concepts.title: zeroth-order optimization
concepts.one_liner: In zeroth-order optimization, the update function only observes the value $J(\theta)$ and finds minima by sampling different $\theta$ values and moving toward lower values.
concepts.content: In the simplest setting, called **zeroth-order optimization**, the update function only gets to observe the value $J(\theta)$. The only way, then, to find $\theta$'s that minimize the loss is to sample different values for $\theta$ and move toward the values that are lower.

concepts.title: gradient-based optimization
concepts.one_liner: Gradient-based optimization uses the gradient $\nabla_{\theta}J(\theta)$ at the current operating point to move in the direction of steepest descent to minimize the loss.
concepts.content: For **gradient-based optimization**, also called **first-order optimization**, the update function takes as input the gradient of the cost with respect to the parameters at the current operating point, $\nabla_{\theta}J(\theta)$. This reveals hugely useful information about the loss that directly tells us how to minimize it: just move in the direction of steepest descent, that is, the gradient direction.

concepts.title: Basic Gradient Descent
concepts.one_liner: Basic gradient descent takes steps proportional to the gradient magnitude in the gradient direction to minimize a cost function.
concepts.content:
The simplest version of gradient descent just takes a step in the gradient direction of length proportional to the gradient magnitude. This algorithm is described in @alg-gradient_descent_basic_gradient_descent.

(see figure: Gradient descent `GD`. Optimizing a cost function $J: \theta \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ by descending the gradient $\nabla_{\theta} J$.)

This algorithm has two hyperparameters, the **learning rate** $\eta$, which controls the step size (learning rate times gradient magnitude), and the number of steps $K$. If the learning rate is sufficiently small and the initial parameter vector $\theta^0$ is random, then this algorithm will almost surely converge to a local minimum of $J$ as $K \rightarrow \infty$~\cite{lee2016gradient}. However, to descend more quickly, it can be useful to set the learning rate to a higher value.
concepts.motivation_md: Basic gradient descent provides a straightforward method to minimize a cost function by iteratively moving parameters in the direction of steepest descent scaled by a learning rate.
concepts.recap_md:
- Basic gradient descent steps in the gradient direction proportional to gradient magnitude.
- It uses hyperparameters: learning rate $\eta$ and number of steps $K$.
- With a small enough learning rate and random start, it converges to a local minimum as $K \to \infty$.

concepts.title: learning rate schedule
concepts.one_liner: A learning rate schedule adjusts the learning rate $\eta^k$ over iterations to take smaller steps as the minimizer is approached.
concepts.content:
A generally useful strategy is to start with a high value for $\eta$ and then decay it until convergence according to a **learning rate schedule**. Researchers have come up with innumerable schedules, and they generally work by calling some function $\texttt{lr}(\eta^0,k)$ to get the learning rate on each iteration of descent:
$$
\eta^{k} = \texttt{lr}(\eta^0,k)
$$
Generally, we want an update rule where $\eta^{k+1} < \eta^k$, so that we take smaller steps as we approach the minimizer. A few simple and popular approaches are given below:


$$
\begin{aligned}
    \texttt{lr}(\eta^0,k) &= \beta^{-k} \eta^0 &\quad\quad \triangleleft\quad \text{exponential decay}\\
    \texttt{lr}(\eta^0,k) &= \beta^{-\lfloor k/M \rfloor} \eta^0 &\quad\quad \triangleleft\quad \text{stepwise exponential decay}\\
    \texttt{lr}(\eta^0,k) &= \frac{(K - k)}{K} \eta^0 &\quad\quad \triangleleft\quad \text{linear decay}
\end{aligned}
$$

One downside of linear decay is that it depends on the total number of steps $K$. This makes it hard to compare optimization runs of different lengths. This is something to also be aware of in more advanced learning rate schedules, such as cosine decay~\cite{loshchilov2016sgdr}, which also have different behavior for different settings of $K$.

The $\beta$ and $M$ are additional hyperparameters of these methods. The general approach of learning rate decay is summarized in @alg-gradient_descent_gradient_descent_with_lr_decay.

(see figure: Gradient descent with learning rate decay algorithm.)

Variations on this algorithm include only decaying the learning rate when a plateau is reached (i.e., when the loss is not decreasing for many iterations in a row), or decaying the learning rate according to more complex nonlinear schedules, such as one shaped like a cosine function~\cite{loshchilov2016sgdr}.
concepts.motivation_md: Learning rate schedules help optimize convergence by reducing step sizes over time, preventing overshooting as the algorithm approaches a minimum.
concepts.recap_md:
- Learning rate schedules decay $\eta^k$ over iterations to take smaller steps near minima.
- Common schedules include exponential decay, stepwise decay, and linear decay.
- Advanced schedules like cosine decay adapt learning rates based on loss plateaus or iteration count.

concepts.title: momentum
concepts.one_liner: Momentum means that we set the parameter update to be a direction given by a weighted combination of the previous update direction plus the current negative gradient.
concepts.content:
Could we do a smarter update than just taking a step in the direction of the gradient? Of the countless ideas that have been proposed, one of the few that has stuck is momentum~\cite{polyak1964some,sutskever2013importance}. Momentum makes the analogy to skiing even more precise: momentum is like the inertia of the skier, carrying them over the little bumps and imperfections in the ski slope and increasing their speed as they descend along a straight path. In math, momentum just means that we set the parameter update to be a direction $\mathbf{v}^{k+1}$, given by a weighted combination of the previous update direction, $\mathbf{v}^{k}$, plus the current negative gradient:
$$
\mathbf{v}^{k+1} = \mu \mathbf{v}^{k} - \eta\nabla_{\theta} J(\theta^k)
$$
The weight $\mu$ in this combination is a new hyperparameter, sometimes simply called the momentum. The full algorithm is given in @alg-gradient_descent_gradient_descent_with_momentum.
concepts.motivation_md: Momentum improves gradient descent by carrying updates over bumps and imperfections, increasing optimization speed and stability. It helps avoid slow progress caused by noisy or oscillating gradients. (llm_inferred)
concepts.recap_md:
- Momentum updates parameters using a weighted sum of the previous update and the current negative gradient.
- The momentum hyperparameter $\mu$ controls the influence of past updates.
- Momentum helps accelerate descent and smooth out optimization trajectories.

concepts.title: Gradient-Like Optimization for Functions without Good Gradients

position.section_title: What Kinds of Functions Can Be Minimized with Gradient Descent?

concepts.one_liner: Most gradient-based optimizers don't really need true gradients; instead, their update functions are compatible with a broader family of local loss-minimizing directions, $\mathbf{v}$.
concepts.content:
What about minimizing functions like @fig-gradient_descent-grad_descent_simple_examples (d), where the gradient is zero almost everywhere? This is a case where gradient descent truly struggles. However, it is often possible to transform such a problem into one that can be treated with gradient descent. Remember that the key property of a gradient, from the perspective of optimization, is that it is a locally loss-minimizing direction in parameter space. Most gradient-based optimizers don't really need true gradients; instead, their update functions are compatible with a broader family of local loss-minimizing directions, $\mathbf{v}$. 

Besides the true gradient, what are some other good choices for $\mathbf{v}$? One common idea is to set $\mathbf{v}$ to be the gradient of a **surrogate loss** function, which is a function, $J_{\texttt{surr}}$, with meaningful (non-zero) gradients that approximates $J$. An example might be a smoothed version of $J$. Another way to get $\mathbf{v}$ is to compute it by sampling perturbations of $\theta$, and seeing which perturbation leads to lower loss. In this strategy, we evaluate $J(\theta+\epsilon)$ for a set of perturbations $\epsilon$, then move toward the $\epsilon$'s that decreased the loss. Approaches of this kind are sometimes called **evolution strategies**~\cite{beyer2002evolution, salimans2017evolution}, and a basic version of this algorithm is given in @alg-gradient_descent_ES.

(see figure: Evolution strategy algorithm.)

As shown in @fig-gradient_descent-sampling_out1, this algorithm can successfully minimize the function in @fig-gradient_descent-grad_descent_simple_examples (c).

(see figure: Using @alg-gradient_descent_ES) to minimize a nondifferentiable (zero-gradient) loss, using $\sigma=1$, $M=10$, and $\eta=0.02$.)
concepts.motivation_md: Some functions have zero gradients almost everywhere, making gradient descent ineffective; gradient-like optimization methods use alternative local directions to enable optimization in such cases.
concepts.recap_md:
- Gradient descent struggles when gradients are zero almost everywhere.
- Update directions $\mathbf{v}$ can come from surrogate losses or sampled perturbations.
- Evolution strategies use sampling to find descent directions when gradients are unavailable.

Approaches of this kind are sometimes called **evolution strategies**~\cite{beyer2002evolution, salimans2017evolution}, and a basic version of this algorithm is given in @alg-gradient_descent_ES.
concepts.motivation_md: Surrogate losses provide meaningful gradients when the original loss has poor or zero gradients, enabling gradient-based optimization methods to work effectively. (llm_inferred)
concepts.recap_md:
- Surrogate loss functions approximate the original loss with meaningful gradients.
- They enable gradient-based updates when the true gradient is zero or uninformative.
- Surrogate losses can be smoothed versions of the original loss.

What about @fig-gradient_descent-grad_descent_simple_examples (e), where the gradient explodes near the optimum? Is there anything we can do to improve the optimization of this function? To combat exploding gradients, a useful trick is **gradient clipping**, which just means clamping the magnitude of the gradient to some maximum value. @alg-gradient_descent_grad_clipping describes this approach.

(see figure: Gradient clipping algorithm.)

`clip` is the "clipping" function: $\texttt{clip}(v, -m, m) = \max(\min(v,m),-m)$

- It helps stabilize optimization when gradients explode near optima.
- The clipping function clamps values between specified bounds.

concepts.title: stochastic gradient descent
concepts.one_liner: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) uses a randomly sampled batch of training data to estimate the gradient at each iteration.
concepts.content:
The variant of gradient descent that uses this idea is called **stochastic gradient descent** (SGD), because each iteration of descent uses a different randomly (stochastically) sampled batch of training data to estimate the gradient. 

The full description of SGD is given in @alg-gradient_descent_SGD.

(see figure: Stochastic gradient descent algorithm. Stochastic gradient descent estimates the gradient from a stochastic subset (batch) of the full training data, and makes an update on that basis.)

`SGD` has a number of useful properties beyond just being faster to compute than `GD`. Because each step of descent is somewhat random, $\texttt{SGD}$ can jump over small bumps in the loss landscape, as long those bumps disappear for some randomly sampled batches. Another important property is that $\texttt{SGD}$ can implicitly regularize the learning problem. For example, for linear problems (i.e., $f_\theta$ is linear), then if there are multiple parameter settings that minimize the loss, $\texttt{SGD}$ will often converge to the solution with minimum parameter norm~\cite{zhang2021understanding}.
concepts.motivation_md: SGD enables efficient training by estimating gradients from random data batches, allowing faster updates and implicit regularization effects. (llm_inferred)
concepts.recap_md:
- SGD estimates gradients using randomly sampled batches of data.
- It can jump over small bumps in the loss landscape due to randomness.
- SGD can implicitly regularize and prefer minimum norm solutions in linear problems.

key_passage.text: The variant of gradient descent that uses this idea is called **stochastic gradient descent** (SGD), because each iteration of descent uses a different randomly (stochastically) sampled batch of training data to estimate the gradient.

Another important property is that $\texttt{SGD}$ can implicitly regularize the learning problem.

concepts.title: overfitting
concepts.one_liner: Overfitting occurs when we fit to properties in the training data that do not exist in the test data, causing poor generalization.
concepts.content:
When we fit to properties in the training data that do not exist in the
 test data, we call this **overfitting**. When this happens, training
 performance will be high, but test performance can be very low, since
 what we learned about the training data does not **generalize** to the
 test data.
concepts.motivation_md: Overfitting explains why models that perform well on training data may fail on unseen test data, highlighting the need for generalization.
concepts.recap_md:
- Overfitting means fitting training data properties not present in test data.
- It results in high training performance but low test performance.
- Overfitting indicates poor generalization to new data.

key_passage.text: When we fit to properties in the training data that do not exist in the test data, we call this **overfitting**.

motivation.text: When this happens, training performance will be high, but test performance can be very low, since what we learned about the training data does not **generalize** to the test data.

concepts.title: underfitting
concepts.one_liner: Underfitting occurs when a learner fails to optimize the objective on the training data.
concepts.content:
A learner may perform poorly for one of two reasons: either it failed to
 optimize the objective on the training data, or it succeeded on the
 training data but in a way that does not generalize to the test setting.
The former is called underfitting and the latter is called overfitting.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding underfitting helps diagnose when a model has not learned enough from training data, distinguishing it from overfitting.
concepts.recap_md:
- Underfitting means failing to optimize the training objective.
- Overfitting means succeeding on training but failing to generalize.
- Poor performance can arise from either underfitting or overfitting.

key_passage.text: The former is called underfitting and the latter is called overfitting.

motivation.text: A learner may perform poorly for one of two reasons: either it failed to optimize the objective on the training data, or it succeeded on the training data but in a way that does not generalize to the test setting.

concepts.title: Learning from Examples
concepts.one_liner: We want to learn an algorithm that fills in missing pixels, but it may be too complex to write by hand, so the machine learns it from many examples.
concepts.content:
We were able to model the behavior of $\star$, on the examples we were given, with a simple algebraic equation. Let's try something rather more complicated. From the three examples in @fig-intro_to_learning-inpainting_example, can you figure out what the operator $F$ does?

(see figure: A complicated function that could be learned from examples. This example is from @hays2007scene.)

You probably came up with something like "it fills in the missing pixels." That's exactly right, but it's sweeping a lot of details under the rug. Remember, we want to learn an *algorithm*, a procedure that is completely unambiguous. How exactly does $F$ fill in the missing pixels?

It's hard to say in words. We may need a very complex algorithm to specify the answer, an algorithm so complex that we could never hope to write it out by hand. This is the point of machine learning. The machine writes the algorithm for us, but it can only do so if we give it many examples, not just these three.
concepts.motivation_md: Learning from examples lets machines discover complex algorithms that are too difficult to specify manually, enabling solutions like filling in missing pixels from image data.
concepts.recap_md:
- Learning from examples aims to discover an unambiguous algorithm from data.
- Complex algorithms, like filling missing pixels, may be too hard to write by hand.
- Machine learning automates algorithm creation by using many examples.

This is the point of machine learning. The machine writes the algorithm for us, but it can only do so if we give it many examples, not just these three.

concepts.title: unsupervised learning
concepts.one_liner: In unsupervised learning, we are given examples of input data but not the target outputs, and the learner must find a useful model or representation of the inputs.
concepts.content: In unsupervised learning, we are given examples of *input data* $\{x^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}$ but we are not told the target outputs $\{y^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}$. Instead the learner has to come up with a model or representation of the input data that has useful properties, as measured by some **objective function**. The objective could be, for example, to compress the data into a lower dimensional format that still preserves all information about the inputs. We will encounter this kind of learning in part @sec-generative_modeling_and_representation_learning of this
concepts.motivation_md: Unsupervised learning helps discover patterns or representations from input data without needing labeled outputs, enabling data compression or feature extraction.
concepts.recap_md:
- Unsupervised learning uses input data without target outputs.
- The learner finds a model or representation with useful properties.
- Objectives include compressing data while preserving information.

key_passage.text: In unsupervised learning, we are given examples of *input data* $\{x^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}$ but we are not told the target outputs $\{y^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}$. Instead the learner has to come up with a model or representation of the input data that has useful properties, as measured by some **objective function**.

motivation.text: The objective could be, for example, to compress the data into a lower dimensional format that still preserves all information about the inputs.

concepts.title: reinforcement learning
concepts.one_liner: In reinforcement learning, a reward function measures output quality, and the learner tries to maximize this reward.
concepts.content: In reinforcement learning, we suppose that we are given a **reward function** that explicitly measures the quality of the learned function's output. To be precise, a reward function is a mapping from outputs to scores: $r: \mathcal{Y} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$. The learner tries to come up with a function that maximizes rewards. This book will not cover reinforcement learning in detail, but this kind of learning is becoming an important part of computer vision, especially in the context of vision for robots. We direct the interested reader to @sutton2018reinforcement to learn more.
concepts.motivation_md: Reinforcement learning addresses learning when feedback is given as rewards rather than explicit examples, useful for tasks like robotic vision.
concepts.recap_md:
- Reinforcement learning uses a reward function mapping outputs to scores.
- The learner aims to maximize the reward.
- It's important in computer vision, especially for robotics.

key_passage.text: In reinforcement learning, we suppose that we are given a **reward function** that explicitly measures the quality of the learned function's output.

motivation.text: This book will not cover reinforcement learning in detail, but this kind of learning is becoming an important part of computer vision, especially in the context of vision for robots.

concepts.title: Learning without Examples
concepts.one_liner: Unsupervised learning has training data, while reinforcement learning usually does not and must collect its own data.
concepts.content: At first glance unsupervised learning and reinforcement learning look similar: both maximize a function that scores desirable properties of the input-output mapping. The big difference is that unsupervised learning has access to training data whereas reinforcement learning usually does not; instead the reinforcement learner has to collect its own training data.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the difference clarifies how learning methods handle data availability and feedback mechanisms.
concepts.recap_md:
- Both unsupervised and reinforcement learning maximize a scoring function.
- Unsupervised learning uses given training data.
- Reinforcement learning must collect its own training data.

key_passage.text: At first glance unsupervised learning and reinforcement learning look similar: both maximize a function that scores desirable properties of the input-output mapping.

motivation.text: The big difference is that unsupervised learning has access to training data whereas reinforcement learning usually does not; instead the reinforcement learner has to collect its own training data.

concepts.title: objective function, the loss function, or the loss
concepts.one_liner: The objective function, loss function, or loss scores model outputs or compares them to targets, typically to be minimized.
concepts.content: Commonly, $f$ is referred to as the **learned function**. The objective that the learner optimizes is typically a function that scores model outputs, $\mathcal{L}: \mathcal{Y} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, or compares model outputs to target answers, $\mathcal{L}: \mathcal{Y} \times \mathcal{Y} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$. We will interchangeably call this $\mathcal{L}$ either the **objective function**, the **loss function**, or the **loss**. A loss almost always refers to an objective we seek to *minimize*, whereas an objective function can be used to describe objectives we seek to minimize as well as those we seek to maximize.
concepts.motivation_md: Objective and loss functions quantify how well a model performs, guiding the learning process by providing a measure to optimize.
concepts.recap_md:
- The learned function $f$ is optimized by an objective function $\mathcal{L}$.
- $\mathcal{L}$ scores outputs or compares outputs to targets.
- Loss usually means minimizing the objective, but objective functions can be maximized or minimized.

key_passage.text: We will interchangeably call this \(\mathcal{L}\) either the **objective function**, the **loss function**, or the **loss**.

motivation.text: A loss almost always refers to an objective we seek to *minimize*, whereas an objective function can be used to describe objectives we seek to minimize as well as those we seek to maximize.

concepts.title: Importance of Parameterization
concepts.one_liner: The way we parameterize a hypothesis space affects optimization and learning, even if the space of functions is the same.
concepts.content:
The hypothesis space can be described by a set $\mathcal{F}$ of all the possible functions under consideration by the learner. For example, one hypothesis space might be "all mappings from $\mathbb{R}^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$" and another could be "all functions $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ that satisfy the conditions of being a distance metric." Commonly, however, we will not just specify the hypothesis space, but also how we parameterize the space. For example, we may say that our *parameterized* hypothesis space is $y = \theta_1 x + \theta_0$, where $\theta_0$ and $\theta_1$ are the parameters. This example corresponds to the space of affine functions from $\mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, but this is not the only way to parameterize that space. Another choice could be $y = \theta_2\theta_1 x + \theta_0$, with parameters $\theta_0$, $\theta_1$, and $\theta_2$. These two choices parameterize *exactly the same space*, that is, any affine functions can be represented by either parameterization and both parameterizations can only represent affine functions. However, these two parameterizations are not equivalent, because optimizers and objectives may treat different parameterizations differently. Because of this, to fully define a learning algorithm, it is important to specify how the hypothesis space is parameterized.

**Overparameterized** models, where you use more parameters than the minimum necessary to fit the data, are especially important in modern computer vision; most neural networks @sec-neural_nets are overparameterized.
concepts.motivation_md: Parameterization affects how learning algorithms optimize models, making it crucial to specify for effective training and understanding of model behavior.
concepts.recap_md:
- Hypothesis spaces define possible functions the learner considers.
- Parameterization specifies how functions are represented by parameters.
- Different parameterizations of the same space affect optimization behavior.
- Overparameterized models use more parameters than minimally needed.

key_passage.text: Because of this, to fully define a learning algorithm, it is important to specify how the hypothesis space is parameterized.

motivation.text: Because of this, to fully define a learning algorithm, it is important to specify how the hypothesis space is parameterized.

Another choice could be $y = \theta_2\theta_1 x + \theta_0$, with parameters $\theta_0$, $\theta_1$, and $\theta_2$. These two choices parameterize *exactly the same space*, that is, any affine functions can be represented by either parameterization and both parameterizations can only represent affine functions.

concepts.title: Empirical Risk Minimization: A Formalization of Learning from Examples

position.section_title: Empirical Risk Minimization: A Formalization of Learning from Examples

concepts.one_liner: Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) minimizes average loss over training data to learn a function from examples.
concepts.motivation_md: ERM formalizes learning from examples by minimizing average loss over training data, providing a principled approach to supervised learning.
concepts.recap_md:
- ERM minimizes average loss over training examples.
- $\mathcal{F}$ is the hypothesis space; $\mathcal{L}$ is the loss function.
- The goal is to find $f$ that best fits the training data.

motivation.text: The idea is to minimize the average error (i.e., risk) we incur over all the training data (i.e., empirical distribution).

concepts.title: maximum likelihood learning
concepts.one_liner: Maximum likelihood learning finds the function that assigns the highest probability to the observed data.
concepts.motivation_md: Maximum likelihood learning provides a probabilistic framework to infer the best model explaining observed data, linking statistical inference with ERM.
concepts.recap_md:
- Maximum likelihood learning finds $f$ maximizing data likelihood.
- Likelihood is the probability of outputs given inputs and model.
- ERM can be interpreted as maximum likelihood inference depending on loss.

key_passage.text:
The term
$p\big(\{\mathbf{y}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N \bigm | \{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N, f\big)$
is called the **likelihood** of the $\mathbf{y}$ values given the model
$f$ and the observed $\mathbf{x}$ values, and maximizing this quantity
is called **maximum likelihood learning**.

motivation.text: Depending on the loss function, there is often an interpretation of ERM as doing maximum likelihood probabilistic inference. In this interpretation, we are trying to infer the hypothesis $f$ that assigns the highest probability to the data.

concepts.title: Derivative of Y along a 3D horizontal edge
concepts.one_liner: In a 3D horizontal edge, the coordinate $Y$ will not change, so the derivative along the edge is zero: $\partial Y / \partial {\bf t} = 0$.
concepts.motivation_md: Knowing that $Y$ does not change along a 3D horizontal edge helps establish boundary conditions for surface orientation inference.
concepts.recap_md:
- Along a 3D horizontal edge, $Y$ remains constant.
- Therefore, the derivative $\partial Y / \partial {\bf t} = 0$ along that edge.

key_passage.text: In a 3D horizontal edge, the coordinate $Y$ will not change. Therefore, the derivative along the edge should be zero:

concepts.title: Tangent vector to edge
concepts.one_liner: The vector $\mathbf{t} = (-n_y, n_x)$ denotes the direction tangent to the edge.
concepts.content: The vector $\mathbf{t}$ denotes the direction tangent to the edge and is given by ${\bf t} = (-n_y, n_x)$.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the tangent vector to an edge is essential to express derivatives along edges in image coordinates.
concepts.recap_md:
- The tangent vector to an edge is $\mathbf{t} = (-n_y, n_x)$.
- It defines the direction along the edge in the image plane.

key_passage.text: where the vector $\bf t$ denotes direction tangent to the edge, ${\bf t}=(-n_y, n_x)$.

concepts.title: Expression for derivative of Y along edge tangent vector
concepts.one_liner: The derivative of $Y$ along the tangent vector $\mathbf{t}$ can be expressed as $\partial Y / \partial {\bf t} = \nabla Y \cdot {\bf t} = -n_y \partial Y / \partial x + n_x \partial Y / \partial y$.
concepts.content:
We can write the derivative of $Y$ along the tangent vector $\mathbf{t}$ as a function of derivatives along the $x$ and $y$ image coordinates:

$$\begin{aligned}
\partial Y / \partial {\bf t} =  \nabla Y \cdot {\bf t} = -n_y \partial Y / \partial x + n_x \partial Y / \partial y
\end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Expressing the derivative along the edge tangent in terms of $x$ and $y$ derivatives allows computation from image data.
concepts.recap_md:
- Derivative along tangent vector: $\partial Y / \partial {\bf t} = \nabla Y \cdot {\bf t}$.
- Expanded: $-n_y \partial Y / \partial x + n_x \partial Y / \partial y$.

concepts.title: Constraint Propagation
concepts.one_liner: Most of the image consists of flat regions without edge constraints, so criteria are needed to propagate 3D structure information from boundaries into flat interiors.
concepts.content: Most of the image consists of flat regions where we do not have edge constraints and thus lack enough local information to infer the surface orientation. Therefore, we need criteria to propagate information from the boundaries, where 3D structure information is available, into the interior of flat image regions. This problem is common in many visual domains.
concepts.motivation_md: Because flat image regions lack local 3D orientation information, constraint propagation is necessary to infer surface structure from boundary data.
concepts.recap_md:
- Flat image regions lack edge constraints and local 3D information.
- Information must be propagated from boundaries into interiors.
- This propagation problem is common in visual domains.

key_passage.text: Therefore, we need some criteria in order to propagate information from the boundaries, where we do have information about the 3D structure, into the interior of flat image regions.

motivation.text: Most of the image consists of flat regions where we do not have such edge constraints and we thus don't have enough local information to infer the surface orientation.

example.text: This problem is common in many visual domains.

concepts.title: Planarity constraints for flat image regions
concepts.one_liner: Flat image regions impose planarity constraints requiring the second derivatives of $Y$ to be zero: $\partial^2 Y / \partial x^2 = 0$, $\partial^2 Y / \partial y^2 = 0$, and $\partial^2 Y / \partial y \partial x = 0$.
concepts.content:
We assume that object faces are planar. Thus, flat image regions impose the following constraints on the local 3D structure:

$$\begin{aligned}
\partial^2 Y / \partial x^2 &= 0  \\
\partial^2 Y / \partial y^2 &= 0 \\
\partial^2 Y / \partial y \partial x &= 0 
\end{aligned}$$

That is, the second order derivatives of $Y$ should be zero.
concepts.motivation_md: Planarity constraints enforce that flat regions correspond to planar surfaces by requiring zero second derivatives of $Y$.
concepts.recap_md:
- Flat regions imply planar surfaces.
- Planarity means $\partial^2 Y / \partial x^2 = \partial^2 Y / \partial y^2 = \partial^2 Y / \partial y \partial x = 0$.
- Second derivatives of $Y$ vanish in flat regions.

concepts.title: Approximation of second order derivatives for planarity constraints
concepts.one_liner: Second order derivatives can be approximated by applying first order derivative approximations twice, e.g., $\partial^2 Y / \partial x^2 \simeq 2Y(x,y)-Y(x+1,y)-Y(x-1,y)$.
concepts.content:
The second order derivatives are zero as stated. To approximate these continuous partial derivatives, we apply the first order derivative approximations twice (as given by equations (@eq-image_partial_derivatives_aprox)). The result is:

$$\partial^2 Y / \partial x^2 \simeq 2Y(x,y)-Y(x+1,y)-Y(x-1,y),$$

and similarly for $\partial^2 X / \partial x^2$.
concepts.motivation_md: Approximating second order derivatives numerically allows enforcing planarity constraints on discrete image data.
concepts.recap_md:
- Second derivatives are approximated by applying first order approximations twice.
- For example, $\partial^2 Y / \partial x^2 \simeq 2Y(x,y)-Y(x+1,y)-Y(x-1,y)$.
- Similar approximations apply for $X$ derivatives.

key_passage.text: The approximation to the second derivative can be obtained by applying twice the first order derivative approximated by equations ( The result is $\partial^2 Y / \partial x^2 \simeq 2Y(x,y)-Y(x+1,y)-Y(x-1,y)$, and similarly for $\partial^2 X / \partial x^2$.

motivation.text: As before, we want to approximate the continuous partial derivatives.

concepts.title: A Simple Inference Scheme
concepts.one_liner: All constraints can be written as an overdetermined linear system $\mathbf{A} \mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{b}$ and solved by minimizing $J = \sum_i w_i (\mathbf{a}_i \mathbf{Y} - b_i)^2$ using the pseudoinverse.
concepts.motivation_md: Formulating constraints as a linear system allows efficient computation of the 3D structure by solving an overdetermined system.
concepts.recap_md:
- Constraints form an overdetermined linear system $\mathbf{A} \mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{b}$.
- Solve by minimizing weighted least squares cost $J = \sum_i w_i (\mathbf{a}_i \mathbf{Y} - b_i)^2$.
- Solution computed via pseudoinverse: $\mathbf{Y} = (\mathbf{A}^T \mathbf{A})^{-1} \mathbf{A}^T \mathbf{b}$.

motivation.text: Our formulation has resulted on a big system of linear constraints (there are more equations than there are pixels in the image).

example.text: For instance, if the index $i$ corresponds to one of the pixels inside one of the planar faces of a foreground object, then there will be three equations. One of the planarity constraint can be written as $\mathbf{a}_i = [0, \dots, 0, -1, 2, -1, 0, \dots, 0]$, $b_i=0$, and analogous equations can be written for the other two.

concepts.title: Results of simple 3D inference approach
concepts.one_liner: The simple 3D inference approach produces world coordinate images $X(x,y)$, $Y(x,y)$, and $Z(x,y)$ that can be visually verified by rendering from different viewpoints.
concepts.motivation_md: Visualizing the inferred 3D world coordinates and rendering from different viewpoints helps verify the accuracy of the 3D inference method.
concepts.recap_md:
- The method produces world coordinate images $X$, $Y$, and $Z$.
- Visual verification includes rendering the 3D scene from new viewpoints.
- The approach works well but relies on assumptions; improvements are needed for general images.

key_passage.text: shows the resulting world coordinates $X(x,y)$, $Y(x,y)$, $Z(x,y)$ for each pixel. The world coordinates are shown here as images with the gray level coding the value of each coordinate (black corresponds to the value 0).

motivation.text: It works. At least it seems to work pretty well. Knowing how well it works will require having some way of evaluating performance. This will be important.

question.text: One thing to think about is if information about 3D orientation is given in the edges, how does that information propagate to the flat areas of the image in order to produce the correct solution in those regions?

Here, one simple way to visually verify that the solution is correct is to render the objects under new view points. shows the reconstructed 3D scene rendered under different view points to show that the 3D structure has been accurately captured.

concepts.title: Looking at Individual Pixels
concepts.one_liner: The image in @fig-pexels-retha-ferguson is a tiny image with just $32 \times 32$ pixels.
concepts.content:
Before we build systems that can see, it is good to learn to look at images and to pay attention to individual pixels. The image in @fig-pexels-retha-ferguson is a tiny image with just $32 \times 32$ pixels.

What is the minimum number of pixels needed to form a recognizable image? The answer depends on the image. It is possible to create visually recognizable images with very few pixels @torralba_2009.

It is so small that we can actually look at each single pixel and think about how it is that we can make sense of it. For instance, let's look at the pixel in row 13 counting from the bottom, and column 12 counting from the left. That pixel corresponds to a dark gray pixel, which is near a couple of other pixels with similar intensity, surrounded by a set of white pixels. That pixel seems to be a pen, but how do we know what it is? The pen is barely three pixels long and one pixel wide. How can that provide enough information?

![A tiny image with 32 $\times$ 32 color pixels. Despite the very low resolution, we can still recognize most of its content. *Source*: Original image created with Dall-E, and downsampled with Photoshop.](figures/visionscience/DALLE_32x32.png){#fig-pexels-retha-ferguson width="90%"}

Same image as in @fig-pexels-retha-ferguson but shown small and blurred to remove the artifacts due to the square pixels.

[FIGURE:5ebf18ba45aa5415 | A very low-resolution, 32 by 32 pixel image of a person sitting at a desk. Despite the extreme blurriness, one can discern a person's head and shoulder on the right, a blue mug in the center, a pen...]

Reducing the size and blurring helps better recognizing the objects despite containing the same visual information.

Recognition of the meaning of that pixel can not come just from the intensity of that pixel or the few pixels nearby. There are way too many possible situations in which different objects in the world could map to a similar set of pixel intensities. concepts.title: The More You Look, the More You See

position.section_title: The More You Look, the More You See

concepts.one_liner: The longer you look at an image, the more details you see and the better you understand the scene.
concepts.content:
Visual perception cannot be formulated as a simple input-output function over predefined domains. Vision is a dynamical system, even when looking at a static image. The longer you look at an image, the more details you see and the better you understand the scene. Just look at the image shown in @fig-street_in_paris and try to write down everything you see down to the smallest detail.

(see figure: A street in Paris. Is everything fine in this picture?)

But this feeling of unlimited and effortless understanding of a picture is also an illusion. Do you truly understand everything you see? For instance, are you sure you can make sense of all the chair legs in @fig-street_in_paris? In fact, this image has been manipulated so that some of legs do not correspond to any chair.

When solving a task, as the **visual cognitive load** increases we are more likely to make judgment mistakes.

As you look around the image, notice that each patch you look at is actually a small photo in its own right. In fact, a big image like this contains thousands of tiny images within it (@fig-tiny_images). A single photo can be *big data*; if you chop up this photo you get a big dataset of tiny images. A common trick in computer vision is to take a method that was developed for processing a dataset and instead apply it to the set of patches in an image, or vice versa.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept highlights how visual understanding deepens over time and how complex images contain many smaller images, which is crucial for tasks in computer vision and perception.
concepts.recap_md:
- Vision is dynamic; longer viewing reveals more details.
- Visual cognitive load can cause judgment errors.
- Large images contain many tiny images, useful for computer vision methods.

concepts.title: The Eye of the Artist
concepts.one_liner: Learning to paint is a great way of learning to see.
concepts.content:
Learning to paint is a great way of learning to see. You start from a white piece of canvas and a finite set of acrylic paints, and your goal is to paint an object that should look real, with shadows, 3D shape, and reflections. What mixtures of paint and what strokes can accomplish that? Artists learn to see the world not by what it represents, but as why it looks the way it does.

The following sequence @fig-agata_painting painted by Agata Lapedriza, shows different steps in the painting process of a strawberry. Layer after layer, the artist replicates the light that will fool your eye into seeing a strawberry instead of acrylic paint. It is interesting to see that the realism does not increase monotonically as the painting progresses. For instance, from step 3 to 4, the right side of the strawberry has lost realism. However, those new strokes will become the shading that will make the strawberry pop out from the canvas.


![The following sequence shows different steps in the process
concepts.motivation_md: Learning to paint trains observation skills, helping one understand how light and materials create visual perception, which enhances visual understanding.
concepts.recap_md:
- Painting teaches seeing by replicating light and shadows.
- Artists focus on why objects look as they do, not just what they are.
- Realism in painting can fluctuate before improving.

concepts.title: pinhole cameras
concepts.one_liner: The tiny holes between the leaves of a tree create a multitude of pinholes that project images like pinhole cameras.
concepts.content:
One of the most common situations that we often encounter is the **pinhole cameras** formed by the spacing between the leaves of a tree. The tiny holes between the leaves of a tree create a multitude of pinholes. The pinholes created by the leaves project different copies of the sun on the floor. When the openings between leaves are small enough, the shape of the projected spot light is dominated by the shape of the sun. This is something we see often but rarely think about the origin of the spotlights that we see on the floor.

In fact, the leaves of a tree create pinholes that produce images in many other situations. We will talk about pinhole cameras in .
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains how natural pinhole cameras form, illustrating basic image projection principles important in vision science and optics.
concepts.recap_md:
- Pinhole cameras can be formed by tiny holes between leaves.
- These pinholes project images, such as multiple copies of the sun.
- The shape of the projected light depends on the sun's shape when openings are small.

concepts.title: Motion Blur
concepts.one_liner: Blur in photos taken from a moving car occurs because the camera captures light over time while the scene moves relative to it.
concepts.content:
## Motion Blur

When we are in a moving car and we take a picture from the passenger window, often images will appear blurring, especially when taken at night (@fig-Paris_from_moving_car). Blur is due to the fact that the camera sensor is collecting light during a period of time while the car is moving and the picture that results is the average of several translated copies of the same image. However, note that not all of the objects are equally blurry. Things that are far away might still look sharp while things nearby appear very blurry.

![Picture of Paris taken from a moving car.](figures/visionscience/motion_blur.jpg){#fig-Paris_from_moving_car width="100%"}

The amount of blur is related to the car speed, the exposure time, and the distance between the camera and each object in the scene. We will
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains why motion blur occurs in photos from moving vehicles, linking blur amount to speed, exposure time, and object distance.
concepts.recap_md:
- Motion blur occurs when the camera moves during exposure.
- Objects farther away appear less blurry than nearby ones.
- Blur depends on car speed, exposure time, and object distance.

concepts.title: light field cameras
concepts.one_liner: Light field cameras capture what the scene looks like from hundreds of different viewing angles using an array of tiny lenses, enabling tricks like depth triangulation and synthetic refocusing.
concepts.content: These cameras, called **light field cameras**, use an array of tiny lenses rather than raindrops, but the result is similar: they capture what the scene looks like from hundreds of different viewing angles. From that density of information, they can achieve many interesting tricks, such as triangulating the depth of objects in the scene and synthetically refocusing the image after it has been taken.
concepts.motivation_md: Light field cameras exist to capture rich visual information from many angles, enabling advanced image processing like depth estimation and refocusing after capture.
concepts.recap_md:
- Light field cameras use arrays of tiny lenses to capture scenes from many viewing angles.
- They enable depth triangulation of objects in the scene.
- They allow synthetic refocusing of images after capture.

concepts.title: Plato's Cave
concepts.one_liner: An image is a crude projection of the underlying physical state, collapsing 3D geometry into a flat 2D grid of pixels, much like the shadows in Plato's Allegory of the Cave.
concepts.content:
In the *Allegory of the Cave*, Plato imagined a group of prisoners chained up in a cave whose only experience of the outside world is through shadows cast on the cave's wall. When we look at images, we think we are directly seeing reality, but actually the situation is much more like Plato's cave. An image is a crude projection of the underlying physical state. It collapses all the 3D geometry into a flat 2D grid of pixels. From any given viewing angle, most of the scene is occluded. Materials are only depicted in terms of how photons bounce off their surfaces; what's below the surface may be completely omitted. When you look at a picture, think about all the things you cannot see. There's more you don't see than you do. One job of a vision system is to infer everything you can't see given everything you can.

The allegory of the cave has several layers of indirection: the shadows are cast by puppets that are controlled by puppeteers who act out interpretations of the broader reality outside.
concepts.motivation_md: Images only show a limited, flattened view of reality, similar to shadows on a cave wall, so vision systems must infer unseen aspects of the scene.
concepts.recap_md:
- Plato's Allegory of the Cave illustrates how images are projections, not direct reality.
- Images collapse 3D scenes into 2D pixel grids, hiding occluded parts.
- Vision systems aim to infer unseen information from visible data.

concepts.title: Algorithmic Fairness
concepts.one_liner: Algorithmic Fairness studies the performance and fairness of algorithms across people, groups, and cultures to address biases and ensure equitable computer vision.
concepts.content: The field of **Algorithmic Fairness** studies the performance and fairness of algorithms across people, groups, and cultures. It seeks to address algorithmic biases, and to develop strategies to ensure that computer vision algorithms don't reflect or create biases against different groups of people or cultures. Entry points to this literature include a number of text and video sources, including
concepts.motivation_md: Algorithmic Fairness exists to identify and mitigate biases in algorithms to promote equitable treatment across diverse populations.
concepts.recap_md:
- Algorithmic Fairness studies how algorithms perform fairly across diverse groups.
- It aims to address and reduce algorithmic biases.
- Ensures computer vision algorithms do not create or reflect cultural biases.

key_passage.text: The field of **Algorithmic Fairness** studies the performance and fairness of algorithms across people, groups, and cultures.

motivation.text: It seeks to address algorithmic biases, and to develop strategies to ensure that computer vision algorithms don't reflect or create biases against different groups of people or cultures.

concepts.title: Facial Analysis
concepts.one_liner: Facial analysis measures attributes like pose and identity beyond face detection and must be evaluated for bias across demographic groups.
concepts.content: Facial detection asks whether there is a face in some image region, while facial analysis refers to measuring additional attributes of the face, including pose and identity. It is important to characterize the performance of facial analysis systems across demographic groups, as certain studies have done @Klare2012. A large Face Recognition Vendor Test by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) @Grother2019 examined the accuracy of face recognition algorithms for different demographic groups defined by sex, age, and race or country of birth. For one dataset, they found false positive rates were highest in West and East African and East Asian people, and lowest in Eastern European individuals. For the systems offered by many vendors, this effect was large, with differences of up to a factor of 100 in the recognition false positive rates between different countries of birth. In addition, the more accurate face recognition systems showed less bias and some developers supplied highly accurate identification algorithms for which false positive differentials were undetectable. Certain studies @Grother2019 have stressed the importance of reporting both false negative and false positive rates for each demographic group at that threshold. Others @Cavazos2021 have provided a checklist for measuring bias in face recognition algorithms. It is clearly important to understand the biases of any facial analysis system that is put into use, as these characteristics can vary greatly from system to system.
concepts.motivation_md: Facial analysis systems must be evaluated for bias across demographic groups to ensure fair and accurate performance.
concepts.recap_md:
- Facial analysis measures attributes like pose and identity beyond simple detection.
- Studies show significant demographic biases in face recognition false positive rates.
- Reporting false negative and false positive rates per group is crucial for fairness.

concepts.one_liner: Algorithmic bias can stem from biases in training datasets, which may reflect the backgrounds of researchers and underrepresent certain populations.
concepts.content:
One cause of algorithmic bias can be a bias in the contents of the training dataset. There are many subtleties in the creation and labeling of computer vision datasets @Ramaswamy2021b. Any dataset represents only one slice of the possible images and labels that one could capture from the world @Torralba2011. Furthermore, the samples taken may well be influenced by the background of the researchers gathering the dataset. The text shows examples of common objects from four different households across the globe. From left to right, the photographs are shown in decreasing order of the average household income of the region from which the photo was taken. The object recognition results for six different commercially available image recognition systems are listed below each photograph, showing that the performance is much better for the images from first-world households @DeVries2019, possibly due to a better representation of imagery from such households in the training datasets of the image recognition systems.

- Dataset bias affects algorithm performance across different populations.
- Recognition systems perform better on images from higher-income, Western households.

concepts.title: Generative Adversarial Networks to Create Unbiased Datasets and Algorithms
concepts.one_liner: Generative adversarial networks (GANs) can synthetically produce balanced datasets to mitigate bias and improve fairness in algorithms.
concepts.content:
One way to mitigate a biased dataset is to synthetically produce the images needed to provide the necessary balance or coverage. Generative adversarial networks (GANs), described in , can operate on a dataset to generate sets of images similar to those of the dataset, but differing from each other in controlled ways, for example, with changes in the apparent gender, age, or race of depicted people. Such GANs have been used to develop debiased datasets and algorithms.

Sattigeri et al. @Sattigeri2019 proposed an algorithm they called Fairness GAN, which included a classifier trained to perform *as poorly as possible* on predicting the classification result based on a protected attribute. For example, the algorithm was designed to predict an attractiveness label while gaining no benefit from knowing the gender or skin tone. The resulting debiased dataset showed some improvement in fairness metrics.

Another study @Ramaswamy2021 took an alternative approach to the problem of removing correlations between a protected attribute and a target label. The authors used GANs to generate pairs of realistic looking images that were balanced with respect to each protected attribute. The text shows an example of this. If "wearing hat" is deemed to be the protected attribute, it is desired to remove its correlation in the data with the attribute, "wearing glasses." If no debiasing steps were taken, the algorithm would learn to associate wearing hats with wearing glasses. The GAN is used to augment the dataset with paired examples of images of people wearing hats both with and without glasses. When this augmented dataset is combined with the original dataset, performance in a variety of fairness measures is improved.

Still another approach to dataset fairness, by @Zhao2017, injects constraints to require that the model predictions follow the distributions observed within the training data, assuming that the training data has the desired distribution. See also @Wang2020 for a benchmark and comparison of techniques for dataset bias mitigation.
concepts.motivation_md: GANs enable synthetic data generation to balance datasets and reduce bias, improving fairness in computer vision algorithms.
concepts.recap_md:
- GANs can generate synthetic images to balance datasets and mitigate bias.
- Fairness GAN trains classifiers to ignore protected attributes, improving fairness.
- Augmenting datasets with paired images removes unwanted correlations between attributes.

concepts.title: Counterfactuals for Analyzing Algorithmic Biases
concepts.one_liner: Counterfactual studies using GANs allow experimental intervention to assess algorithmic bias by modifying variables in probe images and observing classification changes.
concepts.content:
It may be difficult to distinguish whether a given biased result is caused by algorithmic bias or by biases in the testing dataset @Balakrishnan2020. One way to disentangle those is through experimentation, that is, modifying variables of a probe image and examining the algorithm's decision. GAN models, when coupled with human labeling to learn directions in the latent space corresponding to changes in the desired attributes, allow for such experimental intervention. Researchers @Balakrishnan2020 have shown that such counterfactual studies may lead to very different conclusions than observational studies alone, which can be influenced by biased correlations in the testing dataset. (See also related work in counterfactual reasoning by @Denton2019.) shows several **transects** from @Balakrishnan2020, paths through the GAN's latent space where only one face variable is modified. The variation in an algorithm's classification results along the images of the transect provides a clean assessment of any bias related to the variable being modified.

(see figure: A GAN creates sequences of faces, called **transects**, where only one attribute changes @Balakrishnan2020)
concepts.motivation_md: Counterfactual analysis using GANs helps isolate algorithmic bias from dataset bias by experimentally modifying image attributes and observing algorithm responses.

- Distinguishing algorithmic bias from dataset bias is challenging.
- GANs enable experimental modification of image attributes for analysis.
- Counterfactual transects reveal how classification changes with single attribute variation.

concepts.title: Differential privacy
concepts.one_liner: Differential privacy allows extracting aggregated information about a population from a database without revealing information about any single individual.
concepts.content:
Differential privacy allows extracting aggregated information about a population from a database without revealing information about any single individual.

A very successful theoretical privacy framework, called differential privacy, addresses these issues. Following the techniques of differential privacy @Dwork2014, researchers can guarantee to the participants of a study that they will not be affected by allowing their data to be used in a study or analysis, no matter what other studies, datasets, or information sources are available.

Algorithms can be designed for which it can be shown that the guarantee of differential privacy is met @Kearns2020, @Dwork2014. One approach is to inject enough randomness into each recorded observation to guarantee that no individual's data can be reconstructed (with probabilistic guarantees that can be made as stringent as desired, at the cost of data efficiency), while still allowing scientific conclusions to be formed by averaging over the many data samples. A simple example of this approach, described in @Kearns2020, is the following procedure to query a set of adults to determine what fraction of them have cheated on their partner. Each surveyed adult is instructed to flip a coin. If the coin shows heads, they are instructed to answer the question, "Have you cheated on your partner?", truthfully. If the coin shows tails, they are asked to answer "yes" or "no" at random, by flipping the coin again and answering "yes" if heads and "no" if tails. The resulting responses for each individual are stored.

There are also risks associated with the wrong use of differential privacy @Dwork_Kohli_Mulligan_2019.

If the stored data were hacked, or accidentally leaked, no harm would come to the surveyed individuals even though their data from this sensitive survey had been revealed. Any "yes" answer could very plausibly be explained as being a result of the subject having been instructed by the protocol to flip a coin to select the answer. Yet it is still possible to infer the true percentage of "yes" answers in the surveyed population from the stored data: the expected value of the measured percentages will be the true "yes" and "no" answers in the population. The price for this differential privacy is that more data must be collected to obtain the same accuracy guarantees in the estimate of the true population averages.
concepts.motivation_md: Differential privacy exists to enable researchers to extract useful aggregate information from sensitive databases without compromising the privacy of any individual participant, ensuring strong privacy guarantees even if data leaks occur.
concepts.recap_md:
- Differential privacy allows aggregated data extraction without revealing individual information.
- It works by injecting randomness to protect individual data while preserving overall statistical accuracy.
- More data is needed to maintain accuracy under differential privacy guarantees.

motivation.text: Following the techniques of differential privacy researchers can guarantee to the participants of a study that they will not be affected by allowing their data to be used in a study or analysis, no matter what other studies, datasets, or information sources are available.

The resulting responses for each individual are stored.

concepts.title: Ethics
concepts.one_liner: Ethics are important for vision scientists to think through and grapple with.
concepts.content: Many ethical issues are outside of the traditional training and education of scientists or engineers, but ethics are important for vision scientists to think through and grapple with. Scientists have a distinguished history of engaging with ethical and moral issues.
concepts.motivation_md: Ethics guides vision scientists to consider the moral implications of their work beyond technical challenges, ensuring responsible and conscientious research and application.
concepts.recap_md:
- Ethics often lie outside traditional scientific training.
- Vision scientists must actively engage with ethical and moral issues.
- Ethical awareness is crucial for responsible research.

concepts.title: Concerns beyond Algorithmic Bias
concepts.one_liner: Even if algorithms recognize people equally well regardless of attributes, many concerns remain beyond algorithmic bias.
concepts.content:
Suppose the research community developed algorithms that could recognize and analyze people or objects equally well, regardless of displayed gender, race, age, culture or other class attributes. Is the community's work toward fairness completed? Unfortunately, there are still many issues of concern, as pointed out by many authors and speakers @Gebru2020, @Gebru2021, @Benjamin2019. To list a few of these issues:

- Face analysis for job hiring. Companies have used automated facial analysis methods (analyzing expressions and length of responses) as part of their proprietary algorithms for resume screening, although, at least for some cases, that process has stopped after criticism of the fairness of these methods for screening @Kahn2021.

- Automated identification of faces can be used to compile a list of the participants at a public protest, potentially allowing retribution for attendance @Garvie2016, @Mozur2019.

- People can show a bias toward believing the output of a machine @Cummings2004, making it more difficult for a person to correct an algorithm's mistake.

- There are concerns whether labeling the gender of a person from their appearance could cause distress or harm to some in the LGBTQ community @Hamidi2018, @Bennett2021.

We provide a subsequent list of questions for thought and discussion. We
concepts.motivation_md: Even with fair algorithms, concerns like misuse in hiring, surveillance, overreliance on machines, and harm to marginalized groups remain, requiring ongoing ethical consideration.
concepts.recap_md:
- Fair algorithms do not resolve all ethical concerns.
- Uses like job hiring and protest surveillance raise fairness and privacy issues.
- Machine output bias and harm to LGBTQ individuals are additional concerns.

concepts.title: Some Ethical Issues in Computer Vision
concepts.one_liner: Researchers and engineers should consider many ethical questions regarding privacy, fairness, consent, and societal impact in computer vision.
concepts.content:
The following are an (incomplete) set of questions that researchers and engineers may keep in mind:

- Would you prefer that a person identify someone from a photograph, with the potential biases and assumptions that the individual may have, or for an algorithm to do so, based on training from a dataset which may include biases of its own? See @Kearns2020, @Mullainathan2019 for related discussions.

- What privacy safeguards must be in place to accept always-on camera and voice recording inside people's homes? Inside your own home?

- Traffic fatalities in the US currently result in the tragedy of approximately 30,000 deaths annually, with most of those fatalities being caused by driver error. If every vehicle were self-driving, fatalities caused by human error could fall dramatically, yet there will surely still be fatalities caused by machine errors, albeit far fewer than had been caused by humans. Is that a tradeoff society should make? What should be our threshold of fatalities caused by machine? This moral question is a societal-scale version of "the trolley problem" @Thomson1985: A bystander can choose to divert a trolley from the main track to a side track, saving five people who are on that main track, but killing one person who is on the side track. Should the bystander actively divert the trolley, intentionally killing the person on the side track, who would otherwise have been spared if no action were taken? These issues are also present for automobile airbags, which save many lives but sometimes injure a small number of people @Dalmotas1995, and in other public health issues.

- Algorithms will never perform exactly as well among all groups of people. Within what tolerance must the performance of human analysis algorithms be for an algorithm to be considered fair? Is algorithmic bias being less than human bias sufficient for deployment?

- Some image datasets have contained offensive material @Birhand2021, @Barber2019. How should we decide which concepts or images can be part of a training set? Is there any need for algorithms to understand offensive words or concepts?

- Could potential categorization tasks of humans in photographs (e.g., gender identity, skincolor, age, height) bring harm to individuals, and how?

- Should computer vision systems ever be used in warfare? In policing? In public surveillance?

- What is the role of machines in society? Regarding decisions of person identification, do we want people making decisions, with their own difficult-to-measure biases, or do we want machines involved, with biases that may be measurable?

- Do face recognition algorithms suppress public protests? Consider a world where any face shown in public is always recorded and identifiable. (We are almost in that world). What are the consequences of that for personal safety, speech, assembly, and liberties?

- What are the most beneficial uses of computer vision?

- Which uses have the most potential for harm, or currently cause the most harm?

- Is it ok to use computer vision to monitor workers in order to improve their productivity? In order to improve workplace safety? In order to prevent workplace harassment?

- What criteria would you use to evaluate the pros and cons of using machines or humans for a given task?

- Should datasets represent real-world disparities, or represent the world as we want it to be? How might these choices amplify existing economic disparities?

- When should consent be required (and from whom) before using an image to train a computer vision algorithm?
concepts.motivation_md: Ethical questions in computer vision guide researchers to consider privacy, fairness, consent, and societal impact, helping to mitigate harm and promote beneficial uses.
concepts.recap_md:
- Ethical questions cover privacy, fairness, and societal impact.
- Consider tradeoffs in machine vs. human decision-making.
- Consent and dataset representation are key concerns.

concepts.title: Concluding Remarks
concepts.one_liner: Computer vision can cause harm as well as bring many benefits, so researchers must be aware and mitigate potential harms.
concepts.content: Computer vision, with its expanding roles in society, can both cause harm as well as bring many benefits. It is important that every computer vision researcher be aware of the potentials for harm, as well as learn techniques to mitigate against those possibilities. It is our responsibility to bring this technology into our society with care and understanding.

- Computer vision has both harmful and beneficial societal impacts.
- Researchers should be aware of potential harms.
- Mitigation techniques are essential for responsible deployment.

concepts.title: light ray
concepts.one_liner: A light ray is an abstraction describing light radiation heading in a particular direction from a particular location in space.
concepts.content: Introduce the abstraction of a light ray, describing the light radiation heading in a particular direction from a particular location in space (@fig-lightSpray). A light ray is specified by its position, direction, and intensity as a function of wavelength and polarization. In this treatment, we ignore diffraction effects.
concepts.motivation_md: The concept of a light ray simplifies the complex behavior of light by focusing on its direction, position, and intensity, enabling analysis of light transport without diffraction effects.
concepts.recap_md:
- A light ray describes light traveling from a specific location in a specific direction.
- It is characterized by position, direction, and intensity (wavelength and polarization).
- Diffraction effects are ignored in this treatment.

concepts.title: bidirectional reflection distribution function
concepts.one_liner: The bidirectional reflection distribution function (BRDF) describes how outgoing light power depends on incoming light, surface normal, wavelength, and directions.
concepts.motivation_md: BRDF models how surfaces reflect light depending on direction, wavelength, and surface properties, essential for realistic rendering and vision analysis.
concepts.recap_md:
- BRDF, $F$, defines outgoing light power based on incoming light and surface properties.
- Depends on surface normal $\mathbf{n}$, incoming/outgoing directions, wavelength, and incoming power.
- Expressed as $\ell_{\texttt{out}} = F(\ell_{\texttt{in}}, \mathbf{n}, \lambda, \mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q})$.

key_passage.text: $\mathbf{q}$, is determined by what is called the **bidirectional reflection distribution function** (BRDF), $F$, of the surface.

motivation.text: If the surface normal is $\mathbf{n}$, then outgoing power is some function, $F$, of the surface normal, the incoming and outgoing ray directions, the wavelength, and the incoming light power:

example.text:
$$\ell_{\texttt{out}} = F \left( \ell_{\texttt{in}}, \mathbf{n}, \lambda, \mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q} \right)
$$

concepts.title: Lambertian Surfaces
concepts.one_liner: The Lambertian model approximates diffuse reflection with a simple BRDF where outgoing intensity depends on surface orientation and reflectance.
concepts.content:
In general, BRDFs can be quite complicated (see @Matusik2002), describing both diffuse and specular components of reflection. Even surfaces with completely diffuse reflections can give complicated reflectance distributions @Oren1994. A useful approximation describing diffuse reflection is the Lambertian model, with a particularly simple BRDF, which we denote as $F_L$. The outgoing ray intensity, $\ell_{\texttt{out}}$, is a function only of the surface orientation relative to the incoming and outgoing ray directions, the wavelength, a scalar surface reflectance, and the incoming light power:
$$
\ell_{\texttt{out}} = F_{L} \left( \ell_{\texttt{in}} (\lambda), \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{p} \right)  = a \ell_{\texttt{in}}(\lambda) \left( \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{p} \right),
$$ {#eq-lambert}

where $a$ is the surface reflectance, or albedo, $\mathbf{n}$ is the surface normal vector, and $\mathbf{p}$ points toward the source of the incident light. Note that the brightness of the outgoing light ray depends on the orientation of the surface relative to the incident ray, as well as the reflectance, $a$, of the surface. For a Lambertian surface, the intensity of the reflected light is a function of the direction of the incoming light ray, but not a function of the outgoing direction of the ray, $\mathbf{q}$.
concepts.motivation_md: The Lambertian model simplifies complex surface reflectance by assuming purely diffuse reflection, making it easier to analyze and simulate light reflection.
concepts.recap_md:
- BRDFs describe complex reflection including diffuse and specular components.
- Lambertian model approximates diffuse reflection with a simple BRDF $F_L$.
- Outgoing intensity depends on surface reflectance $a$, surface normal $\mathbf{n}$, and incoming light direction $\mathbf{p}$.

key_passage.text: A useful approximation describing diffuse reflection is the **Lambertian model**, with a particularly simple BRDF, which we denote as $F_L$. The outgoing ray intensity, $\ell_{\texttt{out}}$, is a function only of the surface orientation relative to the incoming and outgoing ray directions, the wavelength, a scalar surface reflectance, and the incoming light power: $$ \ell_{\texttt{out}} = F_{L} \left( \ell_{\texttt{in}} (\lambda), \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{p} \right) = a \ell_{\texttt{in}}(\lambda) \left( \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{p} \right), $$ where $a$ is the surface **reflectance**, or **albedo**, $\mathbf{n}$ is the surface normal vector, and $\mathbf{p}$ points toward the source of the incident light.

concepts.title: Spatial Resolution and Color
concepts.one_liner: Color interacts with our perception of spatial resolution, with the eye sensitive to fine spatial modulations in some color directions but relatively insensitive in others.
concepts.content:
Color interacts with our perception of spatial resolution. For some directions in color space, the eye is very sensitive to fine spatial modulations, while for other color space directions, the eye is relatively insensitive. Some color coordinate systems take advantage of this disparity to enable efficient representation of images by sampling image data sparsely along color axes where human perception is insensitive to blurring.

In a red-green-blue (RGB) representation, the eye is sensitive to high spatial frequency changes in both red and green, as shown in figures @fig-girls1 and @fig-girls2. A rotation of the color coordinates of the image, followed by a nonlinear stretching, can put the image into a color space called L, a, b. In that space, the eye is very sensitive to any blurring of the L color component, called luminance, but is relatively insensitive to blurring of the a or b components, as demonstrated in @fig-girls3 and @fig-girls4. This effect is commonly exploited in image compression, allowing some image components to be sampled more coarsely than others.

(see figure: (a) Original image. (b) RGB components. (c) RGB components, each blurred. These sharp and blurred components are used in the color images of @fig-girls2)

(see figure: Color images composed of sharp and blurred components from figures @fig-girls1 (b) and @fig-girls1 (c). (a) R component blurred, G and B components sharp. (b) G component blurred, R and B components...)

(see figure: (a) Original image. (b) Lab components. (c) Lab components, each blurred. These sharp and blurred components are used in the color images of @fig-girls4)

(see figure: Color images composed of sharp and blurred components from figures @fig-girls3 (b) and @fig-girls3 (c). Fig (a) L component blurred, a and b components sharp. (b) a component blurred, L and b...)
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding how color perception affects spatial resolution helps optimize image representation and compression by exploiting the eye's varying sensitivity to color blurring.
concepts.recap_md:
- The eye's sensitivity to spatial resolution varies across color directions.
- RGB space is sensitive to high-frequency changes in red and green.
- L, a, b space separates luminance (L) from color components (a, b), allowing efficient image compression.

concepts.title: Concluding Remarks
concepts.one_liner: The three classes of color sensors in our eyes project light spectra into a 3-dimensional color space, and humans observe different colors with different spatial resolutions.
concepts.content:
The three classes of color sensors in our eyes project light spectra into a 3-dimensional color space. While human perception of color depends on more than just the spectrum of the light being observed, most systems for color matching achieve good results by assuming that the spectrum is all that matters. Linear algebra can find the best controls for a display or printing device in order to match the color measured by a set of sensors.

As would be expected from the spatial varying pattern of color sensors in our eyes--we have few blue or short-wavelength sensors--humans observe different colors with different spatial resolutions, a fact that is exploited in image compression methods.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding how human color sensors work and their spatial resolution differences helps improve color matching and image compression techniques.
concepts.recap_md:
- Human eyes have three classes of color sensors projecting light spectra into 3D color space.
- Color perception depends mostly on light spectrum, enabling color matching.
- Spatial variation in sensors causes different spatial resolutions for colors, used in image compression.
