concepts.title: Regularizers as Probabilistic Priors
concepts.one_liner: Regularizers can be interpreted as priors that prefer, a priori, some solutions over others.
concepts.content: Regularizers can be interpreted as priors that prefer, a priori (before looking at the data), some solutions over others. Under this interpretation, the data fit loss (e.g., $L_2$ loss) is a likelihood function $p(\{y^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1} \bigm | \{x^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}, \theta)$ and the regularizer is a prior $p(\theta)$. Bayes' rule then states that the posterior $p(\theta \bigm | \{x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1})$ is proportional to the product of the prior and the likelihood. The log posterior is then the sum of the log likelihood and the log prior, plus a constant. Hence we arrive at the form of @eq-problem_of_generalization-regularized_objective.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains how regularization in learning algorithms can be viewed probabilistically as imposing priors, connecting optimization objectives to Bayesian inference.
concepts.recap_md:
- Regularizers act as priors preferring some solutions before seeing data.
- Data fit loss corresponds to a likelihood function.
- Posterior is proportional to prior times likelihood; log posterior sums log prior and log likelihood.

key_passage.text: Regularizers can be interpreted as **priors** that prefer, a priori (before looking at the data), some solutions over others.

motivation.text: Under this interpretation, the data fit loss (e.g., $L_2$ loss) is a likelihood function $p(\{y^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1} \bigm | \{x^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}, \theta)$ and the regularizer is a prior $p(\theta)$.

concepts.title: Bayesian Occam's razor
concepts.one_liner: The Bayesian Occam's razor derives priors by noting that more complex hypothesis spaces assign less prior mass to any single hypothesis.
concepts.content: These priors are not arbitrarily chosen. The notion of the Bayesian Occam's razor derives such priors by noting that more complex hypothesis spaces must cover more possible hypotheses, and therefore must assign less prior mass to any single hypothesis (the prior probability of all possible hypotheses in the hypothesis space must sum to 1) @jefferys1992ockham, @mackay2003information. This is why, probabilistically, simpler hypotheses are more likely to be true.
concepts.motivation_md: Bayesian Occam's razor explains why simpler hypotheses are preferred probabilistically, guiding the choice of priors in learning.
concepts.recap_md:
- Bayesian Occam's razor links hypothesis complexity to prior mass.
- More complex hypothesis spaces spread prior mass thinner.
- Simpler hypotheses have higher prior probability and are more likely true.

key_passage.text: The notion of the **Bayesian Occam's razor** derives such priors by noting that more complex hypothesis spaces must cover more possible hypotheses, and therefore must assign less prior mass to any single hypothesis (the prior probability of all possible hypotheses in the hypothesis space must sum to 1).

motivation.text: This is why, probabilistically, simpler hypotheses are more likely to be true.

concepts.title: Rethinking Generalization
concepts.one_liner: Some complex hypothesis spaces, like deep nets, tend not to overfit despite having more parameters than data points.
concepts.content: A recent empirical finding is that some seemingly complex hypothesis spaces, such as deep nets (which we will see in later chapters), tend not to overfit, even though they have many more free parameters than the number of datapoints they are fit to. Exactly why this happens is an ongoing topic of research @zhang2016understanding. But we should not be too surprised. The number of parameters is just a rough proxy for model capacity (i.e., the expressivity of the hypothesis space). A single parameter that has infinite numerical precision can parameterize an arbitrarily complex function. Such a parameter defines a very expressive hypothesis space and will be capable of overfitting data. Conversely, if we have a million parameters, but they are regularized so that almost all are zero, then these parameters may end up defining a simple class of functions, which does not overfit the data. So you can think of the number of parameters as a rough estimate of model capacity, but it is not at all the full story. See @belkin2018reconciling for more discussion on this point.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept challenges the simplistic view that more parameters always mean overfitting, highlighting the role of regularization and effective model capacity.
concepts.recap_md:
- Deep nets can avoid overfitting despite many parameters.
- Number of parameters is a rough proxy for model capacity.
- Regularization can reduce effective complexity, preventing overfitting.

concepts.title: Three Tools in the Search for Truth: Data, Priors, and Hypotheses

position.section_title: Three Tools in the Search for Truth: Data, Priors, and Hypotheses

concepts.one_liner: Learning uses data, priors, and hypotheses together to pinpoint the true function generating observations.
concepts.content:
In this section, we introduce a perspective on learning and generalization that puts all our tools together. We consider learning as akin to searching for the proverbial needle in a haystack. The haystack is our search space (i.e., the hypothesis space). The needle is the "truth" we are seeking, that is, the true function that generates our observations.

We have several tools at our disposal to help us pinpoint the location of the needle, focusing on three: data, priors, and hypotheses.

The first tool, data, was the topic of @sec-intro_to_learning. In vision, the data is observations of the world like photos and videos. Finding explanations consistent with the observed data is the centerpiece of learning-based vision.

The second tool at our disposal was introduced earlier in this chapter—priors (a.k.a. regularizers) that prefer some solutions over others a priori.

The last tool at our disposal is the set of hypotheses under consideration for what the true function may be. The hypothesis space constrains which solutions we can possibly find. If the true solution is not in our hypothesis space, then no amount of data or priors can help us find it. This situation is like the old joke of a drunk man looking for his lost keys under a lamppost @freedman2010wrong. "Why are you looking there," a cop asks. "Because this is where the light is."

Together these three tools allow us to pinpoint one (or a few) good solutions in the space of all possibilities, as depicted in the cartoon in @fig-problem_of_generalization-search_space_tools.

In this cartoon, we are learning a mapping from some domain $\mathcal{X}$ to another domain $\mathcal{Y}$. The hypothesis space, $\mathcal{F}$ (white circle; "the lamppost's light") places a hard constraint on the subset of possible mappings under consideration, the prior (yellow ellipse) places a soft constraint on which mappings are preferred over which others, and the data (green ellipse) also places a soft constraint on the space, preferring mappings that well fit the data.

(see figure: A cartoon of the tools for honing in on the truth.)

Approximation error is low within the green region. If we didn't care about generalization, then it would be sufficient just to select any solution in this green region. But since we do care about generalization, we bias our picks toward the yellow region, which corresponds to a prior that selects points we believe to be closer to the true solution, even if they might not fit the data perfectly well. These tools isolate the area outlined in bright yellow as the region where we may find our needle of truth. A learning algorithm, which
concepts.motivation_md: Learning is like searching for a needle in a haystack; data, priors, and hypotheses help narrow down the search for the true function generating observations.
concepts.recap_md:
- Learning involves data, priors, and hypothesis space.
- Hypothesis space constrains possible solutions; priors bias preferences.
- Together, these tools help locate the true function in the search space.

concepts.title: Experiment 1: Effect of Data

position.section_title: Three Tools in the Search for Truth: Data, Priors, and Hypotheses

concepts.one_liner: The more data you have, the less you need other modeling tools to pinpoint the true solution.
concepts.content:
Training data is the main source of information for a learner, and a learner is just like a detective: as it observes more and more data, it gets more and more evidence to narrow in on the solution. Here we look at how data shapes the objective function $J$ for the following empirical risk minimization problem: $$\begin{aligned}
    J(\theta; \{x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}) &= \frac{1}{N}\sum_i \lvert f_{\theta}(x^{(i)}) - y^{(i)}\rvert^{0.25} \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad\text{objective}:error_fn_1\\
    f_{\theta}(x) &= \theta_0 x + \theta_1 \sin(x)  \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad\text{hypothesis space}
\end{aligned}$$

We use the exponent $0.25$, rather than the more common squared error, so that the plots in @fig-problem_of_generalization-more_data_more_constraints show more clearly the linear constraints (the dark lines) added by each datapoint to the objective $J$.

In @fig-problem_of_generalization-more_data_more_constraints, bottom row, we plot $J$ as a heatmap over the values obtained for different settings of $\theta$. On the top row we plot the data being fit, $\{x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}$, along with the function $f_{\theta}$ that achieves the best fit, and a sample other settings of $\theta$ that achieve within 0.1 of the cost of the best fit. Each column corresponds to some amount of training data $N$. Moving to the right, we increase $N$.

(see figure: More data, more (soft) constraints.)

The heatmaps here are reminiscent of a classic computer vision algorithm called the Hough transform @hough1959machine, @duda1972use. This transform can be used to find geometric primitives that fit feature points in images. In fact, the bottom row is exactly the generalized Hough transform~\cite{duda1972use} of the data points in the top row, using $\theta_0 x + \theta_1 \sin(x)$ as the family of geometric primitives we are fitting.

The first thing to look at is the leftmost column, where $N=1$. For a single datapoint, there are an infinite number of functions in our hypothesis space that perfectly fit that point. This shows up in the heatmaps as a line of settings of $\theta$ that all achieve zero loss. The learning algorithm we used in this example picks a random solution from the set of solutions that achieve zero loss. Unfortunately, here it got unlucky and picked a solution that happens to be far from the true solution.

Next, look at the second column where we have $N=5$ training points. Ideally we want to find a curve that exactly passes through each point. Each single datapoint adds one constraint to this problem, and each constraint shows up as a line in the heatmap for $J$ [the line of solutions that satisfy the constraint $y^{(i)} = \theta_0 x^{(i)} + \theta_1 \sin(x^{(i)})$ for that datapoint $i$]. The intersection of all these constraints pinpoints the setting of parameters that fits all that data. In this example, with five datapoints, there is no location where all the constraint lines intersect, which means there is no curve in our hypothesis space that can perfectly fit this data. Instead we settle for the curve that best approximates the data, according to our loss function. Notice that the learned solution is now pretty close to the true function that generated the data. It is not an exact match, because the data is generated by taking noisy samples from the true data generating function.

Finally, let's look at the third column, where we are fitting 20 datapoints. Now the intersection (or, more precisely, average) of the losses for all the datapoints gives a relatively smooth cost function $J(\theta)$, and the learned solution is almost right on top of the true solution. This illustrates a very important point:

::: center
*The more data you have, the less you need other modeling tools.*

With enough data, the true solution will be pinpointed by data alone. However, when we don't have enough data, or when the data is noisy or incorrectly labeled, we can turn to our two other tools, which we will see next.
concepts.motivation_md: This experiment shows how increasing data quantity sharpens the objective function and reduces reliance on other modeling tools like priors or regularizers.
concepts.recap_md:
- More data adds more constraints, narrowing solutions.
- Few data points allow many perfect fits; many points reduce ambiguity.
- With enough data, the true solution is identified by data alone.

concepts.title: ridge regularizer

position.section_title: Three Tools in the Search for Truth: Data, Priors, and Hypotheses

concepts.one_liner: The ridge regularizer prefers solutions with small parameter norm, pulling learned solutions closer to the origin as regularization strength increases.
concepts.content: We look at the effect of the ridge regularizer $\left\lVert\theta\right\rVert_2^2$. We plot the energy landscape and function fit for this problem in @fig-problem_of_generalization-more_regularizer_more_constraints, fitting to a single datapoint. The ridge regularizer prefers solutions with small parameter norm, so its contribution to the energy landscape is to place a quadratic bowl around the origin. As we increase $\lambda$ (moving left to right in the subplots), the effect of the regularizer becomes stronger and pulls the learned solution closer and closer to the origin.
concepts.motivation_md: Ridge regularization helps control model complexity by penalizing large parameter values, encouraging simpler solutions.
concepts.recap_md:
- Ridge regularizer penalizes the squared norm of parameters.
- It creates a quadratic bowl energy landscape centered at zero.
- Increasing $\lambda$ strengthens the pull toward the origin.

key_passage.text: We will look at the effect of the ridge regularizer $\left\lVert\theta\right\rVert_2^2$.

motivation.text: The ridge regularizer prefers solutions with small parameter norm, so its contribution to the energy landscape is to place a quadratic bowl around the origin.

concepts.one_liner: Priors help only when they are good guesses; overreliance ignores data; and there is an optimal regularization strength.
concepts.content:
You can take away a few lessons from this example:

1.  Priors help only when they are good guesses as to the truth.

2.  Overreliance on the prior means ignoring the data, and this is generally a bad thing.

3.  For any given prior, there is a sweet spot where the strength is optimal. Sometimes this ideal strength can be derived from modeling assumptions and other times you may need to tune it as a hyperparameter.

concepts.recap_md:
- Priors are helpful only if they approximate the truth well.
- Ignoring data by overusing priors is detrimental.
- Optimal regularization strength balances prior and data influence.

concepts.title: complex exponentials form an orthogonal basis
concepts.one_liner: The complex exponentials form an orthogonal basis for discrete signals and images of finite length.
concepts.content:
A remarkable property is that the complex exponentials form an orthogonal basis for discrete signals and images of finite length. For images of size $N \times M$,
$$\left<e_{u,v}, e_{u',v'} \right> = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} e_{u,v}\left[n,m\right] e^*_{u',v'}\left[n,m\right] = MN \delta \left[u-u'\right]\delta \left[v-v'\right]$$
Therefore, any finite length discrete image can be decomposed as a linear combination of complex exponentials.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding that complex exponentials form an orthogonal basis allows us to represent any finite discrete image as a sum of these basis functions, enabling powerful signal decomposition and analysis.
concepts.recap_md:
- Complex exponentials form an orthogonal basis for discrete signals and images.
- Orthogonality is expressed as $\left<e_{u,v}, e_{u',v'} \right> = MN \delta[u-u']\delta[v-v']$.
- Any finite discrete image can be decomposed into a linear combination of complex exponentials.

concepts.title: Discrete Fourier Transform
concepts.one_liner: The Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) transforms a finite size image into its complex Fourier transform.
concepts.content:
The **Discrete Fourier Transform** (DFT) transforms an image $\ell\left[n,m \right]$, of finite size $N \times M$, into the complex image Fourier transform $\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]$ as:
$$\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] =  
\mathcal{F} \left\{ \ell\left[n,m \right] \right\}
=
\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} \, \ell\left[n,m \right] 
\exp{ \left( -2\pi j \left( \frac{u\, n}{N} + \frac{v\, m}{M} \right) \right)}
$$
We will call $\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]$ the Fourier transform of $\ell\left[m,n \right]$. We often represent the relationship between the signal and its transform as:
$$\ell\left[n,m \right] \xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}} \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]$$
By applying $\frac{1}{MN} \sum_{u=0}^{M-1} \sum_{v=0}^{N-1}$ to both sides of the equation above and exploiting the orthogonality between distinct Fourier basis elements, we find the **inverse Fourier transform** relation:
$$\ell\left[n,m \right] = 
\mathcal{F}^{-1} \left\{ \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] \right\}
=
\frac{1}{NM} \sum_{u=0}^{N-1} \sum_{v=0}^{M-1} \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] 
\exp{ \left(+2\pi j \left(\frac{u\, n}{N} + \frac{v\, m}{M} \right) \right) }
$$
concepts.motivation_md: The DFT converts finite discrete images into frequency domain representations, enabling analysis and processing using complex exponentials as basis functions.
concepts.recap_md:
- The DFT transforms an image $\ell[n,m]$ into $\mathscr{L}[u,v]$ using sums of complex exponentials.
- The transform is defined as $\mathscr{L}[u,v] = \sum \ell[n,m] e^{-2\pi j(\frac{un}{N}+\frac{vm}{M})}$.
- The inverse DFT reconstructs the image from $\mathscr{L}[u,v]$ using a similar sum with positive exponentials.

key_passage.text: The Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) transforms an image \ell\left[n,m \right], of finite size N \times M, into the complex image Fourier transform \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] as: $$\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] = \mathcal{F} \left\{ \ell\left[n,m \right] \right\} = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} \, \ell\left[n,m \right] \exp{ \left( -2\pi j \left( \frac{u\, n}{N} + \frac{v\, m}{M} \right) \right)} $$ We will call \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] the Fourier transform of \ell\left[m,n \right].

concepts.title: inverse Fourier transform
concepts.one_liner: The inverse Fourier transform reconstructs the original image from its Fourier transform.
concepts.content:
Distinct Fourier basis elements allow us to find the **inverse Fourier transform** relation:
$$\ell\left[n,m \right] = 
\mathcal{F}^{-1} \left\{ \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] \right\}
=
\frac{1}{NM} \sum_{u=0}^{N-1} \sum_{v=0}^{M-1} \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] 
\exp{ \left(+2\pi j \left(\frac{u\, n}{N} + \frac{v\, m}{M} \right) \right) }
$$
concepts.motivation_md: The inverse Fourier transform is essential to recover the original image from its frequency domain representation.
concepts.recap_md:
- The inverse Fourier transform reconstructs $\ell[n,m]$ from $\mathscr{L}[u,v]$.
- It uses a sum over all frequencies with positive complex exponentials.
- The formula includes a normalization factor $\frac{1}{NM}$.

concepts.title: periodicity of the Fourier transform and inverse
concepts.one_liner: The Fourier transform and its inverse are periodic functions with periods related to the image size.
concepts.content: As $\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]$ is obtained as a sum of complex exponentials with a common period of $N,M$ samples, the function $\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]$ is also periodic: $\mathscr{L}\left[u+aN,v+bM \right] = \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]$ for any $a,b \in \mathbb{Z}$. Also, the result of the inverse DFT is a periodic image. Indeed, you can verify from equation (@eq-inversefourier) that $\ell\left[n+aN,m+bM \right] = \ell\left[n,m \right]$ for any $a,b \in \mathbb{Z}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Periodicity in the Fourier transform and its inverse reflects the discrete and finite nature of signals, ensuring consistent reconstruction and interpretation.
concepts.recap_md:
- $\mathscr{L}[u,v]$ is periodic with periods $N$ and $M$ in $u$ and $v$.
- The inverse DFT result $\ell[n,m]$ is also periodic with periods $N$ and $M$.
- Periodicity holds for any integer shifts $a,b \in \mathbb{Z}$.

Also the result of the inverse DFT is a periodic image.

concepts.title: arrangement of Fourier coefficients in the complex plane
concepts.one_liner: Fourier coefficients can be arranged so the zero frequency is at the center, representing slow variations near the origin.
concepts.content:
Especially useful for the inverse that can be written as:
$$\ell\left[n,m \right] = \frac{1}{NM} \sum_{u=-N/2}^{N/2} \sum_{v=-M/2}^{M/2} \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]\exp{ \left(+2\pi j \left(\frac{u\, n}{N} + \frac{v\, m}{M} \right) \right) }
$$
This formulation allows us to arrange the coefficients in the complex plane so that the zero frequency, or DC, coefficient is at the center. Slow, large variations correspond to complex exponentials of frequencies near the origin. If the amplitudes of the complex conjugate exponentials are the same, then their sum will represent a cosine wave; if their amplitudes are opposite, it will be a sine wave. Frequencies further away from the origin represent faster variation with movement across space. The DFT and its inverse in 1D are defined in the same way as shown in @tbl-tableFamilyFT.
concepts.motivation_md: Arranging Fourier coefficients with zero frequency at the center helps interpret frequency components as slow or fast spatial variations, aiding signal analysis.
concepts.recap_md:
- Fourier coefficients can be arranged with zero frequency at the center.
- Frequencies near the origin correspond to slow variations; farther frequencies correspond to faster variations.
- Equal amplitudes of conjugate exponentials form cosine waves; opposite amplitudes form sine waves.

concepts.title: uniqueness of decomposition into complex exponentials
concepts.one_liner: The decomposition of a signal into a sum of complex exponentials is unique.
concepts.content: One very important property is that the decomposition of a signal into a sum of complex exponentials is unique: there is a unique linear combination of the exponentials that will result in a given signal.
concepts.motivation_md: Uniqueness ensures that the Fourier decomposition precisely and unambiguously represents the original signal, which is critical for analysis and reconstruction.
concepts.recap_md:
- Decomposition into complex exponentials is unique.
- There is only one linear combination of exponentials for a given signal.
- This property guarantees precise signal representation.

concepts.title: Fast Fourier Transform
concepts.one_liner: The Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) algorithm reduces the computation cost of the DFT from $O(N^2)$ to $O(N \log N)$.
concepts.content: The DFT became very popular thanks to the **Fast Fourier Transform** (FFT) algorithm. The most common FFT algorithm is the Cooley–Tukey algorithm @Cooley1965 that reduces the computation cost from $O(N^2)$ to $O(N \log N)$.
concepts.motivation_md: The FFT algorithm exists to efficiently compute the DFT, making Fourier analysis practical for large signals and images.
concepts.recap_md:
- FFT is an algorithm to compute the DFT efficiently.
- The Cooley–Tukey algorithm is the most common FFT method.
- It reduces computation from $O(N^2)$ to $O(N \log N)$.

key_passage.text: The DFT became very popular thanks to the **Fast Fourier Transform** (FFT) algorithm.

motivation.text: The most common FFT algorithm is the Cooley–Tukey algorithm that reduces the computation cost from $O(N^2)$ to $O(N \log N)$.

concepts.title: Matrix Form of the Fourier Transform
concepts.one_liner: The DFT can be expressed as a matrix multiplication where each row is a basis vector of complex exponentials.
concepts.content:
As the DFT is a linear transform we can also write the DFT in matrix form, with one basis per row. In 1D, the matrix for the DFT is as follows:

$$\mathbf{F} = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & \dots & 1\\ %u=0
1 & \exp{ \left(-2\pi j \frac{1}{N} \right)} & \exp{ \left(-2\pi j \frac{2}{N} \right)} & \dots & \exp{ \left(-2\pi j \frac{N-1}{N} \right)}\\ %u=1
1 & \exp{ \left(-2\pi j \frac{2}{N} \right)} & \exp{ \left(-2\pi j \frac{4}{N} \right)} & \dots & \exp{ \left(-2\pi j \frac{2\, (N-1)}{N} \right)}\\ %u=2
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & ~ & \vdots \\
1 & \exp{ \left(-2\pi j \frac{(N-1)}{N} \right)} & \exp{ \left(-2\pi j \frac{(N-1)\, 2}{N} \right)} & \dots & \exp{ \left(-2\pi j \frac{(N-1)\, (N-1)}{N} \right)}\
\end{bmatrix}$$ 

Each entry in the matrix is
$\mathbf{F}_{u,n} = \exp{ \left(-2\pi j \frac{u\, n}{N} \right)}$, with $u$ indexing rows and $n$ indexing columns. Note that $\mathbf{F}$ is a symmetric matrix. The inverse of the DFT is the complex conjugate: $\mathbf{F}^{-1} = \mathbf{F}^{*}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Expressing the DFT as a matrix multiplication clarifies its linear algebraic structure and facilitates efficient computation and theoretical analysis.
concepts.recap_md:
- The DFT can be represented as a matrix $\mathbf{F}$ with entries $\exp(-2\pi j \frac{u n}{N})$.
- Each row of $\mathbf{F}$ is a Fourier basis vector.
- The inverse DFT is given by the complex conjugate matrix $\mathbf{F}^*$.

key_passage.text: As the DFT is a linear transform we can also write the DFT in matrix form, with one basis per row.

concepts.title: Background: The Polynomial Regression Learning Problem
concepts.one_liner: Polynomial regression is like linear regression except the hypothesis space is polynomial functions rather than linear functions, i.e., $y = f_{\theta}(x) = \sum_{k=0}^K \theta_k x^k$.
concepts.content:
Polynomial regression is similar to linear regression except that the hypothesis space consists of polynomial functions rather than linear functions, expressed as:
$$\begin{aligned}
y = f_{\theta}(x) = \sum_{k=0}^K \theta_k x^k
\end{aligned}$$
where $K$, the degree of the polynomial, is a hyperparameter of the hypothesis space. Considering the least-squares ($L_2$) loss function, polynomial regression is closely related to linear regression; in fact, it can be transformed into a linear regression problem.

This is seen by rewriting the polynomial as:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \sum_{k=0}^K \theta_k x^k = \theta^\mathsf{T}\phi(x)\\
    \quad\quad\quad\quad \phi(x) = \begin{bmatrix}
                            1 \\ x \\ x^2 \\ \vdots \\ x^K
                        \end{bmatrix}
\end{aligned}$$

Now the function $f_{\theta}$ takes the form $f_{\theta}(x) = \theta^\mathsf{T}\phi(x)$, which is linear in the parameters $\theta$. By featurizing $x$ into the feature vector $\phi(x)$, the polynomial regression problem becomes a linear regression problem in this feature space. The learning problem and closed form optimizer for $L_2$ polynomial regression closely resemble those of $L_2$ linear regression:

where
$$\mathbf{\Phi} = 
     \begin{bmatrix}
        1 & x^{(1)} & x^{(1)^2} & ... & x^{(1)^K} \\
        1 & x^{(2)} & x^{(2)^2} & ... & x^{(2)^K} \\
        \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\
        1 & x^{(N)} & x^{(N)^2} & ... & x^{(N)^K}  \\
    \end{bmatrix}$$

The matrix $\mathbf{\Phi}$ contains the features (columns) for each datapoint (rows) and plays the same role as the data matrix $\mathbf{X}$ in linear regression. Such matrices of feature representations are often called data matrices. As an exercise, one can derive the closed form optimizer using the same steps as for linear regression.
concepts.motivation_md: Polynomial regression generalizes linear regression by allowing polynomial hypothesis spaces, enabling more flexible fits to data while retaining a linear structure in parameters for efficient optimization.
concepts.recap_md:
- Polynomial regression models $y$ as a polynomial function $f_{\theta}(x) = \sum_{k=0}^K \theta_k x^k$.  
- By featurizing inputs as $\phi(x) = [1, x, x^2, ..., x^K]^\mathsf{T}$, polynomial regression becomes linear regression in feature space.  
- The data matrix $\mathbf{\Phi}$ contains these polynomial features for all datapoints, enabling closed form solutions analogous to linear regression.

motivation.text: It turns out polynomial regression is highly related to linear regression; in fact, we can transform a polynomial regression problem into a linear regression problem!

question.text: As an exercise, you can derive the closed form of the optimizer, given above, using the same steps as we did for linear regression in chapter.

concepts.title: Polynomial Regression as a Lens into Generalization
concepts.one_liner: As the polynomial degree $K$ increases, the hypothesis space expands, allowing better data fits but risking overfitting by fitting noise, illustrating generalization challenges.
concepts.content:
Increasing the order of the polynomial $K$ means using $K+1$ basis functions $x^0, \ldots, x^K$. For $K=1$, this reduces to linear regression; for $K=2$, quadratic functions (parabolas) are fit to the data. As $K$ increases, the hypothesis space expands to include increasingly curvy fits, as shown in @fig-under_and_overfitting.

(see figure: Underfitting and overfitting.)

In the figure, the black line is the model's fit, the green line is the true underlying relationship between random variables $X$ and $Y$, and the black points are observed data sampled from the green line plus observation noise. The full data generating process is:
$$\begin{aligned}
    Y &= X^2 + 1 &\triangleleft \quad\text{true underlying relationship}\\
    \epsilon &\sim \mathcal{N}(0,1) &\triangleleft \quad\text{observation noise}\\
    Y^\prime &= Y + \epsilon &\triangleleft \quad\text{noisy observations}\\
    x,y &\sim p(X,Y^{\prime}) &\triangleleft \quad\text{data-generating process}
\end{aligned}$$

As $K$ increases, the model fits the data points better but eventually overfits, perfectly interpolating the data but deviating from the true data-generating line. This occurs because for high $K$ (e.g., $K=10$), the curve can fit not only the true relationship but also the noise $\epsilon$, which does not generalize to test data. This is overfitting.

Additionally, for large $K$, many polynomial functions fit the data equally well, leading to non-unique solutions. The optimizer may select an arbitrary, often very curvy hypothesis due to optimization details rather than the objective, which is undesirable when the true function is smoother.
concepts.motivation_md: Studying polynomial regression with varying degree $K$ illustrates how model complexity affects generalization, demonstrating underfitting, overfitting, and the importance of balancing fit and smoothness.
concepts.recap_md:
- Increasing polynomial degree $K$ expands the hypothesis space, allowing more complex fits.  
- High-degree polynomials can overfit by fitting noise, reducing generalization.  
- Multiple equally good fits exist for large $K$, causing optimizer-dependent solutions.

key_passage.text: As we increase $K$ we fit the data points better and better, but eventually start *overfitting*, where the model perfectly interpolates the data (passes through every datapoint) but deviates more and more from the true data-generating line.

motivation.text: Why does that happen? It's because for $K=10$ the curve can become wiggly enough to not just fit the true underlying relationship but also to *fit the noise*, the minor offsets $\epsilon$ around the green line.

concepts.title: Approximation error
concepts.one_liner: Approximation error is the total cost incurred on the training data, measuring the gap between the model's predictions and training points.
concepts.content:
Approximation error is the gap between the model's predictions (black line) and the training data points (black points). Given training data $\{x_{(\texttt{train})}^{(i)}, y_{(\texttt{train})}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$, the approximation error $J_{\texttt{approx}}$ is defined as the total cost incurred on this training data:

$$\begin{aligned}
    J_{\texttt{approx}} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(x_{(\texttt{train})}^{(i)}), y_{(\texttt{train})}^{(i)})
\end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Approximation error quantifies how well the model fits the training data, indicating the model's capacity to capture observed patterns.
concepts.recap_md:
- Approximation error measures the cost on training data points.  
- It quantifies the difference between model predictions and training labels.  
- Defined as $J_{\texttt{approx}} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(x_{(\texttt{train})}^{(i)}), y_{(\texttt{train})}^{(i)})$.

key_passage.text: **Approximation error** is the gap between the black line and the training data points.

concepts.title: Generalization error
concepts.one_liner: Generalization error is the expected cost on new test points from the true data generating process, often approximated by heldout data performance.
concepts.content:
Generalization error is the gap between the model's predictions (black line) and the true underlying relationship (green line), representing the expected cost incurred when sampling a new test point from the true data generating process. It is often approximated by measuring performance on heldout data $\{x_{(\texttt{val})}^{(i)}, y_{(\texttt{val})}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$, which is a subset of data not used for training or testing:

$$\begin{aligned}
    J_{\texttt{gen}} &= \mathbb{E}_{x,y \sim p_{\texttt{data}}} [ \mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(x), y)]\\
                        &\approx \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(x_{(\texttt{val})}^{(i)}), y_{(\texttt{val})}^{(i)})
\end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Generalization error measures how well the model performs on unseen data, reflecting its ability to generalize beyond training samples.
concepts.recap_md:
- Generalization error is the expected loss on new data from the true distribution.  
- It is approximated by evaluating on heldout validation data.  
- Defined as $J_{\texttt{gen}} = \mathbb{E}_{x,y \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(x), y)]$.

key_passage.text: Generalization error is the gap between the black line and the green line, that is, the expected cost we would incur if we sampled a new test point at random from the true data generating process.

motivation.text: Generalization error is often approximated by measuring performance on a heldout , $\{x_{(\texttt{val})}^{(i)}, y_{(\texttt{val})}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$, which can simply be a subset of the data that we don't use for training or testing:

example.text:
$$\begin{aligned} J_{\texttt{gen}} &= \mathbb{E}_{x,y \sim p_{\texttt{data}}} [ \mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(x), y)]\\ &\approx \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(x_{(\texttt{val})}^{(i)}), y_{(\texttt{val})}^{(i)})
\end{aligned}$$

concepts.title: Regularization
concepts.one_liner: Regularization refers to mechanisms that penalize function complexity to avoid learning overly flexible functions that overfit.
concepts.content: Regularization refers to mechanisms that penalize function complexity to avoid learning overly flexible functions that overfit. Typically, regularizers are terms added to the objective function that prefer simpler functions within the hypothesis space, all else being equal. This embodies the principle of Occam's razor.
concepts.motivation_md: Regularization exists to prevent overfitting by discouraging overly complex models, promoting simpler, more generalizable solutions.
concepts.recap_md:
- Regularization penalizes function complexity to prevent overfitting.  
- It adds terms to the objective favoring simpler hypotheses.  
- Embodies Occam's razor by preferring simpler models.

key_passage.text: Regularization refers to mechanisms that penalize function complexity so that we avoid learning too flexible a function that overfits.

motivation.text: Typically, regularizers are terms we add to the objective that prefer simple functions in the hypothesis space, all else being equal.

concepts.title: regularized objective function
concepts.one_liner: A regularized objective function combines data fit loss with a regularizer weighted by a hyperparameter $\lambda$.
concepts.motivation_md: Regularized objectives balance fitting the data well with controlling model complexity to improve generalization.
concepts.recap_md:
- Regularized objective = data fit loss + $\lambda$ times regularizer.  
- $\lambda$ controls the strength of regularization.  
- Encourages simpler models while fitting data.

concepts.title: $L_p$ norm regularizer
concepts.one_liner: An $L_p$ norm regularizer penalizes the $L_p$ norm of the model parameters $\theta$, i.e., $R(\theta) = \lVert\theta\rVert_p$.
concepts.content:
One of the most common regularizers penalizes the $L_p$ norm of the model parameters $\theta$:
$$
R(\theta) = \left\lVert\theta\right\rVert_{p}.
$$
concepts.motivation_md: Penalizing the $L_p$ norm of parameters encourages simpler models by shrinking parameter magnitudes, reducing overfitting.
concepts.recap_md:
- $L_p$ norm regularizer penalizes $\lVert\theta\rVert_p$.  
- Encourages smaller parameter values.  
- Commonly used to control model complexity.

key_passage.text:
One of the most common regularizers is to penalize the $L_p$ norm of the parameters of our model, $\theta$:
$$
R(\theta) = \left\lVert\theta\right\rVert_{p}.
$$

concepts.title: Tikonov regression
concepts.one_liner: When $p=2$, the $L_p$ norm regularizer is called Tikhonov regression, also known as ridge regression in neural networks.
concepts.content: An especially common choice is $p=2$, in which case the regularizer is called Tikhonov regression (also known as ridge regression). In the context of neural networks, this regularizer is called weight decay. When $p=1$, the ...
concepts.motivation_md: Tikhonov regression ($p=2$) is widely used because it penalizes large parameter values smoothly, improving generalization and numerical stability.
concepts.recap_md:
- $p=2$ norm regularizer is called Tikhonov or ridge regression.  
- Known as weight decay in neural networks.

concepts.title: Relative importance of amplitude and phase in images

position.section_title: Fourier Analysis as an Image Representation

concepts.one_liner: The amplitude contains very useful information as shown in @fig-phasevsamp, and the relative importance of phase and amplitude depends on the image.
concepts.content:
However, this does not mean that all the information of the image is contained inside the phase only. The amplitude contains very useful information as shown in @fig-phasevsamp. To get an intuition of the information available on the amplitude and phase, let's do the following experiment: take an image, compute the Fourier transform, and create two images by applying the inverse Fourier transform when removing one of the components while keeping the other original component. For the amplitude image, we randomize the phase. For the phase image, we replace the amplitude by a noninformative $A \left[u,v \right] = 1/(u^2+v^2)^{1/2}$ for all images. This amplitude is better than a random amplitude because a random amplitude produces a very noisy image hiding the information available, while this generic form for the amplitude will produce a smoother image, revealing its structure while still removing any information available on the original amplitude. @fig-phasevsamp shows different types of images and how the DFT amplitude and phase contribute to defining the image content. The top image is inline with the observation from @fig-phaseoramp where phase seems to be carrying most of the image information. However, the rest of the images do not show the same pattern. As we move down along the examples in the figure, the relative importance between the two components changes. And for the bottom image (showing a pseudo-periodic thread texture) the amplitude is the most important component.

The amplitude is great for capturing images that contain strong periodic patterns. In such cases, the amplitude can be better than the phase. This observation has been the basis for many image descriptors @Gorkani94, @oliva01. The amplitude is somewhat invariant to location (although it is not invariant to the relative location between different elements in the scene). However the phase is a complex signal that does not seem to make explicit any information about the image.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the relative importance of amplitude and phase in images helps reveal how different image components contribute to visual content, aiding in image analysis and descriptor design.
concepts.recap_md:
- The amplitude contains useful information and can be more important for images with strong periodic patterns.
- Phase often carries most image information but its importance varies by image.
- Amplitude is somewhat location-invariant; phase is complex and less explicit.

concepts.title: Campbell and Robson chart
concepts.one_liner: The Campbell and Robson chart is an image with amplitude varying vertically and frequency varying horizontally, illustrating contrast sensitivity.
concepts.content:
$$\ell\left[n,m\right] = A\left[m\right] \sin(2 \pi f\left[n\right] n/N)$$
with
$$A\left[m\right] = A_{min} \left(\frac{A_{max}}{A_{min}}\right)^{m/M}$$
and
$$f\left[n\right] = f_{min} \left(\frac{f_{max}}{f_{min}}\right)^{n/N}$$
This image is separable and it is composed of two factors: an amplitude, $A\left[m\right]$, that varies only along the vertical dimension, $m$, and a wave with a frequency, $f\left[n\right]$, that varies along the horizontal component, $n$. The amplitude, $A\left[m\right]$, goes from $A_{max}$ to $A_{min}$ on a logarithmic scale. The frequency function, $f\left[n\right]$, is defined as an increasing function that starts from $f_{min}=1$ and grows up to $f_{max}=60$ (with $N=2,048$ being the number of horizontal pixels in the image). This image is shown in @fig-csfchart and it is also called the **Campbell and Robson chart**. It appears to an observer as a signal with a wave that oscillates slow at the left and faster toward the right and that has high contrast a the bottom and loses contrast towards the top becoming invisible.
concepts.motivation_md: The Campbell and Robson chart visually demonstrates how contrast sensitivity varies with spatial frequency and amplitude, aiding vision research.
concepts.recap_md:
- The image amplitude varies vertically from $A_{max}$ to $A_{min}$ logarithmically.
- Frequency varies horizontally from $f_{min}=1$ to $f_{max}=60$.
- The chart illustrates waves oscillating slower on the left and faster on the right with contrast decreasing upward.

concepts.title: spatiotemporal filter that will do exactly what we were looking for
concepts.one_liner: We get a kernel $h(x,y,t;v_x,v_y)$ that we can use as a spatiotemporal filter that will do exactly what we were looking for.
concepts.content:
$$
h(x,y,t;v_x,v_y) = g_t+v_xg_x+v_yg_y = \nabla  g \left( 1,v_x,v_y \right)^\top
$$ {#eq-spt_nulling_filter}

We get a kernel $h(x,y,t;v_x,v_y)$ that we can use as a spatiotemporal filter that will do exactly what we were looking for. Indeed, if we convolve it with the input sequence $\text{img}_0 (x-v_x t,y-v_y t)$ we get a zero output (using @eq-brightnessconstancy):

$$
\begin{split}
\ell _0 (x-v_x t, y-v_y t) \circ h & = \ell _0 (x-v_x t, y-v_y t) \circ \left( g_t + v_x g_x + v_y g_y \right) \\
& = \left( \frac{\partial \ell _0}{\partial t} + v_x \frac{\partial \ell _0}{\partial x} + v_y \frac{\partial \ell _0}{\partial y} \right) \circ g \\
& = 0
\end{split}
$$
concepts.motivation_md: A spatiotemporal filter kernel $h(x,y,t;v_x,v_y)$ is constructed to cancel out motion at a specific velocity, enabling zero output when convolved with an image sequence moving at that velocity.

- Convolution of $h$ with the shifted input sequence yields zero output.
- This uses the brightness constancy assumption in its derivation.

concepts.title: nulling filter
concepts.one_liner: Such a filter $h$ will cancel any objects moving at the velocity $(v_x,v_y)$.
concepts.content:
Such a filter $h$ will cancel any objects moving at the velocity $(v_x,v_y)$. By using different filters, each one computing derivatives along different space-time orientations, we can create output sequences where specific objects disappear, as shown in @fig-tunedfilter. This filter is called a **nulling filter** [@Darrell93].

(see figure: (a) Input sequence. (b) Output to $h$ with $v_x=v_y=0$. (c) $v_x=1$ pixels/frame. (d) $v_x=-1$ pixel/frame.)

Note that despite assuming that the sequence contained a single moving object when deriving the formulation for the nulling filter, the filter also works in sequences with multiple objects moving at different speeds, as shown in @fig-tunedfilter. This is because the operations are local (the kernel $h$ has a small size), and the behavior will be correct if in a local image patch there is only one velocity present. In fact, it is easy to show that the method will also work if the sequence is a sum of several moving transparent layers.

concepts.title: sampling period
concepts.one_liner: The sampling period $T_s$ is the interval at which a continuous signal is sampled to produce a discrete sequence.
concepts.content: Let's consider a one-dimensional (1D) continuous time signal $\ell (t)$ and its sampled version $\ell [n] = \ell(n T_s)$, where $T_s$ is the **sampling period**. Intuitively, it is clear that in this sampling process, some information will get lost. If no information was lost, then we should be able to recover the continuous signal $\ell (t)$ from its sampled version $\ell [n]$ by doing some kind of interpolation. One way of ensuring that information is not lost is to decrease $T_s$, which will result in a more accurate approximation of the continuous signal $\ell (t)$ at the expense of the amount of memory needed to store $\ell [n]$. Decreasing $T_s$ will also result in an increase in the computational cost of processing the signal $\ell [n]$. Therefore, it is important to choose the appropriate $T_s$. Understanding the sampling process and how to reconstruct the continuous signal is necessary as it will allow us to find the optimal sampling parameters.
concepts.motivation_md: Choosing the right sampling period balances accuracy and resource use, ensuring the continuous signal can be reconstructed from discrete samples.
concepts.recap_md:
- Sampling period $T_s$ is the interval between samples of a continuous signal.
- Smaller $T_s$ means better approximation but higher storage and computation costs.
- Proper $T_s$ choice is crucial for accurate signal reconstruction.

concepts.title: sampling theorem
concepts.one_liner: The sampling theorem states that the sampling frequency must be greater than twice the maximum frequency present in the input signal to perfectly reconstruct it.
concepts.content:
The **sampling theorem** (also known as Nyquist theorem) states that for a signal to be perfectly reconstructed from a set of samples (under the slow and smooth prior), the sampling frequency $w_s = 2 \pi /T_s$ has to be $w_s > 2w_{max}$ when $w_{max}$ is the maximum frequency present in the input signal [@Shannon1948].

The same theorem can be stated in terms of periods: the sampling period, $T_s$, has to be $T_s < T_{min} / 2$, i.e., smaller than half of the period of the highest frequency component, $T_{min} = 2 \pi /w_{max}$. Note that our previous example did not satisfy the **Nyquist condition**.
concepts.motivation_md: The sampling theorem ensures that sampling is done at a rate sufficient to perfectly reconstruct the original signal without loss of information.
concepts.recap_md:
- Sampling frequency $w_s$ must satisfy $w_s > 2w_{max}$ for perfect reconstruction.
- Equivalently, sampling period $T_s < T_{min}/2$.
- This is known as the Nyquist condition.

concepts.title: discrete time sine wave
concepts.one_liner: The discrete time sine wave is $s[n] = A \sin(w n - \theta)$ and is periodic only if $w = 2 \pi K / N$ for integers $K,N$.
concepts.content:
In discrete time, the **discrete time sine wave** is as follows
$$s\left[n\right] = A \sin\left(w ~n  - \theta \right)$$ Note that the discrete sine wave will not be periodic for any arbitrary value of $w$. A discrete signal $\ell\left[n\right]$ is periodic, if there exists $T \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $\ell\left[n\right] = \ell\left[n+mT\right]$ for all $m \in \mathbb{Z}$. For the discrete sine (and cosine) wave to be periodic the frequency has to be $w = 2 \pi K / N$ for $K,N \in \mathbb{N}$. If $K/N$ is an irreducible fraction, then the period of the wave will be $T = N$ samples. Although $\theta$ can have any value, here we will consider only the values $\theta=0$ and $\theta = \pi/2$, which correspond to the sine and cosine waves, respectively.
concepts.motivation_md: Discrete sine waves model signals sampled at discrete times, with periodicity conditions depending on frequency ratios.
concepts.recap_md:
- Discrete sine wave: $s[n] = A \sin(w n - \theta)$.
- Periodic only if $w = 2\pi K / N$ for integers $K,N$.

concepts.title: Sines and Cosines in 2D
concepts.one_liner: In 2D, discrete sine and cosine waves are $s_{u,v}[n,m] = A \sin(2\pi(\frac{u n}{N} + \frac{v m}{M}))$ and $c_{u,v}[n,m] = A \cos(2\pi(\frac{u n}{N} + \frac{v m}{M}))$.
concepts.content:
The same analysis can be extended to two dimensions (2D). In 2D, the discrete sine and cosine waves are as follows:
$$s_{u,v}\left[n,m\right] = A \sin \left(2 \pi \left( \frac{u\,n}{N}  + \frac{v\,m}{M}  \right) \right)$$
$$c_{u,v}\left[n,m\right] = A \cos \left(2 \pi \left( \frac{u\,n}{N}  + \frac{v\,m}{M}  \right) \right)$$
where $A$ is the amplitude and $u$ and $v$ are the two spatial frequencies and define how fast or slow the waves change along the spatial dimensions $n$ and $m$. @fig-disc2Dsignal shows some examples.

(see figure: 2D sine waves with $N=M=20$. The frequency values are (a) $u=2, v=0$; (b) $u=3, v=1$; (c) $u=7,v=-5$.)

- 2D discrete cosine wave: $c_{u,v}[n,m] = A \cos(2\pi(\frac{u n}{N} + \frac{v m}{M}))$.
- $u,v$ are spatial frequencies controlling wave variation in $n,m$.

concepts.title: Complex Exponentials
concepts.one_liner: The complex exponential wave is $e_u[n] = \exp\left(2 \pi j \frac{u n}{N}\right)$ and relates to sine and cosine waves by Euler's formula.
concepts.content:
### Complex Exponentials

Another important signal is the complex exponential wave:
$$e_{u}\left[n\right] = \exp \left(2 \pi j   \frac{u\, n}{N}   \right)$$

Complex exponentials are related to cosine and sine waves by Euler's formula: $$
\exp \left(j a\right) = \cos (a) + j \sin (a)$$@fig-complexexponential shows the one dimensional (1D) discrete complex exponential function (for $v=0$). As the values are complex, the plot shows in the $x$-axis the real component and in the $y$-axis the imaginary component. As $n$ goes from 0 to $N-1$ the function rotates along the complex circle of unit magnitude.


(see figure: Complex exponential wave with (a) $N=40$, $k=1$, $A=1$; and (b) $N=40$, $k=3$, $A=1$. The red and green curves show the real and imaginary waves. The black line is the complex exponential. The dots...)
concepts.motivation_md: Complex exponentials unify sine and cosine waves and are fundamental in signal processing and Fourier analysis.
concepts.recap_md:
- Complex exponential: $e_u[n] = \exp(2\pi j \frac{u n}{N})$.
- Related to sine and cosine by Euler's formula.
- Rotates on the complex unit circle as $n$ varies.

key_passage.text: Another important signal is the complex exponential wave: $$e_{u}\left[n\right] = \exp \left(2 \pi j \frac{u\, n}{N} \right)$$ Complex exponentials are related to cosine and sine waves by Euler's formula: $$ \exp \left(j a\right) = \cos (a) + j \sin (a)$$

motivation.text: As the values are complex, the plot shows in the $x$-axis the real component and in the $y$-axis the imaginary component. As $n$ goes from 0 to $N-1$ the function rotates along the complex circle of unit magnitude.

concepts.title: complex exponential wave
concepts.one_liner: In 2D, the complex exponential wave is $e_{u,v}[n,m] = \exp\left(2 \pi j \left( \frac{u n}{N} + \frac{v m}{M} \right)\right)$ and can be separated into products of 1D signals.
concepts.content:
In 2D, the complex exponential wave is
$$e_{u,v}\left[n,m\right] = \exp \left(2 \pi j \left(  \frac{u\, n}{N}  + \frac{v\,m}{M}  \right) \right)$$where $u$ and $v$ are the two spatial frequencies. Note that complex exponentials in 2D are separable. This means they can be written as the product of two 1D signals:
$$e_{u,v}\left[n,m\right]   = e_{u}\left[n\right] e_{v}\left[m\right]$$

A remarkable property is that the complex exponentials form an orthogonal basis for discrete signals and images of finite length. For images of size $N \times M$,
$$\left<e_{u,v}, e_{u',v'} \right> = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} e_{u,v}\left[n,m\right] e^*_{u',v'}\left[n,m\right] = MN \delta \left[u-u'\right]\delta \left[v-v'\right]$$
concepts.motivation_md: 2D complex exponentials provide an orthogonal basis for representing discrete signals and images, enabling efficient analysis and synthesis.
concepts.recap_md:
- 2D complex exponential: $e_{u,v}[n,m] = \exp\left(2 \pi j \left( \frac{u n}{N} + \frac{v m}{M} \right)\right)$.
- Separable into products of 1D signals.
- Form an orthogonal basis for discrete signals and images.

concepts.title: Associative
concepts.one_liner: Convolutions can be applied in any order: $$\ell_1 [n] \circ \ell_2 [n] \circ \ell_3 [n] = \ell_1[n] \circ (\ell_2[n] \circ \ell_3[n]) = (\ell_1[n] \circ \ell_2[n]) \circ \ell_3[n]$$
concepts.content:
-   **Associative**. Convolutions can be applied in any order:
    $$\ell_1 \left[n\right] \circ \ell_2 \left[n\right] \circ \ell_3 \left[n\right] = \ell_1\left[n\right] \circ (\ell_2\left[n\right] \circ \ell_3\left[n\right]) = (\ell_1\left[n\right] \circ \ell_2\left[n\right]) \circ \ell_3\left[n\right]$$
    In practice, for finite length signals, the associative property might be affected by how boundary conditions are implemented.
concepts.motivation_md: The associative property ensures that the order in which convolutions are applied does not affect the final result, simplifying analysis and implementation of multiple convolutions.
concepts.recap_md:
- Convolution is associative: order of applying convolutions does not matter.
- For finite signals, boundary conditions can affect associativity.
- Expressed as: $\ell_1 \circ (\ell_2 \circ \ell_3) = (\ell_1 \circ \ell_2) \circ \ell_3$.

key_passage.text: Convolutions can be applied in any order: $$\ell_1 \left[n\right] \circ \ell_2 \left[n\right] \circ \ell_3 \left[n\right] = \ell_1\left[n\right] \circ (\ell_2\left[n\right] \circ \ell_3\left[n\right]) = (\ell_1\left[n\right] \circ \ell_2\left[n\right]) \circ \ell_3\left[n\right]$$

motivation.text: In practice, for finite length signals, the associative property might be affected by how boundary conditions are implemented.

concepts.title: Distributive
concepts.one_liner: Distributive with respect to the sum: $$\ell_1[n] \circ (\ell_2[n] + \ell_3[n]) = \ell_1[n] \circ \ell_2[n] + \ell_1[n] \circ \ell_3[n]$$
concepts.content:
-   **Distributive** with respect to the sum:
    $$\ell_1\left[n\right] \circ (\ell_2\left[n\right] + \ell_3\left[n\right] ) = \ell_1\left[n\right] \circ \ell_2\left[n\right] +  \ell_1 \left[n\right] \circ \ell_3 \left[n\right]$$
concepts.motivation_md: The distributive property allows convolution to distribute over addition, enabling linear combination of signals before or after convolution.
concepts.recap_md:
- Convolution distributes over addition: $\ell_1 \circ (\ell_2 + \ell_3) = \ell_1 \circ \ell_2 + \ell_1 \circ \ell_3$.
- This property simplifies analysis of linear systems.
- Useful for decomposing signals into sums.

key_passage.text: **Distributive** with respect to the sum: $$\ell_1\left[n\right] \circ (\ell_2\left[n\right] + \ell_3\left[n\right] ) = \ell_1\left[n\right] \circ \ell_2\left[n\right] + \ell_1 \left[n\right] \circ \ell_3 \left[n\right]$$

concepts.title: Shift
concepts.one_liner: If the input signal is shifted by $n_0$, the convolution output shifts by the same amount: $$\ell_{\texttt{out}}[n-n_0] = h[n] \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}[n-n_0] = h[n-n_0] \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}[n]$$
concepts.content:
-   **Shift**. Another interesting property involves shifting the two convolved functions. Let's consider the convolution
    $\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n\right] = h\left[n\right] \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n\right]$.
    If the input signal, $\ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n\right]$, is translated by a constant $n_0$, i.e.
    $\ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n - n_0\right]$, the result of the
    convolution with the same kernel, $h\left[n\right]$, is the same
    output as before but translated by the same constant $n_0$:
    $$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n-n_0\right] =  h\left[n\right] \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n-n_0\right]$$
    Translating the kernel is equivalent:
    $$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n-n_0\right] =  h\left[n\right] \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n-n_0\right]  = h\left[n-n_0\right] \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n\right]$$
concepts.motivation_md: The shift property shows how translating the input or kernel shifts the output correspondingly, important for understanding signal translation effects.
concepts.recap_md:
- Shifting the input signal shifts the convolution output by the same amount.
- Shifting the kernel instead produces the same shifted output.
- Expressed as: $\ell_{out}[n-n_0] = h[n] \circ \ell_{in}[n-n_0] = h[n-n_0] \circ \ell_{in}[n]$.

key_passage.text: Another interesting property involves shifting the two convolved functions. Let's consider the convolution $\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n\right] = h\left[n\right] \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n\right]$. If the input signal, $\ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n\right]$, is translated by a constant $n_0$, i.e. $\ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n - n_0\right]$, the result of the convolution with the same kernel, $h\left[n\right]$, is the same output as before but translated by the same constant $n_0$: $$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n-n_0\right] = h\left[n\right] \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n-n_0\right]$$ Translating the kernel is equivalent: $$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n-n_0\right] = h\left[n\right] \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n-n_0\right] = h\left[n-n_0\right] \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n\right]$$

concepts.title: Support
concepts.one_liner: The convolution of a discrete signal of length $N$ with another of length $M$ results in a signal of length $L \leq M+N-1$.
concepts.content:
-   **Support**. The convolution of a discrete signal of length $N$ with
    another discrete signal of length $M$ results in a discrete signal
    with length $L \leq M+N-1$.
concepts.motivation_md: Knowing the length of the convolution output helps in signal processing and system design, especially for finite signals.
concepts.recap_md:
- Convolution output length $L \leq M+N-1$ for signals of lengths $N$ and $M$.
- This bounds the size of the resulting signal.
- Important for finite discrete signals.

key_passage.text: The convolution of a discrete signal of length $N$ with another discrete signal of length $M$ results in a discrete signal with length $L \leq M+N-1$.

concepts.title: Identity
concepts.one_liner: The convolution identity is the impulse $\delta[n]$, which satisfies $\delta[n] \circ \ell[n] = \ell[n]$.
concepts.content:
-   **Identity**. The convolution also has an identity function, that is the **impulse**, $\delta \left[n\right]$, which takes the value 1 for $n=0$ and it is zero everywhere else:
    $$\delta \left[n\right] =
      \begin{cases}
        1       & \quad \text{if } n=0\\
        0       & \quad \text{if } n \neq 0 \\
      \end{cases}$$
    The convolution of the impulse with any other signal, $\ell\left[n\right]$, returns the same signal:
    $$\delta \left[n\right] \circ \ell\left[n\right] = \ell\left[n\right]$$
concepts.motivation_md: The identity property defines an impulse signal that leaves any signal unchanged when convolved, fundamental for signal analysis.
concepts.recap_md:
- The impulse $\delta[n]$ equals 1 at $n=0$ and 0 elsewhere.
- Convolution with $\delta[n]$ returns the original signal.
- Acts as the identity element for convolution.

key_passage.text: The convolution also has an identity function, that is the impulse, $\delta \left[n\right]$, which takes the value 1 for $n=0$ and it is zero everywhere else: $$\delta \left[n\right] = \begin{cases} 1 & \quad \text{if } n=0\\ 0 & \quad \text{if } n \neq 0 \\ \end{cases}$$

motivation.text: The convolution of the impulse with any other signal, $\ell\left[n\right]$, returns the same signal: $$\delta \left[n\right] \circ \ell\left[n\right] = \ell\left[n\right]$$

concepts.title: Circular Convolution
concepts.one_liner: Circular convolution uses circular padding and is defined as $$\ell_{\texttt{out}}[n] = h[n] \circ_N \ell_{\texttt{in}}[n] = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} h[(n-k)_N] \ell_{\texttt{in}}[k]$$ with period $N$.
concepts.content:
### Circular Convolution

Writing the circular convolution in matrix form will look like:
[FIGURE:adb812066d7186ad | A square diagram representing a circulant matrix structure. A thick black main diagonal is flanked by two red diagonals and two green diagonals. Small segments of the red and green diagonals wrap...]

When convolving a finite length signal with a kernel, we have seen that it can be convenient to extend the signal beyond its boundary to reduce boundary artifacts. This trick is also very useful analytically and conduces to a special case of the convolution: the **circular convolution** uses circular padding. The circular convolution of two signals, $h$ and $\ell_{\texttt{in}}$, of length $N$ is defined as follows:

$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n\right] = h \left[n\right] \circ_N \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n\right] =  \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} h \left[(n-k)_N \right] \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[k \right]$$

In this formulation, the signal $h \left[ (n)_N \right]$ is the infinite periodic extension, with period $N$, of the finite length signal $h \left[n \right]$. The output of the circular convolution is a periodic signal with period $N$, $\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n \right] = \ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[(n)_N \right]$.

The circular convolution has the same properties than the convolution (e.g., is commutative.)
concepts.motivation_md: Circular convolution handles finite signals with circular padding, avoiding boundary artifacts and producing periodic outputs, useful in signal processing and analysis.
concepts.recap_md:
- Circular convolution uses circular padding and sums over one period.
- Output is periodic with period $N$.
- Shares properties with standard convolution, such as commutativity.

key_passage.text: The circular convolution of two signals, $h$ and $\ell_{\texttt{in}}$, of length $N$ is defined as follows: $$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n\right] = h \left[n\right] \circ_N \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n\right] = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} h \left[(n-k)_N \right] \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[k \right]$$ In this formulation, the signal $h \left[ (n)_N \right]$ is the infinite periodic extension, with period $N$, of the finite length signal $h \left[n \right]$. The output of the circular convolution is a periodic signal with period $N$, $\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n \right] = \ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[(n)_N \right]$.

motivation.text: When convolving a finite length signal with a kernel, we have seen that it can be convenient to extend the signal beyond its boundary to reduce boundary artifacts. This trick is also very useful analytically and conduces to a special case of the convolution: the **circular convolution** uses circular padding.

concepts.title: Convolution in the Continuous Domain
concepts.one_liner: The continuous convolution is defined as $$\ell_{\texttt{out}}(t) = h(t) \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(t-\tau) \ell_{\texttt{in}}(\tau) d\tau$$ and shares properties with discrete convolution.
concepts.content:
### Convolution in the Continuous Domain

The convolution in the continuous domain is defined in the same way as with discrete signals but replacing the sums by integrals. Given two continuous signals $h(t)$ and $\ell_{\texttt{in}}(t)$, the convolution operator is defined as follows:
$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}(t) = h(t) \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(t-\tau) \ell_{\texttt{in}}(\tau) d\tau$$

The properties of the continuous domain convolution are analogous to the properties of the discrete convolution, with the commutative, associative and distributive relationships still holding.

We can also define the impulse, $\delta (t)$, in the continuous domain such that $\ell(t) \circ \delta(t) = \ell(t)$. 

The impulse is defined as being zero everywhere but at the origin where it takes an infinitely high value so that its integral is equal to 1:
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(t) dt = 1$$ The impulse function is also called the impulse distribution (as it is not a function in the strict sense) or the Dirac delta function.  


The delta distribution is usually represented with an arrow of height 1, indicating that it has an finite value at that point, and a finite area equal to 1:

[FIGURE:3bb6012ff85cabfe | A graph of the Dirac delta function $\delta(t-a)$ on a coordinate system with horizontal axis $t$ and vertical axis $\delta(t-a)$. A single blue vertical arrow is positioned at $t=a$ on the...]

The impulse has several important properties:

-   Scaling property: $\delta (at) =  \delta (t) / |a|$

-   Symmetry: $\delta (-t) = \delta (t)$

-   Sampling property: $\ell(t) \delta (t-a) = \ell(a) \delta (t-a)$ where $a$ is a constant. From this, we have the following:
    $$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \ell(t) \delta (t-a) dt = \ell(a)$$

-   As in the discrete case, the continuous impulse is also the identity for the convolution: $\ell(t) \circ \delta (t) = \ell(t)$.

The impulse will be useful in analytical derivations and we will see it again in chapter @sec-sampling when we discuss sampling.
concepts.motivation_md: Continuous convolution generalizes discrete convolution to continuous signals, enabling analysis and processing of continuous-time systems.
concepts.recap_md:
- Continuous convolution replaces sums with integrals: $\ell_{out}(t) = \int h(t-\tau) \ell_{in}(\tau) d\tau$.
- Shares commutative, associative, and distributive properties with discrete convolution.
- The impulse $\delta(t)$ acts as the identity element in continuous convolution.

key_passage.text:
The convolution in the continuous domain is defined in the same way as with discrete signals but replacing the sums by integrals. Given two continuous signals $h(t)$ and $\ell_{\texttt{in}}(t)$, the convolution operator is defined as follows:
$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}(t) = h(t) \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(t-\tau) \ell_{\texttt{in}}(\tau) d\tau$$

motivation.text: The impulse will be useful in analytical derivations and we will see it again in chapter when we discuss sampling.

concepts.title: cross-correlation
concepts.one_liner: The cross-correlation operator between image $\ell_{\texttt{in}}$ and kernel $h$ is $$\ell_{\texttt{out}}[n,m] = \ell_{\texttt{in}} \star h = \sum_{k,l=-N}^N \ell_{\texttt{in}}[n+k,m+l] h[k,l]$$ without kernel inversion.
concepts.content:
The **cross-correlation** operator (denoted by $\star$) between the image $\ell_{\texttt{in}}$ and the kernel $h$ is written as follows:
$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n,m\right] = \ell_{\texttt{in}}\star h =  \sum_{k,l=-N}^N \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n+k,m+l \right] h \left[k,l \right]$$
where the sum is done over the support of the filter $h$, which we assume is a square $(-N,N)\times(-N,N)$. In the convolution, the kernel is inverted left-right and up-down, while in the cross-correlation is not. Remember that the convolution between image $\ell_{\texttt{in}}$ and kernel $h$ is written as follows:
$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n,m\right] = \ell_{\texttt{in}}\circ h = \sum_{k,l=-N}^N \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n-k,m-l \right] h \left[k,l \right]$$
concepts.motivation_md: Cross-correlation measures similarity between an image and a kernel without flipping the kernel, useful in pattern matching and feature detection.
concepts.recap_md:
- Cross-correlation sums products of image and kernel without kernel inversion.
- Denoted by $\star$, differs from convolution which flips the kernel.
- Formula: $\ell_{out}[n,m] = \sum \ell_{in}[n+k,m+l] h[k,l]$.

key_passage.text: The cross-correlation operator (denoted by $\star$) between the image $\ell_{\texttt{in}}$ and the kernel $h$ is written as follows: $$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n,m\right] = \ell_{\texttt{in}}\star h = \sum_{k,l=-N}^N \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n+k,m+l \right] h \left[k,l \right]$$ where the sum is done over the support of the filter $h$, which we assume is a square $(-N,N)\times(-N,N)$.

motivation.text: In the convolution, the kernel is inverted left-right and up-down, while in the cross-correlation is not.

concepts.title: Activation Layers
concepts.one_liner: Activation layers add nonlinearity by applying pointwise scalar-to-scalar functions on each input dimension, enabling neural nets to compute nonlinear functions.
concepts.motivation_md: Activation layers introduce nonlinearity into neural networks, enabling them to model complex functions beyond linear mappings, which is essential for learning rich representations.
concepts.recap_md:
- Activation layers add nonlinearity to neural nets, enabling them to compute nonlinear functions.
- They apply scalar-to-scalar pointwise functions on each input dimension.
- Common activations include threshold, sigmoid, tanh, relu, and leaky-relu.

key_passage.text: Activation layers add nonlinearity. Activation layers are typically pointwise functions, applying a scalar to scalar mapping on each dimension of the input vector.

motivation.text: If a net only contained linear layers then it could only compute linear functions. This is because the composition of $N$ linear functions is a linear function.

concepts.title: batchnorm
concepts.one_liner: Batchnorm standardizes each neural activation with respect to its mean and variance over a batch of datapoints.
concepts.motivation_md: Batchnorm improves training by normalizing activations within a batch, stabilizing learning and accelerating convergence.
concepts.recap_md:
- Batchnorm standardizes activations by subtracting the batch mean and dividing by the batch standard deviation.
- It includes learnable scale ($\gamma$) and shift ($\beta$) parameters.
- This normalization is computed over a batch of datapoints.

key_passage.text: Batchnorm **standardizes** each neural activation with respect to its mean and variance over a batch of datapoints.

concepts.title: L2 normalization

concepts.title: Why Are Neural Networks a Good Architecture?

position.section_title: Why Are Neural Networks a Good Architecture?

concepts.one_liner: Deep nets are good architectures because they are high capacity, differentiable, have good inductive biases, run efficiently on parallel hardware, and build abstractions.
concepts.content:
## Why Are Neural Networks a Good Architecture?

As you will soon learn, almost all modern computer vision algorithms involve deep nets in one way or another. So you may be wondering: why are deep nets such a good architecture? We will highlight here five reasons:

1.  They are high capacity (big enough nets are universal approximators).

2.  They are differentiable (the parameters can be optimized via gradient descent).

3.  They have good inductive biases (neural architectures reflect real structure in the world).

4.  They run efficiently on parallel hardware.

5.  They build abstractions.

Let's look at reasons 1-3 in light of the discussion of searching for truth from chapter @sec-problem_of_generalization (see @fig-problem_of_generalization-search_space_tools). Reason 1 relates to the size of the hypothesis space. The hypothesis space can be made very big if we use a large neural network with many parameters. So we can usually be sure that our true solution (or a close approximation to it) does indeed lie in the space spanned by the neural net architecture.
Reason 2 says that searching for the solution within this space is relatively easy, since we can use gradients to direct us toward ever better fits to the data. Reason 3 is one we will only come to appreciate later in the book as we investigate more advanced neural net architectures. It turns out that these architectures impose constraints and regularizers that bias our search toward solutions that capture true structure about the visual world, and this leads to learned solutions that generalize.

Reason 4 is equally important to the first three: it says we can do all of this *efficiently* because most computations can be parallelized on modern hardware; in particular both matrix multiplies (linear layers) and pointwise operations (e.g., relu layers) are easy to parallelize on graphical processing units. Further, most operations are applied to image batches, where each item in the batch can be sent to a different parallel compute node.

Reason 5 is perhaps the most subtle. It is related to the layered structure of neural nets. Layer by layer, neural nets build up increasingly abstracted representations of the input data, and these abstractions tend to be increasingly useful. This argument is not easy to appreciate at first glance, but it will be a major theme of the subsequent chapters in this book, especially those on representation learning. For now, just keep in mind that the *internal representations* that are built up layer by layer in deep nets are useful and important beyond just the net's overall input-output behavior.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding why deep neural networks are effective helps appreciate their design: they combine capacity, differentiability, inductive biases, computational efficiency, and abstraction-building.
concepts.recap_md:
- Neural nets are universal approximators with high capacity.
- They are differentiable, enabling gradient-based optimization.
- They encode inductive biases and build useful abstractions layer by layer.

Reason 2 says that searching for the solution within this space is relatively easy, since we can use gradients to direct us toward ever better fits to the data. Reason 3 is one we will only come to appreciate later in the book as we investigate more advanced neural net architectures. It turns out that these architectures impose constraints and regularizers that bias our search toward solutions that capture true structure about the visual world, and this leads to learned solutions that generalize.

concepts.title: Concluding Remarks
concepts.one_liner: Neural nets are simple, universal approximators trained by gradient descent and are effective especially in computer vision due to architectures reflecting visual world structure.
concepts.content:
## Concluding Remarks

Neural nets are a very simple and useful parameterized hypothesis space. They are universal approximators that can be trained via gradient descent and run on parallel hardware. *Deep* nets are especially effective in computer vision; as we will soon see, deep architectures can be constructed that specifically reflect structure in the visual world, making visual processing highly efficient and performant.
Artificial neural nets also have connections to the real neural nets in our brains. This connection runs deeper than merely sharing a name: the deep net architectures we will see later in this book (e.g., convolutional networks, transformers) are our best current models of computation in animal brains, in the sense that they explain brain data better than any competing models @Schrimpf2020integrative. This is a class of models truly worth paying attention to.
concepts.motivation_md: Neural nets provide a powerful, trainable model class that is both computationally efficient and biologically inspired, making them central to modern AI and neuroscience.
concepts.recap_md:
- Neural nets are simple, universal approximators trained via gradient descent.
- Deep nets reflect structure in the visual world, enhancing efficiency.
- They model brain computation better than competing models.

concepts.title: Fourier transform of a real image
concepts.one_liner: The DFT results in a complex representation, which can be written using the real and imaginary components or using a polar decomposition.
concepts.content:
When computing the DFT of a real image, we will not be able to write the analytic form of the result, but there are a number of properties that will help us to interpret the result. @fig-DFT_a shows the Fourier transform of a $64 \times 64$ resolution image of a cube. As the DFT results in a complex representation, there are two possible ways of writing the result. Using the real and imaginary components:
$$\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] = Re \left\{\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] \right\}  + j \, Imag \left\{\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] \right\}$$
where $Re$ and $Imag$ denote the real and imaginary part of each Fourier coefficient. Or using a polar decomposition:
$$\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]  = A \left[u,v \right] \, \exp{\left( j \, \theta\left[u,v \right]  \right)}$$
where $A \left[u,v \right] \in \mathbb{R}^+$ is the amplitude and $\theta \left[u,v \right] \in \left[-\pi, \pi \right]$ is the phase. @fig-DFT_a shows both decompositions of the Fourier transform.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the complex-valued DFT of real images requires decomposing it into real/imaginary parts or amplitude/phase to interpret the frequency content effectively.
concepts.recap_md:
- The DFT of a real image is complex-valued.
- It can be expressed as real plus imaginary parts.
- Or equivalently as amplitude and phase in polar form.

key_passage.text: When computing the DFT of a real image, we will not be able to write the analytic form of the result, but there are a number of properties that will help us to interpret the result. As the DFT results in a complex representation, there are two possible ways of writing the result. Using the real and imaginary components: $$\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] = Re \left\{\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] \right\} + j \, Imag \left\{\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] \right\}$$ where $Re$ and $Imag$ denote the real and imaginary part of each Fourier coefficient. Or using a polar decomposition: $$\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] = A \left[u,v \right] \, \exp{\left( j \, \theta\left[u,v \right] \right)}$$ where $A \left[u,v \right] \in \mathbb{R}^+$ is the amplitude and $\theta \left[u,v \right] \in \left[-\pi, \pi \right]$ is the phase.

motivation.text: When computing the DFT of a real image, we will not be able to write the analytic form of the result, but there are a number of properties that will help us to interpret the result.
