concepts.title: partial sums of Fourier components for image reconstruction
concepts.one_liner: One can synthesize any image as a sum of complex exponentials (sines and cosines) using partial sums of Fourier components.
concepts.content: Upon first learning about Fourier transforms, it may be a surprise for readers to learn that one can synthesize any image as a sum of complex exponentials (i.e., sines and cosines). To help gain insight into how that works, it is informative to show examples of partial sums of complex exponentials. @fig-DFT_b shows partial sums of the Fourier components of an image. In each partial sum of $N$ components, we use the largest N components of the Fourier transform. Using the fact that the Fourier basis functions are orthonormal, it is straightforward to show that this is the best least-squares reconstruction possible from each given number of Fourier basis components. This first image shows what is reconstructed from the largest Fourier component which turns out to be $\mathscr{L}\left[0,0 \right]$. This component encodes the DC value of the image, therefore the resulting image is just a constant. The next two components correspond to two complex conjugates of a very slow varying wave. And so on. As more components get added, the figure slowly emerges. In this example, the first 127 coefficients are sufficient for recognizing this $64 \times 64$ resolution image.
concepts.motivation_md: Showing partial sums of Fourier components illustrates how images can be reconstructed progressively from frequency components, deepening understanding of Fourier synthesis.
concepts.recap_md:
- Images can be synthesized as sums of complex exponentials.
- Partial sums use the largest Fourier components.
- The first component encodes the image's DC value (constant).

concepts.title: Delta Distribution
concepts.one_liner: The Fourier transform of the delta function $\delta \left[n,m \right]$ is 1.
concepts.content:
The Fourier transform of the delta function $\delta \left[n,m \right]$ is
$$\mathcal{F} \left\{ \delta \left[n,m \right] \right\} = 
\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} \, \delta \left[n,m \right] 
\exp{ \left( -2\pi j \left( \frac{u\, n}{N} + \frac{v\, m}{M} \right) \right)} = 1$$
where the Fourier transform of the delta signal is 1.
$$\delta \left[n,m \right] \xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}} 1$$
If we think in terms of the inverse Fourier transform, this means that if we sum all the complex exponentials with a coefficient of 1, then all the values will cancel but the one at the origin, which results in a delta function:
$$\delta \left[n,m \right] = \frac{1}{NM} \sum_{u=-N/2}^{N/2} \sum_{v=-M/2}^{M/2}
concepts.motivation_md: The delta function's Fourier transform being 1 shows that summing all complex exponentials equally reconstructs a single spike, fundamental for understanding frequency-domain representations.
concepts.recap_md:
- The delta function $\delta[n,m]$ transforms to 1 in the Fourier domain.
- Summing all complex exponentials with coefficient 1 yields a delta.
- This links time-domain spikes to uniform frequency components.

concepts.title: Cosine and Sine Waves
concepts.one_liner: The Fourier transform of cosine and sine waves results in delta functions at positive and negative frequencies.
concepts.motivation_md: Expressing cosine and sine waves in terms of delta functions in the frequency domain clarifies their frequency content and aids in signal analysis.
concepts.recap_md:
- Cosine transforms to two delta functions at $\pm (u_0,v_0)$.
- Sine transforms to a difference of delta functions scaled by $1/(2j)$.
- Euler's formula and orthogonality prove these relationships.

concepts.title: Box Function
concepts.one_liner: The box function is defined as 1 inside the interval $[-L,L]$ and 0 outside.
concepts.motivation_md: The box function models a simple finite interval signal, serving as a fundamental example for studying Fourier transforms and periodic extensions.
concepts.recap_md:
- The box function equals 1 for $n \in [-L,L]$ and 0 otherwise.
- Its duration is $2L+1$.
- It can be viewed as a finite-length signal with periodic extension.

key_passage.text:
The box function is defined as follows:
$$\text{box}_{L} \left[n \right] = \begin{cases} 1 & \quad \text{if } -L \leq n \leq L \\ 0 & \quad \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$$ The box function takes values of 1 inside the interval
$\left[ -L,L \right]$ and it is 0 outside. The duration of the box is
$2L+1$.

motivation.text:
The box function is a very useful function that we will use several
times in this book. It is good to be familiar with its Fourier transform

concepts.one_liner: The DFT of the box function is the discrete sinc function.
concepts.motivation_md: Knowing the DFT of the box function as the discrete sinc function helps analyze finite signals and their frequency characteristics.

concepts.title: The Full Algorithm: Forward, Then Backward

position.section_title: The Full Algorithm: Forward, Then Backward

concepts.one_liner: The full backpropagation algorithm consists of a forward pass through the network followed by a backward pass computing gradients for each layer.
concepts.content:
We can compute the gradient update for parameters $\theta_l$ once we have the arrays $\mathbf{L}_l$ and $\mathbf{g}_l$ for layer $l$. To ensure these arrays are ready when updating layer $l$, we first perform a forward pass through the entire network, starting with input data $\mathbf{x}_0$ and evaluating layer by layer to produce the sequence $\mathbf{x}_0, \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_L$. (see figure: Forward pass.)

Data/activations passed forward through the network are shown in green.

Next, we compute a backward pass, iteratively evaluating the gradients $\mathbf{g}$ to obtain the sequence $\mathbf{g}_L, \mathbf{g}_{L-1}, \ldots$, as well as the parameter gradients for each layer. (see figure: A schematic diagram of the backpropagation process in a neural network. Red arrows flow from right to left, starting with a value of 1 entering a loss derivative block $\mathcal{L}'$, then passing...)

The full algorithm is summarized in algorithm @alg-backpropagation-backprop_for_chains.
concepts.motivation_md: Backpropagation computes gradients efficiently by first running a forward pass to calculate activations, then a backward pass to propagate gradients, enabling parameter updates for training neural networks.
concepts.recap_md:
- The algorithm first performs a forward pass to compute activations $\mathbf{x}_0, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_L$.
- Then it performs a backward pass to compute gradients $\mathbf{g}_L, \mathbf{g}_{L-1}, \ldots$.
- Parameter gradients for each layer are computed during the backward pass.

key_passage.text:
We use the color for data/activations being passed forward through the network. Next, we compute a **backward pass**, iteratively evaluating the
$\mathbf{g}$'s and obtaining the sequence
$\mathbf{g}_L, \mathbf{g}_{L-1}, \ldots$, as well as the parameter
gradients for each layer.

motivation.text:
So, we just need to order our operations so that when we get to updating
layer $l$ we have these two arrays ready.

concepts.title: Backpropagation Over Data Batches
concepts.one_liner: The gradient of a sum of terms is the sum of the gradients of each term.
concepts.content:
So far, we have only examined computing the gradient of the loss for a single datapoint $\mathbf{x}$. The total cost function we wish to minimize is typically the average of the losses over all datapoints in a training set $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$. Once we know how to compute the gradient for a single datapoint, we can compute the gradient for the whole dataset using the identity:

$$\frac{\partial \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N J_i(\theta)}{\partial \theta} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{\partial J_i(\theta)}{\partial \theta}$$

where $J_i(\theta)$ is the loss for a single datapoint $\mathbf{x}^{(i)}$. Therefore, to compute a gradient update for algorithms like stochastic gradient descent, we apply backpropagation in batch mode by running it over each datapoint in the batch (which can be done in parallel) and then averaging the results.

In the remaining sections, we focus on backpropagation for the loss at a single datapoint, keeping in mind that batch backpropagation simply requires applying the above averaging.
concepts.motivation_md: To train on datasets with many datapoints, we compute gradients over batches by averaging individual gradients, enabling efficient updates with stochastic gradient descent.
concepts.recap_md:
- The total loss is the average over all datapoints' losses.
- Gradient of the average loss equals the average of the gradients.
- Batch backpropagation applies backprop to each datapoint and averages results.

key_passage.text:
However, once we know how to compute the gradient for a single datapoint, we can easily compute the gradient for the whole dataset, due to the following identity: $$\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N J_i(\theta)}{\partial \theta} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{\partial J_i(\theta)}{\partial \theta}
\end{aligned}$$ The gradient of a sum of terms is the
sum of the gradients of each term. where $J_i(\theta)$ is
the loss for a single datapoint $\mathbf{x}^{(i)}$. Therefore, to
compute a gradient update for an algorithm like stochastic gradient
descent , we apply backpropagation in
batch mode, that is, we run it over each datapoint in our batch (which
can be done in parallel) and then average the results.

motivation.text:
As you may recall from and , the total cost function we wish
to minimize will typically be the *average* of the losses over *all* the
datapoints in a training set, $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$.

concepts.title: Backpropagation for a Linear Layer
concepts.one_liner: Forward for a linear layer is $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}= \mathbf{W} \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}+ \mathbf{b}$, and backward gradients can be computed using matrix multiplies involving $\mathbf{W}$ and the input/output gradients.
concepts.content:
A linear layer's forward operation is defined as:
$$\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}= \mathbf{W} \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}+ \mathbf{b}$$
where $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$ is $N$-dimensional, $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}$ is $M$-dimensional, $\mathbf{W}$ is an $[M \times N]$ matrix, and $\mathbf{b}$ is an $M$-dimensional vector.

The gradients of this function with respect to inputs and parameters are:

$$\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{W} \quad [M \times N], \quad \mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{b}} = \mathbf{I} \quad [M \times M]$$

There is no simple shorthand for $\mathbf{L}^\mathbf{W}$, but the backward operation can be implemented by plugging these into the backpropagation equations:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}} &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}} \mathbf{W} \\
    \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{W}} &= \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}} \\
    \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{b}} &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}
\end{aligned}$$

The gradient $\frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{W}}$ is an outer product between $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$ and $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$. This avoids building a large sparse matrix for $\mathbf{L}^\mathbf{W}$.

(see figure: The forward and backward matrix multiples for a linear layer.)

(see figure: Matrix multiply for parameter gradient of a linear layer.)

(see figure: Linear layer forward and backward.)

All these operations mainly involve matrix multiplies and are straightforward to implement using any library that provides matrix multiplication (`matmul`).
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding backpropagation for linear layers is essential because they form the building blocks of neural networks; their gradients can be efficiently computed using matrix operations.
concepts.recap_md:
- Forward pass: $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}= \mathbf{W} \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}+ \mathbf{b}$.
- Backward pass gradients: $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}} = \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}} \mathbf{W}$, $\frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{W}} = \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$, $\frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{b}} = \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$.
- The parameter gradient is an outer product of input activations and output gradients.

key_passage.text:
The definition of a linear layer, in forward direction, is as follows:
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}= \mathbf{W} \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}+ \mathbf{b}
\end{aligned}$$ We have separated the parameters into $\mathbf{W}$ and
$\mathbf{b}$ for clarity, but remember that we could always rewrite the
following in terms of $\theta = \texttt{vec}[\mathbf{W}, \mathbf{b}]$.

motivation.text:
Unlike the other equations, at first glance

concepts.title: Backpropagation for a Pointwise Nonlinearity
concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation for a pointwise nonlinearity involves multiplying the output gradient by a diagonal matrix of derivatives of the nonlinearity applied elementwise.
concepts.content:
Pointwise nonlinearities have simple backward functions. Let a scalar nonlinearity be $h: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ with derivative $h^{\prime}: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$. Define a pointwise layer as
$$f(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}) = [h(x_{\texttt{in}}[0]), \ldots, h(x_{\texttt{in}}[N-1])]^\mathsf{T}$$

Then the Jacobian matrix is diagonal:
$$\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}} = f^{\prime}(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}) = \texttt{diag}([h^{\prime}(x_{\texttt{in}}[0]), \ldots, h^{\prime}(x_{\texttt{in}}[N-1])]^{\mathsf{T}}) \triangleq \mathbf{H}^{\prime}$$

There are no parameters to update, so the backward operation computes:
$$\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}} = \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}} \mathbf{H}^{\prime}$$

For example, for a ReLU layer:
$$h^{\prime}(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } x \geq 0 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

This corresponds to masking gradients where the activation was negative. The backward operation is a matrix multiply with this diagonal matrix.

(see figure: Matrix multiply for `backward` of a pointwise layer.)

Simplified elementwise:
$$\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}[i] = \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}[i] h^{\prime}(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[i]) \quad \forall i$$

(see figure: Matrix multiply for `backward` of a pointwise layer.)
concepts.motivation_md: Pointwise nonlinearities are common in neural networks, and their backpropagation is simple and efficient, involving elementwise multiplication by derivatives.
concepts.recap_md:
- The Jacobian of a pointwise nonlinearity is a diagonal matrix of derivatives.
- Backward pass multiplies output gradient by this diagonal matrix.
- For ReLU, the derivative is 1 where input is nonnegative, else 0.

concepts.title: Backpropagation for Loss Layers
concepts.one_liner: The backward pass for an $L_2$ loss layer computes the gradient as $2(\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y})$, the per-dimension error between prediction and target.
concepts.content:
The loss layer for an $L_2$ loss function is defined as $\left\lVert \hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y} \right\rVert^2_2$, where $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is the network output and $\mathbf{y}$ is the ground truth.

This layer has no parameters, so we only derive the backward gradient:

$$\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}} = \frac{\partial \left\lVert \hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y} \right\rVert^2_2}{\partial \hat{\mathbf{y}}} = 2(\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y}) \quad [1 \times |\mathbf{y}|]$$

The backward gradient signal is:

$$\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}} = \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}} * 2(\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y}) = 2(\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y})$$

Here, $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}} = \frac{\partial J}{\partial J} = 1$ since the output of the loss layer is the cost $J$.

Thus, the backward signal is a row vector of per-dimension errors between prediction and target.

(see figure: Matrix multiply for `backward` of an $L_2$ loss layer.)
concepts.motivation_md: Loss layers provide the final error signal for training; their backward pass computes gradients that propagate error back through the network.
concepts.recap_md:
- The $L_2$ loss is $\left\lVert \hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y} \right\rVert^2_2$.
- Backward gradient is $2(\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y})$.
- The loss layer has no parameters; gradient is the error vector.

key_passage.text: As a simple example, we will derive backprop for an $L_2$ loss function: $\left\lVert\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y}\right\rVert^2_2$, where $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is the output of the network (prediction) and $\mathbf{y}$ is the ground truth.

motivation.text:
This layer has no parameters so we only need to derive for this layer: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}} &= \frac{\partial \left\lVert\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y}\right\rVert^2_2}{\partial \hat{\mathbf{y}}} = 2(\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y}) \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad [1 \times |\mathbf{y}|]\\ \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}} &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}*2(\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y}) = 2(\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y})
\end{aligned}$$ Here we have made use of the fact that
$\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}} = \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}} = \frac{\partial J}{\partial J} = 1$,
since the output of the loss layer *is* the cost $J$.

example.text: So, the backward signal sent by the $L_2$ loss layer is a row vector of per-dimension errors between the prediction and the target.

concepts.title: Putting It All Together: Backpropagation through an MLP
concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation through an MLP involves a forward pass computing activations and a backward pass computing gradients, with backward operations corresponding to transposed weight matrices and gating from nonlinearities.
concepts.content:
Consider an MLP with input $\mathbf{x}$ (4-dimensional), hidden layers $\mathbf{z}$ and $\mathbf{h}$ (3-dimensional each), and output $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ (2-dimensional). The forward pass computes activations layer by layer. (see figure: Forward pass through an MLP.)

For the backward pass, gradients $\mathbf{g}$ are treated as column vectors (transposed from the usual row vector convention). Using the matrix identity $(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})^\mathsf{T} = \mathbf{B}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}$, the backward operation is:

$$\mathbf{g}^\mathsf{T}_{\texttt{in}} = (\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}} \mathbf{W})^\mathsf{T} = \mathbf{W}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{g}^\mathsf{T}_{\texttt{out}}$$

This shows that backward for a linear layer is the same as forward but with transposed weights (biases are ignored in backward to activations).

Nonlinearities like ReLU act as gating matrices in backward, masking gradients where activations were negative. All backward operations are matrix multiplies, regardless of the forward operation.

Parameter gradients at each backward step are outer products of input activations and output gradients. 

This unifies forward and backward passes as matrix operations within the network.

### Forward-Backward Is Just a Bigger Neural Network {#sec-backpropagation-backprop_as_neural_net}
concepts.motivation_md: Combining forward and backward passes clarifies the structure of backpropagation and reveals that backward computations are closely related to forward ones, aiding understanding and implementation.
concepts.recap_md:
- Backward pass gradients are column vectors and computed using transposed weight matrices.
- Nonlinearities gate gradients by masking where activations were negative.
- Parameter gradients are outer products of activations and output gradients.

key_passage.text: This reveals an interesting connection between `forward` and `backward` for linear layers: `backward` for a linear layer is the same operation as `forward`, just with the weights transposed!

concepts.title: Forward-Backward Is Just a Bigger Neural Network
concepts.one_liner: The full backpropagation algorithm can be viewed as one big neural network combining the forward and backward passes.
concepts.content:
The backward pass through a neural network can itself be implemented as another neural network—a linear network with parameters determined by the original network's weights and activations. Therefore, the full backward pass is a neural network.

Since the forward pass is also a neural network (the original network), the full backpropagation algorithm—a forward pass followed by a backward pass—can be viewed as one big neural network.

Parameter gradients can be computed from this combined network via one additional matrix multiply (`matmul`) for each layer of the backward network.

The full network for a three-layer MLP is shown in @fig-backpropagation-backprop_as_neural_net.

concepts.title: Box Filter
concepts.one_liner: The box convolution kernel can be written as: $$\text{box}_{N,M} \left[n,m \right] = \begin{cases} 1 & \quad \text{if } -N \leq n \leq N  \text{~and~}  -M \leq m \leq M\\ 0 & \quad \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$$
concepts.content:
Let's start with a very simple low-pass filter, the box filter.  The box convolution kernel can be written as:

$$
\text{box}_{N,M} \left[n,m \right] = 
\begin{cases}
    1       & \quad \text{if } -N \leq n \leq N  \text{~and~}  -M \leq m \leq M\\
    0       & \quad \text{otherwise.} 
\end{cases}
$$

The box filter with $N=M=1$ is:

[FIGURE:c8dd7ad0f0cc82dd | A 3D stem plot of a 2D discrete box filter $\text{box}_{1,1}[n,m)$. The plot shows a $3 \times 3$ grid of blue stems, each with a height of 1, centered at $(n,m) = (0,0)$ and extending from $-1$ to...]

Filtering an input image, $\ell_{\text{in}}$, with a box filter results in the following:
$$\begin{aligned}
\ell_{\text{out}} \left[n,m\right] &= 
\text{box}_{N,M} \left[n,m\right] \circ \ell_{\text{in}} \left[n,m\right]  \\
&= \sum_{k,l} \ell_{\text{in}} \left[n-k,m-l \right] \text{box}_{N,M} \left[k,l \right] \\
&= \sum_{k=-N}^N \sum_{l=-M}^M \ell_{\text{in}} \left[n-k,m-l \right]
\end{aligned}$$
That is, the output value on each location $(n,m)$ is the sum of the input pixels within the rectangle around that location.
concepts.motivation_md: The box filter is a simple low-pass filter that averages pixel values in a rectangular neighborhood, useful for smoothing images by attenuating high-frequency content.
concepts.recap_md:
- Box filter kernel is 1 inside a rectangle and 0 outside.
- Filtering sums input pixels within the rectangle around each location.
- It acts as a simple low-pass filter for images.

motivation.text: That is, the output value on each location $(n,m)$ is the sum of the input pixels within the rectangle around that location.

concepts.title: Properties
concepts.one_liner: The box filter is a low-pass filter that attenuates high spatial-frequency content of the input image.
concepts.content:
### Properties

The box filter is a low-pass filter. That is, it attenuates the high spatial-frequency content of the input image. 

As we already mentioned in @sec-box_function, the two-dimensional (2D) box filter is separable as it can be written as the convolution of two 1D kernels: $\text{box}_{N,M} \left[n,m \right]  = \text{box}_{N,0} \circ \text{box}_{0,M}$. When the box is large, it can be implemented efficiently using the integral image [@Viola01].

One important property of a low-pass filter is the **DC gain**, that is, the gain it has for a constant value input (i.e., the lowest possible input frequency). If the input signal is a constant, i.e., $\ell[n,m] = a$, where $a$ is a real number, the result of convolving the image with the box filter $h_{N,M}$ is also a constant:

$$
\ell_{\text{out}} \left[n,m\right] = \sum_{k,l} a \text{box}_{N,M} \left[k,l \right] = a \sum_{k,l} \text{box}_{N,M} \left[k,l \right]  = a (2N+1)(2M+1)
$$

Remember that the DC value of a signal is its mean value. DC is an old name derived from Direct Current.

In general, the DC gain of an arbitrary filter $h [n,m]$ is the sum of its kernel values:

$$
\text{DC~gain} = \sum_{n,m} h [n,m]
$$

In the example of the box filter with $N=1$, the DC gain is 3. 

In the frequency domain, the DC gain of a filter refers to its gain at a frequency of 0. This gain is represented by the value $H[0,0]$, where $H$ is the result of applying the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) to the filter's kernel $h$. This can be easily proven by checking the definition of the DFT and setting the spatial frequencies to zero. One can verify in @fig-boxfilter that the value of $\left| \text{Box}_1[0] \right|$ is $3$. The DC gain of a filter will change the mean value of the input signal.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the properties of the box filter, including its low-pass nature and DC gain, helps in analyzing its effects on images and its efficient implementation.
concepts.recap_md:
- Box filter attenuates high spatial frequencies (low-pass).
- It is separable into two 1D kernels.
- DC gain equals the sum of kernel values and affects the mean signal value.

concepts.title: Limitations
concepts.one_liner: The box filter is simple to implement and understand, but it has a number of limitations.
concepts.content:
### Limitations

The box filter is simple to implement and to understand, but it has a number of limitations:

- **The box filter is not a perfect blurring filter.** A blur filter should attenuate high spatial frequencies with stronger attenuation for higher spatial frequencies. However, if you consider the highest spatial frequency, which will be an oscillating signal that takes successively on the values 1 and $-1$: $\left[..., 1, -1, 1, -1, 1, -1, ... \right]$ when filtered with the box filter $\text{box}_{1}$ the result is the same oscillating signal! However, if you filter a wave with lower frequency such as $\left[..., 0.5, 0.5, -1, 0.5, 0.5, -1, ... \right]$ then the result is $\left[..., 0,0,0,0, ...\right]$. Therefore, the attenuation is not monotonic with spatial frequency as shown in @fig-boxfilter. This is not a desirable behavior for a blurring filter, and it can cause artifacts to appear. This could be addressed using an even size box filter $\left[1,1 \right]$. However, an even box filter is not centered around the origin and the output image will have a half-pixel translation. Therefore, odd filter sizes are preferred.

The oscillating signal:

[FIGURE:b08aebefbd75544f | A discrete 1D signal plot representing a box filter. It shows blue stems with circular heads at integer positions along the horizontal $n$-axis. Stems at $n = -1, 0, 1$ have a height of 1, while all...]

convolved with the kernel $[1,1,1]$ results in:

[FIGURE:87007ce110b1a43f | A discrete stem plot representing a 1D signal on a horizontal axis labeled $n$. The signal alternates between positive and negative values at integer intervals, with blue dots at the end of each...]

- **If you convolve two boxes, you do not get another box.** Instead, you get a triangle. You can easily check this by convolving two box filters. For instance, in the simple case where $N=1, M=0$:

$$
\text{box}_{1,0} \circ \text{box}_{1,0} = \left[1, 1, 1\right] \circ \left[1, 1, 1\right] = \left[1,2,3,2,1\right]
$$

The output is a **triangular filter** \index{Filter!Triangular filter} with length $2 \times (L-1)$, with $L=3$ the length of the box filter. When convolving two box filters of different lengths, the result will be a truncated triangle. Although that is not a problem at first sight, it means that if you blur an image twice with box filters, what you get is not the equivalent to blurring only once with a larger box filter.

The next low-pass filter addresses both of these issues.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the limitations of the box filter motivates the development of better low-pass filters that avoid artifacts and provide more consistent blurring.
concepts.recap_md:
- Box filter does not attenuate highest spatial frequencies properly.
- Convolving two box filters produces a triangular filter, not a larger box.
- Even-sized box filters cause half-pixel shifts; odd sizes are preferred.

concepts.title: Template Matching and Normalized Correlation
concepts.one_liner: The normalized cross-correlation is the dot product between a zero-mean, unit-norm template and a unit-norm local image patch, scaled by the local standard deviation, to detect template occurrences robustly.
concepts.content:
The goal of template matching is to find a small image patch within a larger image. @fig-normcorr shows how to use template matching to detect all the occurrences of the letter "a" with an image of text, shown in @fig-normcorr (b). @fig-normcorr (a) shows the template of the letter "a".

(see figure: Fig (a) Template. (b) Input image. (c) Correlation between input (b) and template (a). (d) Normalized correlation. e) Locations with cross-correlation above 75 percent of its maximum value.)

Cross-correlation is a potential method for template matching, but it has certain flaws. Consider matching the "a" template in @fig-normcorr (a) in a given input image. Just by increasing the brightness of the image in different parts we can increase the filter response since correlation is essentially a multiplication between the kernel $h$ and any input image patch $p$ (note that all the values are positive in $p$ and $h$). In bright image regions we will have the maximum correlation values regardless of regions' content as shown in @fig-normcorr (c).

The normalized cross-correlation, at location $(n,m)$, is the dot product between a template, $h$, (normalized to be zero mean and unit norm) and the local image patch, $p$, centered at that location and with the same size as the kernel, normalized to be unit norm. This can be implemented with the following steps: First, we normalize the kernel $h$. The normalized kernel $\hat h$ is the result of making the kernel $h$ zero mean and unit norm. Then, the normalized cross-correlation is as follows (@fig-normcorr (d)): 

$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n,m\right] 
                = 
                \frac{1}{\sigma \left[n,m \right]}
                \sum_{k,l=-N}^N
                \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n+k,m+l \right]
                \hat{h} \left[k,l \right]$$ 
                
Note that this equation is similar to the correlation function, but the output is scaled by the local standard deviation, $\sigma \left[m,n \right]$, of the image patch centered in $(n,m)$ and with support $(-N,N)\times(-N,N)$, where $(-N,N)\times(-N,N)$ is the size of the kernel $h$. To compute the local standard deviation, we first compute the local mean, $\mu \left[n,m \right]$, as follows:
$$\mu \left[n,m \right] = \frac{1}{(2N+1)^2} \sum_{k,l=-N}^N \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n+k,m+l \right]$$
And then we compute:
$$\sigma^2 \left[n,m \right] = \frac{1}{(2N+1)^2} \sum_{k,l=-N}^N \left( \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n+k,m+l \right] - \mu \left[n,m \right] \right) ^2$$

@fig-normcorr (e) shows the detected copies of the template @fig-normcorr (a) in the image @fig-normcorr (b). The red bounding boxes in @fig-normcorr (e) correspond to the location with local maximum values of the normalized cross-correlation (@fig-normcorr (d) that are above a threshold chosen by hand.

In the example of @fig-normcorr, all the instances of the letter 'a' have been correctly detected. But this method is very fragile when used to detect objects and is useful only under very limited conditions. Normalized correlation will detect the object independently of location, but it will not be robust to any other changes such as rotation, scaling, and changes in appearance. Just changing the font of the letters will certainly make the approach fail.
concepts.motivation_md: Template matching aims to locate small image patches within larger images, but simple cross-correlation is sensitive to brightness variations. Normalized correlation addresses this by adjusting for local brightness and contrast, improving detection accuracy.
concepts.recap_md:
- Template matching finds small image patches within larger images.
- Cross-correlation can detect templates but is sensitive to brightness changes.
- Normalized cross-correlation uses zero-mean, unit-norm templates and local image patches, scaled by local standard deviation, to improve robustness.

key_passage.text: The normalized cross-correlation, at location $(n,m)$, is the dot product between a template, $h$, (normalized to be zero mean and unit norm) and the local image patch, $p$, centered at that location and with the same size as the kernel, normalized to be unit norm. This can be implemented with the following steps: First, we normalize the kernel $h$. The normalized kernel $\hat h$ is the result of making the kernel $h$ zero mean and unit norm. Then, the normalized cross-correlation is as follows ( (d)): $$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n,m\right] = \frac{1}{\sigma \left[n,m \right]} \sum_{k,l=-N}^N \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n+k,m+l \right] \hat{h} \left[k,l \right]$$ Note that this equation is similar to the correlation function, but the output is scaled by the local standard deviation, $\sigma \left[m,n \right]$, of the image patch centered in $(n,m)$ and with support $(-N,N)\times(-N,N)$, where $(-N,N)\times(-N,N)$ is the size of the kernel $h$.

motivation.text: Cross-correlation is a potential method for template matching, but it has certain flaws. Consider matching the "a" template in (a) in a given input image. Just by increasing the brightness of the image in different parts we can increase the filter response since correlation is essentially a multiplication between the kernel $h$ and any input image patch $p$ (note that all the values are positive in $p$ and $h$). In bright image regions we will have the maximum correlation values regardless of regions' content as shown in (c).

concepts.title: System Identification
concepts.one_liner: For an unknown system, one way of finding the convolution kernel $h$ consists in computing the output of the system when the input is an impulse.
concepts.content:
One important task that we will study is that of explaining the behavior of complex systems such as neural networks. For an LTI filter with kernel $h\left[n\right]$, the output from an impulse is $y\left[n\right] = h\left[n\right]$. The output of a translated impulse $\delta \left[n -n_0 \right]$ is $h \left[n -n_0 \right]$. This is why the kernel that defines an LTI system, $h\left[n\right]$, is also called the impulse response of the system.

![LTI system with impulse response $h\left[n\right]$.](figures/linear_image_filtering/genericfilterH2.png){width="30%" #fig-genericfilterH}

For an unknown system, one way of finding the convolution kernel $h$ consists in computing the output of the system when the input is an impulse.

Let's start with a beautiful example from acoustics @TraerE7856. When you are in a room you often hear that sounds are distorted with echos (@fig-impulse_response_room_a). The number and strength of the echos depend on the geometry of the room, whether it is full or empty and the materials in the walls and ceilings.

(see figure: As shown in the sketch, sounds produced by one speaking person reach a listener via multiple paths. What the person hears is the superposition of all those signals. Figure modified from @TraerE7856.)

Interestingly the relationship between the sounds that are originated in one location and what a listener hears in another position are related by an LTI system. If you are in a room and you clap (which is a good approximation to an impulse of sound), the echoes that you hear are very close to the impulse response of the system formed by the acoustics of the room. Any sounds that originates at the location of your clap will produce a sound in the room that will be qualitatively similar to the convolution of the acoustic signal with the echoes that you hear before when you clapped. @fig-impulse_response_room_a2 shows a recording made in a restaurant in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

(see figure: Fig (a) Apparatus used to measure the impulse response generated by a battery-powered speaker and a portable digital recorder. (b) Recorded acoustic impulse response of a room. Figure modified from...)  

@fig-impulse_response_room_b, adapted from @TraerE7856, shows a sketch of how a voice signal gets distorted by the impulse response of a room before it reaches the listener. The impulse response, $h (t)$, is modeled here as a sequence of four impulses, the first impulse corresponds to the direct path and the remaining three to the different paths inside the room, modeled with different delays ($T_i$) and amplitudes ($0 < a_i < 1$): 

$$h (t) = a_0 \delta (t)
+ a_1 \delta \left(t-T_1 \right) 
+ a_2 \delta \left( t-T_2 \right)
+ a_3 \delta \left( t-T_3 \right)$$ 

The sound that reaches the listener is the superposition of four copies of the sound emitted by the speaker. This can be written as the convolution of the input sound, $\ell_{\texttt{in}}(t)$, with room impulse response, $h (t)$:
$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}(t) = \ell_{\texttt{in}}(t) \circ h(t) = a_0 \ell_{\texttt{out}}(t)
+ a_1 \ell_{\texttt{in}}(t-T_1) 
+ a_2 \ell_{\texttt{in}}(t-T_2)
+ a_3 \ell_{\texttt{in}}(t-T_3)$$ which is shown graphically in @fig-impulse_response_room_b.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding system behavior by identifying its impulse response helps explain complex systems and predict outputs from inputs, such as how room acoustics distort sounds via echoes.
concepts.recap_md:
- The kernel $h[n]$ of an LTI system is its impulse response.
- For unknown systems, applying an impulse input reveals the convolution kernel.
- Room acoustics act as an LTI system where echoes represent the impulse response.

concepts.title: spatial frequency
concepts.one_liner: A spatial frequency describes how quickly a signal varies over space.
concepts.content: While temporal frequency describes how quickly signals vary over time, a spatial frequency describes how quickly a signal varies over space. The Fourier transform lets us describe a signal as a sum of complex exponentials, each of a different spatial frequency.
concepts.motivation_md: Spatial frequency helps analyze signals that vary over space, enabling decomposition into components with different rates of spatial change, which is essential in image and signal processing.
concepts.recap_md:
- Spatial frequency describes how quickly a signal varies over space.
- It is analogous to temporal frequency but for spatial domains.
- Fourier transform decomposes signals into sums of complex exponentials at different spatial frequencies.

motivation.text: The Fourier transform lets us describe a signal as a sum of complex exponentials, each of a different spatial frequency.

concepts.title: Fourier series
concepts.one_liner: Fourier showed that any function defined on $(0,\pi)$ can be expressed as an infinite sum of harmonically related sinusoids.
concepts.content:
*Theorie de la Chaleur* @Fourier09, and the **Fourier series** has become one of the most important mathematical tools in science and engineering.

Fourier showed that any function, $\ell(t)$ defined in the interval $t \in (0,\pi)$, could be expressed as an infinite linear combination of harmonically related sinusoids,
$$\ell(t) = a_1 \sin (t) + a_2 \sin (2t) + a_3 \sin (3t) + ...$$ and that the value of the coefficients $a_n$ could be computed as the area of the curve $\ell(t) \sin (nt)$. Precisely,
$$a_n = \frac{2}{\pi} \int_0^\pi  \ell(t) \sin (nt) dt$$ However, the sum is only guaranteed to converge to the function $\ell(t)$ within the interval $t \in (0,\pi)$. In fact, the resulting sum, for any values $a_n$, is a **periodic function** with period $2\pi$ and is anti-symmetric with respect to the origin, $t=0$.
concepts.motivation_md: Fourier series provide a powerful way to represent functions as sums of sinusoids, enabling analysis and synthesis of signals in science and engineering.
concepts.recap_md:
- Fourier series express functions on $(0,\pi)$ as sums of sinusoids.
- Coefficients $a_n$ are computed via integrals involving $\ell(t) \sin(nt)$.
- The resulting sum is a periodic function with period $2\pi$ and is anti-symmetric about $t=0$.

Precisely, $$a_n = \frac{2}{\pi} \int_0^\pi \ell(t) \sin (nt) dt$$ However, the sum is only guaranteed to converge to the function $\ell(t)$ within the interval $t \in (0,\pi)$.

concepts.title: sine series
concepts.one_liner: The sine series expresses the ramp signal as an infinite sum of weighted sine functions with increasing frequency.
concepts.content:
One of Fourier's original examples of **sine series** is the expansion of the ramp signal $\ell(t)=t/2$. This series was first introduced by Euler. Fourier showed that his theory explained why a ramp could be written as the following infinite sum:
$$\frac{1}{2} t =  \sin (t) - \frac{1}{2}  \sin (2t) + \frac{1}{3} \sin (3t) - \frac{1}{4}  \sin (4t) + ...$$
The result of this series approximates the ramp with increasing accuracy as we add more terms. The plots in @fig-FourierSeries6 show each of the weighted sine functions (on top) and the resulting partial sum (bottom graphs). We can see how adding **higher frequency** sines adds more details to the resulting function making it closer to the ramp. These plots show the signal in the interval $t \in (-4 \pi, 4 \pi)$ to reveal the periodic nature of the result of the sine series.

(see figure: Reconstruction of a ramp with the first five sine functions.)
concepts.motivation_md: The sine series demonstrates how complex signals like ramps can be represented as sums of sine waves, illustrating the power of Fourier analysis for signal approximation.
concepts.recap_md:
- The ramp signal $\ell(t)=t/2$ can be expanded as a sine series.
- The series is an infinite sum of weighted sine functions with increasing frequency.
- Adding more terms improves the approximation and reveals periodicity.

Fourier showed that his theory explained why a ramp could be written as the following infinite sum: $$\frac{1}{2} t = \sin (t) - \frac{1}{2} \sin (2t) + \frac{1}{3} \sin (3t) - \frac{1}{4} \sin (4t) + ...$$

concepts.title: change of representation
concepts.one_liner: The Fourier series of a signal can be viewed as a change of representation from time domain values to an infinite sequence of coefficients.
concepts.content:
It is useful to think of the **Fourier series** of a signal as a **change of representation** as shown in @fig-FourierSeries5_representation. Instead of representing the signal by the sequence of values specified by the original function $\ell(t)$, the same function can be represented by the infinite sequence of coefficients $a_n$. The coefficients $a_n$ give us an alternative description of the function $\ell(t)$ and the rest of this chapter will be devoted to understand what this **transformation** has to offer.

(see figure: Two representations for the ramp function. (left) Time domain. (right) Fourier domain with coefficients of the sine series.)
concepts.motivation_md: Viewing the Fourier series as a change of representation allows us to analyze signals in the frequency domain, offering insights and tools not evident in the time domain.
concepts.recap_md:
- Fourier series represent signals as infinite sequences of coefficients.
- This is a change from time domain values to frequency domain representation.
- The transformation provides alternative insights into signal properties.

concepts.title: continuous time sine wave
concepts.one_liner: A continuous time sine wave is defined as $s(t) = A \sin(w t - \theta)$ with amplitude $A$, frequency $w$, and phase $\theta$.
concepts.content:
The **continuous time sine wave** is
$$s\left(t\right) = A \sin\left(w ~t - \theta \right)$$ where $A$ is the **amplitude**, $w$ is the **frequency**, and $\theta$ is the **phase**. The wave signal is periodic with a period $T=2 \pi / w$.

[FIGURE:61cdacec6e8491fb | A graph of a continuous sine wave $s(t)$ plotted against time $t$. A horizontal double-headed arrow between two consecutive peaks is labeled 'Period', and a vertical double-headed arrow from the...]
concepts.motivation_md: Continuous time sine waves are fundamental building blocks for representing and analyzing periodic signals in many fields, including physics and engineering.
concepts.recap_md:
- A continuous time sine wave is given by $s(t) = A \sin(w t - \theta)$.
- $A$ is amplitude, $w$ is frequency, and $\theta$ is phase.
- The wave has period $T = 2\pi / w$.

$$s\left(t\right) = A \sin\left(w ~t - \theta \right)$$ where $A$ is the

concepts.title: Fourier Transform for Continuous Signals
concepts.one_liner: For infinite length signals defined on the continuous domain, the Fourier transform is defined as an integral transform with a continuous frequency variable $w$.
concepts.content:
The continuous domain is convenient when working with functions and operations that are not defined in the discrete domain. For instance, the derivative operator is well defined in the continuous domain but we can only approximate it in the discrete domain. Another example is when using the Gaussian distribution, which is defined as a continuous function. For this reason, sometimes some formulation is easier when done in the continuous domain.

For infinite length signals defined on the continuous domain, the Fourier transform is defined as:

$$\mathscr{L}(w) =  \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \ell(t) \exp{ \left( - j w t \right)} \, dt $$

where $\mathscr{L}(w)$ is a continuous function on the frequency $w$ (in radians). As before, this transform also has an inverse. The inverse Fourier transform is as follows:

$$\ell(t) = \frac{1}{2 \pi} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathscr{L}(w) \exp{ \left( j w t \right) } \, dw$$

Most of the properties that we have seen for the DFT also apply to the continuous domain, replacing sums with integrals.

The convolution between two continuous signals is defined as

$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}(t) =  \ell_1 \circ \ell_2 = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \ell_1 (t-t') \ell_2(t') \, d t'$$

Those definitions can be extended to 2D dimensions by making all the integrals double and integrating across the spatial variables $x$ and $y$. Although, in practice, images and filters will be discrete signals, many times it is convenient to think of them as continuous signals.
concepts.motivation_md: Continuous Fourier transforms allow analysis and operations on signals where derivatives and continuous distributions like Gaussian are naturally defined, enabling easier and more precise formulations than discrete approximations. (llm_inferred)
concepts.recap_md:
- The continuous Fourier transform uses integrals instead of sums for infinite length signals.
- The frequency variable $w$ is continuous and in radians.
- Convolution in continuous signals is defined by an integral over all time shifts.

concepts.title: Fourier Transform for Infinite Length Discrete Signals
concepts.one_liner: For discrete signals with infinite length, the Fourier transform is defined as an infinite sum with a continuous frequency variable $w$ and is periodic with period $2 \pi$.
concepts.content:
Another useful tool is the Fourier transform for discrete signals with infinite length. In this case, the sum becomes infinite, and by replacing $w = 2 \pi u / N$ in equation (@eq-fourier), we can write:

$$\mathscr{L}(w) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} \ell\left[n \right] \exp{(- j w n)}$$

The frequency $w$ is now a continuous variable. The Fourier transform $\mathscr{L}(w)$ is a periodic function with period $2 \pi$.

The inverse Fourier transform is

$$\ell\left[n \right] = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{2 \pi} \mathscr{L}(w) \exp{(j w n)} d w$$

where the integral is done only in one of the periods.
concepts.motivation_md: This transform extends Fourier analysis to infinite discrete signals, allowing frequency analysis with continuous frequency variables and periodic spectra. (llm_inferred)
concepts.recap_md:
- The infinite discrete Fourier transform sums over all integer indices $n$.
- The frequency variable $w$ is continuous and periodic with period $2\pi$.
- The inverse transform integrates over one period of $w$.

In this case, the sum becomes infinite, and by replacing $w = 2 \pi u / N$ in equation ( we can write: $$\mathscr{L}(w) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} \ell\left[n \right] \exp{(- j w n)}$$The frequency $w$ is now a continuous variable. The Fourier transform $\mathscr{L}(w)$ is a periodic function with period $2 \pi$.

concepts.one_liner: There are several Fourier transforms including discrete finite, continuous infinite, and discrete infinite length variants, each with corresponding forward and inverse formulas.

| Time Domain                       | FT                                                                                                 | FT$^{-1}$                                                                                          | Frequency Domain                  |

concepts.one_liner: The Fourier transform has been extensively used as an image representation, revealing explicit information about the picture.
concepts.content:
The Fourier transform has been extensively used as an image representation. In this section we will discuss the information about the picture that is made explicit by this representation.

As we discussed before, the Fourier transform of an image can be written in polar form:

$$\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]  = A \left[u,v \right] \, \exp{\left( j\, \theta\left[u,v \right]  \right)}$$

concepts.title: Decomposing the Fourier transform of a signal in its amplitude and phase

position.section_title: Fourier Analysis as an Image Representation

concepts.one_liner: Decomposing the Fourier transform into amplitude and phase reveals that phase carries location information while amplitude carries intensity scaling.
concepts.content:
Decomposing the Fourier transform of a signal in its amplitude and phase can be very useful. It has been a popular image representation during the early days of computer vision and image processing.

If we think in terms of the inverse of the Fourier transform, $A \left[u,v \right]$ gives the strength of the weight for each complex exponential and the phase $\theta \left[u,v \right]$ translates the complex exponential. The phase carries the information of where the image contours are by specifying how the phases of the sinusoids must line up in order to create the observed contours and edges. In fact, as shown in @sec-DFTproperties, translating the image in space only modifies the phase of its Fourier transform. In short, one can think that location information goes into the phase while intensity scaling goes into the magnitude.
concepts.motivation_md: Separating amplitude and phase helps understand how image features and spatial information are encoded in the Fourier transform, aiding image analysis. (llm_inferred)
concepts.recap_md:
- Amplitude indicates the strength of each frequency component.
- Phase encodes spatial location and contour information.
- Translating an image changes only the phase of its Fourier transform.

concepts.title: Phase dominance in image appearance

position.section_title: Fourier Analysis as an Image Representation

concepts.one_liner: The phase of the Fourier transform mostly determines the appearance of an image, more than the magnitude.
concepts.content:
One might ask which is more important in determining the appearance of the image, the magnitude of the Fourier transform, or its phase. @fig-phaseoramp shows the result of a classical experiment that consists of computing the Fourier transform for two images and building two new images by swapping their phases @Oppenheim1981.

(see figure: Swapping the amplitude and the phase of the Fourier Transform of two images. Each color channel is processed in the same way.)

The first output image is the inverse Fourier transform of the amplitude of the first input image and the phase of the DFT of the second input image. The second output image contains the other two terms. The figure shows that the appearance of the resulting images is mostly dominated by the phase of the image they come from. The image built with the phase of the stop sign looks like the stop sign even if the amplitude comes from a different image. @fig-phaseoramp shows the result in color by doing the same operation over each color channel (red, green, and blue) independently. The phase signal determines where the edges and colors are located in the resulting image. The final colors are altered as the amplitudes have changed.
concepts.motivation_md: This experiment illustrates that phase information is crucial in preserving image structure and appearance, highlighting the importance of phase in image processing. (llm_inferred)
concepts.recap_md:
- Swapping phases between images preserves the main visual structure.
- Phase determines edges and spatial layout.
- Amplitude affects color and intensity but not overall shape.

concepts.title: A remarkable property of natural images: the magnitude of their DFT

position.section_title: Fourier Analysis as an Image Representation

concepts.one_liner: Natural images typically have a DFT magnitude that peaks at the origin and decays inversely proportional to radial frequency.
concepts.content:
A remarkable property of natural images: the magnitude of their DFT generally has its maximum at the origin and decays inversely proportional to the radial frequency.

One remarkable property of real images is that the magnitude of the DFT of natural images is quite similar and can be approximated by $A \left[u,v \right] = a/ (u^2+v^2)^b$ with $a$ and $b$ being two constants. We will talk more about this property when discussing statistical models of natural images in @sec-stat_image_models. This typical structure of the DFT magnitude of natural images has been used as a prior for many tasks such as image denoising.
concepts.motivation_md: Recognizing the typical decay pattern of natural image spectra helps in modeling and processing images, such as in denoising and statistical analysis. (llm_inferred)
concepts.recap_md:
- Natural images have DFT magnitudes peaking at zero frequency.
- Magnitude decays roughly as $a/(u^2+v^2)^b$.
- This property is useful as a prior in image processing tasks.

concepts.title: The Perceptron: A Simple Model of a Single Neuron

position.section_title: The Perceptron: A Simple Model of a Single Neuron

concepts.one_liner: A perceptron is a neuron with $n$ inputs and one output that maps inputs to outputs according to a linear layer followed by a threshold activation function.
concepts.motivation_md: The perceptron models a single neuron that maps multiple inputs to a binary output, enabling simple classification tasks by applying a weighted sum followed by a threshold function.
concepts.recap_md:
- A perceptron maps $n$ inputs to one output using weights and bias.
- It computes a linear combination $z = \mathbf{w}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{x} + b$.
- The output $y$ is 1 if $z > 0$, else 0, acting as a threshold activation.

concepts.title: The Perceptron as a Classifier

position.section_title: The Perceptron: A Simple Model of a Single Neuron

concepts.one_liner: A perceptron with two inputs and one output acts as a classifier assigning class labels based on the sign of a weighted sum of inputs.
concepts.content:
People got excited about perceptrons in the late 1950s because it was shown that they can learn to classify data @rosenblatt1958perceptron. Let's see how that works. We will consider a perceptron with two inputs, $x_1$ and $x_2$, and one output, $y$. Let the incoming connection weights be $w_1 = 2$, $w_2 = 1$, and $b=0$. The values of $z$ and $y$, as a function of $x_1$ and $x_2$, are shown in @fig-neural_nets-perceptron_as_classifier.

(see figure: Value of hidden unit ($z$) and output unit ($y$) in a perceptron, as a function of the input data.)

Notice that $y$ takes on values 0 or 1, so you can think of this as a classifier that assigns a class label of 1 to the upper-right half of the plotted region.
concepts.motivation_md: The perceptron can classify data points into two classes by assigning outputs 0 or 1 based on a linear combination of inputs, enabling early neural network classification.
concepts.recap_md:
- Perceptrons classify data by outputting 0 or 1.
- With weights $w_1=2$, $w_2=1$, and $b=0$, the output separates the input space.
- The output $y=1$ corresponds to one side of the decision boundary.

concepts.title: Learning with a Perceptron

position.section_title: The Perceptron: A Simple Model of a Single Neuron

concepts.one_liner: Learning with a perceptron involves adjusting weights and bias to minimize classification loss over data, typically using general-purpose optimizers like gradient descent.
concepts.content:
So a perceptron acts like a classifier, but how can we use it to learn? The idea is that given data, $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$, we will adjust the weights $\mathbf{w}$ and the bias $b$, in order to minimize a classification loss, $\mathcal{L}$, that scores the number of misclassifications: 

$$\begin{aligned}    \mathbf{w}^*, b^* = \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{\mathbf{w}, b} \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{x}^{(i)} + b, y^{(i)})
\end{aligned}$$ 

In @fig-neural_nets-fitting_a_perceptron, this optimization process corresponds to shifting and rotating the **decision boundary**, until you find a line that separates data labeled as $y = 0$ from data labeled as $y = 1$.

(see figure: Different possible decision surfaces of a perceptron.)

You might be wondering, what's the exact optimization algorithm that will find the best line that separates the classes? The original perceptron paper proposed one particular algorithm, the "perceptron learning algorithm." This was an optimizer tailored to the specific structure of the perceptron. Older papers on neural nets are full of specific learning rules for specific architectures: the delta rule, the Rescorla-Wagner model, and so forth @rescorla1972theory. Nowadays we rarely use these special-purpose algorithms. Instead, we use *general-purpose* optimizers like gradient descent (for differentiable objectives) or zeroth-order methods (for nondifferentiable objectives). concepts.recap_md:
- Learning adjusts weights $\mathbf{w}$ and bias $b$ to minimize classification loss.
- The decision boundary shifts and rotates to separate classes.
- Modern learning uses general-purpose optimizers like gradient descent.

concepts.title: Multilayer Perceptrons
concepts.one_liner: Multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) are networks with multiple layers of perceptrons, using linear layers and nonlinear activation functions to produce multiple outputs.
concepts.content:
Perceptrons can solve linearly separable binary classification problems, but they are otherwise rather limited. For one, they only produce a single output. What if we want multiple outputs? We can achieve this by adding edges that fan out after the perceptron (@fig-neural_nets-fan_out).

(see figure: Multiple outputs fan out from a neuron.)

This network maps an input **layer** of data $\mathbf{x}$ to a layer of outputs **y**. The neurons in between inputs and outputs are called **hidden units**, shaded in gray. Here, $z$ is a hidden unit and $h$ is a hidden unit, that is, $h = g(z)$ where $g(\cdot)$ is an activation function like in @eq-neural_nets-perceptron_activation.

More commonly we might have many hidden units in stack, which we call a (@fig-neural_nets-MLP1).

(see figure: Mutilayer perceptron.)

How many layers does this net have? Some texts will say two [$\mathbf{W}_1$, $\mathbf{W}_2$], others three [$\mathbf{x}$, $\{\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{h}\}$, $\mathbf{y}$], others four [$\mathbf{x}$, $\mathbf{z}$, $\mathbf{h}$, $\mathbf{y}$]. We must get comfortable with the ambiguity.

Because this network has multiple layers of neurons, and because each neuron in this net acts as a perceptron, we call it a **multilayer perceptron** (**MLP**). The equation for this MLP is: 
$$\begin{aligned}    \mathbf{z} &= \mathbf{W}_1\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}_1 &\triangleleft \quad \text{linear layer}\\
    \mathbf{h} &= g(\mathbf{z}) &\triangleleft \quad \text{activation function}\\
    \mathbf{y} &= \mathbf{W}_2\mathbf{h} + \mathbf{b}_2 &\triangleleft \quad \text{linear layer}
\end{aligned}$$

In general, MLPs can be constructed with any number of layers following this pattern: linear layer, activation function, linear layer, activation function, and so on.

The activation function $g$ could be the threshold function like in @eq-neural_nets-perceptron_activation, but more generally it can be any pointwise nonlinearity, that is, $g(\mathbf{h}) = [\tilde{g}(h_1), \ldots, \tilde{g}(h_N)]$ and $\tilde{g}$ is any nonlinear function that maps $\mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$.

Beyond MLPs, this kind of sequence (linear layer, pointwise nonlinearity, linear layer, pointwise nonlinearity, and so on) is the prototypical motif in almost all neural networks, including most we will see later in this book.
concepts.motivation_md: MLPs extend perceptrons to multiple layers and outputs, enabling them to solve more complex, nonlinear problems by stacking linear transformations and nonlinear activations.
concepts.recap_md:
- MLPs have multiple layers including hidden units.
- Layers alternate linear transformations and nonlinear activations.
- Activation functions can be any pointwise nonlinearity, not just thresholds.

concepts.title: Activations Versus Parameters
concepts.one_liner: Activations are neuron output values representing data, while parameters are the learned weights and biases of the network.
concepts.content:
When working with deep nets it's useful to distinguish *activations* and *parameters*. The activations are the values that the neurons take on, $[\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z}_1, \mathbf{h}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{z}_{L-1}, \mathbf{h}_{L-1}, \mathbf{y}]$; slightly abusing notation, we use this term for both preactivation function neurons and postactivation function neurons. The activations are the neural representations of the data being processed. Often, we will not worry about distinguishing between inputs, hidden units, and outputs to the net, and simply refer to all data and neural activations in a network, layer by layer, as a sequence $[\mathbf{x}_0, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_L]$, in which case $\mathbf{x}_0$ is the raw input data

[FIGURE:e4b298598d24ed71 | A multilayer network is a sequence of transformations $f_1, \ldots, f_L$ that produce a series of activations $\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_L$.]

Conversely, parameters are the weights and biases of the network. These are the variables being learned. Both activations and parameters are tensors of variables.

Often we think of a layer as a function $\mathbf{x}_{l+1} = f_{l+1}(\mathbf{x}_l)$, but we can also make the parameters explicit and think of each layer as a function:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{x}_{l+1} = f_{l+1}(\mathbf{x}_{l}, \theta_{l+1})
\end{aligned}$$ 

That is, each layer takes the activations from the previous layer, as well as parameters of the current layer as input, and produces activations of the next layer. Varying either the input activations or the input parameters will affect the output of the layer. From this perspective, anything we can do with parameters, we can do with activations instead, and vice versa, and that is the basis for a lot of applications and tricks. For example, while normally we learn the values of the parameters, we could instead hold the parameters fixed and learn the values of the activations that achieve some objective. In fact, this is what is done in many methods such as network prompting, adversarial attacks, and network visualization, which we will see in more detail in later chapters.
concepts.motivation_md: Distinguishing activations and parameters clarifies their roles: activations represent processed data, while parameters define the network's learned transformations, enabling various learning and analysis techniques.
concepts.recap_md:
- Activations are neuron outputs representing data at each layer.
- Parameters are the learned weights and biases.
- Layers can be viewed as functions of activations and parameters.

concepts.title: Fast Activations and Slow Parameters
concepts.one_liner: Activations are fast functions of individual data points, while parameters are slow functions learned over entire datasets.
concepts.content:
So what's different about activations versus parameters? One way to think about it is that activations are *fast* functions of a data*point*: they are the result of a few layers of processing this datapoint. Parameters are *also* functions of the data (they are learned from data) but they are *slow* functions of data*sets*: the parameters are arrived at via an optimization procedure over a whole dataset. So, both activations and parameters are statistics of the data, that is, information extracted about about the data that organizes or summarizes it. The parameters are a kind of metasummary since they specify a functional transformation that produces activations from data, and activations themselves are a summary of the data.
@fig-neural_nets-params_vs_activations shows how this looks.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the difference between fast activations and slow parameters helps clarify how neural networks process individual data points quickly while learning parameters more slowly over datasets.
concepts.recap_md:
- Activations are fast functions of individual data points.
- Parameters are slow functions learned from entire datasets.
- Parameters define transformations producing activations.

concepts.title: Deep Nets
concepts.one_liner: Deep nets stack many layers of linear transformations and nonlinearities to perform complex nonlinear mappings.
concepts.content:
Deep nets are neural nets that stack the linear-nonlinear motif many times (@fig-deep_nets):

(see figure: Deep nets consist of linear layers interleaved with nonlinearities.)

Each layer is a function. Therefore, a deep net is a composition of many functions: 
$$\begin{aligned}
    f(\mathbf{x}) = f_{L}(f_{L-1}(\ldots f_2(f_1(\mathbf{x}))))
\end{aligned}$$

The $L$ is the number of layers in the net.

These functions are parameterized by weights $[\mathbf{W}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{W}_L]$ and biases $[\mathbf{b}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{b}_L]$. Some layers we will see later have other parameters. Collectively, we will refer to the concatenation of all the parameters in a deep net as $\theta$.

Deep nets are powerful because they can perform nonlinear mappings. In fact, a deep net with sufficiently many neurons can fit almost any desired function arbitrarily closely, a property we will investigate further in @sec-neural_nets-universal_approximation.

now let's make the two classes not linearly separable. Our new dataset is shown in @fig-neural_nets-nonseparable_dataset.

(see figure: Dataset that is not linearly separable.)

Here there is no line that can separate the zeros from the ones. Nonetheless, we will demonstrate a multilayer network that can solve this problem. The trick is to just add more layers! We will use the two layer MLP shown in @fig-neural_nets-simple_MLP_network.

(see figure: A simple MLP network.)

Consider using the following settings for $\mathbf{W}_1$ and $\mathbf{W}_2$: $$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{W}_1 = 
        \begin{bmatrix}
            1 & -1 \\
            2 & 1
        \end{bmatrix}
    ,\quad\quad
    \mathbf{W}_2 = 
        \begin{bmatrix}
            1 & -1
        \end{bmatrix}
\end{aligned}$$ The full net then performs the following operation:
$$\begin{aligned}
    z_1 &= x_1 - x_2, \quad z_2 = 2x_1 + x_2 &\triangleleft \quad \texttt{linear}\\
    h_1 &= \max(z_1,0), \quad h_2 = \max(z_2,0) &\triangleleft \quad \texttt{relu}\\
    z_3 &= h_1-h_2 &\triangleleft \quad \texttt{linear}\\
    y &= \mathbb{1}(z_3 > 0) &\triangleleft \quad \text{\texttt{threshold}}
\end{aligned}$$  


The $\mathbb{1}$ is the indicator function, which we define as: 
$$\begin{equation*}
    \mathbb{1}(x) = \begin{cases}
                1 & \text{if $x$ is true} \\
                0 & \text{otherwise}
             \end{cases}
\end{equation*}$$

Here we have introduced a new pointwise nonlinearity, the **Rectified linear unit** (**relu**), which is like a graded version of a threshold function, and has the advantage that it yields non-zero gradients over half its domain, thus being amenable to gradient-based learning.

We visualize the values that the neurons take on as a function of $x_1$ and $x_2$ in @fig-neural_nets-simple_MLP_network_values:

(see figure: Values of hidden units and output unit for the MLP shown in \fig{\ref{fig-neural_nets-simple_MLP_network}}.)

As can be seen in the rightmost plot, at the output $y$, this neural net successfully assigns a value of 1 to the region of the dataspace where the datapoints labeled as 1 live. This example demonstrates that is possible to solve nonlinear classification problems with a deep net. In practice, we would want to *learn* the parameter settings that achieve this classification. One way to do so would be to enumerate all possible parameter settings and pick one that successfully separates the zeros from the ones. This kind of exhaustive enumeration is a slow process, but don't worry, in @sec-backpropagation we will see how to speed things up using gradient descent. But it's worth remarking that enumeration is always a sufficient solution, at least when the possible parameter values form a finite set.
concepts.motivation_md: Deep nets enable solving complex nonlinear problems by stacking many layers of linear and nonlinear transformations, vastly increasing representational power.
concepts.recap_md:
- Deep nets compose many layers of linear and nonlinear functions.
- Parameters include weights and biases for each layer.
- Deep nets can approximate almost any function with enough neurons.

concepts.title: intrinsic images decomposition
concepts.one_liner: Decomposing an image into different physical causes is known as intrinsic images decomposition.
concepts.content: Decomposing an image into different physical causes is known as **intrinsic images decomposition**. The intrinsic image decomposition, proposed by Barrow and Tenenbaum [@Barrow1978], aims to recover intrinsic scene characteristics from images, such as occlusions, depth, surface normals, shading, reflectance, reflections, and so on.
concepts.motivation_md: Intrinsic images decomposition helps separate an image into its fundamental physical components, enabling better understanding and analysis of scene properties like shading and reflectance.
concepts.recap_md:
- Intrinsic images decomposition separates an image into physical causes.
- It recovers intrinsic scene characteristics like shading and reflectance.
- Proposed by Barrow and Tenenbaum in 1978.

concepts.title: Concluding Remarks
concepts.one_liner: Image derivatives (first order, second order, and the Laplacian) provide a powerful image representation used in applications such as image inpainting and explaining visual illusions.
concepts.content: In this chapter we have covered a very powerful image representation: image derivatives (first order, second order, and the Laplacian) and their discrete approximations. Despite the simplicity of this representation, we have seen that it can be used in a number of applications such as image inpainting, separation of illumination and reflectance, and it can be used to explain simple visual illusions. It is not surprising that similar filters like the ones we have seen in this chapter emerge in convolutional neural networks when trained to solve visual tasks.
concepts.motivation_md: Image derivatives provide a simple yet powerful way to analyze images, enabling tasks like inpainting and understanding visual illusions, and they connect to modern neural network filters.
concepts.recap_md:
- Image derivatives include first order, second order, and Laplacian.
- They enable applications like image inpainting and illumination separation.
- Similar filters appear in convolutional neural networks for vision tasks.

concepts.title: constant brightness assumption
concepts.one_liner: The constant brightness assumption states that the brightness of pixels does not change while the scene is moving.
concepts.content:
We use continuous values for $x$, $y$, and $t$, and continuous images, $\ell _0(x,y)$, because it allows us to deal with any velocity values. This function also assumes that the brightness of the pixels does not change while the scene is moving (**constant brightness assumption**).

The constant brightness assumption is the initial hypothesis of most motion estimation algorithms. We will devote multiple chapters in [Part Understanding Geometry](/part_understanding_geometry.html)  to study motion in depth.
concepts.motivation_md: The constant brightness assumption simplifies motion estimation by assuming pixel brightness remains unchanged during movement, enabling analysis of velocity and motion.
concepts.recap_md:
- Assumes pixel brightness remains constant during motion.
- Uses continuous spatial and temporal variables for velocity handling.
- Basis for most motion estimation algorithms.

concepts.title: Modeling sequences in the Fourier domain

position.section_title: Modeling sequences in the Fourier domain

concepts.one_liner: The Fourier transform of a globally moving image equals the product of the static image's 2D FT and a delta wall defined by the motion parameters.
concepts.content:
## Modeling sequences in the Fourier domain

The FT of a globally moving image is (using the shift property):
$$
\mathscr{L} (w_x,w_y,w_t) = \mathscr{L}_0 (w_x, w_y) \delta (w_t + v_x w_x + v_y w_y)
$$
The continuous FT of the sequence is equal to the product of the 2D FT of the static image $\ell _0(x,y)$ and a delta wall. To better understand this function, let's look at a simple example in only one spatial dimension, as shown in @fig-mov_pulse_012.

(see figure: Fig (a) A sequence with one spatial dimension showing a static rectangular pulse. b) The rectangular pulse moves to the left at a speed $v=-0.5$ and c) moving towards the left, $v=-1$. As we work...)

@fig-mov_pulse_012 shows the FT for a sequence with one spatial dimension, $\ell (x,t)$, that contains a blurry rectangular pulse moving at three different speeds towards the left. @fig-mov_pulse_012 (a) shows a sequence when the pulse is static, and @fig-mov_pulse_012 (d) shows its FT. Across the spatial frequency $w_x$, the FT is approximately a sinc function. 

Across the temporal frequency $w_t$, as the signal is constant, its FT is a delta function. Therefore, the FT is a sinc function contained inside a delta wall in the line $w_t=0$. @fig-mov_pulse_012 (b) shows the same rectangular pulse moving towards the left, $v_x=0.5$. @fig-mov_pulse_012 (e) shows the sinc function but skewed along the frequency line $w_t+0.5w_x=0$. concepts.title: Temporal filters
concepts.one_liner: Temporal filters are spatio-temporal convolutions characterized by causality, with causal, non-causal, and anti-causal types.
concepts.content:
## Temporal filters

Linear spatio-temporal filters can be written as spatio-temporal convolutions between the input sequence and a convolutional kernel (impulse response). Discrete spatiotemporal filters have an impulse response $h \left[n,m,t \right]$. The extension from 2D filters to spatio-temporal filters does not have any additional complications. We can also classify filters as low-pass, high-pass, etc. But in the case of time, there is another attribute used to characterize filters: causality.

- **Causal filters**: These are filters with output variations that only depend on the past values of the input. This puts the following constraint: $h \left[n,m,t \right]=0$ for all $t<0$. This means that if the input is an impulse at $t=0$, the output will only have non-zero values for $t>0$. If this condition is satisfied, then the filter output will only depend on the input's past for all possible inputs.
- **Non-causal filters**: When the output has a dependency on future inputs.
- **Anti-causal filters**: This is the opposite, when the output only depends on the future: $h \left[n,m,t \right]=0$ for all $t>0$.

Many filters are non-causal and have both causal and anti-causal components (e.g., a Gaussian filter). Note that non-causal filters cannot be implemented in practice and, therefore, any filter with an anti-causal component will have to be approximated by a purely causal filter by bounding the temporal support and shifting in time the impulse response.

In this chapter, we have written all the filters as convolutions. However, some filters are better described as difference equations (this is especially important in time). An example of a difference equation is:
$$
\ell _{out} \left[n,m,t \right] = \ell _{in} \left[n,m,t \right] + \alpha \, \ell _{out} \left[n,m,t-1 \right]
$$
where the output $g$ at time $t$ depends on the input at time $t$ and the output at the previous time instant $t-1$ multiplied by a constant $\alpha$. We can easily evaluate the impulse response, $h \left[n,m,t \right]$, of such a filter by replacing $\ell \left[n,m,t \right]$ with an impulse, $\delta \left[n,m,t \right]$. The impulse response is:
$$
h \left[n,m,t \right] = \alpha^t  \delta \left[n,m \right] u \left[t \right]
$$
where $u\left[t \right]$, called the Heaviside step function, is:
$$
u \left[t \right] = \begin{cases}
    0     & \quad \text{if }  t <0 \\
    1     & \quad \text{otherwise }\\
\end{cases}
$$

The Heaviside step function, $u \left[t\right]$, is an infinite length function with the form

[FIGURE:3bdfa12be361a5d6 | A discrete-time stem plot of the unit step function $u[t)$. For integer values $t < 0$, the signal is zero, and for $t \ge 0$, the signal is constant at 1. The plot shows blue dots at $t = -5, -4...]

Most filters described by difference equations have an impulse response with infinite support. They are called IIR (Infinite Impulse Response) filters. IIR filters can be further classified as stable and unstable. Stable filters are the ones that given a bounded input, $| \ell _{in} \left[n,m,t \right] |<A$, produce a bounded output, $| \ell _{out} \left[n,m,t \right] | <B$. For this to happen, the impulse response has to be bounded. In unstable filters, the amplitude of the impulse response diverges to infinity. In the previous example, the filter is stable if and only if $| \alpha | < 1$.

Let's now describe some spatio-temporal filters.

- Temporal filters are spatio-temporal convolutions with impulse response $h[n,m,t]$.
- Causal filters depend only on past inputs; non-causal depend on future inputs.
- Difference equations describe some filters; stable IIR filters have bounded impulse responses.

concepts.title: rectangular sampling
concepts.one_liner: If $a=T,b=0,c=0,d=T$, then we will have a regular rectangular sampling.
concepts.content:
$$
\ell_s [n,m] = \ell (an+bm, cn+dm)
$$

where $a,b,c,d$ are constants. For instance, if $a=T,b=0,c=0,d=T$, then we will have a regular **rectangular sampling**. But we could have other patterns. We can also place the samples at random locations (**irregular sampling**). @fig-sampling_grids shows different sampling patterns.
