concepts.title: Steering Theorem
concepts.one_liner: The steering condition is the requirement that the rotated filter be a linear combination of a set of basis filters that are rotated versions of itself.
concepts.content:
Let's consider a filter with impulse response $h(x,y)$. For convenience, it is better to write the filter response in polar coordinates, $h(r,\phi)$. The steering condition is the requirement that the rotated filter, $h(r,\phi - \theta)$, be a linear combination of a set of basis filters that are rotated versions of itself, $h(r,\phi - \theta_m)$ with $m \in (1,M)$. The steering condition is:
$$h(r,\phi - \theta) = \sum_{m=1}^{M} k_{m}(\theta) h(r,\phi - \theta_m) .$$

If we express the filter to be steered as a Fourier series in angle (using complex exponentials for notational convenience), we have
$$h(r,\phi) = \sum_{n=-N}^{N} a_n(r) \exp \left( j n \phi \right)$$

Substituting this Fourier series into the steering condition, we obtain an equation for the interpolation functions $k_{j}(\theta)$. The steering condition holds for functions expandable in this Fourier form if and only if the interpolation functions $k_{j}(\theta)$ satisfy:

$$\left[
\begin{array}{c}
1 \\
\exp (j \theta) \\
\ldots \\
\exp (j N \theta) \\
\end{array}
\right]
=
\left[ 
\begin{array}{cccc}
1 & 1 & \ldots & 1 \\
\exp (j \theta_{1}) & \exp (j \theta_{2}) & \ldots & \exp (j \theta_{M}) \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\
\exp (j N \theta_{1}) & \exp (j N \theta_{2}) & \ldots & \exp (j N \theta_{M})
\end{array}
\right]
\left[
\begin{array}{c}
k_{1}(\theta) \\ k_{2}(\theta) \\ \vdots \\ k_{M}(\theta) 
\end{array}
\right].$$
concepts.motivation_md: Steering theorems quantify how many basis filters are needed to synthesize any rotated version of a filter, depending on its orientation sharpness.
concepts.recap_md:
- The steering condition requires rotated filters to be linear combinations of basis filters.
- Filters can be expressed as Fourier series in angle to analyze steering.
- Interpolation functions $k_j(\theta)$ solve a matrix equation derived from the Fourier expansion.

key_passage.text:
The steering condition is the requirement that the rotated filter, $h(r,\phi - \theta)$, be a linear combination of a set of basis filters that are rotated versions of itself, $h(r,\phi - \theta_m)$ with $m \in (1,M)$. The steering condition is:
$$h(r,\phi - \theta) = \sum_{m=1}^{M} k_{m}(\theta) h(r,\phi - \theta_m) .$$

motivation.text: You could imagine that will depend on how sharply oriented the filter is. A circularly symmetric filter takes just one basis function to synthesize all other orientation responses, and a very narrow filter will take quite a few. This is quantified by steering theorems.

question.text: Let's make the previous observation more precise and general. How many basis filters does it take to steer any given filter?

concepts.title: Steerable Quadrature Pairs
concepts.one_liner: Steerable-quadrature filters allow for arbitrary shifts both in orientation and in phase.
concepts.content:
As in the case of Gabor filters, it is useful to build quadrature pairs of steerable filters. Steerable-quadrature filters allow for arbitrary shifts both in orientation and in phase. We can design such filters. For instance, consider the second-order derivatives of a Gaussian with $\sigma^2=1/2$ and normalized so that the integral over all the space of its squared magnitude equals 1:

$$\begin{split}
g_{xx}(x,y) &= 0.9213(2x^2-1) \exp \left(-(x^2+y^2) \right) \\
g_{xy}(x,y) &= 1.843 (x y) \exp \left(-(x^2+y^2) \right) \\
g_{yy}(x,y) &= 0.9213(2y^2-1) \exp \left(-(x^2+y^2) \right)
\end{split}$$

It is possible to get a good approximation to its Hilbert transform using a Gaussian times a third-order odd polynomial. The approximation to the Hilbert transform of $g_{xx}(x,y)$ is:

$$h_{xx}(x,y) = -0.9780 (-2.254 x+x^3) \exp \left(-(x^2+y^2) \right)$$

Here, $g_{xx}(x,y)$ and its Hilbert transform $h_{xx}(x,y)$ have the same spectral content but opposite phase. The figure @fig-steerg2h2 analyzes the quality of the approximation. It shows the quadrature pair, $g_{xx}$ and $h_{xx}$, sampled in space and cropped into a window of $13\times13$ pixels, and its Fourier transform. The DFT is computed by zero padding to $256\times256$ pixels. In @fig-steerg2h2 (a), $g_{xx}$ is the even phase, and in (b) $h_{xx}$ is the odd phase. (c) illustrates that the sum of their squares reveals the square of their Gaussian envelopes. (d) illustrates a section of the magnitude of their Fourier transforms along the $u$ axis for $v=0$. The $h_{xx}$ is a sampled third-order polynomial approximation to the Hilbert transform of $g_{xx}$, so their power spectra may not be exactly the same. The blue line shows the magnitude of the analytic filter $g_{xx}+jh_{xx}$. It has double amplitude, and the content for negative frequencies is close to zero.

![Quadrature pair, $g_{xx} \left[n,m \right]$ and $h_{xx} \left[n,m \right]$. The filters are sampled in space and cropped into a window of $13\times13$ pixels.](figures/spatial_filter_sets/steer_quad_aprox_a.png){width=100% #fig-steerg2h2}
concepts.motivation_md: Steerable quadrature pairs enable flexible filtering with arbitrary orientation and phase shifts, useful for signal analysis.
concepts.recap_md:
- Steerable-quadrature filters allow arbitrary orientation and phase shifts.
- Second-order Gaussian derivatives can form such pairs.
- Hilbert transform approximations provide the quadrature (odd) phase filter.

concepts.title: basis functions for steerability
concepts.one_liner: To steer $h_{xx}(x,y)$ to an angle $\theta$, this approximation requires four basis functions, not just three as for the second-order derivative of a Gaussian.
concepts.content:
To steer $h_{xx}(x,y)$ to an angle $\theta$, this approximation requires four basis functions, and not just three as for the second-order derivative of a Gaussian. The other three functions needed are:

$$\begin{split}
h_2(x,y) &= -0.9780(-0.7515+x^2) y \exp \left(-(x^2+y^2) \right) \\
h_3(x,y) &= -0.9780(-0.7515+y^2) x \exp \left(-(x^2+y^2) \right) \\
h_4(x,y) &= -0.9780 (-2.254 y+y^3) \exp \left(-(x^2+y^2) \right) 
\end{split}$$
concepts.motivation_md: More basis functions are needed to steer certain filters accurately, reflecting their complexity beyond simple Gaussian derivatives.
concepts.recap_md:
- Steering $h_{xx}(x,y)$ requires four basis functions.
- This is more than the three needed for second-order Gaussian derivatives.
- The additional basis functions involve polynomial terms multiplied by Gaussians.

key_passage.text: To steer $h_{xx}(x,y)$ to an angle $\theta$, this approximation requires four basis functions, and not just three as for the second-order derivative of a Gaussian.

The other three functions needed are:
$$\begin{split}

h_3(x,y) &= -0.9780(-0.7515+y^2) x \exp \left(-(x^2+y^2) \right) \\
h_4(x,y) &= -0.9780 (-2.254 y+y^3) \exp \left(-(x^2+y^2) \right) \end{split}$$

concepts.title: The basis function for steerability are not unique
concepts.one_liner: The basis functions for steerability are not unique; different sets can span the same space of rotated filters.
concepts.motivation_md: Different basis sets can represent the same steerable filter space, offering flexibility in design and optimization.
concepts.recap_md:
- Basis functions for steerability are not unique.
- Separable and non-separable bases can span the same filter space.
- Spatial scaling affects the filter parameter $\sigma$.

key_passage.text: The basis function for steerability are not unique.

example.text: For instance, figures (a and c) show two basis functions that span all rotations of $g_{xx}$. (a) has separable filters corresponding to $g_{xx}$, $g_{xy}$ and $g_{yy}$, and (c) shows three rotated versions of $g_{xx}$ at 0, 60, and 120 degrees. (c) is a non-separable basis spanning the same space as the filters of (a). Figures (b and d) show two basis functions that span all rotations on $h_{xx}$ spanning the same space as the filters of (b).

concepts.title: oriented energy as a function of angle
concepts.one_liner: Oriented energy as a function of angle can be computed from the squared sum of steerable quadrature pair filter responses.
concepts.content:
Putting it all together, we can compute oriented energy as a function of angle, for all angles, just from the seven basis filter responses shown in @fig-steer_quad_basis.

$$E(x,y,\theta) = g_{xx}(x,y,\theta)^2 + h_{xx}(x,y,\theta)^2$$

concepts.title: Cross terms in oriented energy from multiple oriented structures
concepts.one_liner: Cross terms arise in oriented energy when multiple oriented structures interact within the filter passband.
concepts.content: When there are two oriented structures within the passband of the quadrature pair filters, the sum of the energies of the individual structures is not the same as the energy of the sum of the structures. Because we're squaring to find the energies, the combination of multiple structures isn't linear. As @fig-multioriflorets (a) shows, when there are two oriented structures within the passband, squaring the filter responses causes the convolution in the Fourier domain to pick up extra cross-terms from the interaction between the structures, in addition to the desired terms from squaring each frequency response individually within the passband. These cross terms appear as spurious spatial frequencies in the energy term, and we can eliminate them by spatially low-pass filtering the squared oriented energy responses. Using the blurred squared basis filter responses, we get much cleaner oriented energy as a function of angle plots, even with the $g_{xx}$, $h_{xx}$ filters in the junctions, as shown in @fig-multioriflorets (b).
concepts.motivation_md: Cross terms complicate oriented energy measurements when multiple structures overlap; low-pass filtering helps clean the energy response.
concepts.recap_md:
- Multiple oriented structures cause cross terms in energy.
- Squaring filter responses introduces nonlinear interactions.
- Spatial low-pass filtering reduces spurious cross terms.

concepts.title: Gaussian Filter
concepts.one_liner: One of the important blurring (low-pass) filters in computer vision is the Gaussian filter.
concepts.content: One of the important blurring (low-pass) filters in computer vision is the Gaussian filter. The Gaussian filter is important because it is a good model for many naturally occurring filters. It also has several properties, as we will discuss here, that make it unique.
concepts.motivation_md: The Gaussian filter is widely used because it models many natural blurring processes and has unique mathematical properties that make it effective for image processing tasks.
concepts.recap_md:
- The Gaussian filter is a key low-pass filter in computer vision.
- It models many naturally occurring filters well.
- It has unique properties that distinguish it from other filters.

key_passage.text: One of the important blurring (low-pass) filters in computer vision is the Gaussian filter.

motivation.text: The Gaussian filter is important because it is a good model for many naturally occurring filters.

concepts.title: Gaussian distribution
concepts.one_liner: The Gaussian distribution is defined in continuous variables.
concepts.content:
The Gaussian distribution is defined in continuous variables. In one dimension:

$$
g(x; \sigma) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^2}} \exp{ \left( -\frac{x^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right) }
$$

and in two dimensions:

$$
g(x,y; \sigma) = \frac{1}{2 \pi \sigma^2} \exp{ \left(-\frac{x^2 + y^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right) }
$$
concepts.motivation_md: The Gaussian distribution models many natural phenomena and forms the basis for the Gaussian filter used in image processing.
concepts.recap_md:
- Gaussian distribution is defined continuously in 1D and 2D.
- 1D formula involves $\exp(-x^2/(2\sigma^2))$ normalized by $1/\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}$.
- 2D formula extends this with $x^2 + y^2$ in the exponent and normalization $1/(2\pi\sigma^2)$.

concepts.title: Discretization
concepts.one_liner: In practice, we only need to consider samples within three standard deviations $x \in (-3\sigma, 3\sigma)$ for the discrete Gaussian filter.
concepts.content:
In order to use the Gaussian filter in practice, we need to consider discrete locations and approximate the function by a finite support function. In practice, we only consider samples within three standard deviations $x \in (-3\sigma, 3\sigma)$ because at $3\sigma$, the amplitude of the Gaussian filter is around 1 percent of its central value. Many properties of the Gaussian filter discussed later are only true in the continuous domain and are only approximated in the discrete form.

For a given standard deviation parameter $\sigma$, the discretized Gaussian kernel is $g \left[n, m; \sigma \right]$:

$$
g \left[ n,m; \sigma \right] = \exp{ \left( -\frac{n^2 + m^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right) }
$$

1D Gaussian with $\sigma=1$ and its discretized version:

[FIGURE:750fb1caf06dd3e4 | A discrete stem plot of a 1D Gaussian function $g[n)$ centered at $n=0$. The plot shows blue dots at integer values from $n=-4$ to $n=4$, with a peak value of 1 at $n=0$ and values decreasing...]
concepts.motivation_md: Discretization is necessary to implement the Gaussian filter on digital images, approximating the continuous function with finite samples while maintaining key properties as closely as possible.
concepts.recap_md:
- Discretize Gaussian filter by sampling within $\pm 3\sigma$.
- Discrete Gaussian kernel: $g[n,m;\sigma] = \exp\left(-\frac{n^2+m^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)$.
- Many continuous properties only approximately hold for discrete versions.

key_passage.text: In order to use this filter in practice, we need to consider discrete locations and also approximate the function by a finite support function. In practice, we only need to consider samples within three standard deviations $x \in (-3\sigma, 3\sigma)$. At $3\sigma$, the amplitude of the Gaussian filter is around 1 percent of its central value.

motivation.text: Unfortunately, many of the properties of the Gaussian filter that we will discuss later are only true in the continuous domain and are only approximated when using its discrete form.

concepts.title: Properties of the Continuous Gaussian
concepts.one_liner: The continuous Gaussian has unique properties such as separability, its Fourier transform being Gaussian, and convolution of Gaussians resulting in another Gaussian.
concepts.content:
Here are some key properties of the Gaussian filter:

- The $n$-dimensional Gaussian is the only completely circularly symmetric operator that is separable.

- The continuous Fourier transform (FT) of a Gaussian is also a Gaussian. For a 1D Gaussian, its Fourier transform is:

$$
G (w; \sigma) = \exp{ \left( -\frac{w^2 \sigma^2} {2} \right) }
$$

and in 2D the Fourier transform is:

$$
G (w_x, w_y; \sigma) = \exp{ \left(- \frac{(w_x^2+w_y^2) \sigma^2} {2} \right) }
$$

Note that this function is monotonically decreasing in magnitude for increasing frequencies, and it is also radially symmetric.

- The width of the Gaussian Fourier transform decreases with $\sigma$ (this is the opposite behavior to the Gaussian in the spatial domain).

- The convolution of two $n$-dimensional Gaussians is an $n$-dimensional Gaussian:

$$
g (x,y; \sigma_1 ) \circ g (x,y; \sigma_2)  = g (x,y; \sigma_3)
$$

where the variance of the result is the sum $\sigma_3^2 = \sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2$. This property is the basis of the Gaussian pyramid.

- The Gaussian is the solution to the heat equation.

- Repeated convolutions of any function concentrated in the origin result in a Gaussian (central limit theorem).

- In the limit $\sigma \rightarrow 0$ the Gaussian becomes an impulse.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding these properties explains why the Gaussian filter is fundamental in image processing and signal analysis, enabling efficient and mathematically tractable operations.
concepts.recap_md:
- Gaussian is the only circularly symmetric separable operator.
- Its Fourier transform is also Gaussian and radially symmetric.
- Convolution of Gaussians sums variances: $\sigma_3^2 = \sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2$.
- Gaussian solves the heat equation and converges to an impulse as $\sigma \to 0$.

key_passage.text:

The continuous Fourier transform (FT) of a Gaussian is also a Gaussian.
The convolution of two $n$-dimensional Gaussians is an $n$-dimensional Gaussian.
The Gaussian is the solution to the heat equation.
Repeated convolutions of any function concentrated in the origin result in a Gaussian (central limit theorem).
In the limit $\sigma \rightarrow 0$ the Gaussian becomes an impulse.

motivation.text: This is a remarkable property of Gaussian filters and is the basis of the Gaussian pyramid that we will see later in

concepts.title: Limitations
concepts.one_liner: Many properties of the continuous Gaussian do not hold exactly for its discrete approximation obtained by sampling.
concepts.content:
Many properties are only true for the continuous Gaussian and do not hold for its discrete approximation $g\left[n,m;\sigma \right]$ obtained by sampling the Gaussian at discrete locations. For example, consider a 1D Gaussian with variance $\sigma^2=1/2$ approximated by five samples, called $g_5$, with values:

$$
g_5\left[ n \right] = \left[0.0183, \; 0.3679, \; 1.0000, \; 0.3679, \; 0.0183 \right] 
$$

If you compute the approximation for $\sigma^2=1$ by discretizing the Gaussian, the result is not equal to $g_5 \circ g_5$. Thus, successive convolutions of discretized Gaussians accumulate errors and the convolution is not exactly Gaussian anymore.

Also, the convolution of $g_5\left[ n \right]$ with the wave $\left[1,-1,1,-1,...\right]$ is not zero, unlike the continuous case. This is expected from the Fourier transform of the Gaussian. While not a strong limitation in many applications, it matters when completely canceling highest frequencies, such as in antialiasing.

The next low-pass filter addresses these limitations of the box and Gaussian filters.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept highlights the practical limitations of discrete Gaussian filters, motivating the search for better discrete approximations with desirable properties.
concepts.recap_md:
- Discrete Gaussian approximations do not preserve all continuous properties.
- Convolution of discrete Gaussians accumulates errors and is not exactly Gaussian.
- Some frequency cancellation properties fail in discrete case, important for antialiasing.

key_passage.text: However, many of these properties are only true for the continuous version of the Gaussian and do not work for its discrete approximation $g\left[n,m;\sigma \right]$ obtained by directly sampling the values of the Gaussian at discrete locations.

motivation.text: Therefore, as you apply successive convolutions of discretized Gaussians the errors will accumulate. That is, the convolution of discretized Gaussians is not a Gaussian anymore.

example.text:
Let's consider a Gaussian with variance $\sigma^2=1/2$. It can be approximated by five samples. We will call this approximation $g_5$ and it takes the values: $$
g_5\left[ n \right] = \left[0.0183, \, 0.3679, \, 1.0000, \, 0.3679, \, 0.0183 \right] $$ You can check that if you compute the approximation for $\sigma^2=1$ by discretizing the Gaussian, the result obtained is not equal to doing $g_5 \circ g_5$.

concepts.title: Binomial Filters
concepts.one_liner: Binomial filters are efficient discrete approximations to the Gaussian filter using binomial coefficients.
concepts.content:
In practice, there are very efficient discrete approximations to the Gaussian filter that, for certain $\sigma$ values, have nicer properties than discretized Gaussians. One common approximation uses binomial coefficients [@Chehikian91]. Binomial filters are obtained by successive convolutions of the box filter $\left[1,1\right]$.

The binomial coefficients use the central limit theorem to approximate a Gaussian as successive convolutions of a very simple function. The binomial coefficients form the Pascal's triangle as shown in @fig-pascaltriangle.
concepts.motivation_md: Binomial filters provide a computationally efficient and mathematically sound discrete approximation to the Gaussian filter, improving on direct discretization.
concepts.recap_md:
- Binomial filters approximate Gaussian filters efficiently.
- They are formed by successive convolutions of $[1,1]$.
- Binomial coefficients relate to Pascal's triangle.

key_passage.text: One common approximation of the Gaussian filter is to use **binomial coefficients**. Binomial filters are obtained by successive convolutions of the box filter \left[1,1\right].

motivation.text: In practice, there are very efficient discrete approximations to the Gaussian filter that, for certain $\sigma$ values, have nicer properties than when working with discretized Gaussians.

concepts.one_liner: The binomial coefficients form the Pascal's triangle.

concepts.recap_md:

motivation.text: Binomial coefficients. To build the Pascal's triangle, each number is the sum of the number above to the left and the one above to the right.

concepts.title: Properties
concepts.one_liner: Binomial coefficients provide a compact integer approximation to Gaussian coefficients with useful convolution and frequency properties.
concepts.content:
- Binomial coefficients provide a compact approximation of the Gaussian coefficients using only integers. Note that the values of $b_2$ differ from $g_5$ despite both approximating a Gaussian with variance $\sigma^2 = 1/2$. The variance of $g_5$ is not exactly $1/2$ despite being obtained by discretizing a Gaussian with that variance.

- The sum of all coefficients (DC gain) for each binomial filter $b_n$ is $2^n$, and their spatial variance is $\sigma^2 = n/4$.

- One remarkable property is that $b_n \circ b_m = b_{n+m}$, so $\sigma_n^2 + \sigma_m^2 = \sigma_{n+m}^2$, analogous to the continuous Gaussian property. The convolution of two binomial filters is another binomial filter.

- The simplest Gaussian approximation is the 3-tap binomial kernel:

$$
b_2 = \left[1, 2, 1\right] 
$$

This filter is even (no translation when applied) and its discrete Fourier transform (DFT) is:

$$
B_2 \left[u\right] = 2+2 \cos (2 \pi u/N)
$$

The frequency gain decreases monotonically with spatial frequency $u$ and becomes zero at the highest frequency, $G_3 \left[ 10 \right]=0$.

(see figure: 1D Binomial Filter.)

(see figure: Fourier Transform of Binomial Filter.)

Fig (a) A one-dimensional three-tap approximation to the Gaussian filter ($\left[1,2,1\right]$) and, (b) its Fourier transform for $N=20$ samples.

- All even binomial filters can be written as successive convolutions with $\left[1,2,1\right]$. Their Fourier transform is a power of that filter's transform and is monotonic:

$$
B_{2n} \left[u\right] = (2+2 \cos (2 \pi u/N))^n
$$

The filter transfer function $B_{2n}$ is real, positive, and a zero-phase filter.

- For all binomial filters $b_n$, convolution with the wave $\left[1,-1,1,-1,...\right]$ yields the zero signal $\left[0,0,0,0,...\right]$. This property is useful for downsampling images.
concepts.motivation_md: These properties make binomial filters practical and mathematically elegant discrete approximations to Gaussian filters, with benefits in convolution behavior and frequency response.
concepts.recap_md:
- Binomial filters approximate Gaussian coefficients using integers.
- Convolution adds indices: $b_n \circ b_m = b_{n+m}$.
- The 3-tap binomial filter $[1,2,1]$ has monotonic frequency response.
- Even binomial filters are powers of the 3-tap filter's transform.
- Convolution with alternating wave yields zero signal.

key_passage.text: Binomial coefficients provide a compact approximation of the Gaussian coefficients using only integers. The sum of all the coefficients (DC gain) for each binomial filter $b_n$ is $2^n$, and their spatial variance is $\sigma^2 = n/4$. One remarkable property of the binomial filters is that $b_n \circ b_m = b_{n+m}$, and, therefore, $\sigma_n^2 + \sigma_m^2 = \sigma_{n+m}^2$, which is analogous to the Gaussian property in the continuous domain.

motivation.text: Binomial coefficients provide a compact approximation of the Gaussian coefficients using only integers.

example.text:
The simplest approximation to the Gaussian filter is the 3-tap binomial kernel: $$
b_2 = \left[1, 2, 1\right] $$ This filter is interesting because it is even (so it can be applied to an image without producing any translation) and its discrete Fourier transform (DFT) is: $$
B_2 \left[u\right] = 2+2 \cos (2 \pi u/N)
$$ The frequency gain is shown in Fig (b). The gain decreases monotonically (there are no ripples) with spatial frequency, $u$, and it becomes zero at the highest frequency, $G_3 \left[ 10 \right]=0$.

concepts.title: difference equations for filters
concepts.one_liner: Some filters are better described as difference equations, where the output at time $t$ depends on the input and output at previous times, leading to infinite impulse response (IIR) filters.
concepts.content:
In this chapter, we have written all the filters as convolutions. However, some filters are better described as difference equations (this is especially important in time). An example of a difference equation is:
$$
\ell _{out} \left[n,m,t \right] = \ell _{in} \left[n,m,t \right] + \alpha \, \ell _{out} \left[n,m,t-1 \right]
$$
where the output $g$ at time $t$ depends on the input at time $t$ and the output at the previous time instant $t-1$ multiplied by a constant $\alpha$. We can easily evaluate the impulse response, $h \left[n,m,t \right]$, of such a filter by replacing $\ell \left[n,m,t \right]$ with an impulse, $\delta \left[n,m,t \right]$. The impulse response is:
$$
h \left[n,m,t \right] = \alpha^t  \delta \left[n,m \right] u \left[t \right]
$$
where $u\left[t \right]$, called the Heaviside step function, is:
$$
u \left[t \right] = \begin{cases}
    0     & \quad \text{if }  t <0 \\
    1     & \quad \text{otherwise }\\
\end{cases}
$$

The Heaviside step function, $u \left[t\right]$, is an infinite length function with the form

[FIGURE:3bdfa12be361a5d6 | A discrete-time stem plot of the unit step function $u[t)$. For integer values $t < 0$, the signal is zero, and for $t \ge 0$, the signal is constant at 1. The plot shows blue dots at $t = -5, -4...]

Most filters described by difference equations have an impulse response with infinite support. They are called IIR (Infinite Impulse Response) filters. IIR filters can be further classified as stable and unstable. Stable filters are the ones that given a bounded input, $| \ell _{in} \left[n,m,t \right] |<A$, produce a bounded output, $| \ell _{out} \left[n,m,t \right] | <B$. For this to happen, the impulse response has to be bounded. In unstable filters, the amplitude of the impulse response diverges to infinity. In the previous example, the filter is stable if and only if $| \alpha | < 1$.

Let's now describe some spatio-temporal filters.

- Impulse response of such filters often has infinite support, called IIR filters.
- Stability requires bounded impulse response; for example, $|\alpha|<1$ ensures stability.

concepts.title: Spatiotemporal Gaussian
concepts.one_liner: The spatiotemporal Gaussian filter extends the spatial Gaussian by incorporating temporal width, allowing efficient 3D separable convolution for video smoothing.
concepts.content:
As with the spatial case, we can define the same low-pass filters: the box filter, triangular filters, etc. As an example, let's focus on the Gaussian filter. The spatio-temporal Gaussian is a trivial extension of the spatial Gaussian filter we have seen in \@sec-spt_gaussian:
$$
g(x,y,t; \sigma_x,\sigma_t) = \frac{1}{(2 \pi)^{3/2} \sigma_x^2\sigma_t} \exp{-\frac{x^2 + y^2}{2 \sigma_x^2}} \exp{-\frac{t^2}{2 \sigma_t^2}}
$$
Where $\sigma_x$ is the width of the Gaussian along the two spatial dimensions, and $\sigma_t$ is the width in the temporal domain. As the units for $t$ and $x,y$ are unrelated, it does not make sense to set all the $\sigma$s to have the same value.

We can discretize the continuous Gaussian by taking samples and building a 3D convolutional kernel. We can also use the binomial approximation. The 3D Gaussian is separable, so it can be implemented efficiently as a convolutional cascade of 3 one-dimensional kernels. @fig-seq_filtered_kernel (a) shows a spatio-temporal Gaussian. The temporal Gaussian is a non-causal filter; therefore, it is not physically realizable. This is not a problem when processing a video stored in memory. However, if we are processing a streamed video, we will have to bound and shift the filter to make it causal, which will result in a delay in the output.

@fig-sec_filtered_blur (a) shows one sequence, and @fig-sec_filtered_blur (b) shows the sequence filtered with the Gaussian from @fig-seq_filtered_kernel (a). This Gaussian has a small spatial width, $\sigma=1$, and a large temporal width, $\sigma_t=4$, so the sequence is strongly blurred across time. The moving objects show motion blur and are strongly affected by the temporal blur, while the static background is only affected by the spatial width of the Gaussian.

(see figure: Fig (a) Spatio-temporal Gaussian with $\sigma=1$ and $\sigma_t=4$. b) Same Gaussian parameters but skewed by the velocity vector $v_x=-1, v_y=0$ pixels/frame, c) and $v_x=1, v_y=0$ pixel/frame.)

How could we create a filter that keeps sharp objects that move at some velocity $(v_x,v_y)$ while blurring the rest? @fig-sec_filtered_blur(c) shows the desired output of such a filter. The bottom image shows one frame for a sequence filtered with a kernel that keeps sharp objects moving left at 1 pixel/frame while blurring the rest. This filter can be obtained by skewing the Gaussian:
$$
g_{v_x,v_y}(x,y,t) = g(x - v_xt,y - v_yt, t)
$$
This directional blur is not a rotation of the original Gaussian as the change of variables is not unitary, but the same effect could be obtained with a rotation. @fig-sec_filtered_blur(c) shows the effect when $v_x=-1, v_y=0$. The Gaussian is shown in @fig-seq_filtered_kernel(b). The space-time section shows how the sequence is blurred everywhere except one oriented band corresponding to the person walking left. @fig-sec_filtered_blur(d) shows the effect when $v_x=1, v_y=0$. The output of this filter looks as if the camera was tracking one of the objects while the shutter was open, producing a blurry image of all the other objects.

concepts.motivation_md: Extending Gaussian filters to spatiotemporal domains allows smoothing video data while preserving motion information, enabling selective blurring based on object velocity.
concepts.recap_md:
- Spatiotemporal Gaussian extends spatial Gaussian with temporal width $\sigma_t$.
- The 3D Gaussian is separable and can be efficiently implemented.
- Skewing the Gaussian by velocity $(v_x,v_y)$ preserves sharpness of moving objects.

key_passage.text:
The spatio-temporal Gaussian is a trivial extension of the spatial Gaussian filter we have seen in \
$$
g(x,y,t; \sigma_x,\sigma_t) = \frac{1}{(2 \pi)^{3/2} \sigma_x^2\sigma_t} \exp{-\frac{x^2 + y^2}{2 \sigma_x^2}} \exp{-\frac{t^2}{2 \sigma_t^2}}
$$
Where \(\sigma_x\) is the width of the Gaussian along the two spatial dimensions, and \(\sigma_t\) is the width in the temporal domain.

motivation.text: The temporal Gaussian is a non-causal filter; therefore, it is not physically realizable. This is not a problem when processing a video stored in memory. However, if we are processing a streamed video, we will have to bound and shift the filter to make it causal, which will result in a delay in the output.

question.text: How could we create a filter that keeps sharp objects that move at some velocity \((v_x,v_y)\) while blurring the rest?

example.text: This Gaussian has a small spatial width, \(\sigma=1\), and a large temporal width, \(\sigma_t=4\), so the sequence is strongly blurred across time. The moving objects show motion blur and are strongly affected by the temporal blur, while the static background is only affected by the spatial width of the Gaussian.

concepts.title: Temporal derivatives
concepts.one_liner: Temporal derivatives approximate changes over time and can be used to locate moving objects.
concepts.content:
Spatial derivatives were useful to find regions of image variation such as object boundaries. Temporal derivatives can be used to locate moving objects. We can approximate a temporal derivative for discrete signals as:
$$
\ell \left[m,n,t\right] - \ell \left[m,n,t-1\right]
$$

concepts.title: spatio-temporal gradient of a Gaussian
concepts.one_liner: The spatio-temporal gradient of a Gaussian is given by \( \nabla g = (g_x, g_y, g_t) = (-x/\sigma^2, -y/\sigma^2, -t/\sigma_t^2) g(x,y,t) \).
concepts.content:
The spatio-temporal gradient of a Gaussian is:
$$
\nabla  g = \left( g_x(x,y,t), g_y(x,y,t), g_t(x,y,t) \right) =  \left(-x/\sigma^2, -y/\sigma^2, -t/\sigma_t^2 \right) g(x,y,t)
$$
concepts.motivation_md: The gradient of a spatio-temporal Gaussian captures changes in space and time, useful for detecting motion and edges in video data.
concepts.recap_md:
- Gradient components: $g_x, g_y, g_t$.
- Each component scales with $-x/\sigma^2$, $-y/\sigma^2$, and $-t/\sigma_t^2$ respectively.
- Multiplied by the Gaussian function $g(x,y,t)$.

key_passage.text:
$$
\nabla g = \left( g_x(x,y,t), g_y(x,y,t), g_t(x,y,t) \right) = \left(-x/\sigma^2, -y/\sigma^2, -t/\sigma_t^2 \right) g(x,y,t)
$$

concepts.title: using nulling filters to remove objects moving at particular velocity
concepts.one_liner: Nulling filters use a linear combination of temporal and spatial derivatives to produce zero output for objects moving at a target velocity.
concepts.content:
To answer that question, we will first assume the sequence contains a single object moving at a constant velocity. We will then compute the derivatives along $x$, $y$, and $t$ of the sequence and we will find out what particular linear combination of those derivatives makes the output go to zero only when the input sequence moves at a target velocity.

In the case of a moving image with velocity $(v_x, v_y)$, the sequence is 
$$
\ell (x,y,t) = \ell _0 (x-v_xt,y-v_yt)
$$
We can compute the temporal derivative of $f(x,y,t)$ as:
$$
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial t} = \frac{\partial \ell _0}{\partial t} = -v_x \frac{\partial \ell _0}{\partial x} - v_y \frac{\partial f_0}{\partial y}
$$

This result is interesting because it shows that for a moving image there is a relationship between the temporal derivative of the sequence and the spatial derivatives a long the direction of motion. We can use this relationship to find a linear combination of the temporal and spatial derivatives so that the output is zero. 

In fact, if we compute the gradient of the Gaussian along the vector $\left[1,v_x,v_y\right]$:

$$
 h(x,y,t;v_x,v_y) = g_t+v_xg_x+v_yg_y = \nabla  g \left( 1,v_x,v_y \right)^\top
$$ 

we get a kernel $h(x,y,t;v_x,v_y)$ that we can use as a spatiotemporal filter that will do exactly what we were looking for. Indeed, if we convolve it with the input sequence $\text{img}_0 (x-v_x t,y-v_y t)$ we get a zero output (using @eq-brightnessconstancy):

$$
\begin{split}
\ell _0 (x-v_x t, y-v_y t) \circ h & = \ell _0 (x-v_x t, y-v_y t) \circ \left( g_t + v_x g_x + v_y g_y \right) \\
& = \left( \frac{\partial \ell _0}{\partial t} + v_x \frac{\partial \ell _0}{\partial x} + v_y \frac{\partial \ell _0}{\partial y} \right) \circ g \\
& = 0
\end{split}
$$

The filter $h$ from @eq-spt_nulling_filter is shown in @fig-gaussian_seq. As this filter is 3D, we show it as a sequence for different velocities. Each row in the figure corresponds to one particular velocity $v_x, v_y$. In the example shown in @fig-gaussian_seq (a), the Gaussian has a width of $\sigma^2=\sigma_t^2=1.5$ and has been discretized as a 3D array of size $7 \times 7 \times 7$. Figures @fig-gaussian_seq (b, c, and d) show the filter $h$ for different velocities: $(v_x, v_y) = (0,0)$, $(1,0)$, and $(-1,0)$.


(see figure: Visualization of the space-time Gaussian. The Gaussian has a width of $\sigma^2=\sigma_t^2=1.5$, and has been discretized as a 3D array of size $7 \times 7 \times 7$. Each image shows one frame. a)...)

@fig-gaussian_xyt_section shows a different visualization of the same filter $h$ from @eq-spt_nulling_filter. Each image in @fig-gaussian_xyt_section shows a space-time section of the same spatiotemporal Gaussian derivatives as the ones shown in @fig-gaussian_seq. Both visualizations are equivalent and help to understand how the filter works.


![Spatio-temporal Gaussian $g\left[ n,t \right]$ and derivatives. a) Gaussian with $\sigma^2=1.5$. b) Partial derivative with respect to $t$. c) Partial derivative along $(1,-1)$, d) Partial derivative along $(1,1)$.](figures/temporal_filters/gaussians_xyt_section.png){#fig-gaussian_xyt_section}

Such a filter $h$ will cancel any objects moving at the velocity $(v_x,v_y)$. By using different filters, each one computing derivatives along different space-time orientations, we can create output sequences where specific objects disappear, as shown in @fig-tunedfilter. This filter is called a **nulling filter** [@Darrell93].

(see figure: (a) Input sequence. (b) Output to $h$ with $v_x=v_y=0$. (c) $v_x=1$ pixels/frame. (d) $v_x=-1$ pixel/frame.)


Note that despite assuming that the sequence contained a single moving object when deriving the formulation for the nulling filter, the filter also works in sequences with multiple objects moving at different speeds, as shown in @fig-tunedfilter. This is because the operations are local (the kernel $h$ has a small size), and the behavior will be correct if in a local image patch there is only one velocity present. In fact, it is easy to show that the method will also work if the sequence is a sum of several moving transparent layers.

concepts.title: recurrence
concepts.one_liner: A feedback connection defines a recurrence in the computational graph.
concepts.content:
A feedback connection defines a **recurrence** in the computational graph.

Their computation graphs have cycles. That means that the outputs of one layer can send a message back to earlier in the computational pipeline. To make this well-defined, RNNs introduce the notion of **timestep**. One timestep of running an RNN corresponds to one functional call to each layer (or computation node) in the RNN, mapping that layer's inputs to its outputs.
concepts.motivation_md: Recurrence allows outputs of one layer to influence earlier layers, enabling RNNs to process sequences with feedback loops over time steps.
concepts.recap_md:
- A recurrence is defined by a feedback connection in the computational graph.
- Recurrence introduces cycles where outputs can feed back to earlier layers.
- RNNs use timesteps to make these cycles well-defined.

concepts.title: RNNs are all about adaptation
concepts.one_liner: RNNs are all about adaptation: they allow past computations to influence future computations.
concepts.content: RNNs are all about adaptation. They solve the following problem: What if we want our computations in the past to influence our computations in the future? If we have a stream of data, a feedforward net has no way to adapting its behavior based on what outputs it previously produced.
concepts.motivation_md: RNNs address the problem of adapting computations based on past outputs, which feedforward nets cannot do.
concepts.recap_md:
- RNNs enable adaptation over time.
- They allow past computations to influence future ones.
- Feedforward nets cannot adapt based on previous outputs.

concepts.title: Memory in RNNs via recurrent feedback loops
concepts.one_liner: The recurrent feedback loops in an RNN are a kind of memory, propagating information from timestep $t$ to $t+1$.
concepts.content: The answer is memory. The recurrent feedback loops in an RNN are a kind of memory. They propagate information from timestep $t$ to timestep $t+1$. In other words, they remember information about timestep $t$ when processing new information at timestep $t+1$. Thus, by induction, an RNN can potentially remember information over arbitrarily long time intervals. In fact, RNNs are Turing complete: you can think of them as a little computer. They can do anything a computer can do.
concepts.motivation_md: Recurrent feedback loops provide memory to RNNs, enabling them to remember and use past information over time.
concepts.recap_md:

- They pass information from timestep $t$ to $t+1$.
- RNNs can remember information over arbitrarily long intervals and are Turing complete.

concepts.title: unrolled computation graph
concepts.one_liner: The unrolled computation graph is a DAG representation of an RNN's computation over time, making backpropagation applicable.
concepts.content:
(see figure: RNN with multidimensional inputs, hidden states, and outputs.)

To the left, is the **unrolled computation graph**. To the right, is the computation graph rolled up, with a feedback connection. Typically we will work with unrolled graphs because they are directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), and therefore all the tools we have developed for DAGs, including backpropagation, will extend naturally to them. However, note that RNNs can run for unbounded time, and process signals that have unbounded temporal extent, while a DAG can only represent a finite graph. The DAG depicted above is therefore a *truncated* version of the RNN's theoretical computation graph.
concepts.motivation_md: Unrolling an RNN's computation graph removes cycles, enabling the use of DAG-based tools like backpropagation.
concepts.recap_md:
- The unrolled computation graph represents RNN computations as a DAG.
- DAGs allow use of backpropagation and other DAG tools.
- The unrolled graph is a truncated finite representation of the RNN's infinite computation.

concepts.title: The idea of time in an RNN
concepts.one_liner: Time in an RNN refers to sequential computation steps indexed by timestep $t$, not necessarily clock time.
concepts.content: The idea of a *time* in an RNN does not necessarily mean time as it is measured on a clock. Time just refers to *sequential computation*; the timestep $t$ is an index into the sequence. The sequential computation could progress over a spatial dimension (processing an image pixel by pixel) or over the temporal dimension (processing a video frame by frame), or even over more abstracted computational modules.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding 'time' as sequential steps allows RNNs to process data ordered by any sequence, not just clock time.
concepts.recap_md:
- Time in RNNs means sequential computation, not clock time.
- Timestep $t$ indexes the sequence.
- Sequence can be spatial, temporal, or abstract computational steps.

concepts.title: SRN
concepts.one_liner: An SRN is a recurrent layer where $f$ is a linear layer plus nonlinearity and $g$ is another linear layer.
concepts.content:
One common kind of recurrent layer is the (**SRN**), which was defined by Elman in "Finding Structure in Time" @elman1990finding. For this layer, $f$ is a linear layer followed by a pointwise nonlinearity, and $g$ is another linear layer. The full computation is defined by the following equations: 
$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{h}_t &= \sigma_1(\mathbf{W}\mathbf{h}_{t-1} + \mathbf{U}\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[t]+ \mathbf{b})\\
    \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}[t]&= \sigma_2(\mathbf{V}\mathbf{h}_t + \mathbf{c})
\end{aligned}$$ where $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ are pointwise nonlinearities. In SRNs, tanh is the common choice for the nonlinearity, but relus and other choices may also be used.
concepts.motivation_md: The SRN is a foundational recurrent layer model combining linear transformations and nonlinearities to process sequential data.
concepts.recap_md:
- SRN is a recurrent layer defined by Elman.
- $f$ is a linear layer plus nonlinearity; $g$ is another linear layer.
- Common nonlinearities include tanh and relu.

concepts.title: Discrete Fourier Transform Properties
concepts.one_liner: It is important to be familiar with the properties for the DFT.
concepts.content:
It is important to be familiar with the properties for the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT). The following table summarizes some important transforms and properties.

| $\ell[n]$ | $\mathscr{L}[u]$ |
| :---: | :---: |
| $\ell_1[n] \circ \ell_2[n]$ | $\mathscr{L}_1[u] \mathscr{L}_2[u]$ |
| $\ell_1[n] \ell_2[n]$ | $\frac{1}{N} \mathscr{L}_1[u] \circ \mathscr{L}_2[u]$ |
| $\ell\left[n-n_0\right]$ | $\mathscr{L}[u] \exp \left(-2 \pi j \frac{u n_0}{N}\right)$ |
| $\delta[n]$ | 1 |
| $\exp \left(2 \pi u_0 \frac{n}{N}\right)$ | $\delta\left[u-u_0\right]$ |
| $\cos \left(2 \pi u_0 \frac{n}{N}\right)$ | $\frac{1}{2}\left(\delta\left[u-u_0\right]+\delta\left[u+u_0\right]\right)$ |
| $\sin \left(2 \pi u_0 \frac{n}{N}\right)$ | $\frac{1}{2 j}\left(\delta\left[u-u_0\right]-\delta\left[u+u_0\right]\right)$ |
| $\operatorname{box}_L[n]$ | $\frac{\sin \pi u(2 L+1) / N}{\sin \pi u / N}$ |
: Table of basic DFT transforms and properties

- Convolution in time corresponds to multiplication in frequency, and vice versa.
- Shifts and modulations in one domain correspond to specific transformations in the other.

- Scalars factor out of the transform.

concepts.title: Separability
concepts.one_liner: If an image is separable, then its Fourier transform is separable: $\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] = \mathscr{L}_1 \left[u \right] \mathscr{L}_2 \left[v \right]$.
concepts.content:
An image is separable if it can be written as the product of two 1D signals,
$\ell\left[n,m \right] = \ell_1\left[n \right] \ell_2\left[m \right]$. If an image is separable, then its Fourier transform is separable:
$\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] = \mathscr{L}_1 \left[u \right] \mathscr{L}_2 \left[v \right]$.

concepts.title: Parseval's Theorem
concepts.one_liner: Parseval's theorem states that the dot product and norm are preserved (up to a constant) under the DFT basis change.
concepts.content:
As the DFT is a change of basis, the dot product between two signals and the norm of a vector is preserved (up to a constant factor) after the basis change. This is stated by Parseval's theorem:
$$\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} \,  \ell_1 \left[n,m \right] \ell_2^* \left[n,m \right] = \frac{1}{NM}\sum_{u=0}^{N-1} \sum_{v=0}^{M-1} \,  \mathscr{L}_1 \left[u,v \right] \mathscr{L}_2^* \left[u,v \right]$$
In particular, if $\ell_1=\ell_2$ this reduces to the **Plancherel theorem**:
$$\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} \,  \| \ell\left[n,m \right] \|^2 = \frac{1}{NM}\sum_{u=0}^{N-1} \sum_{v=0}^{M-1} \,  \| \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] \|^2$$
This relationship is important because it tells us that the energy of a signal can be computed as the sum of the squared magnitude of the values of its Fourier transform.
concepts.motivation_md: Parseval's theorem ensures that energy and inner products are preserved under the Fourier transform, linking time and frequency domain analyses.
concepts.recap_md:
- Parseval's theorem relates dot products in time and frequency domains.
- The Plancherel theorem is a special case for signal energy.
- Energy can be computed from the squared magnitudes of Fourier coefficients.

concepts.title: Convolution
concepts.one_liner: The Fourier transform of the convolution of two signals is the product of their Fourier transforms.
concepts.content:
Consider a signal $\ell_{\texttt{out}}$ that is the result of applying (circular) convolution of two signals, $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$, both of size $N \times M$: $$\ell_{\texttt{out}}= \ell_1 \circ \ell_2$$

The question is; how does the Fourier transform of the signal $\ell_{\texttt{out}}$ relate to the Fourier transforms of the two signals $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$?

The relationship between the convolution and the Fourier transform is probably the most important property of the Fourier transform and you should be familiar with it.

If we take the Fourier transform of both sides, and use the definition of the Fourier transform, we obtain
$$\begin{split}
\mathscr{L}_{\texttt{out}}\left[u,v \right] & =  \mathcal{F}  \left\{ \ell_1 \circ_{N,M} \ell_2 \right\} \\
& =  
\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}  \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} 
\left\{
\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \sum_{l=0}^{M-1} 
\ell_1 \left[n-k, m-l \right] \ell_2 \left[k,l \right]
\right\}
\exp \left(-2 \pi j \left(\frac{nu}{N} + \frac{mv}{M} \right) \right)
\end{split}$$

In these sums, the finite signal $\ell_1 \left[n, m \right]$ of size $N \times M$ is extended periodically infinitely. The periodic extension allows us to drop the modulo operators. Changing the dummy variables in the sums (introducing $n' = n - k$ and $m' = m - l$), we have
$$\mathscr{L}_{\texttt{out}}\left[u,v \right] =
\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \sum_{l=0}^{M-1} 
\ell_2 \left[k,l \right]
\sum_{n'=-k}^{N-k-1}  \sum_{m'=-l}^{M-l-1} 
\ell_1 \left[n', m' \right] 
\exp{ \left(-2 \pi j \left(\frac{(n'+k)u}{N} + \frac{(m'+l)v}{M} \right) \right)}$$
Recognizing that the last two summations give the DFT of $x\left[n,m\right]$, using circular boundary conditions, gives
$$\mathscr{L}_{\texttt{out}}\left[u,v \right] = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \sum_{l=0}^{M-1}  \mathscr{L}_1 \left[u,v\right] \exp{ \left(-2 \pi j \left(\frac{ku}{N}+\frac{lv}{M} \right ) \right)} \ell_2 \left[k,l\right]$$
Performing the DFT indicated by the second two summations gives the desired result:
$$\mathscr{L}_{\texttt{out}}\left[u,v\right] = \mathscr{L}_1 \left[u,v\right] \mathscr{L}_2 \left[u,v\right]$$

Thus, the operation of a convolution, in the Fourier domain, is just a multiplication of the Fourier transform of each term in the Fourier domain: $$\ell_1 \left[n,m\right] \circ_{N,M} \ell_2 \left[n,m\right]
\xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}} 
\mathscr{L}_1 \left[u,v\right] \mathscr{L}_2 \left[u,v\right]$$
concepts.motivation_md: This property links convolution in the spatial domain to multiplication in the frequency domain, simplifying filtering and signal processing.
concepts.recap_md:
- Convolution in space corresponds to multiplication in frequency.
- The DFT of a convolution equals the product of DFTs.
- This property is fundamental for efficient signal processing.

concepts.title: Dual Convolution
concepts.one_liner: The Fourier transform of the product of two images is the circular convolution of their DFTs.
concepts.content:
Another common operation with working with images is to do products between images. For instance, this might happen if we are applying a mask to an image (which corresponds to multiplying the image by a mask that has 0 in the pixels that we want to mask out).

It turns out that the Fourier transform of the product of two images is the (circular) convolution of their DFTs:

$$\ell_1 \left[n,m\right] \ell_2 \left[n,m\right]
\xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}} 
\frac{1}{NM} \mathscr{L}_1 \left[u,v\right] \circ \mathscr{L}_2 \left[u,v\right]$$
We leave the proof of this property to the reader.
concepts.motivation_md: This property shows how multiplication in the spatial domain corresponds to convolution in the frequency domain, useful for image masking and filtering.
concepts.recap_md:
- Multiplying two images corresponds to convolving their DFTs.
- The Fourier transform of a product is a circular convolution in frequency.
- This is the dual property to convolution in space.

concepts.title: Shift Property, Translation in Space
concepts.one_liner: Translating a signal in space results in multiplying its Fourier transform by a complex exponential.
concepts.content:
A shift corresponds to a translation in space. This is a very common operation that has a very particular influence on the Fourier transform of the signal. It turns out that translating a signal in the spatial domain results in multiplying its Fourier transform by a complex exponential.

To show this, consider an image $\ell\left[n,m \right]$, with Fourier transform $\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]$ and period $N,M$. When displacing the image by $(n_0, m_0)$ pixels, we get $\ell\left[n-n_0,m-m_0 \right]$ and its Fourier transform is:
$$
\begin{split}
\mathcal{F} \left\{ \ell\left[n-n_0,m-m_0 \right] \right\}
&= \\
 & = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} \, \ell\left[n-n_0,m-m_0 \right] \exp{ \left( -2\pi j \left( \frac{u\, n}{N} + \frac{v\, m}{M} \right) \right)} = \\
& =  \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} \, \ell\left[n,m \right] \exp{ \left( -2\pi j \left( \frac{u\, (n+n_0)}{N} + \frac{v\, (m+m_0)}{M} \right) \right)}  = \\
& =   \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]  \exp{ \left( -2\pi j \left( \frac{u\, n_0}{N} + \frac{v\, m_0}{M} \right) \right)}
   \end{split}$$
Note that as the signal $\ell$ and the complex exponentials have the period $N,M$, we can change the sum indices over any range of size $N \times M$ samples.

In practice, if we have an image and we apply a translation there will be some boundary artifacts. So, in general, this property is only true if we apply a **circular shift**, i.e., pixels that disappear on the boundary due to the translation reappear on the other side. This is a consequence of the periodic structure of the signal $\ell$ assumed by the DFT. In practice, when the translation is due to the motion of the camera, the shift will not be circular and new pixels will appear on the image boundary. Therefore, the shift property will be only an approximation.

To see how good of an approximation it is, let's look at one example of a shift due to camera motion. @fig-shiftFT shows two images that correspond to a translation with $n_0=16$ and $m_0=-4$. Note that at the image boundaries, new pixels appear in (c) not visible in (a). As this is not a pure circular translation, the result from equation (@eq-shift) will not apply exactly. To verify equation (@eq-shift) let's look at the real part of the DFT of each image shown in @fig-shiftFT (b) and (d). If equation (@eq-shift) holds true, then the real part of the ratio between the DFTs of the two translated images should be $\cos{ \left( -2\pi j \left( \frac{u\, n_0}{N} + \frac{v\, m_0}{M} \right) \right)}$ with $N=M=128$ and $[n_0,m_0]=[16,-4]$. @fig-shiftFT (f) shows that the real part of the ratio is indeed very close to a cosine, despite of the boundary pixels which are responsible of the noise (the same is true for the imaginary part). In fact, @fig-shiftFT (e) shows the inverse DFT of the ratio between DFTs, considering both real and imaginary components, which is very close to an impulse at $[16,-4]$.

(see figure: Translation in space. Image (c) corresponds to image (a) after a translation of 16 pixels to the right and four pixels down. Images (b) and (d) show the real parts of their corresponding DFTs (with...)
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding how spatial shifts affect the Fourier transform helps analyze image translations and their effects in frequency domain.
concepts.recap_md:
- Translating a signal multiplies its Fourier transform by a complex exponential.
- This property holds exactly for circular shifts due to periodicity.
- Real-world shifts approximate this with boundary artifacts.

concepts.title: Modulation, Translation in Frequency
concepts.one_liner: Multiplying an image by a complex exponential translates its Fourier transform in frequency.
concepts.content:
If we multiply an image with a complex exponential, its Fourier transform is translated, a property related to the previous one:

$$\ell\left[n,m \right]  \exp{ \left( -2\pi j \left( \frac{u_0\, n}{N} + \frac{v_0\, m}{M} \right) \right)}\xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}}\mathscr{L}\left[u-u_0,v-v_0 \right]
$${#eq-modulation_exp} This can be proven using the dual convolution property from section -sec-dualconv. Note that now the result in equation (@eq-modulation_exp) is not a real signal, and for this reason its Fourier Transform does not have symmetries around $u,v=0$.

A related relationship is as follows:

$$\ell\left[n,m \right]  \cos{ \left( 2\pi j \left( \frac{u_0\, n}{N} + \frac{v_0\, m}{M} \right) \right)}\xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}} 
\mathscr{L}\left[u-u_0,v-v_0 \right] + \mathscr{L}\left[u+u_0,v+v_0 \right]$$

Multiplying a signal by a wave is called signal modulation and it is one of the basic operations in communications. It is also an important property in image analysis and we will see its use later.

@fig-modulation shows an example of modulating an image of a stop sign by multiplying by diagonal wave. The bottom row shows the corresponding Fourier transforms.

(see figure: Modulation in space. Multiplying an image by a cosine wave results in a new image with a Fourier transform with two copies of the Fourier transform of the original image. Only the magnitude of the...)

Note that a shift and a modulation are equivalent operations in different domains. A shift in space is a modulation in the frequency domain and that a shift in frequency is a modulation in the spatial domain.
concepts.motivation_md: Modulation translates the Fourier transform, enabling frequency shifts useful in communications and image processing.
concepts.recap_md:
- Multiplying by a complex exponential shifts the Fourier transform.
- Multiplying by a cosine creates two shifted copies in frequency.
- Shift in space corresponds to modulation in frequency, and vice versa.

concepts.title: Concluding Remarks
concepts.one_liner: Aliasing is a common artifact in sampled images and understanding it is important for avoiding or exploiting it.
concepts.content:
Aliasing is a common artifact that appears whenever an image is captured by sampling a continuous light field. Aliasing also affects images whenever there is upsampling or downsampling. Therefore, understanding how aliasing introduces artifacts and the best way to avoid it is an important skill.

However, aliasing is not always bad and it might be possible to use aliasing to recover high-frequency content that would be otherwise lost. Superresolution algorithms can learn to extract, from the aliasing pattern, fine image details.

Also, when an image is encoded by multiple channels, aliasing in one channel does not mean that the information is lost because multiple channels could contain complementary information that allows the recovery of high-resolution details.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding aliasing is crucial because it commonly appears in image sampling and processing, and can both cause artifacts and be exploited to recover lost details.
concepts.recap_md:
- Aliasing occurs when sampling continuous images and during resampling.
- It can cause artifacts but also help recover lost high-frequency details.
- Multiple image channels can complement and mitigate aliasing effects.

concepts.title: strided convolution
concepts.one_liner: Strided convolution involves convolution, decimation by taking every second pixel, and a ReLU nonlinearity.
concepts.motivation_md: Strided convolution combines filtering and downsampling efficiently, which is important in image processing and neural networks.
concepts.recap_md:
- Strided convolution applies convolution with a kernel.
- Then decimation reduces resolution by taking every second pixel.
- Finally, a ReLU nonlinearity is applied.

key_passage.text: This system has three steps: the first step is a vertical edge filter (convolution of the input, $\ell_{\texttt{in}}$, with a horizontal kernel, $[1, -1]$). The next step is to reduce the resolution of the filter output by taking one pixel every two along each dimension (this operation is called decimation).

motivation.text: Decimation takes an input, $u$, with size $N\times M$, and outputs, $h$, with half the size $N/2 \times M/2$.

example.text:
$$\begin{aligned} u[n,m] &= \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n,m\right] \circ \left[-1, 1 \right] & \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \texttt{conv}\\ h[n,m] &= u[2n,2m] & \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \texttt{decimation}\\ \ell_{\texttt{out}}[n,m] &= \max (0,h[n,m]) & \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \texttt{relu}
\end{aligned}$$

concepts.title: Decimation
concepts.one_liner: Image decimation changes image resolution by dropping samples, reducing size by a factor $k$.
concepts.content:
Image decimation consists of changing the resolution of an image by dropping samples. Decimation of an image of size $N \times M$ by a factor of $k$, where $N$ and $M$ are divisible by $k$, results in a lower resolution image of size $N/k \times M/k$:
$$\ell_{\downarrow k} \left[n,m\right]  = \ell\left[kn, km\right]$$
It is common to use the notations
$\ell_{\downarrow k} \left[n,m\right]   = \ell\left[n,m\right] \downarrow k = \ell\left[kn,km\right]$
to denote the decimation operator by a factor $k$. Decimation could be

concepts.recap_md:
- Decimation reduces image size by dropping samples.
- For factor $k$, size changes from $N \times M$ to $N/k \times M/k$.
- Notations include $\ell_{\downarrow k}$ and $\ell \downarrow k$.

concepts.title: delta train
concepts.one_liner: The delta train is a discrete pattern marking samples retained after decimation.
concepts.content:
$\ell_{\delta_k} \left[n,m\right]$, of same size as the input image, $N \times M$, where we set to zero the samples that will be removed in the decimation operation: 
$$\begin{aligned}
\ell_{\delta_k} \left[n,m\right] &= \ell\left[n,m\right] \sum_{s=0}^{N/k-1} \sum_{r=0}^{M/k-1} \delta \left[n - sk \, ,m - rk \right] \\
&=  \ell\left[n,m\right]  \delta_k \left[n,m\right]\end{aligned}$$ where $\delta_k \left[n,m\right]$ is the discrete version of the **delta train**.

concepts.title: Anti-Aliasing Filters
concepts.one_liner: Anti-aliasing filters blur images before downsampling to remove high-frequency content that causes aliasing.
concepts.content:
### Anti-Aliasing Filters

Anti-aliasing filtering is an essential operation whenever we manipulate the resolution of an image. When decimating a signal of size $N \times N$ with a scaling factor $k$, aliasing is produced by all the content at frequencies that are above $u,v > N/2k$. Therefore, to reduce aliasing, we have to remove any spectral content of the signal present at high spatial frequencies. We will do so by using an anti-aliasing filter that will blur the image before downsampling. Blurring removes high-spatial frequencies in the image.

The ideal anti-aliasing filter is a box in the Fourier domain with a cut-off frequency of $L=N/(2k)$ (using the notation introduced in @sec-sampling). The inverse Fourier transform of a box in the frequency domain, with width $2L+1=N/k+1$, is the **discrete sinc** function of length $N$ in the spatial domain:
$$\frac{1}{N} \frac 
{\sin(\pi n (N/k+1)/N)}
{\sin(\pi n/N)}
\xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}} 
box_{N/2k} \left[ u \right]$$

In 2D, the ideal anti-aliasing filter is separable and is obtained by two consecutive 1D convolutions along each dimension. The discrete sinc is very similar to the continuous sinc described in @sec-sampling. The discrete sinc is periodic, with period $N$. The following plot (@fig-discretesinc) shows the anti-aliasing sinc for $N=32$ and $k=2$ and the magnitude of its Fourier transform:

(see figure: Discrete sinc function for $N=32$ and $k=2$ and the magnitude of its DFT.)

And for $k=4$, the impulse response becomes wider and its Fourier transform has a lower cut-off frequency, $N/2k = 4$:

(see figure: Discrete sinc function for $N=32$ and $k=4$ and the magnitude of its DFT.)

One disadvantage of the ideal anti-aliasing filter is that the it requires convolving the image with a very large filter (as large as the image). We would like to use smaller filters to reduce the computational cost. One method to design anti-aliasing filters with a finite impulse response is to use a window, $w [n]$, and to use as anti-aliasing filter the kernel $w [n] h[n]$, where $h[n]$ is the impulse response of the ideal anti-aliasing filter. Typical windows used are the rectangular, Hamming, Parzen, or Kaiser windows.

The rectangular window sets to zero all the values outside of the interval $\left[-L, L\right]$. When $L=5$, it gives a tap-11 filter (a filter with an impulse response of length 11) with the following profile:

![Kernel $w [n] h[n]$, where $h[n]$ is a sinc and $w [n]$ is a rectangular window of length 11.](figures/upsamplig_downsampling/kernel_sinc_window.png){#fig-discretesinc width=100%}

The Fourier transform of the windowed impulse response, $w [n] h[n]$, is the convolution of Fourier transforms. The Fourier transform of the rectangular window is a sinc function. Therefore, the resulting Fourier transform is the convolution of the rectangle with the sinc function, which produces a smooth rectangle with some oscillations. Using other windows allows trading off the smoothing of the ideal rectangular form of the ideal low-pass filter and the oscillations.

The **Hamming window** is defined as:
$$w  \left[n\right] =  \begin{cases}
    0.54+0.46 \cos (\pi n/L)     & \quad \text{if }  n \in  \left[-L, L\right] \\
    0       & \quad \text{otherwise }\\
\end{cases}$$ The Hamming window ($L=5$) produces a smooth transfer function with oscillations of smaller amplitude in the Fourier domain:
$$h = [1, 0.65, -2.45, -0.82, 8.8, 15, 8.8, -0.82, -2.45, 0.65, 1] / 29.36$$

(see figure: Hamming window ($L=5$) and the magnitude of its DFT.)

In practice, when we need very small anti-aliasing filters, binomial filters are a good choice. The binomial filter $b_2$ has a DFT (length $N$) with a $1+\cos(2\pi/N)$ profile. At the frequency $N/4$ the gain is $1/2$. Therefore, the spectral content responsible for aliasing will not be completely removed, but the attenuation is enough in most cases.


![The binomial kernel $b_2 = \left[1,2,1\right]$, and its DFT.](figures/upsamplig_downsampling/binomial_kernel1.png){#fig-discretesinc2 width=100%}

Or $b_4 = [ 1, 4, 6, 4, 1]$, which attenuates the aliased frequencies even more, also results in an oversmoothed signal.

![The binomial kernel $b_4 = [ 1, 4, 6, 4, 1]$, and its DFT.](figures/upsamplig_downsampling/binomial_kernel4.png){#fig-discretesinc4 width=100%}

When implementing 2D anti-aliasing filters, we apply two consecutive 1D convolutions along each dimension. For efficiency, the anti-aliasing filter only needs to be computed on the samples that will be kept after downsampling ($k$-strided convolution). The necessary amount of attenuation of the aliasing frequencies will have to be decided based on each application.


In 2D, we can apply the binomial filter $b_2$ on each dimension,
$\left[1,2,1\right]/4 \circ \left[1,2,1\right]^\mathsf{T}/4$.


(see figure: Output of three different low-pass anti-aliasing filters. (left) Ideal low-pass filter. (center) Hamming window. (right) Binomial filter.)

The images in @fig-ringing_artifacts show the output of three different low-pass anti-aliasing filters. Note how the ideal low-pass filter introduces **ringing artifacts** in the output image (@fig-ringing_artifacts[a]). Despite that it removes frequencies that will produce aliasing after downsampling, it does that at a high cost because it introduces undesired image structures, which is exactly what we want to prevent with the anti-aliasing filter. The Hamming windowed sinc (shown in @fig-ringing_artifacts[b]) reduces the oscillation but there is still a halo present around edges. This is because there is still one oscillation on the filter impulse response. @fig-ringing_artifacts (c) shows the result applying am anti-aliasing binomial filter.

For most applications using a binomial filter ($b_2$ or $b_4$) is enough because it reduces aliasing and it does not introduce undesired image structures.
concepts.motivation_md: Anti-aliasing filters prevent aliasing artifacts by removing high-frequency content before downsampling, ensuring image quality.
concepts.recap_md:
- Anti-aliasing filters blur images to remove high frequencies causing aliasing.
- The ideal filter is a discrete sinc with a box-shaped frequency response.
- Practical filters use windowing or binomial filters to reduce computation and artifacts.

key_passage.text: Anti-aliasing filtering is an essential operation whenever we manipulate the resolution of an image. When decimating a signal of size $N \times N$ with a scaling factor $k$, aliasing is produced by all the content at frequencies that are above $u,v > N/2k$. Therefore, to reduce aliasing, we have to remove any spectral content of the signal present at high spatial frequencies. We will do so by using an anti-aliasing filter that will blur the image before downsampling. Blurring removes high-spatial frequencies in the image.

concepts.title: recurrent connections and feedback
concepts.one_liner: Recurrent connections allow neural nets to maintain a persistent state and adapt based on feedback from downstream processing.
concepts.content: Recurrent connections give neural nets the ability to maintain a persistent state representation, which can be propagated forward in time or updated with incoming experience. This idea is analogous to the distinction between open-loop and closed-loop control in control theory. Closed-loop control allows the controller to change behavior based on feedback from the consequences of previous decisions. Similarly, recurrent connections allow a neural net to change behavior based on feedback from downstream processing within the same network. Feedback is a fundamental mechanism for making systems adaptive, enabling them to become more competent the longer they run.

concepts.title: The Idea of Attention
concepts.one_liner: Attention is a strategy for processing global information efficiently by focusing on the most salient parts of the signal.
concepts.content:
## The Idea of Attention

Attention is a strategy for processing global information efficiently, focusing just on the parts of the signal that are most salient to the task at hand. The idea can be motivated by attention in human perception. When we look at a scene, our eyes flick around and we attend to certain elements that stand out, rather than taking in the whole scene at once @wolfe2000visual. If we are asked a question about the color of a car in the scene, we will move our eyes to look at the car, rather than just staring passively. Can we give neural nets the same ability?
concepts.motivation_md: Attention allows models to efficiently process global information by selectively focusing on relevant parts, inspired by human perceptual attention. (book-extracted)

- Attention focuses on the most salient parts of a signal.
- Inspired by human visual attention mechanisms.
- Enables efficient global information processing in neural nets.

concepts.title: A New Data Type: Tokens
concepts.one_liner: A token is an encapsulated group of neurons represented as a vector, treated as a new data type in deep learning.
concepts.content:
## A New Data Type: Tokens

We discussed that the main data structures in deep learning are different kinds of groups of neurons: channels, tensors, batches, and so on. Now we will introduce another fundamental data structure, . A token is another kind of group of neurons, but there are particular ways we will operate over tokens that are different from how we operated over channels, batches, and the other groupings we saw before. Specifically, we will think of tokens as *encapsulated* groups of information; we will define operators over tokens, and these operators will be our only interface for accessing and modifying the internal contents of tokens. From a programming languages perspective, you can think of tokens as a new data *type*.

In this chapter we will only consider tokens whose internal content is a vector of neurons. A single token will therefore be represented by a column vector $\mathbf{t} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times 1}$, which is also sometimes called the token's **code vector**.
concepts.motivation_md: Tokens provide a structured way to encapsulate and operate on groups of neurons, enabling new forms of data manipulation in deep learning. (book-extracted)

- Tokens are encapsulated groups of neurons treated as a new data type.
- Operators over tokens define how to access and modify their contents.
- Tokens are represented as column vectors called code vectors.

concepts.title: Spatiotemporal Gabor Filters
concepts.one_liner: Extending the 2D Gabor filter to a 3D $x$-$y$-$t$ Gabor function allows motion analysis but a single Gabor filter cannot disambiguate input velocity.
concepts.content:
Just as with Gaussian derivatives, extending the Gabor filter for motion analysis generalizes the $x$-$y$ 2D Gabor function to a $x$-$y$-$t$ 3D Gabor function. Figure @fig-spacetimefilts (a) shows a $x$-$t$ (cosine and sine) Gabor function in one spatial dimension, and (b) shows a sketch of its Fourier transform. This function is selective to signals translating to the right with speed $v=1$, i.e., $l(x-t)$. The red line in (b) shows a Dirac line containing the energy of the moving signal.

In two spatial dimensions, (c) shows the sketch of the Gabor transfer function. Note that the $x$-$y$-$t$ Gabor filter is not selective to velocity. For a 2D moving signal $l(x-v_x t, y-v_y t)$, the Fourier transform is contained inside a Dirac plane. There are infinitely many such planes passing through the frequencies of the Gabor filter, all intersecting the red line shown in (c). Therefore, a single Gabor filter cannot disambiguate the input velocity.

(see figure: Space-time Gabor filters. (a) Cosine and sine $x$-$t$ Gabor filter, and (b) the sketch of its transfer function. (c) Sketch of the transfer function of a spatiotemporal Gabor filter in two spatial...)
concepts.motivation_md: Spatiotemporal Gabor filters extend 2D spatial filters to 3D space-time to analyze motion, but a single filter cannot uniquely determine velocity, motivating the need for more complex approaches.
concepts.recap_md:
- Spatiotemporal Gabor filters generalize 2D Gabor functions to 3D $x$-$y$-$t$ for motion analysis.
- The $x$-$t$ Gabor function is selective to signals moving at speed $v=1$.
- A single 3D Gabor filter cannot uniquely disambiguate velocity due to overlapping frequency planes.

key_passage.text: Just as we did with Gaussian derivatives, extending Gabor filter for motion analysis is a direct generalization of the $x-y$ 2D Gabor function to a $x-y-t$ 3D Gabor function.

motivation.text: The $x-y-t$ Gabor filter is not selective to velocity. If we have a 2D moving signal $\ell(x-v_xt, y-v_yt)$, the Fourier transform is contained inside a Dirac plane. Therefore, there are an infinite number of planes that will pass by the frequencies of the Gabor filter. All those planes intersect the red line shown in (c). A single Gabor filter cannot disambiguate the input velocity.

This function is selective to signals translating to the right with a speed $v=1$, i.e. $\ell(x-t)$. The red line in (b) shows Dirac line that contains the energy of the moving signal.

concepts.title: Concluding Remarks
concepts.one_liner: Hand-crafted filter banks started as models of human low-level vision and became foundational for many visual tasks but had limited performance compared to learning-based methods.
concepts.content:
In this chapter we have seen the power of using filter banks with some simple nonlinearities.

Hand-crafted filter banks began as models of low-level vision mechanisms in humans and became the basis for many visual tasks such as texture analysis @RG-Heeger-Bergen95, image segmentation @Perona91, motion analysis @Heeger92, orientation analysis @Freeman90c, image denoising @Simoncelli96, and many others.

These approaches had the advantage of being based on first principles and requiring no training data. However, their performance was limited. Many architectures described here can be seen as precursors to learning-based architectures discussed in subsequent chapters.

Before exploring learning-based architectures, we will study multiscale image pyramids in the next chapter.
concepts.motivation_md: Hand-crafted filter banks provide foundational models for visual tasks without training data, but their limited performance motivates studying learning-based architectures.
concepts.recap_md:
- Hand-crafted filter banks model human low-level vision and enable many visual tasks.
- They require no training data but have limited performance.
- They serve as precursors to learning-based architectures.

motivation.text: These approaches had an advantage in that they were based on first principles and required no training data. However, note that performances when using hand-crafted architectures were limited.
