concepts.title: Image Pyramids
concepts.one_liner: Image pyramids provide an efficient representation for space-scale invariant processing by representing images at multiple resolutions and scales.
concepts.content:
In @sec-linear_image_filtering we motivated translation invariant linear filters as a way to account for objects appearing at any location in images. Besides translation invariance, scale invariance is fundamental because objects at different distances appear at different sizes, as shown in @fig-birds_multiscale. To locate all bird instances, an operator invariant to translation and scale is needed. Image pyramids provide an efficient representation for space-scale invariant processing.

Image information occurs over many spatial scales. Image pyramids (multiresolution representations) are useful for analyzing and manipulating images across scales. We discuss three types: Gaussian pyramid (multiple resolutions), Laplacian pyramid (breaks image into isotropic spatial frequency bands), and steerable pyramid (separates scales and orientations).

For example, detecting birds of different sizes with a fixed-size template requires multiple templates or a multiscale image pyramid. The pyramid is constructed by scaling down the image by 25% at each level, reducing pixels to 3/4 the size of the previous image. This approach is computationally efficient since convolutions remain small.

Multiscale image processing and pyramids have many applications beyond scale-invariant object detection. This chapter describes important image pyramids and their uses.

(see figure: Objects in images appear at arbitrary locations and with arbitrary image sizes.)

(see figure: Multiscale image pyramid. Each image is 25 percent smaller than the previous one. The red box indicates the size of a template used for detecting birds. As the size of the template is fixed; it will...)
concepts.motivation_md: Objects appear at arbitrary locations and scales in images; image pyramids enable efficient, scale- and translation-invariant processing to detect and analyze such objects.
concepts.recap_md:
- Image pyramids represent images at multiple resolutions for multiscale analysis.
- Gaussian, Laplacian, and steerable pyramids offer different frequency and orientation decompositions.
- Multiscale pyramids enable efficient detection of objects at varying sizes.

key_passage.text: Image pyramids (i.e., multiresolution representations for images) are a useful data structure for analyzing and manipulating images over a range of spatial scales.

motivation.text: In addition to translation invariance, scale invariance is another fundamental property of images. Due to perspective projection, objects at different distances will appear with different sizes as shown in fig-birds_multiscale. Therefore, if we want to locate all the bird instances in this image, we will have to apply an operator that is invariant in translation and in scale. Image pyramids provide an efficient representation for space-scale invariant processing.

example.text: As a motivating example, let's assume we want to detect the birds from fig-birds_multiscale. If we have a template of a bird, normalized correlation will be able to detect only the birds that have a similar image size than the template. To introduce scale invariance, one possible solution is to change the size of the template to cover a wide range of possible sizes and apply them to the image. Then, the ensemble of templates will be able to detect birds of different sizes. The disadvantage of this approach is that it will be computationally expensive as detecting large birds will require computing convolutions with big kernels, which is very slow. Another alternative is to change the image size as shown in fig-birds_multiscale_processing, resulting in a multiscale image pyramid. Now we can use the pyramid to detect birds at different sizes using a single template. The red box in the figure denotes the size of the template used. The figure shows how birds of different sizes become detectable at, at least, one of the levels of the pyramid. This method will be more efficient as the template can be kept small and the convolutions will remain computationally efficient.

concepts.title: Linear Image Transforms
concepts.one_liner: A linear image transform represents an image as coefficients via projections onto basis vectors and can be invertible, oversampled, or undersampled.
concepts.content:
For an input image $\boldsymbol\ell$ with $N$ pixels, a linear transform is given by:
$$\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{P}^\mathsf{T} \boldsymbol\ell$$
where $\mathbf{r}$ is a vector of dimensionality $M$, and $\mathbf{P}$ is an $N \times M$ matrix. The columns of $\mathbf{P} = [\mathbf{P}_0, \mathbf{P}_1, ..., \mathbf{P}_{M-1}]$ are the projection vectors. The transform coefficients are $\mathbf{r}_i = \mathbf{P}_i^\mathsf{T} \boldsymbol\ell$. Thus, $\mathbf{r}$ is a representation of the image $\boldsymbol\ell$ in a different basis than the original pixels.

We want transforms that are invertible, so the input $\boldsymbol\ell$ can be recovered from coefficients $\mathbf{r}$:
$$\boldsymbol\ell = \mathbf{Q} \mathbf{r} = \sum_{i=0}^{M-1} \mathbf{r}_i \mathbf{Q}_i$$
where columns of $\mathbf{Q} = [\mathbf{Q}_0, \mathbf{Q}_1, ..., \mathbf{Q}_{M-1}]$ are basis vectors. The input is reconstructed as a linear combination of basis vectors weighted by coefficients.

The transform $\mathbf{P}$ is **critically sampled** if $M=N$, **oversampled** if $M > N$, and **undersampled** if $M < N$. The transform is complete (encodes all image structure) if invertible. If critically sampled and complete, then $\mathbf{Q} = (\mathbf{P}^\mathsf{T})^{-1}$. If overcomplete and complete, the inverse is the pseudoinverse $\mathbf{Q} = (\mathbf{P} \mathbf{P}^\mathsf{T})^{-1} \mathbf{P}$.

An important special case is when the transform is **self-inverting**, satisfying $\mathbf{P} \mathbf{P}^\mathsf{T} = \mathbf{I}$. The transform values can be real or complex (e.g., Fourier transform). For complex transforms, replace $\mathbf{P}^\mathsf{T}$ by the conjugate transpose.
concepts.motivation_md: Linear image transforms provide alternate representations of images via projections onto basis vectors, enabling invertible, efficient encoding and reconstruction of image data.
concepts.recap_md:
- Linear image transforms represent images as coefficients via projections onto basis vectors.
- Transforms can be critically sampled ($M=N$), oversampled ($M > N$), or undersampled ($M < N$).
- Invertible transforms allow reconstruction of the original image from coefficients.

key_passage.text: For an input image $\boldsymbol\ell$ with $N$ pixels, a linear transform is: $$\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{P}^\mathsf{T}\boldsymbol\ell$$ where $\mathbf{r}$ is a vector of dimensionality $M$, and $\mathbf{P}$ is a matrix of size $N \times M$. The columns of $\mathbf{P} = \left[\mathbf{P}_0, \mathbf{P}_1, ...,\mathbf{P}_{M-1}\right]$ are the projection vectors. The vector $\mathbf{r}$ contains the transform coefficients: $\mathbf{r}_i = \mathbf{P}_i^\mathsf{T}\boldsymbol\ell$. The vector $\mathbf{r}$ corresponds to a different representation of the image $\boldsymbol\ell$ than the original pixel space.

motivation.text: We are interested in transforms that are invertible, so that we can recover the input $\boldsymbol\ell$ from the projection coefficients $\mathbf{r}$: $$\boldsymbol\ell= \mathbf{Q} \mathbf{r} = \sum_{i=0}^{M-1} \mathbf{r}_i \mathbf{Q}_i$$ The columns of $\mathbf{Q}= \left[\mathbf{Q}_0, \mathbf{Q}_1, ...,\mathbf{Q}_{M-1}\right]$ are the basis vectors. The input signal $\boldsymbol\ell$ can be reconstructed as a linear combination of the basis vectors $\mathbf{Q}_i$ weighted by the representation coefficients $\mathbf{r}_i$.

concepts.title: quadrature mirror filter (QMF) transform
concepts.one_liner: The quadrature mirror filter (QMF) transform is a self-inverting transform equivalent to convolution with orthogonal kernels and has a multiscale version.
concepts.content:
The quadrature mirror filter (QMF) transform is an example of a self-inverting transform @Adelson87b. For 1D signals of length 4, the QMF transform matrix is:
$$
\mathbf{P} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
$$
This corresponds to convolving the input signal with two orthogonal kernels, $[1,1]$ and $[1,-1]$, with stride 2.

This transform also has a multiscale version that is self-inverting.
concepts.motivation_md: The QMF transform provides a self-inverting, efficient way to analyze signals via convolution with orthogonal kernels, useful in multiscale signal processing.
concepts.recap_md:
- The QMF transform is self-inverting and represented by a specific matrix.
- It corresponds to convolution with orthogonal kernels $[1,1]$ and $[1,-1]$ with stride 2.
- A multiscale version of the QMF transform exists and is also self-inverting.

concepts.title: Gaussian Pyramid
concepts.one_liner: A Gaussian pyramid is a recursive multiresolution image representation created by low-pass filtering and downsampling repeatedly.
concepts.content:
A Gaussian pyramid is a recursive algorithm to create multiresolution versions of an image. A Gaussian filter is natural for blurring because successive applications equal a single wider Gaussian filter.

The algorithm involves two steps: convolving the image with a low-pass filter (e.g., the fourth binomial filter $\mathbf{b}_4 = [1,4,6,4,1]/16$, normalized) separably in each dimension, then subsampling by a factor of 2. Each level is obtained by filtering the previous level with the binomial filter and downsampling by 2 in each dimension. Applied recursively, this generates a sequence of images, each smaller and lower resolution than the previous.

@fig-gausspyr shows a Gaussian pyramid with six levels, each half the resolution of the previous. The pyramid is built independently for each color channel.

The two steps can be written in matrix form for a 1D image:
$$\mathbf{g}_{k+1} = \mathbf{D}_k \mathbf{B}_k \mathbf{g}_k = \mathbf{G}_k \mathbf{g}_k$$
where $\mathbf{D}_k$ is the downsampling operator, $\mathbf{B}_k$ is convolution with the binomial filter, and $\mathbf{G}_k = \mathbf{D}_k \mathbf{B}_k$ is the blur-and-downsample operator for level $k$.

One block of Gaussian pyramid computation is shown in the diagram.

The sequence $\mathbf{g}_0, \mathbf{g}_1, ..., \mathbf{g}_N$ is called the Gaussian pyramid.
concepts.motivation_md: Gaussian pyramids enable efficient multiresolution image analysis by recursively blurring and downsampling, capturing image structure at multiple scales.
concepts.recap_md:
- Gaussian pyramids recursively blur and downsample images to create multiresolution representations.
- Each level is half the resolution of the previous.
- The process can be expressed as a matrix operation combining blur and downsampling.

key_passage.text: Here's an elegant, efficient algorithm for making a resolution--reduced version of an input image. It involves two steps: convolving the image with a low-pass filter (e.g., using the fourth binomial filter $\mathbf{b}_4 = [1, 4, 6, 4, 1]$ / 16, normalized to sum to 1, separably in each dimension), and then subsampling by a factor of 2 the result.

motivation.text: We'd like to make a recursive algorithm for creating a multiresolution version of an image. A Gaussian filter is a natural one to use to blur out an image, since the multiple successive application of a Gaussian filter is equivalent to application of a single, wider Gaussian filter.

example.text: Gaussian pyramid with six levels. The first level, $\mathbf{g}_0$, is the input image. The Gaussian pyramid is built for each color channel independently.

concepts.title: Laplacian Pyramid
concepts.one_liner: The Laplacian pyramid represents image details lost between Gaussian pyramid levels by subtracting an upsampled lower-resolution image from a higher-resolution image.
concepts.content:
In the Gaussian pyramid, each level loses some fine image details from the previous level. The Laplacian pyramid @Burt83 represents, at each level, what is present in a Gaussian pyramid image but not in the level below. This is calculated by expanding (upsampling) the lower-resolution Gaussian image to the same size as the higher-resolution image, then subtracting the two. This is done recursively.

To compute the Laplacian pyramid, we calculate the difference between $\mathbf{g}_k$ and $\mathbf{g}_{k+1}$. First, upsample $\mathbf{g}_{k+1}$ to the size of $\mathbf{g}_k$. Let $\mathbf{F}_k = \mathbf{B}_k \mathbf{U}_k$ be the upsample-and-blur operator for level $k$, where $\mathbf{U}_k$ inserts zeros between samples and $\mathbf{B}_k$ is the same blur filter used in the Gaussian pyramid. The Laplacian pyramid coefficients at level $k$ are:
$$\mathbf{l}_k = \mathbf{g}_k - \mathbf{F}_k \mathbf{g}_{k+1} = (\mathbf{I}_k - \mathbf{F}_k \mathbf{G}_k) \mathbf{g}_k = \mathbf{L}_k \mathbf{g}_k$$

One block of Laplacian pyramid computation is shown in the diagram.

@fig-laplacpyr shows the Laplacian pyramid for an image. To compute an $N$-level Laplacian pyramid, first compute a Gaussian pyramid with $N+1$ levels. The last Gaussian level is the low-pass residual.

The Laplacian pyramid is built independently for each color channel.

Matrix forms for 1D inputs and operators are given, showing the detailed computation. The factor 2 compensates for zero insertion reducing average signal value.

Interestingly, the Laplacian pyramid is an invertible transform.
concepts.motivation_md: The Laplacian pyramid captures image details lost between Gaussian pyramid levels, enabling efficient multiscale image representation and reconstruction.
concepts.recap_md:
- The Laplacian pyramid represents differences between Gaussian pyramid levels.
- It is computed by subtracting an upsampled, blurred lower-resolution image from a higher-resolution image.
- The Laplacian pyramid is invertible and built independently per color channel.

key_passage.text: The Laplacian pyramid is simple: it represents, at each level, what is present in a Gaussian pyramid image of one level, but not present at the level below it. We calculate that by expanding the lower-resolution Gaussian pyramid image to the same pixel resolution as the neighboring higher-resolution Gaussian pyramid image, then subtracting the two. This calculation is made in a recursive, telescoping fashion.

motivation.text: In the Gaussian pyramid, each level losses some of the fine image details available in the previous level.

example.text: Let's look at the steps for calculating a Laplacian pyramid. What we want is to compute the difference between \mathbf{g}_k and \mathbf{g}_{k+1}. To do this first we need to upsample the image \mathbf{g}_{k+1} so that it has the same size as \mathbf{g}_k. Let \mathbf{F}_k = \mathbf{B}_k \mathbf{U}_k be the upsample-and-blur operator for pyramid level k. The operator \mathbf{F}_k applies first the upsampling operator \mathbf{U}_k, that inserts zeros between samples, followed by blurring by the same filter \mathbf{B}_k than the one we used for the Gaussian pyramid. The Laplacian pyramid coefficients, \mathbf{l}_k, at pyramid level k, are: $$\mathbf{l}_{k} = \mathbf{g}_k - \mathbf{F}_k \mathbf{g}_{k+1} = (\mathbf{I}_k - \mathbf{F}_k \mathbf{G}_k) \mathbf{g}_{k} = \mathbf{L}_k \mathbf{g}_{k}$$ One **block** of the Laplacian pyramid computation.

concepts.title: low-pass residual
concepts.one_liner: The low-pass residual in the Laplacian pyramid enables recursive reconstruction of the Gaussian pyramid and original image.
concepts.content:
The low-pass residual signal associated with the Laplacian pyramid allows recursive reconstruction of the corresponding Gaussian pyramid. Recall that in the Gaussian pyramid, level 1 is the original image itself, so we can reconstruct the original image from the Laplacian pyramid.

Reconstruction is done recursively from $k = N-1$ down to $k=0$:
$$\mathbf{g}_k = \mathbf{l}_k + \mathbf{F}_k \mathbf{g}_{k+1}$$

The diagram in @fig-laplacian_pyr_architecture shows the Gaussian pyramid, the Laplacian pyramid, and the Laplacian inversion for a three-level Laplacian pyramid. Reconstruction uses the Laplacian pyramid coefficients $\mathbf{l}_0, \mathbf{l}_1, ..., \mathbf{l}_2$ and the low-pass residual $\mathbf{g}_3$ to recover the input signal $\boldsymbol\ell = \mathbf{g}_0$.
concepts.motivation_md: The low-pass residual enables reconstructing the original image from the Laplacian pyramid, making the transform invertible and useful for image processing.
concepts.recap_md:
- The low-pass residual enables recursive reconstruction of the Gaussian pyramid.
- Reconstruction uses Laplacian pyramid coefficients and the low-pass residual.
- This process recovers the original image from the Laplacian pyramid.

key_passage.text: Using the low-pass residual signal associated with the Laplacian pyramid, we can recursively reconstruct the corresponding Gaussian pyramid.

motivation.text: Remember that in the Gaussian pyramid level 1 is just the original image itself, so we can use this to reconstruct the original image from the Laplacian pyramid.

example.text: The diagram in fig-laplacian_pyr_architecture shows the Gaussian pyramid, the Laplacian pyramid and the Laplacian inversion for a three-level Laplacian pyramid. The reconstruction uses the Laplacian pyramid \mathbf{l}_0,\mathbf{l}_1,...,\mathbf{l}_2 and the low pass residual \mathbf{g}_3 to recover the input signal \boldsymbol\ell=\mathbf{g}_0.

concepts.title: equations for an attention layer
concepts.one_liner: The equation for an attention layer is the same as for a linear layer except that the weights are a function of some other data.
concepts.motivation_md: Attention layers generalize linear layers by making the weights depend on other data, enabling dynamic weighting of input tokens based on context or queries.
concepts.recap_md:
- Attention layers compute output as $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}$ where $\mathbf{A}$ depends on other data.
- The weights $\mathbf{A}$ are determined by a function $f$.
- This makes attention layers more flexible than fixed-weight linear layers.

concepts.title: attention allocation function f
concepts.one_liner: $f$ is a function that determines how much attention to apply to each token in $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}$; it determines the weights in this combination.
concepts.content: The key question, of course, is what exactly is $f$? What inputs does $f$ depend on and what is $f$'s mathematical form? Before writing out the exact equations, we start with the intuition: $f$ is a function that determines how much attention to apply to each token in $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}$; because this layer is just a weighted combination of tokens, $f$ is simply determining the weights in this combination. The $f$ can depend on any number of input signals that tell the net what to pay attention to.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding $f$ is crucial because it controls how attention weights are assigned to input tokens, enabling the model to focus on relevant information dynamically.
concepts.recap_md:
- $f$ determines attention weights applied to each token in $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}$.
- Attention layer output is a weighted combination of tokens.
- $f$ can depend on various input signals guiding focus.

concepts.title: attention example: counting animals
concepts.one_liner: The function $f$ produces weights high for tokens representing animal heads to count animals in an image.
concepts.content: As a concrete example, consider that we want to be able to ask questions about different objects in our safari example image, such as how many animals are in the photo. One strategy would be to attend to each token that represents an animal's head, and then just count them up. The $f$ would take as input the text query, and would produce as output weights $\mathbf{A}$ that are high for the $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}$ tokens that correspond to any animal's head and are low for all other $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}$ tokens. If we train such a system to answer questions about counting animals, then the token code vectors might naturally end up encoding a feature that represents the number of animal heads in their receptive field; after all, this would be a solution that would solve our problem (it would minimize the loss and correctly answer the question). Other solutions might be possible, but we will focus on this intuitive solution, which we illustrate in @fig-transformers-attention_layer_safari_query_cartoon.
concepts.motivation_md: This example illustrates how attention weights can be learned to focus on relevant tokens (animal heads) to answer specific queries like counting animals.
concepts.recap_md:
- $f$ outputs weights high for tokens representing animal heads.
- Attention focuses on relevant tokens to answer questions.
- Token vectors may encode features like number of animal heads.

concepts.title: Query-Key-Value Attention
concepts.one_liner: In query-key-value attention, each token is associated with a query vector, a key vector, and a value vector.
concepts.content:
### Query-Key-Value Attention

Transformers use a particular kind of attention based on the idea of queries, keys, and values. In query-key-value attention, each token is associated with a **query** vector, a **key** vector, and a **value** vector.

The idea of queries, keys, and values comes from databases, where a database cell holds a *value*, which is retrieved when a *query* matches the cell's *key*. Tokens are like database cells and attention is like retrieving information from the database of tokens.

We define these vectors as linear transformations of the token's code vector, projecting to query/key/value vectors of length $m$. For a token $\mathbf{t}$, we have: 

$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{W}_q \mathbf{t} \quad\quad \triangleleft \text{ query}\\
    \mathbf{k} &= \mathbf{W}_k \mathbf{t} \quad\quad \triangleleft \text{ key}\\
    \mathbf{v} &= \mathbf{W}_v \mathbf{t} \quad\quad \triangleleft \text{ value}
\end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Query-key-value attention structures tokens with query, key, and value vectors to efficiently retrieve relevant information, inspired by database lookup concepts.
concepts.recap_md:
- Each token has query, key, and value vectors.
- Queries match keys to retrieve values, like a database.
- Vectors are linear projections of token code vectors.

concepts.title: text tokenization for queries
concepts.one_liner: In transformers, all inputs including textual questions are tokenized into tokens.
concepts.content:
In transformers, all inputs to the net are tokenized, so the textual question "How many animals are in the photo?" will also be represented as a token.

We do not cover them in this book, but methods from natural language processing can be used to transform text into a token, or into a sequence of tokens.
concepts.motivation_md: Tokenization converts text into a format the transformer can process, enabling it to handle natural language queries.
concepts.recap_md:
- All inputs to transformers are tokenized.
- Textual questions become tokens.
- NLP methods convert text into tokens or token sequences.

concepts.title: attention similarity measured by dot product
concepts.one_liner: The similarity between a query and a key is most commonly measured by their dot product.
concepts.motivation_md: Measuring similarity by dot product allows the attention mechanism to quantify how relevant each token is to the query, guiding attention weights.
concepts.recap_md:
- Attention weight depends on similarity between query and key.
- Dot product $\mathbf{q}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{k}$ is the common similarity measure.
- Similarities form a vector $\mathbf{s}$ for all tokens in $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}$.

key_passage.text: The most common measure of similarity between a query $\mathbf{q}$ and a key $\mathbf{k}$ is the dot product $\mathbf{q}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{k}$.

motivation.text: The similarity between the query and the key determines the amount of attention weight the query will apply to the token with that key.

example.text:
Querying each token in $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}$ in this way gives us a vector of similarities: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{s} = [s_1, \ldots, s_N]^\mathsf{T}&= [\mathbf{q}_{\texttt{question}}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{k}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_{\texttt{question}}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{k}_N]^\mathsf{T}
\end{aligned}$$

concepts.title: Upsampling
concepts.one_liner: Upsampling consists in the sequence of expansion followed by interpolation.
concepts.motivation_md: Upsampling is used to increase the resolution of a signal or image by expanding it and then interpolating to fill in new values, enabling finer detail representation.
concepts.recap_md:
- Upsampling involves expansion followed by interpolation.
- Expansion is denoted as $z[n,m] = \ell_{\texttt{in}}[n,m] \uparrow k$.
- Interpolation is performed by convolution: $\ell_{\texttt{out}}[n,m] = z[n,m] \circ h_k[n,m]$.

example.text:
$$\begin{aligned} z \left[n,m\right] &= \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n,m\right] \uparrow k & \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \texttt{expansion}\\ \ell_{\texttt{out}}[n,m] &= z \left[n,m\right] \circ h_k \left[n,m\right] & \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \texttt{conv}
\end{aligned}$$

concepts.title: Gabor Filters
concepts.one_liner: Gabor functions are localized in both the spatial and frequency domain and achieve the best simultaneous localization in space and frequency.
concepts.content:
In @sec-fourier_analysis we discussed several useful image representations: representing an image in the frequency domain and decomposing it into amplitude and phase, and also the analysis of image content across different scales and orientations. The Fourier transform is a tool that allows us to extract that information, but only globally. For this information to be useful it needs to be localized. For instance, the analysis of orientations of local image structures can be done using image gradients (@sec-image_derivatives), which are localized in space. In fact, we made use of image derivatives in @sec-simplesystem to recover the three-dimensional (3D) structure of a scene. Here we will discuss another family of filters that has a long history of being used for image analysis: Gabor filters.

@fig-1D_gabor_function (a) shows a one-dimensional (1D) sine function. This function has infinite support. When used as a representation, the Fourier coefficients are obtained as the scalar product between the sine wave and the input image. Each Fourier coefficient involves a point-wise multiplication between the wave and the input image and then the sum of the result. As a consequence of the infinite support of the wave, one single Fourier coefficient does not tell us anything about what happens locally inside the analyzed image.

A good start for a localized image analysis is to restrict the spatial support of a sinusoidal basis function. One function that has a local support (a lot of nice properties as we discussed in @sec-blur_filters) is the Gaussian function (@fig-1D_gabor_function [b]). The product of the Gaussian and the sine wave (or a cosine wave) gives the function with the profile shown in @fig-1D_gabor_function (c) called a Gabor filter. Gabor functions were introduced by Dennis Gabor in 1946 @Gabor1946TheoryOC.

(see figure: Construction of a Gabor function. (a) Sine function. (b) Gaussian function. (c) Gabor function obtained as the product of (a) and (b).)

Gabor functions, originally proposed in 1D, were made popular as an
operator for image analysis by Goesta Granlund in his paper *In Search
of a General Picture Processing Operator* @GRANLUND1978155.

Gabor functions are localized in both the spatial and
frequency domain. One remarkable property of the Gabor function is that
it is the optimal function that achieves the best simultaneous
localization in space and frequency.

Gabor functions can be extended to two dimensions by using 2D Gaussians and waves. We can also use complex waves (@sec-fourier_analysis) as they will give us a more general form of the Gabor function.

We can multiply a complex Fourier
basis function, $\exp{ \left(j  \left(u_0 x + v_0 y \right)  \right)}$,
by a spatially localized 2D Gaussian window,
$\exp{\left(-\frac{x^2 + y^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right) }$ to obtain a Gabor
function, $\psi(x,y)$:
$$\psi(x,y;u_0,v_0) = \frac{1}{2\pi \sigma^2} \exp{\left(-\frac{x^2 + y^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right)} \exp{ \left( j \left(u_0 x + v_0 y \right) \right)}
$$
{#eq-gaborcomplexfilter}

A Gabor function defined as in equation (@eq-gaborcomplexfilter) is a
complex-valued function of location and frequency. We can get the cosine
and sine waves by looking at the real and imaginary components,
$\psi(x,y;u_0,v_0) =  \psi_r(x,y;u_0,v_0) + j \psi_i(x,y;u_0,v_0)$ with
$$\psi_r(x,y;u_0,v_0) = \frac{1}{2\pi \sigma^2} \exp{\left(-\frac{x^2 + y^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right)} \cos{ \left(u_0 x + v_0 y \right) }$$
$$\psi_i(x,y;u_0,v_0) = \frac{1}{2\pi \sigma^2} \exp{\left(-\frac{x^2 + y^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right)} \sin{ \left(u_0 x + v_0 y \right) }$$
Where $\psi_r(x,y;u_0,v_0)$ and $\psi_i(x,y;u_0,v_0)$ are the cosine and
sine phase Gabor filters. @fig-gabors shows the Gaussian window and the
concepts.motivation_md: Gabor filters provide a localized analysis of image content in both space and frequency, overcoming the global limitations of the Fourier transform and enabling detailed orientation and scale analysis.
concepts.recap_md:
- Gabor filters combine a sinusoidal wave with a Gaussian envelope.
- They are localized in both spatial and frequency domains.
- The complex Gabor function has real (cosine) and imaginary (sine) parts.

concepts.title: Quadrature Pairs and the Hilbert Transform
concepts.one_liner: Pairs of filters can be in a relationship to each other that is called quadrature phase.
concepts.content:
Pairs of filters can be in a relationship to each other that is called
**quadrature phase**. This relationship is useful for many low-level
visual processing tasks. When in quadrature phase, pairs of oriented
filters can measure what is called local oriented energy, can identify
contours, independently of the phase of the contour, and can measure
positional changes very accurately. Let's start with the mathematical
definition of quadrature.

For notational simplicity, we'll describe quadrature pair filters in the
time domain, but they extend naturally to two or more dimensions.
Consider an even symmetric zero-mean signal, $\ell(t)$, and with Fourier
transform $\mathscr{L}(\omega)$, with $\mathscr{L}(0)=0$ because the
signal is zero-mean. In the Fourier domain, two functions,
$\mathscr{L}(\omega)$ and $\mathscr{L}_h(\omega)$, are said to be
Hilbert transform pairs if: $$\mathscr{L}_h(\omega) = \begin{cases}
    ~  - j \mathscr{L}(\omega)    & \quad \text{if } \omega >0 \\
    j \mathscr{L}(\omega)    & \quad \text{if } \omega <0 \\
\end{cases}$$We now define the complex signal: $$\ell_a(t) = \ell(t) + j \ell_h(t)
$$
{#eq-analyticsignal} 

where $\ell_h(t)$ is the Hilbert transform of
$\ell(t)$. The signal $\ell_a(t)$ is called the **analytic signal** and
its Fourier transform has no negative frequency components.

It is easy to show that 
$$\mathscr{L}_a(\omega) = \begin{cases}
    ~  2\mathscr{L}(\omega)    & \quad \text{if } \omega >0 \\
    0    & \quad \text{if } \omega <0 \\
\end{cases}$$ 

It is interesting to write the complex signal $\ell_a(t)$
in polar form: $$\ell_a(t) = a(t) \exp \left( j \, \theta (t) \right)
$$
{#eq-analyticsignalpolar} where $a(t)$ is the instantaneous amplitude
(**local amplitude**) and $\theta (t)$ is the instantaneous phase
(**local phase**). This particular representation is common in
communications theory, and it has been used to build image
representations invariant to certain image structures as we will discuss
in the following sections.

The extension of the Hilbert transform to images can be done in several
ways. The most common approach in image processing is to define one
direction, $n$, in the frequency space and then the Hilbert transform is
as follows: 

$$
\mathscr{L}_h(\omega_x,\omega_y) = \begin{cases}
    ~  - j \mathscr{L}(\omega_x,\omega_y)    & \quad \text{if } n^T \cdot (\omega_x,\omega_y) > 0 \\
    j \mathscr{L}(\omega_x,\omega_y)    & \quad \text{if } n^T \cdot (\omega_x,\omega_y) <0 \\
\end{cases}
$$

Two band-pass filters are said to be in quadrature if the impulse
responses are Hilbert transform pairs along some orientation in the
frequency domain. Sine and cosine functions of the same frequency are
Hilbert transform pairs, as are sine and cosine phase Gabor functions,
of the same frequency and Gaussian envelope parameters. Thus, these
filter pairs are also quadrature pairs. When convolving two filters in
quadrature with a signal (or image) the two outputs are also in
quadrature.

The quadrature in the Gabor functions is an approximation that only
holds for $\sigma$ sufficiently large. For small $\sigma$ the filter
does not form a quadrature pair. For large $\sigma$, the real and
imaginary parts of the Gabor filter (cosine and sine phase local
filters) are filters in quadrature with the vector $n=(u_0,v_0)$
pointing in the direction of the central frequency of the Gabor
function.
concepts.motivation_md: Quadrature pairs enable measurement of local oriented energy and contours independent of phase, crucial for accurate visual processing and positional change detection.
concepts.recap_md:
- Quadrature phase describes a relationship between pairs of filters.
- Hilbert transform pairs define quadrature pairs in the frequency domain.
- Gabor filter real and imaginary parts approximate quadrature pairs for large $\sigma$.

When in quadrature phase, pairs of oriented filters can measure what is called local oriented energy, can identify contours, independently of the phase of the contour, and can measure positional changes very accurately.

concepts.title: Local Amplitude
concepts.one_liner: The squared local amplitude is a measure of the image power within the frequency bandwidth of the filters in the local neighborhood.
concepts.content:
Let $h(x,y)$ and $q(x,y)$ be band-pass filters in quadrature, and let
$\ell_h(x,y)$ and $\ell_q(x,y)$ be the result of convolving the signal
$\ell(x,y)$ with $h(x,y)$ and $q(x,y)$, respectively. Then, the squared
local amplitude is a measure of the image power within the frequency
bandwidth of the filters in the local neighborhood of $(x,y)$:
$$a^2(x,y) = \ell_h ^2 (x,y) + \ell_q ^2 (x,y)$$ @fig-quad2 shows the steps
to compute the local amplitude of an input image using Gabor filters.
This is like a two-layer convolutional neural network with two channels
in the first layer, a squaring nonlinearity and then followed by a sum
in the second layer. This very simple system can perform a number of
interesting operations.

concepts.recap_md:
- Local amplitude is computed from the squared sum of filter responses in quadrature.
- It measures image power within the filters' frequency bandwidth locally.
- Computation resembles a two-layer convolutional neural network with squaring and summing.

Then, the squared local amplitude is a measure of the image power within the frequency bandwidth of the filters in the local neighborhood of $(x,y)$: $$a^2(x,y) = \ell_h ^2 (x,y) + \ell_q ^2 (x,y)$$

concepts.title: Local Phase
concepts.one_liner: The local phase is a measure of angle between the real and imaginary components of filter responses.
concepts.content:
The local phase is a measure of angle between the real and imaginary
components (cosine and sine in the case of complex Gabor filters):
$$\theta(x,y) = \angle \left[ \ell_h(x,y) + j \ell_q(x,y) \right]$$
where $\theta (x,y)$ is the instantaneous phase (local phase). This is
another interesting nonlinearity although it is not commonly used in
neural networks. Local image phase has been used to estimate motion
@Fleet89. This information is invariant to local changes of contrast and
it is only sensitive to the local image structure.
concepts.motivation_md: Local phase captures structural information in images invariant to contrast changes, useful for tasks like motion estimation.
concepts.recap_md:
- Local phase is the angle between real and imaginary filter responses.
- It provides contrast-invariant information about local image structure.
- Used in applications such as motion estimation.

concepts.title: Gabor Filter Bank
concepts.one_liner: A filter bank is a collection of filters, each tuned to extract a different image feature, used to build an image representation.
concepts.content:
Another useful concept is the notion of **filter bank**. A filter banks
is a collection of filters, each tuned to extract a different image
feature, and used to build an image representation.

As shown in @fig-gabor_ft, 2D Gabor filters are selective in spatial
frequency. It is very useful to work with sets of Gabor filters, each
selective to a different spatial frequency so that they cover the full
space of spatial frequencies.

@fig-gabor_rectandpolar_tiles shows two different arrangements of Gabor
filters. @fig-gabor_rectandpolar_tiles (a) shows a set of Gabor filters
sampling the frequency domain using a rectangular grid.
@fig-gabor_rectandpolar_tiles (c) shows the corresponding (cosine) Gabor
kernels. All the functions have the same $\sigma$.
@fig-gabor_rectandpolar_tiles (b) shows a polar arrangement of Gabor
functions, and @fig-gabor_rectandpolar_tiles (d) the spatial kernels.
Here, the Gaussian width $\sigma$ is proportional to the distance
between the central frequency and the origin. This produces filters that
are rotated and scaled versions of each other.
concepts.motivation_md: Gabor filter banks allow comprehensive image analysis by covering multiple spatial frequencies and orientations, enabling rich feature extraction.
concepts.recap_md:
- Filter banks are collections of filters tuned to different features.
- Gabor filter banks cover spatial frequencies using rectangular or polar grids.
- Polar arrangements produce rotated and scaled versions of filters.

concepts.title: Steerable Filters and Orientation Analysis
concepts.one_liner: Steerable filters allow continuous rotation of a filter $h(x,y)$ to any orientation $\theta$ by interpolation between a fixed number of predefined orientations.
concepts.content:
One question that arises with oriented filters is how to change their
orientation. More precisely, given a filter $h(x,y)$, we want to
transform it into a continuous function $h(x,y, \theta)$ of angle
$\theta$. The angle $\theta$ specifies the rotation of the original
filter $h(x,y)$.

In the case of the Gabor filters, equation (@eq-gaborcomplexfilter),
each orientation requires convolving the image with a Gabor function
tuned to that orientation. But do we need to create a new Gabor function
for each orientation, or can we interpolate between a fixed number of
predefined oriented filter outputs? How many orientations need to be
sampled?

In this section we will study a generalization of the
Nyquist sampling theorem but applied to dimensions different than
space.

We'd like an analog in orientation for the Nyquist sampling theorem in
space: given a certain number of discrete samples in orientation (or
space), can one interpolate between the samples and synthesize what
would have been found from having a filter (or a spatial sample) at some
arbitrary, intermediate orientation? The answer is yes, and the number
of filter samples needed to interpolate depends on the form of the
filter.

In @sec-image_derivatives, we described the simplest example of an oriented filter: a Gaussian derivative. As we discussed in @eq-steerable_derivative_filter, we can synthesize a directional derivative in any direction as a linear combination of derivatives in the horizontal and vertical directions. By the linearity of convolution, that applies to the derivative applied to any filter or image, as well. It can be seen that the **steering equation** for the first derivative of a Gaussian filter is
concepts.motivation_md: Steerable filters enable efficient computation of filter responses at any orientation by interpolating between a limited set of fixed orientations, reducing computational cost.
concepts.recap_md:
- Steerable filters generalize filter orientation to a continuous angle $\theta$.
- Interpolation between fixed orientations can synthesize responses at arbitrary angles.
- The number of samples needed depends on the filter's form.

concepts.title: encoder-decoder
concepts.one_liner: An encoder-decoder architecture first encodes the input image into a low-dimensional representation, then decodes it back into an image output.
concepts.content: One powerful thing you can do with encoders and decoders is to put them together, forming an **encoder-decoder**. Such an architecture first encodes the input image into a low-dimensional representation, then decodes the representation back into an image output. This is therefore a suitable architecture for image-to-image problems, and it has a few advantages over the image-to-image CNNs we saw in @sec-convolutional_neural_networks-spatial_outputs: 1) by downsampling, the internal feature maps are smaller, using less memory and computation, 2) encoder-decoders introduce an **information bottleneck** -- i.e. the representation between the encoder and decoder is low-dimensional and can only transmit so much information -- and this forces abstraction. This latter concept is one we will study in much greater detail in @sec-representation_learning, where we will see several benefits of compressing a signal. A schematic of the encoder-decoder architecture is shown in
concepts.motivation_md: Encoder-decoder architectures compress input data into a low-dimensional form, enabling efficient memory use and forcing the model to learn abstract representations, which is beneficial for image-to-image tasks.
concepts.recap_md:
- Encoder-decoders encode input images into low-dimensional representations and then decode them back.
- They reduce memory and computation by downsampling internal feature maps.
- The information bottleneck forces the model to abstract important features.

concepts.title: U-Nets
concepts.one_liner: U-Nets add skip connections to encoder-decoders to shuttle information directly across layers, preserving high-frequency details in outputs.
concepts.content:
Encoder-decoders force the signal to pass through a bottleneck, and although this can be a good thing (as discussed above), it also makes the task of the decoder rather difficult. In particular, the decoder may fail to be able to output high frequency details; for a semantic segmentation network, the consequence could be that the predicted label map is very coarse.

To circumvent this problem, we can add that shuttle information directly across blocks of layers in the net. A skip connection $f$ is simply an identity pathway that connects two disparate layers of a net, $f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}$.

Adding skip connections to an encoder-decoder results in an architecture known as a **U-Net** @ronneberger2015u. In this architecture, skip connections are arranged in a mirror pattern, where layer $l$ is connected directly to layer $(L-l)$. The output of a skip connection must somehow be reintegrated into the network. U-nets do this by concatenating the activations from the prior layer to the activations on the later layer, along the channel dimension. This architecture can maintain the information-bottleneck of the encoder-decoder, with its incumbent benefits in terms of memory and compute efficiency and forced abstraction, while also allowing residual information to flow through the skip connections, thereby not sacrificing the ability to output high-frequency spatial predictions. U-Nets look a lot like the steerable pyramids from @sec-image_pyramids, which also consistent of a downsampling *analysis* path followed by an upsampling *synthesis* path, with skip connections in between mirror image stages in the pathways. The main difference is that the U-Net has *learned filters* and *nonlinearities*. A schematic of a U-net is given in @fig-convolutional_neural_nets-unet.

(see figure: U-net architecture. Each block contains a series of layers. The skip connections concatenate activations.)
concepts.motivation_md: U-Nets solve the problem of losing high-frequency details in decoder outputs by adding skip connections that shuttle information directly across layers, preserving fine spatial details.
concepts.recap_md:
- U-Nets add skip connections to encoder-decoders to preserve high-frequency details.
- Skip connections connect layer $l$ to layer $(L-l)$ and concatenate activations.
- This maintains the information bottleneck while allowing detailed spatial predictions.

concepts.title: ResNets
concepts.one_liner: ResNets use residual connections that add the input to the output of a block, enabling very deep networks that can learn identity mappings.
concepts.content:
Another popular architecture that uses skip connections is called **Residual Networks** or **ResNets** @he2016deep. 

See also Highway Networks @srivastava2015highway, a related architecture that uses a form of skip connection but controlled by multiplicative gates.

In the context of ResNets, skip connections are called **residual connections**. This kind of skip connection is *added* to the output of a block of layers $F$:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}= F(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}) + \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \texttt{residual block}
\end{aligned}$$ 

In a **residual block** like this, you can think of $F$ as a *residual* that additively perturbs $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$ to transform it into an improved $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}$. If $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}$ does not have the same dimensionality as $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$, then we can add a linear mapping to convert the dimensions: $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}= F(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}) + \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$.

It is easy for a residual block to simply perform an identity mapping, it just has to learn to set $F$ to zero. Because of this, if we stack many residual blocks in a row, it can end up that the net learns to use only a subset of them. If we set the number of stacked residual blocks to be very large then the net can essentially learn how deep to make itself, using as many blocks as necessary to solve the task. ResNets often exploit this fact by being very deep; for example, they may be hundreds of blocks deep. @fig-convolutional_neural_nets-resnet depicts a 5 block deep ResNet.


(see figure: ResNet architecture. Each block contains a series of layers. The skip connections add activations from one block to the next.)
concepts.motivation_md: ResNets enable very deep neural networks by using residual connections that allow layers to learn identity mappings, preventing degradation and facilitating training.
concepts.recap_md:
- ResNets use residual connections that add input to block outputs.
- Residual blocks can learn identity mappings by setting $F$ to zero.
- Very deep ResNets can learn how many blocks to use, improving performance.

concepts.title: transformer
concepts.one_liner: Transformers are architectures recently supplanting CNNs for vision problems, incorporating stages that process patches independently and globally.
concepts.content: Recently supplanting CNNs as the most successful architectures for vision problems is the **transformer** @sec-transformers. It may be tempting to think, "Why did we bother learning about CNNs then, if transformers are better!" The reason we cover CNNs is not because the exact architecture presented here will last, but because the underlying principles it embodies are ubiquitous in sensory processing. The two key properties mentioned in @sec-convolutional_neural_nets-key_properties are in fact present in transformers and many other architectures beyond CNNs: transformers also include stages that process each patch identically and independently, but they interleave these stages with other stages that globalize information across patches. It comes down to preferences whether you want to call these newer architectures convolutional or not, and there is currently some debate about it in the community. For us it doesn't matter, because if we learn the principles we can recognize them in all the systems we encounter and need not get hung up on names.
concepts.motivation_md: Transformers have become leading architectures for vision tasks by combining local patch processing with global information sharing, embodying principles also found in CNNs.
concepts.recap_md:
- Transformers have recently supplanted CNNs in vision tasks.
- They process patches independently and then globalize information.
- The principles behind CNNs and transformers overlap despite architectural differences.

concepts.title: Recurrent Neural Nets
concepts.one_liner: RNNs are neural nets with feedback connections that model sequences by performing sequential computation.
concepts.content:
RNNs are a neural net architecture for modeling sequences---they perform *sequential* computation (rather than parallel computation).

So far we have seen **feedforward** neural net architectures. These architectures can be represented by directed acyclical computation graphs. (**RNNs**), are neural nets with feedback connections. 

A feedback connection defines a **recurrence** in the computational graph.

Their computation graphs have cycles. That means that the outputs of one layer can send a message back to earlier in the computational pipeline. To make this well-defined, RNNs introduce the notion of **timestep**. One timestep of running an RNN corresponds to one functional call to each layer (or computation node) in the RNN, mapping that layer's inputs to its outputs.
concepts.motivation_md: RNNs model sequential data by introducing feedback connections and timesteps, enabling the network to process sequences over time.
concepts.recap_md:
- RNNs perform sequential computation with feedback connections.
- They have cycles in their computation graphs.
- Timesteps define discrete processing steps mapping inputs to outputs.

motivation.text: Their computation graphs have cycles. That means that the outputs of one layer can send a message back to earlier in the computational pipeline.

concepts.title: graph neural networks
concepts.one_liner: Transformers can also be considered as a special case of graph neural networks (GNNs).
concepts.content: As of this writing, transformers are the dominant architecture in computer vision and in fact in most fields of artificial intelligence. They combine many of the best ideas from earlier architectures—convolutional patchwise processing, residual connections, relu nonlinearities, and normalization layers—with several newer innovations, in particular, vector-valued tokens, attention layers, and positional codes. Transformers can also be considered as a special case of graph neural networks (GNNs). We do not have a separate chapter on GNNs in this book since GNNs, other than transformers, are not yet popular in computer vision. GNNs are a very general class of architecture for processing *sets* by forming a graph of operations over the set. A transformer is doing exactly that: it takes an input set of tokens and, layer by layer, applies a network of transformations over that set until after enough layers a final representation or prediction is read out.
concepts.motivation_md: Graph neural networks (GNNs) generalize architectures like transformers to process sets by forming graphs of operations, enabling powerful representations for complex data structures beyond sequences or grids. (llm_inferred)

- Transformers combine convolutional, residual, nonlinear, and normalization ideas with attention and positional codes.
- GNNs process sets by forming graphs of operations over the set.
- Transformers are a special case of GNNs applying transformations layer by layer to tokens.

concepts.title: natural image
concepts.one_liner: An image is a very high dimensional array of pixels and therefore, the space of all possible images is very large.
concepts.content: First, we need to understand what we mean by a **natural image**. An image is a very high dimensional array of pixels $\ell\left[n,m\right]$ and therefore, the space of all possible images is very large. Even if you consider very small thumbnails of just $32\times32$ pixels and three color channels, with 8 bits per channel, there are more than $10^{7,398}$ possible images. Of course, most of them will just be random noise. @fig-spaces_real_images shows one image, with size $32\times32$ color pixels, sampled from the set of natural images, and on typical example from the set of all images. A typical sample from the set of all images is $32\times32$ pixels independently sampled from a uniform distribution.

- Images are high dimensional arrays of pixels $\ell[n,m]$.
- Even small $32\times32$ color images have over $10^{7,398}$ possible variations.
- Most possible images are random noise, unlike natural images.

concepts.title: Independent Pixels
concepts.one_liner: The simplest image model assumes all pixels are independent and their intensity value is drawn from some stationary distribution.
concepts.content:
The simplest image model will consist in assuming that all pixels are independent and their intensity value is drawn from some stationary distribution (i.e., the distribution of pixel intensities is independent of the location in the image). We can then write the probability, $p_{\theta}(\boldsymbol\ell)$, of an image, $\ell[n,m]$ with size $N \times M$, as follows:
$$p_{\theta}(\boldsymbol\ell) = \prod_{n=1}^{N} \prod_{m=1}^{M} p_{\theta}\left(\ell[n,m] \right)$$
We use $p_{\theta}$ to denote a parameterized probability model. The vector $\theta$ contains the parameters and can be fitted to data using maximum likelihood or other loss functions. We will see many variants of this probability model here and in the following chapters.
concepts.motivation_md: Modeling images by assuming pixel independence and stationary distributions simplifies probability modeling and parameter estimation. (llm_inferred)
concepts.recap_md:
- Assumes all pixels are independent.
- Pixel intensities come from a stationary distribution.
- Probability of image is product of pixel probabilities: $p_{\theta}(\boldsymbol\ell) = \prod p_{\theta}(\ell[n,m])$.

We can then write the probability, $p_{\theta}(\boldsymbol\ell)$, of an image, $\ell[n,m]$ with size $N \times M$, as follows:
$$p_{\theta}(\boldsymbol\ell) = \prod_{n=1}^{N} \prod_{m=1}^{M} p_{\theta}\left(\ell[n,m] \right)$$
We use $p_{\theta}$ to denote a parameterized probability model. The vector $\theta$ contains the parameters and can be fitted to data using maximum likelihood or other loss functions. We will see many variants of this probability model here and in the following chapters.

concepts.title: Receptive Fields
concepts.one_liner: The receptive field of a neuron is the region of the input signal that the neuron is sensitive to, i.e. its support.
concepts.content:
Receptive fields are an important concept when working with CNNs. The receptive field of a neuron is the region of the input signal that the neuron is sensitive to, i.e., its support. In multilayer perceptrons (MLPs), the receptive field of each neuron is the entire input vector since MLPs use fully connected layers. In CNNs, each neuron only sees a portion of the input because each output neuron on a convolutional layer is connected only to a subset of inputs determined by the kernel size of the filter producing that output.

The receptive fields of two example neurons in a CNN are shown below (@fig-convolutional_neural_networks-RFs):

![Receptive fields in a CNN. The black filled neurons are within the receptive fields of each labeled neuron (left: $x_2[3]$, right: $x_1[5]$).](figures/convolutional_neural_nets/RFs.png){width="100%" #fig-convolutional_neural_networks-RFs}

Notice that the receptive field grows deeper in the network. Consider a CNN without nonlinearities: the $l+1$-th layer is the composition of $l$ convolutional filters. Composing filters results in a new filter with larger support (kernel size). The same happens in a CNN with pointwise nonlinearities since pointwise operations do not affect receptive fields (outputs have the same receptive fields as inputs). Whenever there is a downsampling layer by factor $s$, the receptive field of the output is $s$ times larger than that of the input. Because of these properties, receptive field sizes can grow rapidly as we go deeper in CNNs. Generally, we want the final CNN layer to have a receptive field large enough to see the entire input image so output neurons are sensitive to all pixels. This can be achieved with a global average pooling (`gap`) layer, whose output always has a receptive field covering the entire input.
concepts.motivation_md: Receptive fields explain how neurons in CNNs focus on specific input regions, growing larger deeper in the network, enabling the model to capture local and global image features effectively. This concept helps design CNN architectures that cover entire input images.
concepts.recap_md:
- The receptive field of a neuron is the region of the input it is sensitive to.
- In CNNs, receptive fields grow larger with deeper layers and downsampling.
- Final CNN layers typically have receptive fields covering the entire input image.

In CNNs, on the other hand, each neuron only sees a portion of the input, since each output neuron on a conv layer is only connected to a subset of inputs to the conv layer, determined by the kernel size of the filter that produces that output.

concepts.title: Spatial Outputs
concepts.one_liner: To output a spatially varying map of predictions, we can downsample less so the final CNN layer maintains higher spatial resolution and remove global pooling layers.
concepts.content:
In @sec-convolutional_neural_nets-simple_CNN, we saw a CNN outputting a single class probability vector for an image. To output a spatially varying prediction map, we downsample less so the final CNN layer is a feature map maintaining higher spatial resolution. It is also important to remove any global pooling layers.

An example is given below:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{z}_1[c_1,:,:] &= \sum_{c=0}^2 \mathbf{w}_1[c,c_1,:,:] \star \mathbf{x} + b_1[c_1]  &\triangleleft \quad \texttt{conv}\\
    &&[3 \times N \times M] \rightarrow [C_1 \times N \times M]\nonumber\\
    h[c_1,n,m] &= \max(z_1[c_1,n,m],0) &\triangleleft \quad \texttt{relu}\\
    &&[C_1 \times N \times M] \rightarrow [C_1 \times N \times M]\nonumber\\
    \mathbf{z}_2[c_2,:,:] &= \sum_{c_1=0}^{C_1-1} \mathbf{w}_2[c_1,c_2,:,:] \star \mathbf{x} + b_2[c_2] &\triangleleft \quad \texttt{conv}\\
    &&[C_1 \times N \times M] \rightarrow [C_2 \times N \times M]\nonumber\\
    y[k,n,m] &= \frac{e^{-\tau z_2[k,n,m]}}{\sum_{l=1}^K e^{-\tau z_2[l,n,m]}} &\triangleleft \quad \texttt{softmax}\\
    &&[K \times N \times M] \rightarrow [K \times N \times M]\nonumber
\end{aligned}$$

concepts.title: CNN as a Sliding Filter
concepts.one_liner: A CNN made of convolutional layers and pointwise nonlinearities applies the same function independently to each input patch, acting as a nonlinear sliding filter.
concepts.content:
The core of CNNs are convolutional layers. A CNN with only convolutional layers interleaved with pointwise nonlinearities is sometimes called a fully convolutional network (FCN). Such a CNN is just another sliding image filter.

Consider a CNN processing a 1D signal, outputting a feature map $\mathbf{x}_L$. Take two output feature vectors $\mathbf{x}_L[:,i]$ and $\mathbf{x}_L[:,j]$. The feature vector at location $i$ is some function $F$ of the input patch in its receptive field: $\mathbf{x}_L[:,i] = F(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[:,\texttt{RF}(i)])$, where $\texttt{RF}$ returns the input coordinates of the receptive field. The feature vector at $j$ is produced by the same function applied to a different input patch: $\mathbf{x}_L[:,j] = F(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[:,\texttt{RF}(j)])$.

This is illustrated visually in @fig-convolutional_neural_networks-CNN_as_filter (pointwise nonlinearities omitted for clarity):

(see figure: A CNN is a non-linear filter. Edge colors indicate shared weights; two edges with the same color have the same weight. The colors demonstrate that the same function $F$ is applied to each patch of...)

If the CNN had no pointwise nonlinearities, it would be a composition of convolutions, which itself is a convolution (by the associative property of convolution). Thus, a CNN without nonlinearities is a single big convolutional filter processing each input patch independently and identically. Adding pointwise nonlinearities does not change this property because they introduce no interaction between neurons or pixels (they are pointwise). Hence, a CNN made only of convolutional layers and pointwise nonlinearities is a nonlinear operator applying the same transformation independently and identically to each input patch, i.e., a nonlinear filter.

This is why, in the intro to this chapter, we
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding CNNs as nonlinear sliding filters clarifies how they apply the same learned function across all input patches, enabling translation-invariant feature extraction and efficient processing.
concepts.recap_md:
- A CNN with convolutional layers and pointwise nonlinearities applies the same function to each input patch.
- Without nonlinearities, a CNN is equivalent to a single convolutional filter.
- Pointwise nonlinearities preserve the property of independent, identical patch processing.

key_passage.text: Hence it follows that a complete CNN, made up only of convolutional layers and pointwies nonlinearities, is itself a nonlinear operator that applies the same transformation independently and identically to each patch of the input signal, i.e. a nonlinear filter!

motivation.text: The key property of such a system is that it processes each input patch independently and identically.

example.text: To see why, consider a CNN that processes a 1D signal, and outputs a feature map $\mathbf{x}_L$. Take two feature vectors in the output map, $\mathbf{x}_L[:,i]$ and $\mathbf{x}_L[:,j]$. The feature vector at location $i$ is some function, $F$, of the input patch in its receptive field, $\mathbf{x}_L[:,i] = F(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[:,\texttt{RF}(i)])$, where $\texttt{RF}$ returns the coordinates of the receptive field in the input image. It turns out that the feature vector at pixel $j$ is produced by the *same* function, just applied to a different patch of the input: $\mathbf{x}_L[:,j] = F(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[:,\texttt{RF}(j)])$.

concepts.title: Why Process Images Patch by Patch?

position.section_title: Why Process Images Patch by Patch?

concepts.one_liner: A fully convolutional CNN processes each input patch independently and identically, enabling divide-and-conquer and translation-invariant strategies for image understanding.
concepts.content:
A fully convolutional CNN can be thought of as a function that processes each input patch independently and identically. This is a divide-and-conquer strategy: a complex problem (interpreting the whole photo) is split into smaller problems (interpreting each small patch).

Why is this a good strategy?

1. The small problems are easier to solve than the original problem.
2. The small problems can all be solved in parallel.
3. This approach is agnostic to signal length, meaning arbitrarily large problems can be solved by breaking them into bite-sized pieces and solving them individually.

Chopping into small patches works well for many vision problems because the world exhibits locality: related things clump together within a patch, and far apart things can often be assumed independent.

Additionally, convolution is suitable because visual content tends to be translation invariant: objects can appear anywhere in an image and look the same. As objects move across the frame, their position changes but their identity and appearance do not. This justifies processing each patch the same way regardless of position.

Translation invariant means processing each patch identically using the same function $f$. Some texts use the term to describe convolutions, emphasizing that shifting the input shifts the output by the same amount.
concepts.motivation_md: Processing images patch by patch simplifies complex visual tasks by dividing them into smaller, independent, and parallelizable problems, leveraging the locality and translation invariance of visual data.
concepts.recap_md:
- Fully convolutional CNNs process each input patch independently and identically.
- This divide-and-conquer approach simplifies complex image interpretation.
- Visual content's locality and translation invariance justify identical patch processing.

key_passage.text: As we have seen above, a fully convoutional CNN can be thought of a function that processes each patch of the input independently and identically.

motivation.text: This is a divide-and-conquer strategy. If you were to try to understand a complex problem, you might break it up into small pieces and solve each one separately. That's all a CNN is doing. We split up a big problem (i.e. "interpret this whole photo") into a bunch of smaller problems (i.e. "interpret each small patch in the image").

concepts.title: Property #2: Processing Each Patch Identically

position.section_title: Why Process Images Patch by Patch?

concepts.one_liner: Property #2: Processing each patch identically leverages translation invariance, meaning the same function is applied regardless of patch position.
concepts.content:
For images, convolution is especially suitable because visual content tends to be translation invariant, and convolution operators are also translation invariant.

Typically, objects can appear anywhere in an image and look the same, like birds flying across a frame: their position changes but their identity and appearance do not. More generally, as a camera pans across a scene, content shifts in position but remains unchanged.

Because the visual world is roughly translation invariant, it is justified to process each patch the same way regardless of its position (i.e., its translation away from some canonical center patch).

Translation invariant means processing each patch identically using the same function $f$. Some texts use the term to describe convolutions, emphasizing that if the input signal is shifted by some translation, the output signal shifts by the same amount.
concepts.motivation_md: Processing each image patch identically exploits the translation invariance of visual data, enabling consistent recognition of objects regardless of their position.
concepts.recap_md:
- Visual content is roughly translation invariant.
- Processing each patch identically leverages this invariance.
- Convolution operators exhibit translation invariance, shifting outputs with inputs.

concepts.title: Encoder and Decoders
concepts.one_liner: An encoder maps data to a lower-dimensional representation, and a decoder maps from that representation back to data, forming analysis and synthesis pipelines in deep networks.
concepts.content:
In @sec-image_pyramids, we encountered image pyramids with an analysis pipeline converting an image into a multiscale representation of filter responses, and a synthesis pipeline reconstructing the image from those responses. Deep networks may operate similarly in analysis or synthesis directions. The analysis network is called an encoder, and the synthesis network a decoder.

An encoder maps data to a representation, usually lower dimensional, and a decoder performs the inverse, mapping from the representation back to data.

Encoder and decoder networks appear frequently and can be made from many architectures, including non-neural nets. In CNNs, encoders typically take an image input and downsample it layer by layer, producing a lower-dimensional feature map. Decoders do the opposite, upsampling low-dimensional features layer by layer to produce an image output.

An example encoder is an image classifier; an example decoder is an image generator (covered in @sec-generative_models). These architectural patterns are shown in
concepts.motivation_md: Encoders and decoders enable deep networks to transform data into compact representations and reconstruct data from them, facilitating tasks like classification and generation.
concepts.recap_md:
- An encoder maps data to a lower-dimensional representation.
- A decoder maps from the representation back to data.
- CNN encoders downsample images; decoders upsample features to images.

An encoder maps from data to a representation of that data, which is usually lower dimensional, and a decoder performs the inverse operation, mapping from a representation back to the data.

concepts.title: Directed graphical models
concepts.one_liner: Directed graphical models describe factorizations of the joint probability into products of conditional probability distributions.
concepts.content:
In addition to undirected graphical models, another type of graphical model is commonly used. Directed graphical models describe factorizations of the joint probability into products of conditional probability distributions. Each node in a directed graph contributes a well-specified factor in the joint probability: the probability of its variable, conditioned on all the variables originating arrows pointing into it. So this graph

(see figure: A directed graphical model with three variables.)

denotes the joint probability,
$$p(x_1, x_2, x_3) = p(x_2)  p(x_1 \bigm | x_2) p(x_3 \bigm | x_2) $$

The general rule for writing the joint probability described by a directed graph is this: Each node, $x_n$, contributes the factor $p(x_n \bigm | x_{\Xi})$, where $\Xi$ is the set of nodes with arrows pointing in to node $x_n$. You can verify that equation
concepts.motivation_md: Directed graphical models provide a structured way to represent complex joint probability distributions by breaking them down into conditional probabilities, making inference and computation more tractable. (llm_inferred)
concepts.recap_md:
- Directed graphical models factorize joint probabilities into products of conditional probabilities.
- Each node contributes a factor conditioned on its parent nodes.
- The joint probability is the product of all such conditional factors.

concepts.title: minimum mean squared error estimate (MMSE)
concepts.one_liner: The minimum mean squared error estimate (MMSE) minimizes the expected squared error weighted by the posterior probability.
concepts.content:
The average value of that error is called the minimum mean squared error estimate (MMSE). To find this estimate, we seek the $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ that minimizes the squared error, weighted by the probability of each outcome:

$$\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{MMSE} = \mbox{argmin}_{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}} \int_{\mathbf{x}} p(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{y}) (\mathbf{x}-\tilde{\mathbf{x}})'(\mathbf{x}-\tilde{\mathbf{x}}) d\mathbf{x}$$

Differentiating with respect to $\mathbf{x}$ to solve for the stationary point, the global minimum for this convex function, we find

$$\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{MMSE} = \int_{\mathbf{x}} \mathbf{x} p(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{y})  d\mathbf{x}.$$
concepts.motivation_md: The MMSE estimate provides the best average estimate minimizing expected squared error, improving accuracy over other point estimates. (llm_inferred)

- MMSE estimate minimizes expected squared error weighted by posterior.
- The solution is the posterior mean $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{MMSE} = \int \mathbf{x} p(\mathbf{x} | \mathbf{y}) d\mathbf{x}$.

concepts.title: Perception of Sets

position.section_title: A Few Notes about Human Perception

concepts.one_liner: When an image is composed of one or a few distinct objects, we can easily pay attention to each of them individually.
concepts.content:
When an image is composed of one or a few distinct objects, we can easily pay attention to each of them individually. We can also count them in parallel, that is, we can tell if an image has one, two, three, or four elements, very quickly and the time it takes for us to say how many elements are in the display does not depend on the number of elements in the image. That is, if a display has only one element or four elements, we are equally fast at reporting that number (figures @fig-parallel_counting[a, b and c]).

(see figure: When looking at these images, we can count the number of circles at a glance if there are less than five circles. When an image has more than five items, we have to count them one by one.)

But something interesting happens when images are composed of more than five similarly looking elements. If we want to count them we need to look at all of them one by one, and the time to count them grows linearly with the number of elements in the image, as illustrated in @fig-parallel_counting.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains how humans perceive and count small numbers of objects quickly, but counting larger numbers requires serial attention, revealing limits of visual processing.
concepts.recap_md:
- Humans can quickly count up to four elements in an image in parallel.
- Counting more than five similar elements requires serial attention.
- Counting time grows linearly with the number of elements beyond five.

concepts.title: crowding

position.section_title: A Few Notes about Human Perception

concepts.one_liner: Crowding is a visual phenomenon where features of nearby objects get entangled, making it hard to perceive individual items in peripheral vision.
concepts.content:
@fig-crowding illustrates a curious visual phenomenon. Look at the central cross and try to read the letter on the left and right without moving your eyes.

(see figure: Crowding. If you look at the central cross, the letter R on the right can be recognized, however the letter B on the left is hard to read.)

You will notice that the letter R on the right can be recognized easily while the letter B on the left is hard to read. The reason cannot be due to the low resolution of peripheral vision as both letters are at the same distance from the fixation location. The explanation of this phenomena is due to something called **crowding** @Pell2007.

As the letter B is surrounded by other letters, the features of the three letters get entangled as if the pooling window for image features was larger than the three letters together. While you fixate the cross, as you pay attention to the location of the B, you will notice that the features of the three letters are mixed. It is easy to see that it is text, but it is hard to bind the features together to perceive the individual letters. The circles in @fig-crowding represent an approximation of the size of the visual regions over which visual features are pooled. Anything inside the region will suffer from crowding effects. Those regions are larger than what would be predicted by the loss of resolution due to the spacing between receptors in the periphery.

The main message here is for you to feel what it is to perceive what seems to be a statistical representation of the image features present in an image region.
concepts.motivation_md: Crowding explains why objects close together in peripheral vision become hard to recognize individually, revealing limits of feature integration in vision.
concepts.recap_md:
- Crowding occurs when features of nearby objects get mixed in peripheral vision.
- It impairs recognition of individual letters despite equal distance from fixation.
- Visual pooling regions are larger than receptor spacing predicts.

key_passage.text: The explanation of this phenomena is due to something called **crowding**. As the letter B is surrounded by other letters, the features of the three letters get entangled as if the pooling window for image features was larger than the three letters together.

motivation.text: The reason cannot be due to the low resolution of peripheral vision as both letters are at the same distance from the fixation location.

concepts.title: Data Structures and Notation for Working with Tokens
concepts.one_liner: A sequence of tokens is denoted by a matrix \mathbf{T} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}, with each token transposed to become a row of the matrix.
concepts.content:
A sequence of tokens is denoted by a matrix \(\mathbf{T} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}\), in which each token in the sequence, \(\mathbf{t}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{t}_N\), is transposed to become a row of the matrix: 

$$
\mathbf{T} = 
  \begin{bmatrix}
    \mathbf{t}_1^\mathsf{T}\\
    \vdots \\
    \mathbf{t}_N^\mathsf{T}\\
\end{bmatrix}
$$ 

Graphically, \(\mathbf{T}\) is constructed from \(\mathbf{t}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{t}_N\) like this (@fig-transformers-T_notation):

(see figure: In this chapter, we will represent a set of tokens as a matrix whose rows are the token vectors.)

As we will see, transformers are invariant to permutations of the input sequence, so, as far as transformers are concerned, groups of tokens should be thought of as *sets* rather than ordered sequences.

The idea of this notation is that *tokens are to transformers as neurons are to neural nets*. Neural net layers operate over arrays of neurons; for example, an MLP takes as input a column vector \(\mathbf{x}\), whose rows are scalar neurons. Transformers operate over arrays of tokens. A matrix \(\mathbf{T}\) is just a convenient representation of a 1D array of vector-value tokens.
concepts.motivation_md: Representing tokens as rows of a matrix \(\mathbf{T}\) allows transformers to process sequences as sets, reflecting their permutation invariance and enabling operations analogous to those on neurons in neural nets.
concepts.recap_md:
- Tokens in a sequence are represented as rows of a matrix \(\mathbf{T} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}\).
- Transformers treat tokens as sets, invariant to input order.
- This notation parallels neurons in neural nets, facilitating analogous operations.
