The result with stride 1 looks fine, and it is the output we would expect. However, stride 2 starts showing some artifacts on the boundaries, and stride 4 shows very severe artifacts, with some boundaries disappearing. The DFTs make the artifacts more obvious. In the stride 2 result we can see severe aliasing artifacts that introduce

input image.

One can argue that these artifacts might not be important when the kernel is being learned. Indeed, the learning could search for kernels that minimize the artifacts due to aliasing as those probably increase the loss. Also, as each layer is composed of many channels, the set of learned kernels could learn to compensate for the aliasing produced by other channels. However, this reduces the space of useful kernels, and the learning might not succeed in removing all the artifacts.
concepts.motivation_md: Strided convolution reduces output resolution efficiently but can introduce aliasing artifacts, impacting quality; understanding this tradeoff is crucial for neural network design.
concepts.recap_md:
- Strided convolution reduces output resolution by skipping input positions.
- It can reduce computation but may cause aliasing artifacts.
- Larger strides increase artifacts, potentially degrading output quality.

motivation.text:
Strided convolutions can significantly reduce the computational cost and memory requirements when a neural network is large. However, strided
convolution can decrease the quality of the convolution.

concepts.title: tokenization
concepts.one_liner: Tokenization is a convolution operator that converts an input image into tokens by applying a convolution with kernel size and stride equal to K.
concepts.motivation_md: Tokenization converts raw input images into tokens that transformers can process, using convolution to break the image into chunks with stride and kernel size K.
concepts.recap_md:
- Tokenization applies a convolution with kernel and stride $K$ to input images.
- Converts RGB images $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times N \times M}$ into tokens of dimension $d$.
- Assumes input dimensions $N, M$ are divisible by $K$, else padding or resizing is needed.

motivation.text: This math assumes $N$ and $M$ are evenly divisible by $K$; if they aren't then the input can be resized or padded until they are.

concepts.title: Query-Key-Value Projections
concepts.one_liner: The query, key, and value projections in transformers are multichannel convolutions with kernel size 1.
concepts.content:
Next let's look at the query, key, and value projections that are part of the attention layers. For simplicity, we will consider just the query projection, since key and value follow exactly the same pattern.

We wrote this operation as a matrix multiply $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}\mathbf{W}_q^\mathsf{T}$ (@eq-transformers-query_matrix). What this multiply is doing is applying the same linear transformation ($\mathbf{W}_q$) to each token vector (each row of $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}$). Applying the same linear operation to each element in a sequence is exactly what convolution does. Specifically, the query operation can be written as convolving the set of $N$ $d$-channel tokens with a filter bank of $m$ filters, with kernel size 1, producing a new set of $N$ $m$-channel tokens. This equivalence is visualized below (@fig-transformers-conv_matmul_equivalence):


(see figure: The query, key, and value projections in transformers can be written either as a convolution or a matrix multiply.)

Therefore, the query, key, and value projections are all multichannel convolutions with kernels of size 1.

Convolution actually appears all over in linear algebra, and in fact \textit{every matrix product can be written as a convolution}! Whenever you see a product $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}$, you can think of it as the convolution of a multichannel filter bank $\mathbf{B}$ (one filter in each row; kernel size 1) with the signal $\mathbf{A}$ (time indexes rows, channels in the columns).
concepts.motivation_md: Query, key, and value projections apply the same linear transformation to each token, which can be efficiently implemented as convolutions with kernel size 1.
concepts.recap_md:
- Query, key, and value projections are matrix multiplies applying the same linear transform to each token.
- These operations are equivalent to multichannel convolutions with kernel size 1.
- Every matrix product can be interpreted as a convolution with kernel size 1.

key_passage.text: Therefore, the query, key, and value projections are all multichannel convolutions with kernels of size 1.

motivation.text: Applying the same linear operation to each element in a sequence is exactly what convolution does.

example.text: Specifically, the query operation can be written as convolving the set of $N$ $d$-channel tokens with a filter bank of $m$ filters, with kernel size 1, producing a new set of $N$ $m$-channel tokens.

concepts.title: Tokenwise MLP
concepts.one_liner: A token-wise MLP applies the same MLP to each token, which can be written as a series of convolutions with kernel size 1 interleaved with pointwise nonlinearities.
concepts.motivation_md: Token-wise MLPs apply the same linear and nonlinear operations to each token independently, which can be implemented as convolutions with kernel size 1 and pointwise nonlinearities.
concepts.recap_md:
- Token-wise MLP applies the same MLP $F_{\theta}$ to each token.
- Linear layers in the MLP are matrix multiplies equivalent to convolutions with kernel size 1.
- Pointwise nonlinearities act neuronwise, making the token-wise MLP a CNN-like structure.

key_passage.text: A token-wise MLP applies the same MLP $F_{\theta}$ to each token in a sequence. The $F_{\theta}$ consists of linear layers and pointwise nonlinearities.

motivation.text: Notice that this looks just like the query operation we covered in the previous section, Therefore, the same result holds: the linear layers of the token-wise MLP can all be written as convolutions with kernel size 1.

concepts.title: The Similarities between CNNs and Transfomers
concepts.one_liner: Most layers in transformers are convolutional and share operations like normalization and residual connections with CNNs.
concepts.content:
### The Similarities between CNNs and Transfomers

As we have now seen, most layers in transformers are convolutional. These layers break up the signal processing problem into chunks, then process each chunk independently and identically. Some of the other operations in transformers -- normalization layers, residual connections, etc -- are also common in CNNs. So what is *different* between transformers and CNNs?
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the similarities between transformers and CNNs helps clarify how transformers process data and what architectural elements they share.
concepts.recap_md:
- Most transformer layers are convolutional, processing chunks independently.
- Transformers and CNNs share operations like normalization and residual connections.
- Key differences between transformers and CNNs remain despite these similarities.

key_passage.text: As we have now seen, most layers in transformers are convolutional. These layers break up the signal processing problem into chunks, then process each chunk independently and identically.

motivation.text: Some of the other operations in transformers -- normalization layers, residual connections, etc -- are also common in CNNs.

concepts.title: The Differences between CNNs and Transformers
concepts.one_liner: Transformers use 1x1 filters preserving permutation invariance, unlike CNNs which use larger kernels that capture spatial structure.
concepts.content:
#### CNNs can have kernels with non-unitary spatial extent

When we wrote them as convolutions, the query-key-value projections and token-wise MLPs *only used 1x1 filters*.

We use the term "1x1 filter" to refer to any filter whose kernel size is 1 in all its dimensions, regardless of whether the signal is one-dimensional, two-dimensional, three-dimensional, etc.

In fact it cannot be otherwise. If you used a larger kernel it would break the permutation invariance property of transformers, since the output of the filters would depend on which token is next to which. This is one of the key differences between CNNs and transformers. CNNs use $K \times K$ filters, and this makes it so adjacent image regions get processed together. Transformers use 1x1 filters which means the network has no architectural way of knowing about spatial structure (which token is next to which). For vision problems, where spatial structure is often crucially important, transformers can instead be given knowledge of position through the *inputs* to the network, rather than through the architectural structure. We will cover this idea in section [Positional Encodings](#sec-transformers-positional_encodings)
concepts.motivation_md: Transformers maintain permutation invariance by using 1x1 filters, unlike CNNs which use larger kernels to capture spatial relationships; positional information is instead provided via input encodings.
concepts.recap_md:
- Transformers use 1x1 filters to preserve permutation invariance.
- CNNs use larger $K \times K$ filters to process adjacent regions together.
- Transformers rely on positional encodings rather than spatially-aware kernels.

key_passage.text: This is one of the key differences between CNNs and transformers. CNNs use $K \times K$ filters, and this makes it so adjacent image regions get processed together. Transformers use 1x1 filters which means the network has no architectural way of knowing about spatial structure (which token is next to which).

motivation.text: If you used a larger kernel it would break the permutation invariance property of transformers, since the output of the filters would depend on which token is next to which.

example.text: For vision problems, where spatial structure is often crucially important, transformers can instead be given knowledge of position through the *inputs* to the network, rather than through the architectural structure.

concepts.title: Masked Attention
concepts.one_liner: Masked attention restricts which tokens can attend to which by fixing some attention weights to zero, enabling causal prediction and other applications.
concepts.content:
## Masked Attention {#sec-transformers-masked_attention}

Sometimes we want to restrict which tokens can attend to which. This can be done by *masking* the attention matrix, which just means fixing some of the weights to be zero. This can be useful for many settings, including learning features via masked autoencoding @he2022masked, cross-attention between different data modalities @wei2020multi, and for sequential prediction @chen2020generative. To illustrate, we will describe the sequential prediction use case. 

For simplicity, in this section we depict tokens with one-dimensional code vectors, but remember $\mathbf{T}$ would have $d$ columns for $d$-dimensional code vectors.

A common problem is to predict the $(n+1)$-th token in a sequence given the previous $n$ tokens. For example, we may be trying to predict tokens that represent the next frame in a video, the next word in a sentence, or the weather on the next day.


The $\mathbf{T}_{1:n}$ is shorthand for the sequence of tokens $\begin{bmatrix}
    \mathbf{t}_1^\mathsf{T}\\
    \vdots\\
    \mathbf{t}_{n}^\mathsf{T}
\end{bmatrix}$.

A simple way to model this prediction problem is with a linear layer: $\mathbf{y}_{n+1} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{T}_{1:n}$. Here is what this looks like diagrammatically, and on the right is the layer shown as matrix multiplication:


(see figure: Masked prediction of time index 4 from time indices 1-3.)

During training, we will give examples like this: $$\begin{aligned}
    \{\mathbf{t}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{t}_n\} &\rightarrow \mathbf{t}_{n+1}\\
    \{\mathbf{t}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{t}_{n-1}\} &\rightarrow \mathbf{t}_n\\
    \{\mathbf{t}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{t}_{n-2}\} &\rightarrow \mathbf{t}_{n-1}
\end{aligned}$$ and so on. We can make all these predictions at once with a single matrix multiply (@fig-transformers-masked_attn_one_matmul):

(see figure: Masked attention to make multiple causal predictions at once. Black cells are masked; they are filled with zeros.)

This way, one forward pass makes $N$ predictions rather than one prediction. This is equivalent to doing a single next token prediction $N$ times, but it all happens in a single matrix multiply, using the matrix shown on the right.

This kind of matrix is called *causal* because each output index $i$ only depends on input indices $j$ such that $j < i$. If $\mathbf{A}$ is an attention matrix, then this strategy is called **causal attention**. This is a masking strategy where each token can only attend to *previous* tokens in the sequence. This approach can dramatically speed up training because all the sub-sequence prediction problems (predict $\mathbf{t}_{n-1}$ given $\mathbf{T}_{1:n-2}$, predict $\mathbf{t}_{n}$ given $\mathbf{T}_{1:n-1}$, predict $\mathbf{t}_{n+1}$ given $\mathbf{T}_{1:n}$) are supervised at the same time.

This also works for transformers with more than one layer, where the masking strategy looks like shown in @fig-transformers-multilayer_masked_attention.


(see figure: Multilayer masked attention achieves causal prediction with a deep net.)

Notice that the output tokens on every layer $l$ have the property that $\mathbf{t}^l_n$ only depends on $\mathbf{T}^0_{1:n-1}$, where $\mathbf{T}^0$ are the initial set of tokens input into the transformer. Also notice that, after the first layer, all subsequent layers can use causal attention that is not shifted in time, and the previous property is still maintained. Finally, notice that the subnetwork that predicts each subsequent output token overlaps substantially with the subnetworks that predict each previous token. That is, there is sharing of computation between all the prediction problems. We will see a more concrete application of this strategy when we get to autoregressive
concepts.motivation_md: Masked attention enables restricting token interactions to previous tokens only, allowing efficient causal prediction and training of sequential models.
concepts.recap_md:
- Masked attention fixes some attention weights to zero to restrict token dependencies.
- Causal attention ensures each token attends only to previous tokens.
- Enables simultaneous training of multiple next-token predictions in one forward pass.

key_passage.text: Sometimes we want to restrict which tokens can attend to which. This can be done by *masking* the attention matrix, which just means fixing some of the weights to be zero.

motivation.text: This can be useful for many settings, including learning features via masked autoencoding, cross-attention between different data modalities, and for sequential prediction.

concepts.title: Positional Encodings
concepts.one_liner: Positional encodings add a code representing position within the signal to each token, often using sinusoidal functions.
concepts.motivation_md: Positional encodings provide tokens with information about their position in the input sequence or image, which transformers lack due to permutation equivariance.
concepts.recap_md:
- Transformers are permutation equivariant and do not encode token positions by default.
- Positional encodings add position information, often via sinusoidal functions.
- Positional codes can also be learned and are useful beyond transformers, including CNNs.

key_passage.text: Positional encoding concatenates a code representing *position within the signal* onto each token.

motivation.text: Operations over tokens in a transformer are permutation equivariant, which means that we can shuffle the positions of the tokens and nothing substantial changes (the only change is that the outputs get permuted). A consequence is that tokens do not know encode their position within the representation of the signal.

example.text: For example, knowing that a token is a representation of the top region of an image can help us identify that the token is likely to represent sky.

concepts.title: Comparing Fully Connected, Convolutional, and Self-Attention Layers

position.section_title: Comparing Fully Connected, Convolutional, and Self-Attention Layers

concepts.one_liner: Fully connected, convolutional, and self-attention layers can all be represented as affine transformations with different matrix structures.
concepts.content:
## Comparing Fully Connected, Convolutional, and Self-Attention Layers





The shorthand "fc" is often used to indicate a fully-connected linear layer.


 Many layers in deep nets are special kinds of affine transformations. Three we have seen so far are fully-connected layers (`fc`), convolutional layers (`conv`), and self-attention layers (`attn`). All these layers are alike in that their forward pass can be written as $\mathbf{X}_{\texttt{out}}= \mathbf{W}\mathbf{X}_{\texttt{in}}+ \mathbf{b}$ for some matrix $\mathbf{W}$ and some vector $\mathbf{b}$. In `conv` and `attn` layers, $\mathbf{W}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are determined as some function of the input $\mathbf{X}_{\texttt{in}}$. In `conv` layers this function is very simple: just make a Toeplitz matrix that repeats the convolutional kernel(s) to match the dimensionality of $\mathbf{X}_{\texttt{in}}$. In `attn` layers the function that determines $\mathbf{W}$ is a bit more involved, as we saw above, and typically we don't use biases $\mathbf{b}$.

Each of these layers can be represented as a matrix, and examining the structure in these matrices can be a useful way to understand their similarities and differences. The matrix for an `fc` layer is full rank, whereas the matrices for `conv` and `attn` layers have low-rank structure, but different kinds of low-rank structure. In @fig-transformers-affine_layer_comparison, we show what these matrices look like, and also catalog some of the other important properties of each of these layers.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the matrix structures of fully connected, convolutional, and self-attention layers helps clarify their similarities and differences in deep networks.
concepts.recap_md:
- Fully connected, convolutional, and self-attention layers are affine transformations.
- `conv` and `attn` layers have weight matrices determined by input-dependent functions.
- `fc` layers have full-rank weight matrices; `conv` and `attn` have low-rank structures but differ in kind.

key_passage.text: Many layers in deep nets are special kinds of affine transformations. Three we have seen so far are fully-connected layers (`fc`), convolutional layers (`conv`), and self-attention layers (`attn`). All these layers are alike in that their forward pass can be written as $\mathbf{X}_{\texttt{out}}= \mathbf{W}\mathbf{X}_{\texttt{in}}+ \mathbf{b}$ for some matrix $\mathbf{W}$ and some vector $\mathbf{b}$.

motivation.text: Examining the structure in these matrices can be a useful way to understand their similarities and differences.

concepts.title: alignment loss
concepts.one_liner: \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{align}}(f;\alpha) = \mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^+) \sim p_{\texttt{pos}}} [\left\lVert f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{x}^+)\right\rVert_2^{\alpha}]
concepts.content:
The alignment loss is defined as

\[
\mathcal{L}_{\texttt{align}}(f;\alpha) = \mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^+) \sim p_{\texttt{pos}}} [\left\lVert f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{x}^+)\right\rVert_2^{\alpha}]
\]

where the expectation is taken over positive pairs $(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^+)$ sampled from the distribution $p_{\texttt{pos}}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Alignment loss measures how close embeddings of positive pairs are, encouraging similar inputs to have similar representations.
concepts.recap_md:
- Alignment loss measures distance between embeddings of positive pairs.
- Defined as $\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^+) \sim p_{\texttt{pos}}} [\|f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{x}^+)\|_2^{\alpha}]$.
- Encourages embeddings of similar inputs to be close.

key_passage.text: \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{align}}(f;\alpha) &= \mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^+) \sim p_{\texttt{pos}}} [\left\lVert f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{x}^+)\right\rVert_2^{\alpha}]\\

concepts.title: uniformity loss
concepts.one_liner: \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{unif}}(f;t) = \log \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}, \, \mathbf{x}^- \sim p_{\texttt{data}}} [e^{-t\left\lVert f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{x}^-)\right\rVert_2^2}]
concepts.content:
The uniformity loss is defined as

\[
\mathcal{L}_{\texttt{unif}}(f;t) = \log \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}, \, \mathbf{x}^- \sim p_{\texttt{data}}} [e^{-t\left\lVert f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{x}^-)\right\rVert_2^2}]
\]

and the combined loss function is

\[
\mathcal{L}(f;\alpha,t,\lambda) = \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{align}}(f;\alpha) + \lambda \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{unif}}
\]

where $\mathcal{L}_{\texttt{align}}$ is the alignment loss and $\lambda$ is a weighting parameter.
concepts.motivation_md: Uniformity loss encourages embeddings to be spread out, preventing collapse and promoting diversity in representation space.
concepts.recap_md:
- Uniformity loss defined as $\log \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^-}[e^{-t\|f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{x}^-)\|_2^2}]$.
- Combined loss adds alignment and weighted uniformity losses.
- Helps embeddings distribute uniformly and avoid collapse.

concepts.title: perceptual group
concepts.one_liner: A perceptual group is a particular kind of visual representation that groups primitive elements into meaningful structures like contours and objects.
concepts.content:
A particular kind of visual representation, the **perceptual group**, becomes the central object of interest; we will see what these are, how to find them, and how they are related to the representation learning algorithms from the last chapter.

First, what is a perceptual group? Look at the photo in @fig-perceptual_organization-perc_org_teaser and consider what you see. Not what raw pixel values you see, but what structures you see. What are some structures you can name?

(see figure: A few kinds of perceptual organization in the human visual system.)

What a camera sees is the raw RGB pixel values of the photo. But what your mind sees is rather different. You see contours and surfaces, objects and events.

Many of these perceptual structures can be thought of as *groups of primitive elements*: a contour is a group of points that form a line, an object is a group of parts that form a cohesive whole, and so on. Because of this, understanding how humans, and machines, can identify meaningful perceptual groups has been a longstanding area of interest in

- Understanding them is key in vision and representation learning.

concepts.title: Self-Attention
concepts.one_liner: Self-attention computes weighted sums over all tokens for each query, producing output tokens via linear transformations and softmax attention.
concepts.motivation_md: Self-attention enables each token to attend to all others, capturing contextual relationships and producing context-aware output tokens.
concepts.recap_md:
- Self-attention computes $N$ queries and weighted sums over $N$ tokens to produce $N$ output tokens.  
- Queries, keys, and values are computed by linear projections of input tokens.  
- Attention weights are softmax-normalized dot products of queries and keys, applied to values.

key_passage.text: Self-attention is just such an architecture. The idea is that on a self-attention layer, all tokens submit queries, and for each of these queries, we take a weighted sum over all tokens in that layer. If \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}} is a set of N input tokens, then we have N queries, N weighted sums, and N output tokens to form \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}.

concepts.title: Multihead Self-Attention
concepts.one_liner: Multihead self-attention runs $k$ attention layers in parallel and merges their outputs by concatenation and projection.
concepts.motivation_md: Multihead self-attention allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions.
concepts.recap_md:
- Multihead self-attention runs $k$ attention layers in parallel on the same input.  
- Outputs from all heads are concatenated into a matrix $\bar{\mathbf{T}}_{\texttt{out}}$.  
- The concatenated output is projected back to original dimension using $\mathbf{W}_{\texttt{MSA}}$.

key_passage.text: This method simply consists of running $k$ attention layers in parallel. All these layers are applied to the same input $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}$. This results in $k$ output sets of tokens, $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}^1, \ldots, \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}^k$. To merge these outputs, we concatenate all of them and project back to the original dimensionality of $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}$.

concepts.title: The Full Transformer Architecture
concepts.one_liner: A full transformer architecture stacks self-attention layers with tokenwise nonlinearities, normalization, and residual connections.
concepts.content:
## The Full Transformer Architecture {#sec-transformers-ViT_arch}

A full transformer architecture is a stack of self-attention layers interleaved with tokenwise nonlinearities. These two steps are analogous to linear layers interleaved with neuronwise nonlinearities in an MLP, as shown below (@fig-transformers-transformer_vs_MLP):

(see figure: The basic transformer architecture versus an MLP.)

Beyond this basic template, there are many variations that can be added, resulting in different particular architectures within the transformer family. Some common additions are normalization layers and residual connections. In @fig-transformers-ViT_arch we plot the ViT architecture from @dosovitskiy2020vit, showing where these additional pieces enter the picture.


(see figure: The ViT transformer architecture~\cite{dosovitskiy2020vit}. This set of layers forms a computational block, shaded in gray, that can be repeated $L$ times for a depth $L$ ViT. To clarify where the...)

This architecture uses layer normalization (@sec-neural_nets-normalization_layers) before each attention layer and before each token-wise MLP layer. The normalization is done *within* each token (the token code vector is treated as a akin to a layer; each dimension of this vector is standardized by the mean and variance over all dimensions of this vector), so in we refer to this layer as `token norm`. Notice that `token norm` is a tokenwise operation, just like our tokenwise MLP, but it performs a different kind of transformation and does not have learnable parameters. Residual connections are added around each group of layers.

Pseudocode for this a ViT (with single-headed attention) is given below:

``` {.python xleftmargin="0.0" xrightmargin="0.0" fontsize="\\fontsize{8.5}{9}" frame="single" framesep="2.5pt" baselinestretch="1.05"}
# x : input data (RGB image)
# K : tokenization patch size
# d : token/query/key/value dimensionality (setting these all as the same)
# L : number of layers
# W_q_T, W_k_T, W_v_T : transposed query/key/value projection matrices
# mlp: tokenwise mlps
```
concepts.motivation_md: Stacking self-attention layers with nonlinearities, normalization, and residual connections forms powerful transformer models like ViT for complex data processing.
concepts.recap_md:
- Transformer architecture stacks self-attention layers with tokenwise nonlinearities.  
- Includes normalization layers and residual connections for stability.  
- ViT architecture repeats these blocks $L$ times with token normalization and MLPs.

concepts.title: Permutation Equivariance
concepts.one_liner: Transformers are equivariant to permutations of the input token sequence.
concepts.content:
An important property of transformers is that they are equivariant to permutations of the input token sequence. This follows from the fact that both tokenwise layers, $F_{\theta}$, and attention layers, $\texttt{attn}$, are **permutation equivariant**: 

$$\begin{aligned}
    F_{\theta}(\texttt{permute}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}})) &= \texttt{permute}(F_{\theta}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}))\\
    \texttt{attn}(\texttt{permute}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}})) &= \texttt{permute}(\texttt{attn}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}))
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\texttt{permute}$ is a permutation of the order of tokens in $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}$ (i.e., permutes the rows of the matrix). This means that if you scramble (i.e. permute) the patches in the input image then apply attention, the output will be unchanged up to a permutation of the original output. Since the full transformer architecture is just composition of these two types of layers (plus, potentially, residual connections and token normalization, which are also permutation equivariant), and because composing two permutation equivariant functions results in a permutation equivariant operation, we have: 

$$\begin{aligned}
    \texttt{transformer}(\texttt{permute}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}})) &= \texttt{permute}(\texttt{transformer}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}))
\end{aligned}$$ This property is visualized in @fig-transformers-permutation_equivariance.

(see figure: Transformers are permutation equivariant. For notational simplicity, we omit layer indices on the token variables here.)

It is often useful to understand layers in terms of their invariances and equivariances. Convolutational layers are translation equivariant but not necessarily permutation equivariant whereas attention layers are both translation equivariant *and* permutation equivariant (since translation is a special kind of permutation, any permutation equivariant layer is also translation equivariant). Other layers can be catalogued similarly: global average pooling layers are permutation *invariant*, relu layers are permutation equivariant, per-token MLP layers are also permutation equivariant (but with respect to sets of tokens rather than sets of neurons), and so on.

A generally good strategy is to select layers that reflect the symmetries in your data or task: in object detection, translation equivariance makes sense because, roughly, a bird is a bird no matter where it appears in an image. Permutation equivariance might also make sense, for that same reason, but only to an extent: if you break up an image into small patches and scramble them, this could disrupt spatial layout that is important for recognition. We will see in @sec-transformers-positional_encodings how transformers use something called positional codes to reinsert useful information about spatial layout.
concepts.motivation_md: Permutation equivariance ensures transformer outputs rearrange consistently when input tokens are permuted, preserving structural relationships.
concepts.recap_md:
- Tokenwise and attention layers are permutation equivariant: permuting inputs permutes outputs correspondingly.  
- Full transformer composition preserves permutation equivariance.  
- Positional codes are needed to reintroduce spatial layout information.

concepts.title: $K$-Means Segmentation
concepts.one_liner: $K$-means tries to find clusters in this scatter plot and can segment by assigning each pixel to the cluster of its color value.
concepts.content:
$K$-means, which we covered in @sec-representation_learning, is one of the simplest and most useful clustering algorithms, so let's try it for segmentation.

$K$-means operates on a data matrix of $N$ datapoints by $M$ features per datapoint. Our first task is to convert the segmentation problem to that format. The simplest approach is to let each pixel be a datapoint and the pixel's color be its feature vector. For ease of visualization, we use the $ab$ color value as the two-dimensional (2D) feature per pixel. An image represented this way can be plotted as a scatter plot and can be thought of as samples from a distribution over $ab$ colors, as shown in @fig-perceptual_organization-scatter_ab_fruits2.

(see figure: Different regions of coherent color in the image correspond to clusters in the scatter plot of all the $ab$-values of the image's pixels. In general, segmentation can be reduced to the problem of...)

$K$-means tries to find clusters in this scatter plot (and, if you prefer a probabilistic interpretation, it can be thought of as fitting a mixture of Gaussians to the datapoints, which aims to approximate the distribution from which these pixels were sampled). We can segment via $k$-means by simply assigning each pixel to the cluster assignment of its color value. Below we color each pixel in each cluster by the mean color of all pixels assigned to that cluster (@fig-perceptual_organization-kmeans_ab_fruits2).

(see figure: $K$-means segmentation on the fruits example.)

Naturally, $k$-means on $ab$-values finds segments that correspond to regions of roughly a constant color. This simple approach can be surprisingly effective. Notice how it segments a zebra from the background in @fig-perceptual_organization-kmeans_ab_zebra_and_beach (because the black and white stripes have roughly the same $ab$-values). However, it fails to group more complex patterns that are not defined by color similarity, as in the beach photo in @fig-perceptual_organization-kmeans_ab_zebra_and_beach.
concepts.motivation_md: $K$-means segmentation converts image pixels into feature vectors and clusters them by color, enabling simple and effective segmentation of regions with similar colors.
concepts.recap_md:
- $K$-means clusters pixels by their $ab$ color values.
- Each pixel is assigned to the cluster of its color.
- Effective for segmenting regions of roughly constant color.

concepts.title: Affinity-Based Segmentation
concepts.one_liner: Affinity-based segmentation models a distance metric (affinity) that tells us whether two items should be grouped.
concepts.content:
Other clustering methods are based on the idea of affinity, where we try to model a distance metric (the affinity) that tells us whether two items should be grouped. The distance metric usually measures how similar two patterns are, or how likely they are to be part of the same object.

For example, a simple affinity function over pixel pairs could be the Euclidean distance between the color values of the two pixels. There are numerous ways to use such an affinity to group pixels into segments, all sharing the general idea that pixels with high affinity should belong to the same group and pixels with low affinity should belong to different groups. Methods using this idea include those based on graph cuts @shi2000normalized, spectral clustering @arbelaez2010contour, and Markov random field (MRF)-based clustering (@sec-probabilistic_graphical_models).

We do not have time to cover all these methods and in fact they are no longer commonly used. Instead, we focus on a method seen earlier in the book that is in common use: contrastive learning (covered in @sec-representation_learning-contrastive_learning). Contrastive learning fits affinity-based segmentation because it learns from similarities (positive pairs) and differences (negative pairs), which is what an affinity metric provides! Contrastive methods learn an embedding where datapoints with high affinity are nearby and those with low affinity are far apart. Once we have such an embedding, clustering is easy in the embedding space, and almost any off-the-shelf clustering algorithm will work; for simplicity, we use $k$-means in this book.

In this book, we present one way to do affinity-based clustering: first use affinities to supervise an embedding in which the data is nearly clustered, then read off the clusters using a simple quantization method like $k$-means. There are many other affinity-based methods but this simple method often works well.

If we define affinities in terms of color distance, then there's no point in learning such an embedding, because the raw colors themselves are already a great embedding under that notion of affinity. Affinity-based clustering becomes interesting when we have nontrivial affinities to model; for example, given by human judgments about which pixels should go together in natural images.

Because human supervision is expensive and limiting, a popular alternative is to use self-supervised affinity measures, just like in self-supervised contrastive learning. Popular contrastive learning methods like SimCLR @chen2020simple, MoCo @he2020momentum, and DINO @caron2021emerging train a mapping from image patches to embedding vectors such that two patches from the same image embed near each other and patches from different images embed far apart. We can run these methods densely (in a sliding window fashion) across a single image to create a feature map of size $C \times N \times M$, where $N$ and $M$ are spatial dimensions and $C$ is the embedding dimensionality. This creates a new image where each pixel has a value (the embedding vector) similar to other pixels the model thinks would likely appear in the same scene. Effectively, we have learned an affinity metric based on natural patch co-occurrences, then used that affinity metric to obtain a feature map revealing coherent image regions. Applying $k$-means to pixels in this feature map yields effective segmentation. This pipeline is shown in @fig-perceptual_organization-kmeans_dino, using DINO @caron2021emerging as the contrastive embedding.
concepts.motivation_md: Affinity-based segmentation models similarity between pixels to group them, enabling segmentation beyond simple color similarity by learning embeddings that reflect complex affinities.
concepts.recap_md:
- Affinity models a distance metric indicating if items should be grouped.
- Contrastive learning can learn embeddings reflecting affinities.
- Clustering such embeddings (e.g., with $k$-means) yields segmentation.

The distance metric usually measures how similar two patterns are, or how likely they are to be part of the same object.

motivation.text: Affinity-based clustering only really becomes interesting when we have nontrivial affinities to model; for example, they could be given by human judgments about which pixels should go together in natural images.

example.text: Popular contrastive learning methods like SimCLR MoCo and DINO train a mapping from image patches to embedding vectors such that two patches that come from the same image embed near each other and patches from different images embed far apart. We can run these methods *densely* (in a sliding window fashion) across a single image to create a feature map of size $C \times N \times M$, where $N$ and $M$ are the spatial dimensions of the feature map and $C$ is the dimensionality of the embedding vectors. This creates a new image where each pixel has a value (the embedding vector) that is similar to other pixels that the model thinks would be likely to appear in the same scene. In effect, we have learned an affinity metric based on natural patch co-occurrences, then used that affinity metric to obtain a feature map that reveals the coherent regions of an image. If we apply $k$-means to the pixels in this feature map, we can obtain an effective segmentation.

concepts.title: Diffusion Models
concepts.one_liner: Diffusion models use a corruption process that adds noise step-by-step to data and train a neural net to reverse this process, turning noise back into data.
concepts.content:
The strategy of autoregressive models is to break a hard problem into lots of simple pieces. Diffusion models are another class of model that uses this same strategy. They can be understood by looking at autoregressive models in reverse: starting with a complete image, autoregressive models remove one pixel at a time, which is a signal corruption process. Diffusion models use a different corruption process: starting with an uncorrupted image $\mathbf{x}_0$, they add noise $\mathbf{\epsilon}_0$ to produce a noisy image $\mathbf{x}_1$, then add more noise $\mathbf{\epsilon}_1$ to get $\mathbf{x}_2$, and so on. Most commonly, the noise is isotropic Gaussian noise. After $T$ steps, the image $\mathbf{x}_T$ looks like pure noise if $T$ is large enough. Specifically, if the noise process is $$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{x}_t &= \sqrt{(1-\beta_t)}\mathbf{x}_{t-1} + \sqrt{\beta_t}\mathbf{\epsilon}_t\\
    \epsilon_t &\sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})
\end{aligned}$$ with $\beta_t \leq 1$, then $\mathbf{x}_T \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})$ as $T \rightarrow \infty$. Diffusion models train a neural net $f_{\theta}$ to reverse this process by supervised learning on sequences of images becoming noisier. For example, the sequence of images of a bird getting noisier can be reversed to provide training pairs mapping $\mathbf{x}_t \rightarrow \mathbf{x}_{t-1}$, which $f_{\theta}$ learns to predict. This neural net is called a denoiser; it learns to remove noise from an image. Applying the denoiser repeatedly starting from pure noise should produce a noise-less image resembling training data. The training steps are: 1. Generate training data by corrupting images (forward noising). 2. Train a neural net to invert each corruption step (reverse denoising). It helps to let the denoiser observe the time step $t$ as input, so we have $$\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t-1} = f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_t, t)$$ which improves predictions by informing the model how noisy the input is. The denoiser can be trained using an $L_2$ loss or to output Gaussian parameters, yielding probabilistic interpretations. A useful trick is to reparameterize the learning problem to predict the noise rather than the signal: $$\begin{aligned}
    f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_t, t) &= \epsilon_t \\
    \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t-1} &= \mathbf{x}_t + \epsilon_t
\end{aligned}$$ Diffusion models learn a mapping from pure noise to data by creating training sequences from data to noise, which is easier to do than generating data from noise directly.
concepts.motivation_md: Diffusion models exist to generate complex data (like images) by learning to reverse a noise corruption process, which is easier than directly generating structured data from noise. This approach provides a principled way to train models that create realistic samples.
concepts.recap_md:
- Diffusion models corrupt data by adding noise step-by-step until it becomes pure noise.
- A neural net denoiser is trained to reverse this process, removing noise gradually.
- Training involves supervised learning on pairs of noisy and less noisy images, enabling generation from noise to data.

key_passage.text: Diffusion models instead use the following corruption process: starting with an uncorrupted image, $\mathbf{x}_0$, they add noise $\mathbf{\epsilon}_0$ to this image, resulting in a noisy version of the image, $\mathbf{x}_1$. Then they repeat this process, adding noise $\mathbf{\epsilon}_1$ to produce an even noisier signal $\mathbf{x}_2$, and so on. Most commonly, the noise is isotropic Gaussian noise.

motivation.text: One way to look at diffusion models is that we want to learn a mapping from pure noise (e.g., $\mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})$) to data. It is very hard to figure out how to create structured data out of noise, but it is easy to do the reverse, turning data into noise.

concepts.title: GAN learning problem
concepts.one_liner: The GAN learning problem is formulated as a minimax game between the generator and discriminator.
concepts.motivation_md: Formulating GAN training as a minimax game captures the adversarial nature where the generator tries to fool the discriminator and the discriminator tries to detect fakes.
concepts.recap_md:

- The discriminator maximizes classification accuracy.
- The generator minimizes the discriminator's ability to detect fakes.

\end{aligned}$$

\end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: The optimal discriminator maximizes its ability to distinguish real from generated data, providing the best feedback to the generator.

- It is the arg max over discriminator parameters $\phi$.
- Guides the generator by providing accurate discrimination.

concepts.title: GANs are Statistical Image Models
concepts.one_liner: GANs learn mappings from latent noise to samples, amortizing optimization unlike hand-defined statistical image models.
concepts.content: GANs are related to the image and texture models we saw in earlier sections. For example, the Heeger-Bergen model synthesizes images with the same statistics as a source texture by optimizing image pixels until certain statistics match those of a training image. In the Heeger-Bergen model, the objective is to match subband histograms. In the language of GANs, the loss that checks for such a match is a kind of discriminator; it outputs a score related to the difference between a generated image's statistics and the real image's statistics. However, unlike a GAN, this discriminator is hand-defined in terms of certain statistics rather than learned. Additionally, GANs amortize the optimization via learning: GANs learn a mapping $g_{\theta}$ from latent noise to samples rather than arriving at samples via an optimization process starting from scratch each time we want a new sample.
concepts.motivation_md: GANs provide a learned approach to synthesizing images with desired statistics, improving upon hand-crafted statistical models by learning a direct mapping from noise to samples.
concepts.recap_md:
- GANs relate to statistical image models like Heeger-Bergen.
- Heeger-Bergen matches image statistics via optimization with a hand-defined discriminator.
- GANs learn a mapping from noise to samples, amortizing optimization.

concepts.title: VAE training objective with reconstruction and KL terms
concepts.one_liner: The VAE training objective combines a reconstruction error term and a KL divergence term.
concepts.content: $$\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \Big( \log\frac{1}{\sigma_{x^{(i)}}\sqrt{2\pi}} - \frac{\overbrace{(x^{(i)} - \mu_{x^{(i)}})^2}^{\text{reconstruction error}}}{2\sigma_{x^{(i)}}^2} - \underbrace{\frac{1}{2}(\mu_{z^{(i)}}^2 + \sigma_{z^{(i)}}^2 - \log(\sigma_{z^{(i)}}^2) - 1)}_{\text{KL term}} \Big)\end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: The training objective balances reconstruction accuracy with regularization of the latent space to encourage meaningful, structured representations.
concepts.recap_md:
- The objective includes a reconstruction error term measuring how well the model recreates inputs.
- A KL divergence term regularizes the latent distribution towards a unit Gaussian.
- These two terms together enable learning a structured latent space.

concepts.title: Effect of KL term on latent distribution in VAEs
concepts.one_liner: The KL term encourages the encodings $z^{(i)}$ to be near a unit Gaussian distribution.
concepts.content:
The KL term encourages the encodings $z^{(i)}$ to be near a unit Gaussian distribution. To get an intuition for the effect of this term, consider the case where we fix $\sigma_{z^{(i)}}$ to be 1; this is still a valid model for $q_{\psi}(Z|x)$, just with lower capacity because it has fewer free parameters. In this simple case, the KL term reduces to $\frac{1}{2}(\mu_{z^{(i)}}^2 - 1) \propto \mu_{z^{(i)}}^2$. The effect of this term is therefore to encourage the encodings $\mu_{z^{(i)}}$ to be *as close to zero as possible*. In other words, the KL term squashes the distribution of latents ($q_{\psi}(Z)$) to be near the origin.

Minimizing the reconstruction error, on the other hand, requires that the latents do not collapse to the origin; this term wants them to be as spread out as possible so as to preserve information about the inputs $x^{(i)}$ that they encode. The tension between these two terms is what causes the VAE to work. While a standard autoencoder may produce an arbitrary latent distribution, with gaps and tendrils of density (as we saw in @fig-generative_modeling_and_representation_learning-autoencoder_complicated_latent_space), a VAE produces a tightly packed latent space which can be densely sampled from.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the KL term's effect clarifies how VAEs balance latent space regularization with reconstruction fidelity, enabling meaningful sampling and interpolation.
concepts.recap_md:
- The KL term pushes latent encodings $\mu_{z^{(i)}}$ toward zero, encouraging a unit Gaussian latent distribution.
- Reconstruction error pushes latents to spread out to preserve input information.
- The balance between these terms produces a well-structured, densely sampled latent space.

concepts.title: disentanglement
concepts.one_liner: Disentanglement means varying one embedding dimension changes just one independent factor in generated images.
concepts.content: Disentanglement means that we can vary one dimension of the embedding at a time, and just one independent factor of variation in the generated images will change. For example, one dimension might control the direction of light in a scene and another dimension might control the intensity of light.
concepts.motivation_md: Disentanglement helps interpret latent representations by isolating independent factors of variation, making models more understandable and controllable.
concepts.recap_md:
- Disentanglement allows one latent dimension to control a single independent factor.
- Varying one dimension changes only one aspect of generated images.
- Examples include controlling light direction or intensity separately.

concepts.title: Example: Learning a VAE for Rivers
concepts.one_liner: A VAE trained on synthetic river images learns to generate and disentangle latent factors like grass color and river curvature.
concepts.content:
Suppose we have a dataset of aerial views of rivers. We wish to fit this data with a VAE so that (1) we can generate new rivers, and (2) we can identify the underlying latent variables that explain river appearance. In this example we will use data for which we know the true data generating process, which is simply a Python script that procedurally synthesizes cartoon images of rivers given input noise (this is a more elaborate version of the script we saw in @alg-generative_models-simple_rivers_script of @sec-generative_models). The script takes in random values that control the attributes of the scene (the grass color, the heading of the river, the number of trees, etc.) and generates an image with these attributes, as shown in @fig-generative_modeling_and_representation_learning-rivers_dataset.

(see figure: A toy generative model hand-coded in Python.)

Training a VAE on this data (@fig-generative_modeling_and_representation_learning-vae_rivers_samples) learns to recreate the generative process with a *neural net* (rather than a Python script) and maps zero-mean unit-variance *Gaussian noise* to images (rather than taking as input the noise types the script uses).

(see figure: Fitting a VAE to the rivers dataset)

Did the VAE uncover the *true* latent variables that generated the data, that is, did it recover latent dimensions corresponding to the attribute values that were the inputs to the Python script? We can examine this by generating a set of images that walk along two latent dimensions of the VAE's $z$-space, shown in @fig-generative_modeling_and_representation_learning-vae_rivers_latent_walk.

(see figure: Walking along two axes of latent space generates images that show variation in two distinct attributes, demonstrating that this model is, to a degree, disentangled.)

One of the latent dimensions seems to control the grass color, and another controls the river curvature! These two latent dimensions are disentangled in the sense that varying the latent dimension that controls color has little effect on curvature and varying the latent dimension that controls curvature has little effect on color. Indeed, grass color was one of the attributes of the true data generating process (the Python script), and the VAE recovered it. However, interestingly there was no single input to the script that controls the overall river curvature, instead the curves are generating by a vector of Bernoulli variables that rotate the heading left and right as the river extends (using the same algorithm as in @alg-generative_models-simple_rivers_script.) The VAE has discovered a latent dimension that somehow summarizes a more global mode of behavior (i.e., bend left or bend right) than is explicit in the Python script. It is important to realize that VAEs, and most representation learning methods, do not necessarily recover the true causal mechanisms that generated the data but rather might find other mechanisms that can equivalently explain the data. 

A formal name for this issue is the *nonidentifiability* of the true parameters that generated a dataset.

To summarize this section, we have seen that a VAE can be considered two things:
concepts.motivation_md: This example illustrates how VAEs can learn to generate realistic images and discover meaningful latent factors, even when the true data generation process is complex or unknown.
concepts.recap_md:
- A VAE trained on synthetic river images learns to generate new images and identify latent factors.
- Latent dimensions can be disentangled, controlling attributes like grass color and river curvature.
- VAEs may discover latent factors that differ from the true data generating parameters due to nonidentifiability.

concepts.title: InfoNCE loss
concepts.one_liner: The InfoNCE loss treats establishing a contrast as a classification problem, moving points apart until you can classify the positive sample separately from all negatives.
concepts.content:
Hadsell et al.'s contrastive loss and the triplet loss add the concept of a margin to the vanilla formulation: they only push or pull when the distance is less than a specified amount $m$ (called the margin); otherwise, points are considered far enough apart or close enough together. The InfoNCE loss is a variation that treats establishing a contrast as a classification problem: it tries to move points apart until you can classify the positive sample, for a given anchor, separately from all the negatives. The general formulation of these losses takes as input an anchor $\mathbf{x}$, a positive example $\mathbf{x}^+$, and one or more negative examples $\mathbf{x}^-$. The positive and negative may be defined based on transformations, cooccurrences, or something else. The full learning objective is to sum over many samples of anchors, positives, and negatives, producing a sampled set evaluated according to the losses as follows:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^+, \mathbf{x}^-) &= \max(D(f(\mathbf{x}), f(\mathbf{x}^+)-m_{\texttt{pos}},0) - \nonumber \\ &\quad \max(m_{\texttt{neg}} - D(f(\mathbf{x}), f(\mathbf{x}^-),0) \quad \triangleleft \quad \text{Hadsell et al. ``contrastive''}\\
    \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^+, \mathbf{x}^-) &= \max(D(f(\mathbf{x}), f(\mathbf{x}^+)) - D(f(\mathbf{x}), f(\mathbf{x}^-)) + m, 0) \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \text{triplet}\\
    \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^+, \{\mathbf{x}_i^-\}_{i=1}^N) &= -\log \frac{e^{f(\mathbf{x})^\mathsf{T}f(\mathbf{x}^+)/\tau}}{e^{f(\mathbf{x})^\mathsf{T}f(\mathbf{x}^+)/\tau} + \sum_i e^{f(\mathbf{x})^\mathsf{T}f(\mathbf{x}_i^-)/\tau}} \quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\triangleleft \quad \text{InfoNCE}
\end{aligned}$$
Notice that the InfoNCE loss is a log softmax.
concepts.motivation_md: InfoNCE loss reframes contrastive learning as a classification problem, enabling models to distinguish positive samples from negatives effectively by pushing embeddings apart until classification is possible.
concepts.recap_md:
- Contrastive losses use an anchor, positive, and negative samples to learn embeddings.
- InfoNCE loss treats contrastive learning as a classification problem using a log softmax.
- Margins in other losses define thresholds for pushing/pulling embeddings based on distance.

concepts.content: The InfoNCE loss can be understood as a classification problem over a vector of scores $f_1(\mathbf{x})^\mathsf{T}f_2(c)/\tau$ with $c \in \{\mathbf{x}^+, \mathbf{x}_1^-, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_N^-\}$. You can therefore think of this loss as corresponding to a classification problem where the ground truth class is $\mathbf{x}^+$ and the other possible classes are $\{\mathbf{x}_1^-, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_N^-\}$ (refer to @sec-intro_to_learning to revisit softmax classification).
concepts.motivation_md: Viewing InfoNCE as classification clarifies how it separates positive samples from negatives by maximizing the probability of the positive class.
concepts.recap_md:
- InfoNCE loss scores positive and negative samples.
- It treats contrastive learning as a classification problem.
- The positive sample is the ground truth class among negatives.

concepts.title: Alignment and Uniformity
concepts.one_liner: The InfoNCE contrastive loss encourages embeddings to have alignment and uniformity properties.
concepts.content: Wang and Isola @wang2020hypersphere showed that the contrastive loss (specifically the InfoNCE form) encourages two simple properties of the embeddings: alignment and uniformity. Alignment is the property that two views in a positive pair will map to the same point in embedding space, meaning the mapping is invariant to the difference between the views. Uniformity comes from the negative term, which encourages embeddings to spread out and tend toward an evenly spread, uniform distribution. Importantly, for this to work mathematically, the embeddings must be normalized, meaning each embedding vector must be a unit vector. Otherwise, the negative term can push embeddings toward being infinitely far apart from each other. Fortunately, it is standard practice in contrastive learning (and many other forms of representation learning) to apply $L_2$ normalization to the embeddings. The result is that the embeddings will tend toward a uniform distribution over the surface of the $M$-dimensional hypersphere, where $M$ is the dimensionality of the embeddings. See theorem 1 in @wang2020hypersphere for a formal statement of this fact.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding alignment and uniformity helps explain how contrastive losses shape embedding spaces to be both invariant to positive pairs and well-distributed globally.
concepts.recap_md:
- InfoNCE loss encourages alignment and uniformity in embeddings.
- Alignment means positive pairs map to the same point.
- Uniformity means embeddings spread uniformly on a normalized hypersphere.

concepts.title: Evidence Lower Bound or ELBO
concepts.one_liner: The VAE objective, $J$, is often called the Evidence Lower Bound or ELBO, because it is a lower-bound on the data log-likelihood $J_p = \log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$.
concepts.content: The VAE objective, $J$, is often called the **Evidence Lower Bound** or **ELBO**, because it is a lower-bound on the data log-likelihood (i.e. $J_p$, which equals $\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$).
concepts.motivation_md: The ELBO provides a tractable lower bound on the data log-likelihood, allowing us to optimize the VAE objective even when the true likelihood is intractable.
concepts.recap_md:
- The VAE objective $J$ is called the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO).  
- ELBO is a lower bound on the data log-likelihood $\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$.

key_passage.text: The VAE objective, $J$, is often called the **Evidence Lower Bound** or **ELBO**, because it is a lower-bound on the data log-likelihood (i.e. $J_p$, which equals $\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$).

concepts.title: VAE objective form as likelihood minus KL divergence
concepts.one_liner: Using the definition of KL-divergence, we can rewrite $J$ as $J = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim q_{\psi}(Z \mid \mathbf{x})}[\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{z})] - \mathrm{KL}(q_\psi(Z \mid \mathbf{x}) \| p_{\mathbf{z}})$, the VAE objective.
concepts.motivation_md: This form shows the VAE objective as a trade-off between reconstruction likelihood and a KL divergence regularizer, clarifying its interpretation.
concepts.recap_md:
- The VAE objective $J$ equals the expected log-likelihood minus the KL divergence.  
- Formally, $J = \mathbb{E}_{z\sim q_\psi}[\log p_\theta(x|z)] - \mathrm{KL}(q_\psi(Z|x) \| p_z)$.

key_passage.text:
Using the definition of KL-divergence, we can also rewrite $J$ as follows: $$\begin{aligned} J &= \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim q_{\psi}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})}\Big[\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z}) \Big] - \mathrm{KL}\left(q_\psi(Z \mid \mathbf{x}) \| p_{\mathbf{z}}\right) \quad\quad\triangleleft\quad\text{VAE objective}
\end{aligned}$$

concepts.title: Connection to Autoencoders
concepts.one_liner: The VAE uses both an encoder $f_{\psi}$ and a decoder $g_{\theta}$, resembling the two pieces of an autoencoder.
concepts.content: You may have noticed that in the previous sections we made use of both an encoder $f_{\psi}$ (which parameterizes $q_{\psi}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})$) and a decoder $g_{\theta}$ (which parameterizes $p_{\theta}(X \bigm | \mathbf{z})$); it looks like we are using the two pieces of an autoencoder but what's the exact connection?
concepts.motivation_md: This concept highlights the structural similarity between VAEs and autoencoders, helping to understand VAEs as probabilistic autoencoders.
concepts.recap_md:
- The VAE has an encoder $f_\psi$ and decoder $g_\theta$.  
- These correspond to $q_\psi(Z|x)$ and $p_\theta(X|z)$ respectively.  
- This structure resembles an autoencoder.

concepts.title: VAE Gaussian latent and observation models
concepts.one_liner: The VAE uses Gaussian latent and observation models: $p_z = \mathcal{N}(0,1)$, $q_{\psi}(Z|x) = \mathcal{N}(\mu_z, \sigma^2_z)$, and $p_{\theta}(X|z) = \mathcal{N}(\mu_x, \sigma^2_x)$.
concepts.content:
$$\begin{aligned}
    p_z &= \mathcal{N}(0,1)\\
    q_{\psi}(Z \bigm | x) &= \mathcal{N}(\mu_z, \sigma^2_z)\\
    p_{\theta}(X \bigm | z) &= \mathcal{N}(\mu_x, \sigma^2_x)
\end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Using Gaussian distributions for latent and observation models allows tractable inference and learning in VAEs.
concepts.recap_md:
- The prior $p_z$ is standard normal $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$.  
- The encoder $q_\psi(Z|x)$ is Gaussian with parameters $\mu_z, \sigma_z^2$.  
- The decoder $p_\theta(X|z)$ is Gaussian with parameters $\mu_x, \sigma_x^2$.

concepts.title: VAE objective likelihood term and KL term
concepts.one_liner: The VAE objective decomposes into a likelihood term and a KL divergence term for each data point.
concepts.motivation_md: Breaking the objective into likelihood and KL terms clarifies the roles of reconstruction and regularization in training VAEs.
concepts.recap_md:

concepts.title: KL divergence between two normal distributions in closed form
aliases: KL divergence closed form for Gaussians
concepts.one_liner: The KL divergence between two normal distributions $\mathcal{N}(\mu_z, \sigma_z^2)$ and $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ has the closed form $\frac{1}{2}(\mu_z^2 + \sigma_z^2 - \log(\sigma_z^2) - 1)$.
concepts.content:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathrm{KL}\left(q_\psi(Z \mid x) \| p_z\right)&=\operatorname{KL}\left(\mathcal{N}\left(\mu_z, \sigma_z^2\right) \| \mathcal{N}(0,1)\right)\\
    &= \frac{1}{2}(\mu_z^2 + \sigma_z^2 - \log(\sigma_z^2) - 1)
\end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: This closed-form formula allows efficient computation of the KL divergence term in the VAE objective when both distributions are Gaussian.
concepts.recap_md:
- KL divergence between $\mathcal{N}(\mu_z, \sigma_z^2)$ and $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ is closed form.  
- The formula is $\frac{1}{2}(\mu_z^2 + \sigma_z^2 - \log(\sigma_z^2) - 1)$.

concepts.title: VAE sampling and reconstruction error computation
concepts.one_liner: To evaluate the likelihood a VAE places on a datapoint $x$, we encode $x$ into $z$-space, sample $z$, decode back, and compute the reconstruction error.
concepts.motivation_md: This technique shows how to compute the likelihood of a data point under the VAE by encoding, sampling, decoding, and measuring reconstruction error.

- Sample $z \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_z, \sigma_z^2)$.

concepts.title: Photographer Bias
concepts.one_liner: The photographer bias is probably one of the most common biases in image databases, and surprisingly difficult to get rid of it.
concepts.content:
### Photographer Bias

The photographer bias is probably one of the most common biases in image databases, and surprisingly difficult to get rid of it.

In a beautiful study, Steve Palmer et al @Palmer1981 showed participants photographs of objects with different orientations in order to measure what orientations they preferred. For each object there were 12 different orientations. Participants had consistent preferences for particular viewpoints for each object. Interestingly, those preferences also correlated with how easy it was to recognize each object.

In another experiment from the same study, participants were shown one picture and their task was to classify the object as quickly as possible from a fixed set of twelve known possible classes. The average response time and accuracy were measured for each of the $12 \times 12$ images. The speed and accuracy are a measure of how easy it is to recognize an object under a particular viewpoint. The study showed that people recognized objects better when presented in a canonical orientation.

@fig-bias_and_shift-palmer_1981enhanced shows the preferred viewpoint for the 12 objects studied.

(see figure: Cannonical viewpoints for 12 objects. Figure from @Palmer1981)

The views that are recognized faster also match the viewpoints that are preferred when taking a picture of those objects @Palmer1981. Such photographer preferred viewpoint introduces biases on how objects are captured, and this bias makes the statistics of object pose in photographs different from the statistics of how objects are actually seen.

The photographer bias exists for objects and scenes (composed of many objects). When taking pictures of scenes, there are biases on the preferred viewpoint, camera orientation (e.g., the horizon is usually inside the picture frame), object locations (such as the one third rule), object arrangements, positions of shadows, types of occlusions, position of the sun, time of day, weather, and so on. All of those factors are taken in consideration (consciously or not) by photographers when deciding which pictures to take.

When building a benchmark, especially when it is small, it is easy to introduce another photographer bias which is to take pictures that "feel" easier to recognize. This might be the right thing to do at first, when debugging a system, but, if abused, has the risk of leading us in the wrong direction when choosing which approach works best.
concepts.motivation_md: Photographer bias affects how objects and scenes are captured, causing datasets to reflect preferred viewpoints rather than how objects are actually seen, which can mislead model training and evaluation.
concepts.recap_md:
- Photographer bias is common and hard to eliminate in image databases.
- People recognize objects faster in canonical orientations, influencing preferred viewpoints.
- Photographer bias affects object pose statistics and scene composition in images.

concepts.title: Collection Bias
concepts.one_liner: There are many potential data sources, all with different biases; Egocentric videos, internet images, vacation photographs, video captured from a moving vehicle, etc.
concepts.content:
### Collection Bias

There are many potential data sources, all with different biases; egocentric videos, internet images, vacation photographs, video captured from a moving vehicle, etc. The potential biases from each data source can be quite significant, and it's often straightforward to identify the capture technique merely by examining the images in a dataset.

@fig-bias_and_shift-mugs shows the first 22 images returned by Google for the query "mug." It looks far from a diverse and unbiased collection of images. As you can appreciate these pictures of mugs look very different from the visual settings in which one usually encounters mugs (inside cabinets, on top of a table, inside the dishwasher, or dirty inside the sink). Instead the images that appear in the search are taken against a flat background, mostly just white, and under a very canonical point of view. For instance, there are no views directly from above.

Other biases can be a bit subtle, for example, most of the handles appear on the right side, and most of the mugs are fully visible, without any occlusions from hands or other objects, and the only two cases of occlusions from mugs occluded by another mug.

(see figure: Pictures of mugs returned by a Google image search. There are many types of biases present in this small image collection.)

The example of the mug, although a bit of a caricature, helps to understand some of the biases that come from the particular collection protocol used to collect images. In this case, images on the internet have a particular type of bias (at least of the ones that get returned under specific searches).

@fig-bias_and_shift-horses shows images returned when looking for "horse." Interestingly many of the pictures are similar to the horse canonical orientation shown in @fig-bias_and_shift-palmer_1981enhanced.

(see figure: Pictures of horses returned by a Google image search. There are many types of biases present in this small image collection.)
concepts.motivation_md: Different data sources introduce distinct biases, making datasets unrepresentative of real-world diversity and affecting model generalization.
concepts.recap_md:
- Different data sources have distinct biases, e.g., egocentric videos vs. internet images.
- Internet images often show objects in canonical views and clean backgrounds.
- Subtle biases include object orientation and occlusion patterns in collected images.

concepts.title: Annotation Bias
concepts.one_liner: When annotating images, image annotators will choose which images to annotate and which labels to use.
concepts.content:
### Annotation Bias

When annotating images, image annotators will choose which images to annotate and which labels to use. This will also correlate with viewpoint preferences and other photographer biases as those images might be easier to annotate and segment, and this has the risk of compounding with the photographer bias.
concepts.motivation_md: Annotation bias arises because annotators select images and labels, often favoring easier viewpoints, which compounds photographer bias and affects dataset representativeness.
concepts.recap_md:
- Annotators choose which images and labels to use.
- Choices correlate with viewpoint and photographer biases.
- This can compound existing biases in datasets.

concepts.title: Social Bias
concepts.one_liner: Social bias refers to biases associated to how groups of people might be reflected differently in the data.
concepts.content:
### Social Bias

This type of bias can affect both the images and the associated labels. Social bias refers to biases associated to how groups of people might be reflected differently in the data. Social biases can be originated by the data collection protocol or by existing social biases. Images can be captured in certain world regions, or contain stereotypes. Labels can reflect social assumptions and biases. An example of social bias is a dataset of images and labels that associates doctors with males and nurses with females.

These types of biases, besides impacting the overall model performance, can have a negative social impact once they are deployed. It is important to be aware of those biases, and incorporate techniques to mitigate their effects. Now it is a good moment for the reader to revisit @sec-computer_vision_and_society.
concepts.motivation_md: Social bias in datasets reflects and perpetuates stereotypes and social assumptions, impacting model fairness and societal outcomes.
concepts.recap_md:
- Social bias affects images and labels reflecting group stereotypes.
- Biases may arise from collection protocols or existing societal biases.
- Such biases can harm model fairness and have negative social impacts.

motivation.text: These types of biases, besides impacting the overall model performance, can have a negative social impact once they are deployed.

concepts.title: Testing and Benchmark Bias
concepts.one_liner: One usually thinks about the biases in the training set, but biases in the test set can have an even more negative impact on the final system behavior than the training bias.
concepts.content:
### Testing and Benchmark Bias

One usually thinks about the biases in the training set, but biases in the test set can have an even more negative impact on the final system behavior than the training bias. The test set is what researchers and engineers use to decide which algorithm is best, or what data collection is more effective for training. However, there might be little correlation between the performance measured on the test set and the final performance of the system during deployment.

In particular, if we compare two training datasets, one biased and another less biased, by evaluating the performance of a system trained on them using a biased test dataset, we could reach the conclusion that the biased dataset is better.
concepts.motivation_md: Biases in test sets can mislead evaluation and model selection, causing poor real-world performance despite good test results.
concepts.recap_md:
- Test set biases can impact system behavior more than training biases.
- Test sets guide algorithm and data collection choices.
- Biased test sets can falsely favor biased training datasets.

concepts.title: zero-shot
concepts.one_liner: The zero-shot setting refers to when a model works out of the box on a new problem, with zero adaptation whatsoever.
concepts.content: Correspondingly, few-shot learning refers to learning from just a few examples, and the zero-shot setting refers to when a model works out of the box on a new problem, with zero adaptation whatsoever.
concepts.motivation_md: Zero-shot learning enables models to solve new problems immediately without any retraining or adaptation, making them highly flexible and efficient.

- Few-shot means learning from a few examples.
- Zero-shot models work out of the box on new tasks.

concepts.title: Finetuning
concepts.one_liner: Finetuning is making small (fine) adjustments to the parameters of your model to adapt it to do something slightly different than before.
concepts.content: Finetuning consists of initializing a new classifier with the parameter vector from the pretrained model, and then training it as usual. In other words, finetuning is making small (fine) adjustments (tuning) to the parameters of your model to adapt it to do something slightly different than what it did before, or even something a lot different.
concepts.motivation_md: Finetuning refines a pretrained model's parameters to adapt it to new tasks, improving performance without training from scratch.
concepts.recap_md:

- It makes small adjustments to adapt the model.
- Enables adapting to similar or different tasks.

key_passage.text: Finetuning consists of initialializing a new classifier with the parameter vector from the pretrained model, and then training it as usual.

motivation.text: In other words, finetuning is making small (fine) adjustments (tuning) to the parameters of your model to adapt it to do something slightly different than what it did before, or even something a lot different.

concepts.title: Finetuning Subparts of a Network
concepts.one_liner: You can selectively finetune some layers of a network and initialize others from scratch.
concepts.content: You don't have to finetune all layers in your network but can selectively finetune some and initialize others from scratch. This strategy can be applied quite generally, where we initialize some parts of a computation graph from pretrained models and initialize others from scratch. There are many reasons why you might want to do this, or not. Sometimes you might have pretrained models that can perform just certain parts of what your full system needs to do. You can use these pretrained models and compose them together with layers initialized from scratch. Other times you may want to freeze certain layers to prevent them from forgetting their prior knowledge @zhang2023adding.
concepts.motivation_md: Selective finetuning allows efficient reuse of pretrained components while customizing other parts, balancing knowledge retention and task-specific adaptation.
concepts.recap_md:
- Finetune some layers, initialize others from scratch.
- Compose pretrained models with new layers.
- Freezing layers can preserve prior knowledge.

concepts.title: linear probes
concepts.one_liner: Linear probes are linear readout modules used to repurpose or assess neural network features.
concepts.content: One important kind of new module is a read out module that takes some features from the computation graph as input and produces a new prediction as output. When these modules are linear, they are called linear probes. These modules are relatively lightweight (few parameters) and can be optimized with tools from linear optimization (where there are often closed form solutions). Because of this, linear probes are very popular as a way of repurposing a neural net to perform a new task. These modules are also useful as a way of assessing what kind of knowledge each feature map in the original network represents, in the sense that if a feature map can linearly classify some attribute of the data, then that feature maps knows something about that attribute. In this usage, linear probes are probing the knowledge represented in some layer of a neural net.
concepts.motivation_md: Linear probes provide a simple, efficient way to test and repurpose neural network features for new tasks or to understand what knowledge is encoded in each layer.
concepts.recap_md:
- Linear probes are linear readout modules.
- They are lightweight and easy to optimize.
- Used to repurpose or assess neural network features.
