concepts.title: Structured Prediction in Vision
concepts.one_liner: Conditional generative models are suitable for structured prediction problems in vision where outputs are high-dimensional and structured, such as label maps or geometry estimations.
concepts.content:
Whenever you want to make a prediction of an *image*, conditional generative models are a suitable modeling choice. But how often do we really want to predict images? Yes, image colorization is one example, but isn't that more of a graphics problem? Most problems in vision are about predicting labels or geometry, right?

Well yes, but what does label prediction look like? The input is an image and the output is a label map. In image classification the output might just be a single class, but more generally, in object detection and semantic segmentation, we want a label for each part of the image. The target output in these problems is high-dimensional and structured.

Or consider geometry estimation: the output is a depth map, or a voxel grid, or a mesh, and so on. All these are high-dimensional structured objects. The tool we need for solving these problems is structured prediction, and conditional generative models are therefore a good choice. In the next sections we will see two important families of
concepts.motivation_md: Many vision tasks require predicting complex, structured outputs like label maps or geometry, making conditional generative models a natural choice for structured prediction in vision.
concepts.recap_md:
- Vision problems often require predicting structured outputs like label maps or geometry.
- Structured prediction handles high-dimensional, structured outputs.
- Conditional generative models are suitable tools for these structured prediction tasks.

concepts.title: Image-to-Image Translation
concepts.one_liner: Image-to-image translation maps an input image to an output image, treating images as arrays and translating between different views or representations of the data.
concepts.content:
Image-to-image problems are mapping problems where the input is an image and the output is also an image, where we will here think of an image as any array of size $N \times M \times C$ (height by width by number of channels). These problems are very common in computer vision. Examples include colorization, next frame prediction, depth map estimation, and semantic segmentation (a per-pixel label map is also an image, just with $K$ channels, one for each label, rather than three channels, one for each color channel).

One way to think about all these problems is as *translating* from one view of the data to another; for example, semantic segmentation is a translation from viewing the world in terms of its colors to viewing the world in terms of its semantics. This perspective yields the problem of **image-to-image translation** @pix2pix2017; just like we can translate from English to French, can we translate from pixels to semantics, or perhaps from a photographic depiction of scene to a painting of that same scene?
concepts.motivation_md: Image-to-image translation provides a framework to convert images from one representation or style to another, enabling tasks like colorization, segmentation, and style transfer.
concepts.recap_md:
- Image-to-image translation maps images to images, treating them as arrays.
- Common tasks include colorization, next frame prediction, depth estimation, and segmentation.
- It is viewed as translating between different views or representations of the data.

concepts.title: Image-to-Image Translation with a Conditional GAN
concepts.one_liner: Image-to-image translation can be performed using a conditional GAN, where a generator maps an input image to an output image and a discriminator evaluates realism.
concepts.content:
One approach to image-to-image translation is to use a conditional GAN, as was popularized in the "pix2pix" paper @pix2pix2017 (whose method we will follow here). To illustrate this approach, we look at the problem of translating a facade layout map into a photo. In this setting, the conditioning information (input) is a layout map showing where all the architectural elements are positioned on the facade (i.e., a semantic segmentation image of the facade, with colors indicating where the windows, doors, and so on are located), and the output is a matching photo.

The generator therefore maps an image to an image so we will implement it with an image-to-image neural architecture. This could be a convolutional neural network (CNN), or a transformer; following the pix2pix paper we will use a U-Net (a CNN with accordion-shaped skip connections; see @sec-convolutional_neural_nets-unet). The discriminator maps the output image to a real-versus-synthetic score (a scalar), so for the discriminator we will use a regular CNN (just like the ones used for image classification). Here is the full architecture (@fig-conditional_generative_models-pix2pix_facades_arch):

(see figure: The pix2pix @pix2pix2017 model applied to translating a facade layout map into a photo of the facade. The model was trained on the CMP Facades Database @Tylecek13 and the input and ground truth...)

Notice that we have omitted the noise inputs here; instead the generator only takes as input the image $\mathbf{x}$. It turns out that in this setting the noise is not really a necessary input, and many implementations omit it. This is because the input image $\mathbf{x}$ has enough entropy by itself, and you don't necessarily need additional noise to create variety in the outputs of the model. The downside of
concepts.motivation_md: Using a conditional GAN for image-to-image translation enables learning a mapping from input images to output images with realistic outputs, even without explicit noise input.
concepts.recap_md:
- Conditional GANs can perform image-to-image translation by conditioning on input images.
- The generator uses an image-to-image architecture like a U-Net.
- The discriminator scores outputs as real or synthetic using a CNN.

concepts.title: PatchGAN
concepts.one_liner: A PatchGAN discriminator scores each patch in an output image as real or fake and averages these scores as the total loss.
concepts.content:
An architecture for image-to-image tasks is a **PatchGAN** discriminator @pix2pix2017, in which we score each *patch* in the output image as real or fake and take the average over patch scores as our total loss:
$$\begin{aligned}    d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = \frac{1}{NM} \sum_{i=0}^N \sum_{j=0}^M d_{\phi}^{\texttt{patch}}(\mathbf{x}[i:i+k,j:j+k], \mathbf{y}[i:i+k,j:j+k])
\end{aligned}$$
where $k \times k$ is the patch size. Notice that this operation is equivalent to the sliding window action of CNN, so $d_{\phi}^{\texttt{patch}}$ can simply be implemented as a CNN that outputs a $2 \times N \times M$ feature map of real-versus-synthetic scores. Naturally, patches can be sampled at different strides and resolutions, depending on the exact architecture of the CNN $d_{\phi}^{\texttt{patch}}$.
concepts.motivation_md: PatchGAN discriminators focus on local image patches to better capture high-frequency details and texture realism in image-to-image translation tasks.
concepts.recap_md:
- PatchGAN discriminator scores each $k \times k$ patch in the output image as real or fake.
- The total loss is the average over all patch scores.
- Implemented as a CNN producing a feature map of real-versus-synthetic scores.

concepts.title: Unpaired Image-to-Image Translation
concepts.one_liner: Unpaired image-to-image translation learns mappings between image domains without paired training data, enabling style transfer and other tasks where paired data is unavailable.
concepts.content:
In the preceding section we saw how to solve image-to-image translation by treating it just like a supervised regression problem, except using a learned loss function given by a GAN discriminator. This approach works great when we have lots of training data pairs $\{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}\}$ to learn from. Unfortunately, very often, paired training data is hard to obtain. For example, consider the task of translating a photo into a Cezanne painting (@fig-conditional_generative_models-cyclegan_teaser):

(see figure: A style transfer example from the CycleGAN paper @CycleGAN2017 *Input photo source*: Alexei A. Efros.)

The task depicted here is to predict: What would it have looked like if Cezanne had stood at this riverbank and painted it?

How could this be done? We can't have solved it with paired training data because, in this setting, paired data is extremely hard to come by. We would have to resurrect Cezanne and ask him to paint for us a bunch of new scenes, one for each photo in our desired training set. But is all that effort really necessary? You and I, as humans, can certainly imagine the answer to the previous question. We know what Cezanne's style looks like and can reason about the changes that would have to occur to make the photo match his style. Dabs of paint would have to replace the photographic pixels, and the colors should take on more pastel tones. We can imagine the necessary stylistic changes because we have seen many Cezanne paintings before, even though we didn't see them paired with a photograph of the exact same scenes. Let's now see how we can give a machine this same ability. We call this setting the **unpaired translation** setting, and distinguish it from **paired translation** as indicated in @fig-conditional_generative_models-paired_vs_unpaired.
concepts.motivation_md: Unpaired image-to-image translation addresses the challenge of learning mappings between domains when paired training examples are unavailable, enabling tasks like style transfer.
concepts.recap_md:
- Paired image-to-image translation requires matched input-output pairs.
- Unpaired translation learns mappings without paired data.
- This enables style transfer where paired examples are rare or impossible.

concepts.title: ordered array
concepts.one_liner: We will call this representation the ordered array.
concepts.content:
We will call this representation the **ordered array**. It is represented as:
$$\boldsymbol\ell=\left[
\begin{matrix}
\ell[1,1] & \dots & \\
\vdots & \ell[n,m] & \vdots \\
 & \dots  & \ell[N,M] \\
\end{matrix}
\right]$$
Each value is a sample on a regular spatial grid. In this notation, $s$ represents the pixel intensity at one location. This is the representation we are most used to and the typical representation used when taking a signal processing perspective. It makes it simpler to arrays for color images).
concepts.motivation_md: Ordered arrays provide a familiar, grid-based way to represent pixel intensities, simplifying signal processing tasks on images. (LLM-inferred)
concepts.recap_md:
- Ordered arrays represent pixel intensities on a regular spatial grid.
- Each entry corresponds to a sample value at a specific location.
- This is the typical representation used in signal processing for images.

concepts.title: set of pixels
concepts.one_liner: Represented as a set of pixels: $$\left\{ [\ell_i,x_i,y_i] : i \right\}$$ where $\ell_i$ is the pixel intensity (or color) recorded at location $(x_i,y_i)$.
concepts.content:
Represented as a **set of pixels**:
$$\left\{ [\ell_i,x_i,y_i] : i \right\}
$$
where $\ell_i$ is the pixel intensity (or color) recorded at location $(x_i,y_i)$. This representation makes the geometry explicit. It might seem like a trivial representation but it makes some operations easy (and others complex). For instance, we can apply geometric transformations easily by directly working with the spatial coordinates. Imagine you want to translate an image, described by equation (@eq-set_of_pixels), to the right by one pixel, you can do that easily by simply creating the new image defined by the set of translated pixels: $\left\{ [\ell_i,x_i+1,y_i] : i \right\}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Representing images as sets of pixels makes geometric transformations straightforward by manipulating spatial coordinates directly. (LLM-inferred)
concepts.recap_md:
- A set of pixels is represented as $\{ [\ell_i,x_i,y_i] : i \}$.
- $\ell_i$ denotes pixel intensity or color at location $(x_i,y_i)$.
- This explicit geometry aids direct geometric transformations like translations.

motivation.text: This representation makes the geometry explicit. It might seem like a trivial representation but it makes some operations easy (and others complex). For instance, we can apply geometric transformations easily by directly working with the spatial coordinates.

concepts.title: homogeneous coordinate
concepts.one_liner: Homogeneous coordinates represent a vector of length $N$ by a vector of length $N+1$ by adding an additional coordinate, 1, to the heterogeneous coordinates.
concepts.content:
Homogeneous coordinates represent a vector of length $N$ by a vector of length $N+1$. The transformation rule from heterogeneous to homogeneous coordinates is simply to add an additional coordinate, 1, to the heterogeneous coordinates as shown here: 
$$\begin{pmatrix}
    x \\
    y 
    \end{pmatrix}
    \rightarrow 
    \begin{bmatrix}
    x \\
    y \\
    1
    \end{bmatrix}
    $$
It is the same if the vector has three dimensions:
$$\begin{pmatrix}    x \\
    y \\
    z
    \end{pmatrix}
    \rightarrow 
    \begin{bmatrix}
    x \\
    y \\
    z \\
    1
    \end{bmatrix}
    $$
We will refer to conventional Cartesian coordinate descriptions of a point in 2D, such as $(x,y)$, or 3D, such as $(x,y,z)$, as **heterogeneous coordinates** and write with rounded brackets in this chapter. We denote their corresponding **homogeneous coordinate** representations by square bracketed vectors.

August Ferdinand Möbius, a German mathematician and astronomer, introduced homogeneous coordinates in 1827. He also cocreated the famous Möbius strip.

The homogeneous coordinates have the additional rule that all (non-zero) scalings of a homogeneous coordinate vector are equivalent. For example, to represent a 2D point, we have (transforming from heterogeneous to homogeneous coordinates),
$$\begin{bmatrix}
    x \\
    y \\
    1
    \end{bmatrix}
    \equiv 
    \begin{bmatrix}
    \lambda x \\
    \lambda y \\
    \lambda
    \end{bmatrix}$$
for any non-zero scalar, $\lambda$. To go from homogeneous coordinates back to the heterogeneous representation of the point, we divide all the entries of the homogeneous coordinate vector by their last dimension:
$$\begin{bmatrix}
    x \\
    y \\
    w
    \end{bmatrix}
    \rightarrow 
    \begin{pmatrix}
    x/w \\
    y/w 
    \end{pmatrix}$$
@fig-homogeneousAndHeteregeneous illustrates how homogeneous and heterogeneous coordinates relate to each other geometrically. A point in homogeneous coordinates is scale invariant (any point within the line that passes through the origin translates into the same point in heterogeneous coordinates). We can already see that this is closely related to the operation performed by perspective projection.

concepts.title: translation in homogeneous coordinates
concepts.one_liner: We can write this translation in homogeneous coordinates by the product: $$\begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & t_x \\ 0 & 1 & t_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$
concepts.content:
We can write this translation in homogeneous coordinates by the product: 
$$
\begin{bmatrix}
    x' \\
    y' \\
    1
    \end{bmatrix}
    =
    \begin{bmatrix}
    1 & 0 & t_x \\
    0 & 1 & t_y \\
    0 & 0 & 1
    \end{bmatrix}
    \begin{bmatrix}
    x \\
    y \\
    1
\end{bmatrix}
$$ 

What is interesting is that we have transformed an addition into a product by a matrix, $\mathbf{T}$, and a vector, $\mathbf{p}$, in homogeneous coordinates. Rewriting the equation above as: 

$$
\mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{T} \mathbf{p},
$$ with the homogeneous matrix, $\mathbf{T}$, defined as 
$$
\mathbf{T} =             
    \begin{bmatrix}
    1 & 0 & t_x \\
    0 & 1 & t_y \\
    0 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
$$

concepts.title: stereo anaglyph
concepts.one_liner: A stereo anaglyph is an image created from two laterally displaced cameras, viewed with red-cyan filters to produce a 3D stereo effect.
concepts.content: @fig-titanic (a) shows a **stereo anaglyph** of the ill-fated ocean liner, the Titanic, from @McManus2022. This was taken with two cameras, one displaced laterally from the other. The right camera's image appears in red in this image, and the left camera image is in cyan. If you view this image with a red filter covering the left eye, and a cyan filter covering the right (@fig-titanic[b]) then the right eye will see only the right camera's image (analogously for the left eye), allowing the ship to pop-out into a three-dimensional (3D) stereo image. Note that the relative displacement between each camera's image of the smokestacks changes as a function of their depth, which allows us to form a 3D interpretation of the ship when viewing the image with the glasses (@fig-titanic[b]).
concepts.motivation_md: Stereo anaglyphs allow us to perceive depth in a flat image by using two slightly different camera views combined with color filters, enabling a 3D interpretation of scenes.
concepts.recap_md:
- A stereo anaglyph combines two images from laterally displaced cameras using red and cyan colors.
- Viewing with red-cyan filters lets each eye see only one image, creating a 3D effect.
- Depth perception arises from relative displacement of features in the two images.

concepts.one_liner: Random dot stereograms demonstrate that humans can perceive depth from relative displacement even without recognizable features.
concepts.content:
This is illustrated by the **random dot stereograms** (@fig-random_dot_stereogram) introduced by Bela Julesz @Julez1971. concepts.title: Triangulation
concepts.one_liner: Stereo vision triangulates depth by comparing images from two spatially offset cameras.

The task of stereo is to triangulate the depth of points in the world by comparing the images from two spatially offset cameras.

If more than two cameras are used, the task is referred to as multiview stereo.

concepts.title: Density Models
concepts.one_liner: Some generative models not only produce generators but also yield a probability density function $p_{\theta}$, fit to the training data.
concepts.content:
Some generative models not only produce generators but also yield a probability density function $p_{\theta}$, fit to the training data. This density function may play a role in training the generator (e.g., we want the generator to produce samples from $p_{\theta}$), or the density function may be the goal itself (e.g., we want to be able to estimate the probability of datapoints in order to detect anomalies).

In fact, some generative models *only* produce a density $p_{\theta}$ and do not learn any explicit generator function. Instead, samples can be drawn from $p_{\theta}$ using a sampling algorithm, such as **Markov Chain Monte Carlo** (**MCMC**), that takes a density as input and produce samples from it as output. This is a form of the indirect

concepts.title: divergence
concepts.one_liner: A divergence $D$ measures the distance between $p_{\theta}$ and $p_{\texttt{data}}$ while only accessing samples from $p_{\texttt{data}}$.
concepts.content:
**divergence** between the two distributions, $D$, and then solve the following optimization problem:
$$\mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{p_\theta} D(p_{\theta}, p_{\texttt{data}})$$
The problem is that we do not actually have the function $p_{\texttt{data}}$, we only have samples from this function, $\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}$. Therefore, we need a divergence $D$ that measures the distance between $p_{\theta}$ and $p_{\texttt{data}}$ while only accessing samples from $p_{\texttt{data}}$. 

The divergence need not be a proper distance *metric*, and often is not; it can be nonsymmetric, where $D(p,q) \neq D(q,p)$, and need not satisfy the triangle-inequality. In fact, a divergence is defined by just two properties: nonnegativity and $D(p,q) = 0 \iff p=q$.

concepts.title: Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence
concepts.one_liner: A common choice is to use the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, which is defined as follows:
concepts.content:
A common choice is to use the **Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence**, which is defined as follows: 
$$\begin{aligned}
    p_{\theta}^* &= \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{p_\theta} \mathrm{KL}\left(p_{\text {data }} \| p_\theta\right)\\
    &= \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{p_\theta} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}\Big[-\log \frac{p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})}{p_{\texttt{data}}(\mathbf{x})}\Big]\\
    &= \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{p_\theta} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}\big[\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\big] - \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}\big[\log p_{\texttt{data}}(\mathbf{x})\big]\\
    &= \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{p_\theta} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}\big[\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\big] \quad \triangleleft \quad\text{dropped second term since no dependence on $p_{\theta}$}
    \\
    &\approx \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{p_\theta} \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)})
\end{aligned}$$${#eq-generative_models-max_likelihood} where the final line is an empirical estimate of the
expectation by sampling over the training dataset
concepts.motivation_md: KL divergence is widely used to measure how one distribution approximates another, enabling maximum likelihood estimation from data samples.
concepts.recap_md:
- KL divergence measures difference between $p_{\texttt{data}}$ and $p_{\theta}$.  
- Minimizing KL divergence corresponds to maximizing expected log-likelihood.  
- Empirical estimate uses sample average over training data.

concepts.title: Energy-Based Models
concepts.one_liner: Energy-based models learn an unnormalized function $E_{\theta}$ and use it to define relative probabilities without computing the normalizing constant.
concepts.content:
Density models constrain the learned function to be normalized, that is, $\int_{\mathbf{x}} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x} = 1$. This constraint is often hard to realize. One approach is to learn an unnormalized function $E_{\theta}$, then convert it to the normalized density $p_{\theta} = \frac{e^{-E_{\theta}}}{Z(\theta)}$, where $Z(\theta) = \int_{\mathbf{x}} e^{-E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})}d\mathbf{x}$ is the normalizing constant. The $Z(\theta)$ can be very expensive to compute and often can only be approximated.

The parametric form $\frac{e^{-E_{\theta}}}{Z(\theta)}$ is sometimes referred to as a **Boltzmann** or **Gibbs distribution**.

Notice that $Z$ is a function of model parameters $\theta$ but not of datapoint $\mathbf{x}$, since we integrate over all possible data values.

Note that low energy $\Rightarrow$ high probability. So we minimize energy to maximize probability.

**Energy-based models** (**EBM**s) address this by simply skipping the step where we normalize the density, and letting the output of the learner just be $E_\theta$. Even though it is not a true probability density, $E_{\theta}$ can still be used for many of the applications we would want a density for. This is because we can compare *relative probabilities* with $E_\theta$: 

$$\begin{aligned}    \frac{p_\theta(\mathbf{x}_1)}{p_\theta(\mathbf{x}_2)} = \frac{e^{-E_\theta(\mathbf{x}_1)}/Z(\theta)}{e^{-E_\theta(\mathbf{x}_2)}/Z(\theta)}
    = \frac{e^{-E_\theta(\mathbf{x}_1)}}{e^{-E_\theta(\mathbf{x}_2)}}
\end{aligned}$$ Knowing relative probabilities is all that is required for sampling (via MCMC), for outlier detection (the relatively lowest probability datapoint in a set of datapoints is the outlier), and even for optimizing over a space of of data to find the datapoint that is max probability (because $\mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X}} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X}} -E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$).

- Energy-based models learn unnormalized energy functions $E_{\theta}$.  
- Relative probabilities depend only on differences in $E_{\theta}$, enabling many applications.

concepts.title: Adversarial Shifts
concepts.one_liner: The data shift is not just random but adversarial, occurring when a competing agent controls the test setting, such as a hacker or a trader.
concepts.content: The data shifts described previously may be disconcerting, but at least they are not malicious. Unfortunately, things can get worse. Quite often the data shift is not just random but adversarial. This may come up whenever our test setting is under the control of a competing agent, for example, someone trying to hack our system (computer security), another animal trying to eat us (evolution), or a trader trying to outperform us on the stock market (finance).
concepts.motivation_md: Adversarial shifts arise when data changes are controlled by a competing agent, posing challenges beyond random shifts and requiring robust defenses.
concepts.recap_md:
- Adversarial shifts occur when data changes are controlled by an adversary.
- Examples include hackers, predators, or competing traders.
- These shifts are more challenging than random data shifts.

concepts.title: adversarial attacks
concepts.one_liner: Adversarial attacks add imperceptible noise to inputs to fool neural net classifiers into producing any output the attacker desires.
concepts.content:
This was famously demonstrated by @szegedy2014intriguing, who showed that one can add imperceptible noise to an image that fools neural net classifiers despite looking completely innocuous to a human. In fact, the noise pattern can be selected to force the network to produce any output the attacker desires. These are called **adversarial attacks** because we suppose the attacker, who adds the noise, is an adversary that wants to fool or manipulate your system. The adversary can do this by simply optimizing the noise pattern to cause the network to make a particular output, while restricting the noise to be very subtle (within an small $r$-radius ball around the original image). For example, to cause an image classifier $f$ to think the cat in @fig-bias_and_shift-adversarial_perturbation is an ostrich, the attacker could find the noise pattern via the following optimization:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{\mathbf{\epsilon}} H(\mathbf{y}_{\texttt{ostrich}}, f(\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{\epsilon})), \quad\quad \text{subject to} \quad\quad \left\lVert\mathbf{\epsilon}\right\rVert < r
\end{aligned}$$ where $H$ is the cross-entropy loss and

(see figure: An adversarial attack that adds subtle changes to the cat photo to make a neural net classify it instead as an ostrich. The noise image color values are scaled 20x for visualization.)

- Adversarial attacks add subtle noise imperceptible to humans.
- The noise is optimized to force a specific incorrect output.
- Example: fooling a cat classifier into labeling an ostrich.

concepts.one_liner: Adversarial attacks require that the attacker has access to the system to optimize noise patterns that fool it.
concepts.content: This type of attack required that the attacker has access to your system (the neural net $f$) so that they can optimize the noise pattern $\mathbf{\epsilon}$ to fool the system. Unfortunately, if you want to deploy your system to the public, then you have to give people access to it and that makes it vulnerable to attack.

concepts.title: Adversarial attacks are the result of an optimization procedure producing imperceptible noise causing system failure
concepts.one_liner: Adversarial attacks result from optimization procedures that produce imperceptible noise causing system failure with high confidence.
concepts.content: In @sec-neural_nets we described a simple neural network for line classification and showed how, by accessing the architecture and the learned filters, we could manually design input examples that would get wrongly classified. Similarly, in @sec-downsampling_and_upsampling we showed how aliasing could also create vulnerabilities in a network. For large systems, adversarial attacks are not manually designed, instead they are the result of an optimization procedure that optimizes the noise pattern $\mathbf{\epsilon}$ so that it has a small amplitude (i.e., it is imperceptible) and makes the system fail with high confidence.
concepts.motivation_md: Adversarial attacks arise from optimization that finds subtle noise patterns causing confident misclassifications, highlighting systemic vulnerabilities.
concepts.recap_md:
- Small neural networks can be manually fooled by crafted inputs.
- Aliasing can also cause vulnerabilities.
- Large systems face adversarial attacks from optimized imperceptible noise.

concepts.title: Adversarial analysis is worst case analysis and minimizing worst-case error can improve adversarial robustness
concepts.one_liner: Adversarial analysis is worst case analysis, and minimizing worst-case error can improve adversarial robustness.
concepts.content:
Adversarial analysis is worst case analysis. Remember that we typically train our systems to minimize empirical risk, defined as the *mean* error over the training data. Because we only focus on the mean, the *worst case* might be arbitrarily bad. Alternative approaches try to minimize worst-case error, and this can result in systems that are more **adversarially robust**. 

In @sec-data_augmentation we will discuss how **adversarial training** can be used to increase the robustness of the models to adversarial attacks.
concepts.motivation_md: Since typical training minimizes average error, worst-case errors can be large; adversarial analysis focuses on minimizing worst-case error to enhance robustness.
concepts.recap_md:
- Adversarial analysis focuses on worst-case errors.
- Typical training minimizes mean error, ignoring worst cases.
- Minimizing worst-case error improves adversarial robustness.

concepts.title: Concluding Remarks on dataset bias and shift and approaches to reduce their impact
concepts.one_liner: Dataset bias and shift can be reduced by rigorous data collection, domain randomization, and transfer learning, but bias remains a persistent challenge.
concepts.content:
One way to reduce the issues of dataset bias and shift is to implement a rigorous data collection procedure that tries to minimize the biases present in the data. Although it is possible to prevent (or reduce) certain forms of bias, others will remain challenging because it is hard to collect the necessary data or because we are not aware of it. In many cases, deployment will be done in specific settings that might be unknown a priori. Therefore, bias is here to stay and it is important to study forms to reduce its methods in the system performance.

There are two general ways of dealing with dataset bias and shift. The first is called domain randomization, or data augmentation. The second is called transfer learning, or model adaptation. The next two chapters are about these options.
concepts.motivation_md: Bias and shift in datasets affect system performance; understanding methods like data augmentation and transfer learning helps mitigate these issues.
concepts.recap_md:
- Rigorous data collection can reduce but not eliminate bias.
- Bias persists due to unknown or hard-to-collect data.
- Domain randomization and transfer learning address bias and shift.

concepts.title: Data Augmentation
concepts.one_liner: Data augmentation augments a dataset by adding random transformations of each datapoint, simulating more data to improve learning.
concepts.content:
Data augmentation augments a dataset by adding random transformations of each datapoint. For example, below we show some common data augmentations applied to an example image (@fig-data_augmentation-data_aug_examples):

(see figure: A few common types of data augmentation.)

When you do this for every image in a dataset, you are essentially mapping from a smaller dataset to a larger dataset. We know that more data is usually better, so this is a way to simulate the effect of adding more real data to your dataset.

[FIGURE:d88031ceb8315562 | A flowchart showing the process of data augmentation. It starts with a 'Small dataset' represented by the set $\{x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$, which passes through a 'Data augmentation' block...]

Data augmentation might not seem not seem very glamorous, but it is one of the most important tools at our disposal. Machine learning is data-driven intelligence, and the bigger the data the better. Data augmentation is like a philosopher's stone of machine learning: it converts lead (small data) into gold (big data).
concepts.motivation_md: Data augmentation artificially increases dataset size by applying random transformations, improving model generalization when real data is limited.
concepts.recap_md:
- Data augmentation applies random transformations to data points.
- It simulates larger datasets from smaller ones.
- It is a key tool to improve machine learning performance.

concepts.title: invariance to augmentation
concepts.one_liner: The assumption is that target outputs are invariant to augmentations of inputs, meaning $y(\mathbf{x}) = y(T(\mathbf{x},\theta))$ for all $\theta$.
concepts.motivation_md: Assuming output invariance to input augmentations justifies data augmentation methods, but this depends on task-specific properties like symmetry or chirality.
concepts.recap_md:
- Target outputs $\mathbf{y}$ are assumed invariant to input augmentations.
- For scene classification, mirror augmentation preserves class labels.
- For character recognition, mirror augmentation changes labels due to non-invariance.

key_passage.text:
The assumption we are making is that the target outputs \mathbf{y} are **invariant** to the augmentations of the inputs \mathbf{x}. Let y(\mathbf{x}) be the true \mathbf{y} for an input \mathbf{x}; then we are assuming that, $$\begin{aligned} y(\mathbf{x}) = y(T(\mathbf{x},\theta)) \quad \forall \theta \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad\text{$y$ invariant to $T$}
\end{aligned}$$

motivation.text: For example, if our task is scene classification then we would want to only apply augmentations that do not affect the class label of the scene.

example.text:
We could use mirror augmentation, since the mirroring a scene does not change its class. In contrast, if the task were optical character recognition, then mirror augmentation would not be a good idea. That's because the mirror image of the character [b]{.sans-serif} looks just like the character [d]{.sans-serif}. Character recognition is not mirror invariant. In other words, for the task of character recognition, we do not have that
$y(\texttt{mirror}(\mathbf{x})) = y(\mathbf{x})$. The same is true for molecular data that exhibits so-called *chiral* structure: a molecule may behave very differently from its mirror image.

concepts.title: CycleGAN
concepts.one_liner: CycleGAN introduces cycle-consistency, ensuring that translating from $X$ to $Y$ and back returns to the original input.
concepts.content:
Cycle-consistency, introduced by CycleGAN @CycleGAN2017, DualGAN @yi2017dualgan, and DiscoGAN @kim2017learning (all essentially the same model), means that if we translate from domain $X$ to $Y$ and then back from $Y$ to $X$, we should arrive where we started. For example, translating "apple" from English to French yields "pomme," and translating "pomme" back to English returns "apple." In natural language processing, this idea is known as backtranslation.

We can check the quality of a translation system for an unfamiliar language using this trick: if translating back does not return the original word, the translation model likely failed. This is because language translation is roughly one-to-one: each English word usually has an equivalent French word. Cycle-consistency losses act as regularizers encouraging the learned mapping to be roughly one-to-one. The cycle-consistency losses from CycleGAN are:

$$
\begin{aligned}
    \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{cyc}}(\mathbf{x};g_{\theta},f_{\psi}) &= \left\lVert\mathbf{x} - f_{\psi}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}))\right\rVert_1\\
    \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{cyc}}(\mathbf{y};g_{\theta},f_{\psi}) &= \left\lVert\mathbf{y} - g_{\theta}(f_{\psi}(\mathbf{y}))\right\rVert_1
\end{aligned}
$$

Adding this loss to @eq-conditional_generative_models-x_to_y_GAN_learning_problem yields the complete CycleGAN objective:

$$
\begin{aligned}
    \arg\min_{\theta,\psi}\max_{\phi} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} \big[ \log d_{\phi}^{Y}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})) + \log (1 - d_{\phi}^{Y}(\mathbf{y})) + \left\lVert\mathbf{x} - f_{\psi}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}))\right\rVert_1 + \\
    \log d_{\phi}^{X}(f_{\psi}(\mathbf{y})) + \log (1 - d_{\phi}^{X}(\mathbf{x})) + \left\lVert\mathbf{y} - g_{\theta}(f_{\psi}(\mathbf{y}))\right\rVert_1 \big]
\end{aligned}
$$

This model translates from domain $X$ to domain $Y$ and back, such that the outputs in domain $Y$ look realistic according to a domain $Y$ discriminator, and vice versa for domain $X$, and the mappings are cycle-consistent: one complete cycle from $X$ to $Y$ and back should arrive where it started (and vice versa). A diagram for this whole process is given in

(see figure: CycleGAN schematic. Figure derived from @CycleGAN2017)
concepts.motivation_md: Cycle-consistency ensures that translations between domains are reversible, helping to learn mappings that are roughly one-to-one and improving the quality of unsupervised domain translation models like CycleGAN.
concepts.recap_md:
- Cycle-consistency means translating from $X$ to $Y$ and back returns the original input.
- CycleGAN uses cycle-consistency losses as regularizers to enforce one-to-one mappings.
- The full CycleGAN objective combines adversarial losses with cycle-consistency losses for both domains.

concepts.title: general-purpose conditional generative models
concepts.one_liner: Conditional generative models provide a unified and simple solution to diverse structured prediction problems in vision.
concepts.content: Many problems in vision can be phrased as structured prediction, and conditional generative models are a great approach to these problems. They provide a unified and simple solution to a diverse array of problems. A current trend in computer vision (and all of artificial intelligence) is to replace bespoke systems for specific kinds of structured prediction—object detectors, image captioning systems, and so on—with general-purpose conditional generative models. This is one reason why this book does not focus much on special-purpose systems that solve specific problems in vision—because the trend is toward general-purpose modeling tools.
concepts.motivation_md: General-purpose conditional generative models simplify and unify solutions to many vision tasks, replacing specialized systems with flexible, broadly applicable models.
concepts.recap_md:
- Many vision problems are structured prediction tasks.
- Conditional generative models offer a unified approach.
- The trend is toward general-purpose models instead of bespoke systems.

concepts.content: # Data Bias and Shift {#sec-bias_and_shift}

- Understanding bias and shift is crucial for robust learning.

concepts.title: Out-of-Distribution Generalization
concepts.content: ## Out-of-Distribution Generalization
concepts.motivation_md: Out-of-distribution generalization studies how models perform on data distributions different from training, aiming to improve robustness.
concepts.recap_md:
- Out-of-distribution generalization concerns model performance on unseen distributions.
- It is key for deploying models in real-world scenarios.
- Research focuses on methods to improve robustness.

key_passage.text: Out-of-Distribution Generalization

concepts.title: A Toy Example
aliases: toy example for bias and shift
concepts.one_liner: A toy example illustrates the effect of training on one dataset and testing on another with different data distributions.
concepts.content:
Let's start by looking at a toy example. In this toy example, we consider two datasets, each with different data distributions. We study the effect of training on one dataset and testing on another.

Observations $(x,y)$ are sampled from a distribution where $x$ is sampled from a Gaussian and $y$ are noisy observations of the function $f$ applied to $x$:

$$\begin{aligned}
    x &\sim \mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma) \\
    y & = f(x) + \beta \epsilon \\
    \epsilon &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)
\end{aligned}$$

The unknown function $f$ has the form:

$$f_{\theta}(x) = \theta_0 x + \theta_1 x^2 \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad\text{hypothesis space}$$

In the first dataset, the Gaussian parameters are $\mu_A = -1.5$, and the standard deviation is $\sigma_A = 1.5$. In the second dataset, the Gaussian has $\mu_B = 2.5$ and $\sigma_B = 0.5$.

For each dataset, we sample two sets of examples: a training set and a test set, which we use to measure generalization error.

Learning is done by optimizing the loss over the corresponding training set:

$$J(\theta; \{x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i \left\lVert f_{\theta}(x^{(i)}) - y^{(i)}\right\rVert_2^2 + \lambda \left\lVert\theta\right\rVert_2^2 \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad\text{objective}$$

@fig-bias_and_shift-training_test_sets shows training and test examples from both datasets and illustrates the effect of training on one dataset and testing on another. Each plot shows the training samples (circles), used to fit the model, and test samples (triangles) used to measure the generalization error. The diagonal plots show the training and test set corresponding to distribution A, @fig-bias_and_shift-training_test_sets (top-left), and distribution B, @fig-bias_and_shift-training_test_sets (bottom-right). In each case, the fitted model is shown as a dashed line.

(see figure: Training and testing on different datasets. In this illustration, all datasets have 5 samples.)

When training and testing is done using samples from the same distribution (A to A, or B to B) the learned model (best fit) passes near the test samples and the error is small. However, when training and test are coming from different distributions, the error can be large. @tbl-bias_and_shift-training_test_sets shows the generalization error made with different combinations of training and test sets as shown in @fig-bias_and_shift-training_test_sets.

| Training set | Test set A | Test set B |
|--------------|------------|------------|
| A            | 0.18       | 0.7        |
| B            | 1.93       | 0.23       |
: Generalization error for different combinations of training and test sets. {#tbl-bias_and_shift-training_test_sets}

The diagonal elements correspond to the error obtained when training on the training examples of dataset A and testing on the test examples of dataset A, and when training and testing on dataset B.

As shown in @tbl-bias_and_shift-training_test_sets, the error becomes larger for the elements off-diagonal. However, @tbl-bias_and_shift-training_test_sets only gives a partial picture about what is happening because it gives the error only for dataset size equal to 5. What happens if we add more data?

It is interesting in general to look at the performance as a function of training data. If we add more data, does performance improve when training and testing on different datasets? Or does it saturate? The answer will depend on the form of the data distributions and the hypothesis space. But we can check what happens in this toy example.

@fig-bias_and_shift-test_as_function_of_data plots the generalization error (vertical axis) when evaluating on dataset A as a function of the amount of training data (horizontal axis).

(see figure: Generalization error as a function of number of training examples. Test set is dataset A. Each curve shows the performance when training with dataset A and with dataset B (same distributions as in...)

Interestingly, both training sets (A and B) succeed in reducing the generalization error on the test set of dataset A when more training data is available. In this example, even the biased dataset B is still able to train a successful model of dataset A. However, the reduction of the error is slower than when training on dataset A. Examples from dataset B are less valuable than examples from dataset A @Torralba2011. We need approximately 10 times more examples from dataset B in order to reach a particular performance. Another way of saying this is that the value of a training example from dataset B when evaluating on dataset A is around $1/10$ of the value of a sample from A.
concepts.motivation_md: This toy example illustrates how training on one data distribution and testing on another affects generalization error, highlighting the impact of data bias and distribution shift.
concepts.recap_md:
- Training and testing on the same distribution yields low error; cross-distribution testing increases error.
- More training data generally reduces error, but biased datasets require more samples.
- The value of samples depends on their distribution relative to the test set.

concepts.title: Image rectification constraints
concepts.one_liner: Many configurations of the two cameras satisfy the desired image rectification constraints: epipolar lines along image scanlines and matching points within the same rows in each camera image.
concepts.content: Many configurations of the two cameras satisfy the desired image rectification constraints @Zhang2003: (1) that epipolar lines are along image scanlines, and (2) that matching points are within the same rows in each camera image. One procedure that will satisfy those constraints is as follows @wikiRectification2021. First, rotate each camera to be parallel with each other and with optical axes perpendicular to the line joining the two camera centers. Second, rotate each of the cameras about its optical axis to align the rows of each camera with those of the other. Third, uniformly scale one camera's image to be the same size as to the other, if necessary. The resulting image pair will thus satisfy the two requirements above for image rectification. Image rectification
concepts.motivation_md: Image rectification aligns stereo images so that epipolar lines correspond to image rows, simplifying stereo matching and improving correspondence accuracy.
concepts.recap_md:
- Image rectification ensures epipolar lines lie along image scanlines.
- Matching points appear within the same rows in both camera images.
- Achieved by rotating cameras and scaling images to align rows and sizes.

concepts.title: Output Representation
concepts.one_liner: We can estimate disparity or depth; disparity is independent of camera parameters and easier to model noise for, while depth has larger errors for distant points.
concepts.content:
One important question is how we want to represent the output. We are ultimately interested in estimating the 3D structure of the scene. We can estimate the disparity or the depth. Disparity might be easier to estimate as it is independent of the camera parameters. It is also easier to model noise, as we can assume that noise is independent of disparity. However, when using depth, estimation error will be larger for distant points.

Another interesting property of disparity is that for flat surfaces, the second-order derivative along any spatial direction, $\mathbf{x}$, is zero: $$\frac{\partial^2 d}{\partial \mathbf{x}^2}  = 0.$$ This equality does not hold for depth. This property allows introducing a simple regularization term that favors planarity.
concepts.motivation_md: Choosing disparity or depth as output affects noise modeling and error behavior; disparity's planarity property aids regularization.
concepts.recap_md:
- Output can be disparity or depth; disparity is camera-parameter independent.
- Noise modeling is simpler with disparity.
- Disparity's second derivative is zero on flat surfaces, enabling planarity regularization.

concepts.title: Disparity to depth conversion
concepts.one_liner: To convert disparity $d[n,m]$ to depth $z[n,m]$, invert disparity as $z[n,m] = 1/d[n,m]$ and use intrinsic parameters $\mathbf{K}$ to obtain 3D coordinates.

concepts.recap_md:
- Depth is the inverse of disparity: $z[n,m] = 1/d[n,m]$.
- Use intrinsic matrix $\mathbf{K}$ to convert depth and pixel coordinates to 3D points.
- Assumes pinhole camera model.

concepts.title: Two-Stage Networks
concepts.one_liner: Disparity at each location can be computed by a function $\hat{\mathbf{d}} = f_{\theta}(\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2)$ trained to minimize loss against ground truth disparities.
concepts.content:
Given two images, $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$, the disparity at each location can be computed by a function, that is:
$$\hat{\mathbf{d}} = f_{\theta}(\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2)$$

The objective is that the estimated disparities, $\hat{\mathbf{d}}$, should be close to ground truth disparities, $\mathbf{d}$. One example of training set are the KITTI dataset @Geiger2013 and the scene flow dataset @Mayer2016, which contain ground truth disparities from calibrated stereo cameras. One typical loss is:
$$J(\theta) = \sum_t \left| \mathbf{d} - f_{\theta} (\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2) \right|^2$$
This is optimized by gradient descent as usual.

When matching and filtering are implemented separately, one common formulation is to use one neural network to extract features from both images, $g(\mathbf{i}_1)$ and $g(\mathbf{i}_2)$, and one neural network to compute the matching cost and estimate the disparities at every pixel.
$$f(\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2) = c \left( g(\mathbf{v}_1), g(\mathbf{v}_2) \right)$$

A common approach, depicted in block diagram form in @fig-stereo (b)lock,
concepts.motivation_md: Two-stage networks separate feature extraction and matching to improve disparity estimation accuracy in stereo vision.

- Disparity estimation function $\hat{\mathbf{d}} = f_{\theta}(\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2)$ is trained to match ground truth.
- Loss function sums squared errors over training set.
- Separate networks can extract features and compute matching costs.

concepts.one_liner: In this chapter we have reviewed some of the key components of a system trained to estimate depth from single images.
concepts.content: In this chapter we have reviewed some of the key components of a system trained to estimate depth from single images. The methods are similar to other regression problems and most of the challenge consists of identifying how to collect the data needed for training. Supervised methods are more reliable than unsupervised methods for now. Unsupervised methods rely on learning to estimate depth using the constraints present between camera motion, 3D, and photometric consistency. Unsupervised learning allows a system to learn from a very diverse set of data (as the only thing needed is video captured by a moving camera), and to adapt to new environments where ground truth supervision is not available.

concepts.title: reprojection error

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: The reprojection error is the sum of Euclidean distances between observed image points and estimated projected points.
concepts.content:
We already introduced the reprojection error in section @sec-cam_cal_minimizing_reprojection_error when talking about camera calibration. Here the formulation is similar but we optimize over a different set of unknowns. The reprojection error is the sum of Euclidean distances (in heterogeneous coordinates) between the observed image points \(\mathbf{p}^{(j)}_i\) and the estimated projected points \(\hat{\mathbf{p}}^{(j)}_i\):

$$\sum_{j=1}^M \sum_{i=1}^N \left\lVert \mathbf{p}^{(j)}_i - \hat{\mathbf{p}}^{(j)}_i \right\rVert ^2$$

The estimated projected points are obtained using the estimated 3D point locations \(\mathbf{P}^{(j)}_i\) and the estimated camera matrices \(\mathbf{M}^{(j)}\),

$$\sum_{j=1}^M \sum_{i=1}^N \left\lVert \mathbf{p}^{(j)}_i - \pi \left( \mathbf{M}^{(j)} \mathbf{P}^{(j)}_i \right)  \right\rVert ^2 $$

where \(\pi()\) is the function that transforms a vector described with homogeneous coordinates into the corresponding vector in heterogeneous ones.
concepts.motivation_md: Reprojection error quantifies how well estimated 3D points and camera parameters project back to observed image points, guiding optimization in 3D reconstruction.
concepts.recap_md:
- Reprojection error sums Euclidean distances between observed and projected points.
- It involves estimated 3D points \(\mathbf{P}^{(j)}_i\) and camera matrices \(\mathbf{M}^{(j)}\).
- The function \(\pi()\) converts homogeneous to heterogeneous coordinates.

concepts.title: Domain adaptation
concepts.one_liner: Domain adaptation refers to methods for adapting the training domain to be more like the test domain, or vice versa.
concepts.content:
Often, the data we train on comes from a different distribution, or domain, than the data we will encounter at test time. For example, maybe we have trained a recognition system on internet photos and now we want to deploy the system on a self-driving car. The imagery the car sees looks very different than everyday photos you might find on the internet. Domain adaptation refers to methods for adapting the training domain to be more like the test domain, or vice versa. The first option is to adapt the test data, $\{\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{test}}^{(i)},\mathbf{y}_{\texttt{test}}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$, to look more like the training data. Then $f$ should work well on both the training data and the test data. Or we can go the other way around, adapting the training data to look like the test data, *before* training $f$ on the adapted training data. In either case, the trick is to make the distribution of test and train data identical, so that a method that works on one will work just as well on the other.

Commonly, we only have access to labels at training time, but may have plentiful unlabeled inputs $\{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}_i\}_{i=1}^N$ at testing time. This setting is sometimes referred to as unsupervised domain adaptation. Here we cannot make use of test labels but we can still align the test inputs to look like the training inputs (or vice versa). One way to do so is to use a generative adversarial network (GAN; chapter @sec-generative_models) that translates the data in one domain to look identically distributed as the data in the other domain, as has been explored in e.g., @tzeng2017adversarial, @CycleGAN2017, @hoffman2018cycada. A simple version of this algorithm is given in algorithm @alg-transfer_learning-domain_adaptation_by_translation.

(see figure: Unpaired domain adaptation via adversarial translation.)

You may notice that domain adaptation is very similar to prompting. Both edit the model's inputs to make the model perform better. However, while prompting's objective is to improve or steer model performance, domain adaptation's objective is to make the inputs look more familiar. This means domain adaptation is applicable even when we don't have access to the model or even know what the task will be.
concepts.motivation_md: Domain adaptation solves the problem of distribution mismatch between training and test data by making their distributions more similar, improving model performance in new domains.
concepts.recap_md:
- Domain adaptation aligns training and test data distributions.
- Can adapt test data to training data or vice versa.
- Unsupervised domain adaptation uses unlabeled test inputs and GANs for alignment.

concepts.title: Generative Data
concepts.one_liner: Generative data (i.e., synthetic data sampled from a generative model) can be *more* data and *better* data than real data.
concepts.content:
Generative data (i.e., synthetic data sampled from a generative model) is not just a cheap copy of real data. It can be *more* data, and it can be *better* data. It can be *more* data because we can draw an unbounded number of samples from a generative model. These samples are not just copies of the training datapoints but can interpolate and remix the training data in novel ways (chapter @sec-generative_models). Generative models can also produce *better* data because the data comes coupled with a procedure that generated it, and this procedure has structure that can be exploited to understand and manipulate the data distribution.

One such structure is latent variables (chapter @sec-generative_modeling_and_representation_learning). Suppose you have generated a training set of outdoor images with a latent variable generative model. You want to train an object classifier on this data. You notice that the images never show a cow by a beach, but you happen to live in northern California where the cows love to hang out on the coastal bluffs. How can you adapt your training data to be useful for detecting these particular cows? Easy: just edit the latent variables of your model to make it produce images of cows on beaches. If the model is pretrained to produce all kinds of images, it may have the ability to generate cows on beaches with just a little tweaking.

concepts.title: Sequence Models from the Lens of Adaptation

position.section_title: Sequence Models from the Lens of Adaptation

concepts.one_liner: Sequence models like RNNs adapt their behavior based on earlier items in the sequence they have seen.
concepts.content:
There is one more important class of adaptation algorithms: any model of a sequence that updates its behavior based on the items in the sequence it has already seen. We can consider such models as *adapting* to the earlier items in the sequence. CNNs, transformers, and RNNs all have this ability, among many other models, because they can all process sequences and model dependences between earlier items in the sequence and later decisions. However, the ability of sequence models to handle adaptation is clearest with RNNs, which we will focus on in this section.

RNNs update their hidden states as they process a sequence of data. These changes in hidden state change the behavior of the mapping from input to output. Therefore, RNNs *adapt* as they process data. Now consider that learning is the problem of adapting future behavior as a function of past data. RNNs can be run on sequences of frames in a movie or on sequences of pixels in an image. They can also be run on sequences of training points in a training dataset! If you do that, then the RNN is doing *learning*, and learning such an RNN can be considered metalearning. For example, let's see how we can make an RNN do supervised learning. Supervised learning is the problem of taking a set of examples $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)},\mathbf{y}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$ and inferring a function $f: \mathbf{x} \rightarrow \mathbf{y}$. Without loss of generality, we can define an ordering over the input set, so the learning problem is to take the sequence $\{\mathbf{x}^{(1)}, \mathbf{y}^{(1)}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}^{(n)}, \mathbf{y}^{(n)}\}$ as input and produce $f$ as output.

The goal of supervised learning is that after training on the training data, we should do well on any random test query. After processing the training sequence $\{\mathbf{x}^{(1)}, \mathbf{y}^{(1)}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}^{(n)}, \mathbf{y}^{(n)}\}$, an RNN will have arrived at some setting of its hidden state. Now if we feed the RNN a new query $\mathbf{x}^{(n+1)}$, the mapping it applies, which produces an output $\mathbf{y}^{(n+1)}$, can be considered the learned function $f$. This function is defined by the parameters of the RNN along with its hidden state that was learned from the training sequence. Since we can apply this $f$ to any arbitrary query $\mathbf{x}^{(n+1)}$, what we have is a learned function that operates just like a function learned by any other learning algorithm; it's just that in this case the learning algorithm was an RNN.
concepts.motivation_md: Sequence models like RNNs adapt their behavior based on prior inputs, enabling them to perform learning and metalearning by updating hidden states as they process sequences.
concepts.recap_md:
- Sequence models adapt based on earlier sequence items.
- RNNs update hidden states to change input-output mappings.
- RNNs can perform supervised learning by processing training sequences.

$$\mathbf{E} =  \mathbf{T} \times \mathbf{R} = \mathbf{T}_{\times} \mathbf{R}$$
This results in the relationship:
$$\mathbf{P}_2^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{E} \mathbf{P}_1 = 0
$$

concepts.title: Estimation of the essential/fundamental matrix
concepts.one_liner: Given matches between two views, the essential or fundamental matrix can be estimated by solving linear equations and enforcing rank constraints.
concepts.content:
Given a set of matches between the two views we can estimate either the essential or the fundamental matrix by writing a linear set of equations. Any two matching points will satisfy $\mathbf{p}_2^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{E} \mathbf{p}_1 = 0$ and we can use this a linear set of equations for the coefficients of $\mathbf{E}$. However, the matrix $\mathbf{E}$ has a very special structure that allows more efficient and robust methods to estimate the coefficients. The same applies for the fundamental matrix.

As both matrices are rank 2, the minimization the linear set of equations can be done using a constrained minimization or directly optimizing a rank 2 matrix. You can also delete the third singular value $\mathbf{F}$, and, for $\mathbf{E}$, you can delete the third singular value and set the first and second singular values to be equal.

Once $\mathbf{E}$ is estimated, it can be decomposed to recover the translation (skew-symmetric matrix) and rotation (orthonormal matrix) between the two cameras using the singular value decomposition methods.
concepts.motivation_md: Estimating the essential or fundamental matrix from point correspondences is crucial for recovering camera motion and 3D structure in stereo vision.
concepts.recap_md:
- Matches between views satisfy $\mathbf{p}_2^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{E} \mathbf{p}_1 = 0$.
- Both matrices have rank 2 constraints used in estimation.
- $\mathbf{E}$ can be decomposed to recover translation and rotation.

concepts.title: Finding the epipoles
concepts.one_liner: Epipoles satisfy $\mathbf{E} \mathbf{e}_1 = 0$ and $\mathbf{e}_2^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{E} = 0$ and can be found as eigenvectors with smallest eigenvalues of $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{E}^\mathsf{T}$.
concepts.content:
As the epipoles, $\mathbf{e}_1$ and $\mathbf{e}_2$, belong to the epipolar lines, they satisfy
$$\mathbf{p}_2^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{E} \mathbf{e}_1 = 0$$
$$\mathbf{e}_2^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{E} \mathbf{p}_1 = 0$$
and, as the epipoles are the intersection of all the epipolar lines, both relationships shown previously have to be true for any points $\mathbf{p}_1$ and $\mathbf{p}_2$. Therefore,
$$\mathbf{E} \mathbf{e}_1 = 0$$
$$\mathbf{e}_2^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{E} = 0$$
As the matrix $\mathbf{E}$ is likely to be noisy, we can compute the epipoles as the eigenvectors with the smallest eigenvalues of $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{E}^\mathsf{T}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Finding epipoles is essential because they are fixed points where all epipolar lines intersect, helping to define the epipolar geometry between two views.

As the epipoles, $\mathbf{e}_1$ and $\mathbf{e}_2$, belong to the epipolar lines, they satisfy
$$\mathbf{p}_2^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{E} \mathbf{e}_1 = 0$$$$\mathbf{e}_2^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{E} \mathbf{p}_1 = 0$$
and, as the epipoles are the intersection of all the epipolar lines, both relationships shown previously have to be true for any points $\mathbf{p}_1$ and $\mathbf{p}_2$. Therefore,
$$\mathbf{E} \mathbf{e}_1 = 0$$$$\mathbf{e}_2^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{E} = 0$$

motivation.text: As the matrix $\mathbf{E}$ is likely to be noisy, we can compute the epipoles as the eigenvectors with the smallest eigenvalues of $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{E}^\mathsf{T}$.

concepts.title: Epipolar lines: The game
concepts.one_liner: A game to build intuition on epipolar lines by matching camera pairs to sets of epipolar lines.
concepts.content:
In order to build an intuition of how epipolar lines work we propose to play a game. @fig-epipolarlinesgame shows a set of camera pairs and a set of epipolar lines. Can you guess what camera pair goes with what set of epipolar lines?

Answer for the game in @fig-epipolarlinesgame: A-2, B-5, C-4, D-6, E-3, F-1.

(see figure: Epipolar game. The figure shows six camera pair arrangements, and six sets of epipolar lines. Can you identify which camera pairs correspond to each set of epipolar lines?)

To solve the game, visualize mentally the cameras and think about how rays from the origin of one camera will be seen from the other camera. The epipole corresponds to the location where one camera sees the origin of the other camera.

Observe that most of the sets of epipolar lines shown in the figure are symmetric across the two cameras, but it is not always true. What conditions are needed to have symmetric epipolar lines across both cameras? What camera arrangements will break the symmetry? If you were to place two cameras in random locations, do you expect to see symmetric epipolar lines?

It is also useful to use the equations defining the epipolar lines and deduce the equations for the epipolar lines for some of the special cases shown in @fig-epipolarlinesgame.

When building systems, it is crucial to visualize intermediate results in order to find bugs in code. This requires knowing what the results should look like. The game from @fig-epipolarlinesgame helps building that understanding.
concepts.motivation_md: This game helps build intuition on epipolar lines and camera geometry by visualizing and matching camera pairs to epipolar line patterns, aiding debugging and understanding.
concepts.recap_md:
- The game matches camera pairs to epipolar line sets.
- Epipoles are where one camera sees the other's origin.
- Symmetry of epipolar lines depends on camera arrangement.

concepts.title: Image Rectification
concepts.one_liner: Image rectification warps stereo images so epipolar lines align with image scanlines, simplifying stereo matching.
concepts.content:
As described previously, one only needs to search along epipolar lines to find matching points in the second image. If the sensor planes of each camera are coplanar, and if the pixel rows are colinear across the two cameras, then the epipolar lines will be along image scanlines, simplifying the stereo search.

Using the homography transformations (@sec-homography), we can warp observed stereo camera images taken under general conditions to synthesize the images that would have been recorded had the cameras been aligned to yield epipolar lines along scan rows.

Many configurations of the two cameras satisfy the desired image rectification constraints @Zhang2003: (1) that epipolar lines are along image scanlines, and (2) that matching points are within the same rows in each camera image. One procedure that will satisfy those constraints is as follows @wikiRectification2021. First, rotate each camera to be parallel with each other and with optical axes perpendicular to the line joining the two camera centers. Second, rotate each of the cameras about its optical axis to align the rows of each camera with those of the other. Third, uniformly scale one camera's image to be the same size as to the other, if necessary. The resulting image pair will thus satisfy the two requirements above for image rectification. Image rectification uses image warping with bilinear (or other) interpolation as described in @sec-bilinearinterpolation.
concepts.motivation_md: Image rectification simplifies stereo matching by aligning epipolar lines with image rows, reducing the search space for corresponding points.
concepts.recap_md:
- Rectification aligns epipolar lines with image scanlines.
- Achieved by rotating and scaling cameras to meet constraints.
- Uses homography and image warping with interpolation.

concepts.title: Concluding Remarks
concepts.one_liner: A single image contains a lot of information that, in most cases, is enough to estimate metric 3D information from a single 2D image.
concepts.content:
In this chapter we have shown how to use geometric image features such as vanishing points and the horizon line, along with projective invariants like the cross-ratio, to estimate 3D scene properties from a single image. However, most of these steps required some manual intervention. All of these steps can be performed fully automatically by training detectors to localize the full extent of an object, as will be discussed in the section on object recognition, and by detecting points of contact between objects.

One of the key insights from this chapter is that a single image contains a lot of information that, in most cases, is enough to estimate metric 3D information from a single 2D image. In the next chapter, we will discuss learning-based methods for 3D estimation from images.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding how to extract 3D scene properties from a single image is crucial for advancing computer vision and automating 3D reconstruction processes.
concepts.recap_md:
- Geometric features and projective invariants help estimate 3D properties from one image.
- Manual steps can be automated using trained detectors.
- Single images often contain sufficient information for metric 3D estimation.

concepts.title: Monocular Depth Cues

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Monocular depth cues are image features used by the human visual system to interpret the 3D structure of a picture.
concepts.content:
Before delving into the subject of this chapter, let's quickly review some of the image features that are used by the human visual system to interpret the 3D structure of a picture.

For a greater understanding of depth cues, take an art class.

**Shading** refers to the changes in image intensity produced by changes in surface orientation. The amount of light reflected in the direction of the viewer by a surface illuminated by a directional light source is a function of the surface albedo, the light intensity, and the relative angle between the light direction and the surface normal orientation, as discussed in the section on light interacting with surfaces. **Shape from shading** studies how to recover shape by inverting the rendering equations.

Another source of 3D information is **texture gradients**. Since distant things appear smaller than closer things, by measuring the relative size between textural elements that appear in different image regions, we can get a coarse estimate of the 3D scene structure (see figure aerial perspective [a]). Many methods using texture gradient cues have been proposed over time.

Another source of information about the 3D scene structure is shadows and interreflections. An example of how interreflections can inform us about the location of a ball was seen in the section on looking at images. The use of shadows and interreflections by the human visual system has been the focus of many studies. There are also computational approaches that use shadows and interreflections to recover 3D.

When looking at large landscapes, like a mountain range, mountains that are far away have lower contrast due to dispersion by the atmosphere (see figure aerial perspective [b]). This effect gets accentuated when there is fog. Therefore, contrast can be used as a cue to infer relative distances between objects. This depth cue is called **aerial perspective** or atmospheric perspective. One example using haze to infer depth is in Kaiming 2009.

[FIGURE:74c32638e485d003 | A close-up photograph of a textured metal surface with a repeating grid of small, square-based pyramidal bumps. The perspective view shows the bumps receding into the distance, illustrating how...]

[FIGURE:52838648eb2a6dee | A photograph of a deep mountain valley illustrating aerial perspective. The foreground mountains are dark green and high contrast, while the distant mountain peaks appear lighter, bluer, and lower in...]

Fig (a) This image contains multiple 3D cues: shading effects (bump shapes), texture gradients (relative size between bumps), and linear perspective (due to the regular arrangement of the bumps). (b) Aerial perspective. Objects far in the background have lower contrast than objects closer to the camera.

Depth can also be estimated by detecting **familiar objects** with known sizes. One example is people detection. Objects with known sizes can be used to estimate absolute depth while many of the cues that we discussed before can only give relative depth measurements. One example of using object sizes to reason about 3D geometry is Hoiem 2008.

And finally, **linear perspective** provides strong cues for 3D reconstruction as studied earlier.
concepts.motivation_md: Monocular depth cues help humans and algorithms interpret 3D structure from 2D images, enabling depth perception and scene understanding from a single viewpoint.
concepts.recap_md:
- Monocular depth cues include shading, texture gradients, shadows, and aerial perspective.
- Familiar objects with known sizes help estimate absolute depth.
- Linear perspective provides strong 3D reconstruction cues.

concepts.title: Translating the depth map into a point cloud
aliases: depth map to point cloud conversion

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Using homogeneous coordinates, the equation translating a depth map into a 3D point cloud is: $\mathbf{P} = z(\mathbf{p}) \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{p}$.
concepts.content:
Using homogeneous coordinates, the equation translating a depth map into a 3D point cloud is (for each pixel):
$$\mathbf{P} = z(\mathbf{p}) \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{p}$$
where $\mathbf{p}$ are the pixel coordinates of a point, $z(\mathbf{p})$ is the depth measured at that location, and $\mathbf{P}$ are the final 3D point coordinates. In heterogeneous coordinates, and making the pixel locations explicit, equation (@eq-3dcloudpointfromz) can be rewritten as:
$$\begin{aligned}
    X[n,m] &= \left( n-c_x \right) \frac{z[n,m]}{a} \\
    Y[n,m] &= \left( m-c_y \right) \frac{z[n,m]}{a} \\
    Z[n,m] &= z[n,m] 
\end{aligned}$$
where $a$, $c_x$ and $c_y$ are the intrinsic camera parameters (in pixel units). This writing shows that the 3D point coordinates are three images $X[n,m]$, $Y[n,m]$, and $Z[n,m]$ with the same size as the input image.

![Translating the depth map into a point cloud. This requires a calibrated camera (i.e., knowing the intrinsic camera parameters). The sketch shows how one pixel $(n,m)$ is mapped into a 3D point, $\mathbf{P}$, by using the depth, $z[n,m]$, at that location. Colored lines are parallel to the respective axis direction in the camera coordinates system.](figures/learning_3d/from_depthmap_2_pointcloud.png){width="100%" #fig-kinect2}
concepts.motivation_md: Converting depth maps to 3D point clouds allows reconstruction of the 3D scene geometry from 2D images using camera calibration parameters.
concepts.recap_md:
- Depth maps can be converted to 3D point clouds using camera intrinsics.
- Equation: $\mathbf{P} = z(\mathbf{p}) \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{p}$.
- Coordinates $X[n,m], Y[n,m], Z[n,m]$ correspond to 3D points per pixel.

concepts.one_liner: Learning-based methods can extract and combine many cues from images to provide depth estimates from a single image.
concepts.content: Previous computer vision approaches for 3D reconstruction from single images focused on developing the formulation to extract depth using one or few of the cues we discussed in the previous section, and can only be applied to a restricted set of images. Learning-based methods instead have the potential to learn to extract many cues from images, decide which cues are more relevant in each case, and combine them to provide depth estimates. There were a number of early models that applied learning for recovering 3D scene structure @Saxena2008, @Derek2005 but in this chapter we will focus on methods using deep learning although the approaches described here are independent of the particular learning architecture used.

concepts.title: Depth estimation as a pixelwise regression problem

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Supervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Depth estimation becomes a pixelwise regression problem using a learnable function $h_\theta$.
concepts.content:
In the supervised setting we will assume that we have a training set that contains $N$ images, $\ell^{(i)} [n,m]$, and their associated depth maps, $z^{(i)} [n,m]$. In this formulation, depth estimation becomes a pixelwise regression problem. Usually $\mathbf{z}^{(i)}$ and $\boldsymbol\ell^{(i)}$ are images of the same size. Our goal is to estimate depth at each pixel, $\hat{z}^{(i)}[n,m]$, from a single image using a learnable function, $h_\theta$:
$$\hat{\mathbf{z}}^{(i)} = h_\theta \left( \boldsymbol\ell^{(i)} \right)$$
where the parameters $\theta$ are learned by minimizing the loss over a training set:
$$\theta^* = \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{\theta} \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \mathcal{L} \left( \hat{\mathbf{z}}^{(i)}, \mathbf{z}^{(i)} \right)$$
concepts.motivation_md: Formulating depth estimation as pixelwise regression allows learning a function to predict depth from image pixels directly.
concepts.recap_md:
- Depth estimation is formulated as pixelwise regression.
- Learnable function $h_\theta$ maps images to depth maps.
- Parameters $\theta$ are optimized by minimizing loss on training data.

concepts.title: Collecting Training Data

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Supervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Efficient and scalable data collection strategies are crucial for supervised depth estimation.
concepts.content:
Coming up with efficient and scalable data collection strategies is crucial in this task. Several methods for supervised learning from single images differ mostly on how they collect the data. This simplest data capture method is using a depth sensor such as an RGB-D camera or a light detection and ranging (LiDAR) device.

LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging) is a device that calculates distances by measuring the time taken for emitted light to return after reflecting off a surface (time of flight). A LiDAR produces a range image by scanning multiple directions. The output is a point cloud.

Two examples of datasets are the NYUv2 dataset @SilbermanECCV12, captured using a handheld Microsoft Kinect sensor while walking indoors, and the KITTI dataset @Geiger2013, collected from a moving vehicle with a LiDAR scan.

Other methods consist of using stereo pairs for training @Xian2018 or multiview geometry methods that provide more accurate 3D estimates. MegaDepth @MegaDepthLi18 uses scenes captured with multiple cameras to get good 3D reconstructions using structure from motion techniques. This allows creating a dataset of images and associated depth maps that can be used to train depth from single image methods.
concepts.motivation_md: Collecting diverse and accurate training data is essential for supervised learning methods to estimate depth from single images effectively.
concepts.recap_md:
- Data collection methods vary for supervised depth estimation.
- Depth sensors like RGB-D cameras and LiDAR provide ground truth.
- Multi-view and stereo methods also create training datasets.
