concepts.title: Calibration of the Projected World Axis
concepts.one_liner: We will use the cross-ratio to calibrate the projection of the world coordinate system in the image plane.
concepts.content:
Where should we position the tick marks that correspond to 1, 2, 3, ... meters from the origin on each axis in @fig-office_world_calibration? Simply placing them at evenly spaced intervals along the axis in the image won't be correct. Due to geometric distortion introduced by perspective projection, the tick marks are not evenly spaced within the image plane. This distortion affects each axis in a distinct manner.

Let's start assuming we know the location of some arbitrary 3D distance to the origin on each axis that we will denote by $\alpha_X$, $\alpha_Y$ and $\alpha_Z$. The question is, where do we place the ticks for $k\alpha_X$, $k\alpha_Y$ and $k\alpha_Z$ for all $k$? We will use the cross-ratio to calibrate the projection of the world coordinate system in the image plane. For doing this we will need the location of the horizon line of a reference plane (i.e. the ground plane), the position of the orthogonal vanishing point and the real measure of one object in the scene.

As shown in @fig-axis_calibration_procedure (a) we can use the cross-ratio to estimate the location of the points $Y= k \alpha_X$ where $\alpha_X$ is an arbitrary constant as shown in @fig-axis_calibration_procedure (b), and the corresponding image location $r$, for $k=1$, is chosen arbitrarily as shown in @fig-axis_calibration_procedure (a). Due to perspective projection, the image projection of the point $Y= k \alpha_X$ will not be evenly spaced in the image. In this particular example we chose the orientation of the world axis in image coordinates to be aligned with the location of the vanishing points.

(see figure: Using the cross-ratio invariant to project the world coordinates into the image using only the vanishing points.)

In order to calibrate the axis we need to know the dimensions of an object in the scene. We need measurements along the three axis. In this example, we used the bookshelf height (197 cm) and the radius of the table base (50 cm). Using these reference measurements we can solve for the image locations of the ticks $\alpha_X=\alpha_Y=\alpha_Z=1$ m.

@fig-office_all_calibrated_box shows the final calibrated axes with ticks placed each 50 cm along each of the three axes.
concepts.motivation_md: Calibrating the projected world axis corrects for perspective distortion, enabling accurate placement of distance markers in images, which is essential for precise spatial measurements from single images.
concepts.recap_md:
- Perspective projection distorts spacing of tick marks along axes in images.
- Use cross-ratio invariant to calibrate world coordinate projections.
- Reference object measurements enable solving for tick mark placements.

concepts.title: Locating a 3D Point
concepts.one_liner: We can estimate 3D coordinates of a point from a single image by using context such as the object's relation to the ground and vanishing points.
concepts.content:
In the absence of any other information, we cannot recover the 3D location of a single point $\mathbf{P}$ from a single view as illustrated in @fig-locating_a_3d_point [a]. But real world scenes are composed of a multitude of objects providing context, which allows solving the 3D estimation problem even with just a single image. In the previous section we showed how to estimate the height of an object; here we show how to estimate the 3D coordinates of a point.

The basic procedure is illustrated in @fig-locating_a_3d_point [b]. The trick consists in using context (what object is the point part of, where is the horizon line of the scene and where are the vanishing points) to estimate 3D from a single image. It suffices to know that the point $\mathbf{P}$ belongs to an object that is in contact with the ground and the geometry of this object provides the information to localize the projection of the point $\mathbf{P}$ on the ground plane, which we denote with $\mathbf{G}$.

(see figure: Figure (a) In the absence of any other information, we can not recover the 3D location of point $\mathbf{P}$. (b) If we are given a way to project the point P into the ground, then we can read out...)

Once we know the image location of the projection of the 3D point $\mathbf{P}$ to the ground, $\mathbf{G}$, we can project this point to the world-coordinate axis. To estimate the $Y$-coordinate we use a similar method as the one described in the previous section. We first find the line, $\boldsymbol{l}_3$, that passes by the point $\mathbf{G}$ and the origin, and then find the intersection with the horizon line, giving the point $\mathbf{v}$. Next, find the line, $\boldsymbol{l}_4$, that passes by $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{P}$. The intersection of $\boldsymbol{l}_4$ with the $Y_w$-axis gives the coordinate $P_y$. The $P_x$ and $P_z$ coordinates can be obtained by connecting $\mathbf{G}$ with the vanishing points $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$.
concepts.motivation_md: Estimating 3D point locations from a single image is possible by leveraging scene context like object-ground contact and vanishing points, overcoming the inherent ambiguity of single-view 3D reconstruction.
concepts.recap_md:
- A single image alone cannot recover a point's 3D location without context.
- Use object's contact with ground and scene geometry to locate 3D points.
- Project point's ground projection and use vanishing points to find coordinates.

concepts.title: Camera Calibration from Vanishing Points
concepts.one_liner: We can extract camera parameters using only vanishing points under some conditions.
concepts.content:
In the previous chapters, we have seen different methods to calibrate a camera. We saw that we could do it by taking pictures of a calibration pattern, and we also showed that we can extract both the intrinsics and extrinsics from a set of 3D points and their image correspondences. Here we will see a different method that uses only the vanishing points to extract the camera parameters; note that this method will only work under some conditions.

The first step consists in finding the vanishing points in the image. Let's use the office picture from @fig-vanishing_lines. In this particular scene there are many parallel lines in 3D, and they also happen to be parallel to the three directions we used to define the world coordinates system. Therefore, the three vanishing points are also aligned with the world coordinate axis.

Let's assume that we have three orthogonal vanishing directions. That is the vectors $\mathbf{D}_1$, $\mathbf{D}_2$, and $\mathbf{D}_3$ are orthogonal in 3D. From equation (@eq-vanishing_projection), the vanishing points measured on the image are the result of projecting $\mathbf{D}_1$, $\mathbf{D}_2$, and $\mathbf{D}_3$ into the image using the unknown camera projection matrix. We will use the vanishing points to derive a set of constraints on the projection matrix. To do this, we start by inverting equation (@eq-vanishing_projection):
$$\mathbf{D}_i = \mathbf{R}^{-1} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{v}_i
$$ {#eq-vanishing_projection_inv} Because the vectors $\mathbf{D}_i$ are orthogonal, we have that $\mathbf{D}_i^{\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{D}_j = 0$ for $i \neq j$. Therefore, we can write:
$$\mathbf{D}_i^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{D}_j = \mathbf{v}_i^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{K}^{-\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{R}^{-\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{R}^{-1} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{v}_j 
$$ {#eq-vanishing_projection_constraint} As $\mathbf{R}$ is an orthonormal matrix, we have that $\mathbf{R}^{-\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{R}^{-1} = \mathbf{I}$, resulting in a relationship that only depends on the intrinsic camera parameters $\mathbf{K}$:
$$\mathbf{D}_i^T \mathbf{D}_j = \mathbf{v}_i^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{K}^{-\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{v}_j = 0
$$

It is useful to define the following matrix:
$$\mathbf{W} =  \mathbf{K}^{-\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{K}^{-1}$$ This is also known as the **conic matrix** and it has lots of different properties @Hartley2004. 

If we assume that the skew parameter of the intrinsic camera matrix is zero, then the matrix $\mathbf{W}$ has a very particular structure and it has only four different values: $$\mathbf{W} = 
    \begin{bmatrix}
    a & 0 & b\\
    0 & a & c\\
    b & c & d
    \end{bmatrix}$$ Using equation (@eq-vanishing_projection_constraint), we can derive a linear constraint on the values $a,b,c,d$ for each pair of vanishing points. Defining the vector $\mathbf{w}=[a~b~c~d]^\mathsf{T}$, we can rewrite equation (@eq-vanishing_projection_constraint) into a system of linear equations that has the form: $$\mathbf{A} \mathbf{w} = 0$$

The linear equation can be solved with the singular value decomposition (SVD) and the result is the eigenvector with the smallest eigenvalue.

Once we have $\mathbf{W}$, we can find $\mathbf{K}$ by using the Cholesky factorization, which decomposes a matrix as the product of an upper triangular matrix and its transpose. The last step is to normalize the result by normalizing all the matrix values so that the value on the bottom-right side is 1. In our running example of the office picture, we get the following solution for $\mathbf{K}$: 

$$
\mathbf{K} = 
    \begin{bmatrix}
    3{,}054.6    &      0    &     1{,}999.4\\
       0    &       3{,}054.6    &     1{,}528.3\\
       0    &          0    &          1
\end{bmatrix}
$$
concepts.motivation_md: Using vanishing points for camera calibration allows extracting intrinsic parameters without special calibration patterns, useful when only images of scenes with orthogonal directions are available.
concepts.recap_md:
- Vanishing points correspond to directions of parallel lines in 3D.
- Orthogonal vanishing points impose constraints on camera intrinsics.
- Solve linear system from constraints to find intrinsic matrix $\mathbf{K}$.

concepts.title: Representing Radiance Fields With Parameterized Functions

position.section_title: Representing Radiance Fields With Parameterized Functions

concepts.one_liner: We use parameterized functions to represent continuous radiance fields by recording a finite set of parameters that define a function giving field values at any coordinate.
concepts.content:
Continuous fields have infinite resolution, so we cannot explicitly represent them by recording values at all possible positions. Instead, we use parameterized functions to represent continuous fields. These functions take any continuous position as input and output the field's value at that location. This approach is called an implicit representation because we do not explicitly store the field values at all coordinates; rather, we record a finite set of parameters of a function that can provide the field value at any coordinate. Implicit representations are also used in variational autoencoders (VAEs), where an infinite set (an infinite mixture of Gaussians) is represented via a parameterized function from a continuous input domain. You can consider a VAE as a continuous field mapping from latent variables to images.

Many different parameterized functions $L_{\theta}$ can represent our target radiance field $L$. For example, we could use a neural network (e.g., @mildenhall2020nerf), a mixture of Gaussians (e.g., @kerbl20233d), or other function approximators. The key property is that the field $L_{\theta}$ is differentiable with respect to the parameters $\theta$, enabling gradient-based optimization to find parameters that yield a desirable field (used when fitting a radiance field to images). Whatever function family we use, it takes input coordinates and produces colors and densities as output (@fig-nerfs-nerf_module). Because these functions are differentiable, we can view them as modules in a differentiable computation graph (@fig-nerfs-nerf_module). Later, multiple such modules are combined and optimized via backpropagation to fit the field to a set of images.
concepts.motivation_md: Continuous radiance fields have infinite resolution, making explicit storage impossible; parameterized functions provide a finite, differentiable way to represent and optimize these fields.
concepts.recap_md:
- Continuous fields can't be explicitly stored at all positions, so parameterized functions represent them implicitly.
- Parameterized functions take coordinates as input and output field values.
- Differentiable parameterizations enable gradient-based optimization to fit radiance fields to images.

Sometimes this is called an implicit representation of the field, since we don't explicitly store the values of the field at all coordinates. Instead we just record a finite set of parameters of a function that can tell us the value of the field at any coordinate.

position.section_title: Representing Radiance Fields With Parameterized Functions

concepts.one_liner: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) model the radiance field with a neural network, typically a multilayer perceptron (MLP).
concepts.content: We focus on one popular way of parameterizing $L_{\theta}$: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) @mildenhall2020nerf. NeRFs model the radiance field $L$ with a neural network $L_{\theta}$. The original NeRF architecture uses a multilayer perceptron (MLP), but other architectures could also be used. For the MLP formulation, evaluating the color-density at a single coordinate corresponds to a single forward pass through the MLP.

concepts.title: Positional encoding for NeRFs

position.section_title: Representing Radiance Fields With Parameterized Functions

concepts.one_liner: Fourier positional encodings help NeRFs model high-frequency variations abundant in radiance fields.
concepts.content:
NeRF includes a positional encoding layer to transform the raw coordinates into a Fourier representation. It uses the same positional encoding scheme as transformers (see @sec-transformers-positional_encodings). @fig-nerfs-flatland_positional_encoding shows how this scheme translates the $XY$-coordinate field of Flatland to positional encodings:

(see figure: The first layer of NeRF applies positional encoding to the input coordinate values. Here we show the resulting positional codes for all possible input coordinate values $(X,Y)$ within some range.)

Fourier positional encodings are very effective for NeRFs because they help the network model high-frequency variations, which are abundant in radiance fields @tancik2020fourier. Why do such encodings help model high frequencies? Essentially, in regular Cartesian coordinates, the location $(0,0)$ is much closer to $(1,1)$ than to $(100,100)$, but this isn't necessarily the case with Fourier positional codes. Because of this, with Cartesian coordinates as inputs, an MLP will be biased to assign similar values to $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$ and different values to $(0,0)$ and $(100,100)$. Conversely, with Fourier positional codes as input, this bias is reduced. This makes it easier for the MLP, taking Fourier positional codes as input, to fit high-frequency functions that change rapidly, such as assigning very different output values to $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$. See @tancik2020fourier for a more thorough analysis of this phenomenon.
concepts.motivation_md: Fourier positional encodings reduce bias in neural networks, enabling them to fit high-frequency details in radiance fields more effectively.
concepts.recap_md:
- NeRF uses Fourier positional encodings on input coordinates.
- This helps model high-frequency variations in radiance fields.
- Fourier codes reduce bias present with Cartesian inputs, aiding MLP fitting.

concepts.title: Other Ways of Parameterizing Radiance fields

position.section_title: Representing Radiance Fields With Parameterized Functions

concepts.one_liner: Radiance fields can be parameterized by differentiable functions other than neural nets, such as voxel-based representations or mixtures of Gaussians.
concepts.content: In principle, $L_{\theta}$ could be other kinds of functions, including those that are not neural networks. The important property is that it be differentiable so we can optimize its parameters to fit a given scene. One alternative is to parameterize radiance fields using a voxel-based representation, as explored in, e.g., @fridovich2022plenoxels. Another alternative is to use a mixture of Gaussians @kerbl20233d. In this case, each Gaussian represents a semi-transparent ellipsoid of some color $\mathbf{c}$ and some density $\sigma$. When many such Gaussians overlap, their sum can approximate scene content very well.
concepts.motivation_md: Exploring alternative differentiable parameterizations of radiance fields allows for different trade-offs in representation and optimization.
concepts.recap_md:

concepts.title: volume rendering
concepts.one_liner: Volume rendering computes images from radiance fields by integrating radiance values along camera rays weighted by density.
concepts.content:
We use volume rendering to render images from radiance fields, as methods like NeRFs do, though other rendering methods are possible. Volume rendering works by integrating the radiance values along each camera ray. Imagine looking into a hazy volume of colored dust: the integral sums all color values along the ray, weighted by a value related to the dust's density. A cartoon visualization is given in @fig-nerfs-flatland_volume_rendering, and real rendering results are shown in @fig-nerfs-flatland_training. The volume rendering equation is:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \ell(r) = \int_{t_n}^{t_f}\alpha(t) \, \overbrace{L^\sigma(r(t))}^{\text{density}} \, \overbrace{L^c(r(t),\mathbf{D})}^{\text{color}} \, dt\\
    \alpha(t) = \exp \Big(-\int_{t_n}^{t} \underbrace{L^\sigma(r(t))}_{\text{density}} dt\Big)
\end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Volume rendering integrates radiance and density along rays to produce realistic images from radiance fields.
concepts.recap_md:
- Volume rendering integrates radiance values along camera rays.
- The integral weights colors by density, like looking through hazy colored dust.
- This method is used by NeRFs to render images from radiance fields.

motivation.text: For this purpose, we will use volume rendering, which is the strategy that methods like NeRFs use for rendering images from radiance fields (although other rendering methods could be possible).

concepts.title: softmax regression model
concepts.one_liner: The output of $f_{\theta}$ can be interpreted as a probability mass function over $K$ classes.
concepts.content:
This yields the softmax regression model we saw previously in section @sec-intro_to_learning-image_classification. Given the constraint of @eq-object_recognition-sum_to_one_constraint, the output of $f_{\theta}$ can be interpreted as a probability mass function over $K$ classes: 

$$\begin{aligned}
    p_{\theta}(Y \bigm | \mathbf{x}) &= \hat{\mathbf{y}} = f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})
\end{aligned}$$ 

where $Y$ is the random variable indicating the single class per image. This relates to our previous model in @eq-object_recognition-classification_probability_model as:
$$\begin{aligned}
    p(Y_c=1 \bigm | \mathbf{x}) &= p_{\theta}(Y=c \bigm | \mathbf{x})
\end{aligned}$$

concepts.title: Multilabel classification
concepts.one_liner: Multilabel classification can be formulated as $K$ binary classification problems.
concepts.content:
When the image can have multiple labels simultaneously, the classification problem can be formulated as $K$ binary classification problems (where $K$ is the number of classes).

In such a case, the function $f_\theta$ can be a neural network shared across all classes (@fig-class_architecture), and the output vector $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$, of length $K$, is computed using a sigmoid nonlinearity for each output class. In this case the output can still be interpreted as the probability $\hat{y}_c = p_\theta(Y_c=1 \bigm | \mathbf{x})$, but without the constraint that the sum across classes is 1.
concepts.motivation_md: Multilabel classification addresses cases where images contain multiple classes simultaneously, requiring independent probability estimates per class.
concepts.recap_md:
- Multilabel classification treats each class as a binary problem.
- Outputs use sigmoid nonlinearities per class.
- Probabilities per class do not sum to one.

concepts.title: sparse SFM

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Sparse SFM computes 3D reconstruction only for a small subset of reliably detected distinct points across camera poses.
concepts.content: In this chapter, we focused on the most popular variant of SFM used today --- feature-based, or sparse, SFM. In sparse SFM, the 3D reconstruction is computed only for a small subset of the image pixels --- distinct points that may be detected reliably and repeatably across camera pose variations. SFM approaches have also attempted to leverage other kinds of features, such as lines, planes, or objects. Point-based features remain the most popular choice due to their geometric simplicity, and the availability of a wide range of point feature detectors and descriptors.

concepts.title: dense SFM

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Dense SFM computes 3D reconstruction for most or all image pixels, optimizing photometric error rather than 3D reprojection error.
concepts.content: In dense SFM, the 3D reconstruction is computed for every (or most) of the image pixels. The resulting 3D reconstructions are rich and visually informative, and are useful in applications like robot navigation or mixed reality. Dense SFM approaches usually optimize photometric error, that is, the difference in grayscale or red-green-blue (RGB) intensities of corresponding pixels across images. This is in contrast to the point feature-based methods we looked at in this chapter that minimize a 3D reprojection error. However, these dense SFM techniques tend to be much slower than the sparse SFM methods, and often require more assumptions about the scene or the images, such as the scene being Lambertian (i.e., the grayscale or RGB intensity of a 3D point is invariant to the viewing direction) or the images having a substantially smaller baseline motion compared to the range of motions a point feature-based SFM approach can handle. We will talk about dense optimization of the photometric error when discussing motion estimation in

- Requires assumptions like Lambertian surfaces and smaller baseline motions.

concepts.title: plenoptic function
concepts.one_liner: The plenoptic function fully describes all light rays traveling through space by their position, direction, wavelength, and time.
concepts.content: The plenoptic function tries to answer the question: "What information about the world is contained in the light filling a region of space?" Given a scene, the plenoptic function is a full description of all the light rays that travel across the space (@fig-nerfs-plenoptic_function). It tells us the light intensity of a light ray passing through the three-dimensional (3D) point $(X, Y, Z)$ from the direction given by the angles $(\psi, \phi)$, with wavelength $\lambda$, at time $t$: $$L(X, Y, Z, \psi, \phi, \lambda, t)$$ In this chapter we will ignore time and use only three color channels instead of the continuous wavelength. We can represent the plenoptic function with the parametric form $L_{\theta}$ where the parameters $\theta$ have to be adapted to represent each scene.
concepts.motivation_md: The plenoptic function exists to comprehensively represent all light information in a scene, enabling understanding and reconstruction of visual data.
concepts.recap_md:

- Depends on position, direction, wavelength, and time.
- Often simplified by ignoring time and using RGB channels.

concepts.title: vector fields
concepts.one_liner: Vector fields assign a vector to each position in space and are a general way to represent functions varying over space.
concepts.content:
Radiance fields are an example of vector fields, which are functions that assign a vector to each position in space. For example, we might have a vector field $f: X, Y, Z \rightarrow v_1, v_2$, where $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ are coordinates and $v_1$ and $v_2$ are some values. Let's take a moment to consider field-based representations more broadly, since they turn out to be a very important way of representing scenes. Essentially, fields are a way to represent functions that vary over space, and fields appear all over the place in this book. For example, every image is a field: it is a mapping from pixel coordinates to color values. The images we usually deal with in computer vision are discrete fields (the input coordinates are discrete-valued) but in this chapter we will instead deal with continuous fields (the input coordinates are continuous-valued). Unlike regular images, fields can also be more than two-dimensional and can even be defined over non-Euclidean geometries like the surface of a sphere. Because they are such a general-purpose object, fields are used as a scene representation in many contexts. Some examples are the following:

-   **Pixel** images, $f: x, y \rightarrow r, g, b$, are fields with the property that the input domain is discrete, or, equivalently, the field is piecewise constant over little squares that tile the space.

-   **Voxel** fields, $f: X,Y,Z \rightarrow \mathbf{v}$ are discrete fields that can represent values $\mathbf{v}$ like spatial occupancy, flux, or color in a volume. They are like 3D pixels. Like pixels, they have the special property that they are piecewise constant over cubes the size of their resolution.

-   **Optical flow fields**, $f: x, y, t \rightarrow u, v$, measure motion in a video in terms of how scene content flows across the image plane. We encountered these fields in @sec-3D_motion_and_its_2D_projection.

-   **Signed distance functions** (**SDFs**) @curless1996volumetric, $f: X,Y,Z \rightarrow d$, represent the distance to the closest surface to point $[X,Y,Z]^\mathsf{T}$. This is a useful representation of geometry.
    
Notation reminder: we use capital letters for world

- Fields can be discrete or continuous and vary in dimensionality.
- Examples include pixel images, voxel fields, optical flow, and signed distance functions.

concepts.title: Motion Perception in the Human Visual System

position.section_title: Motion Perception in the Human Visual System

concepts.one_liner: Motion perception is a key component of visual perception because the eye constantly moves, fixating different scene locations every 300 ms, providing ever-changing visual information.
concepts.content:
The eye is constantly moving, fixating different scene locations every 300 ms. Therefore, the nature of the input signal to the brain is a sequence of ever-changing visual information. It is not a surprise then that motion perception is a key component of visual perception.

Only when the eye tracks a moving object can it move continuously. Otherwise, the eye jumps from one location to another in saccades. Try moving your eyes smoothly and you will notice that you cannot. However, if you look at your finger you will see that you can follow its motion smoothly.
concepts.motivation_md: Motion perception is essential because our eyes move frequently, causing the brain to receive constantly changing visual input, and understanding motion helps interpret this dynamic information.

- The eye fixates different scene locations every 300 ms, creating changing visual input.
- Motion perception is key to interpreting this dynamic visual information.
- Smooth eye movement occurs only when tracking a moving object; otherwise, eyes jump in saccades.

concepts.title: contrastive divergence
concepts.one_liner: Contrastive divergence modifies the energy function to decrease energy on data samples and increase energy on model samples, approximating the gradient of the log likelihood function.
concepts.content:
One way to fit an energy function to observed data is called contrastive divergence. On each iteration of optimization, this method modifies the energy function to decrease the energy assigned to samples from the data (positive term) and to increase the energy assigned to samples from the model (i.e., samples from the energy function itself; negative term), as shown in @fig-generative_models-contrastive_divergence:

(see figure: Fitting a max likelihood energy function to data, using contrastive divergence. @hinton2002training)

Once the energy function perfectly adheres to the data, samples from the model are identical to samples from the data and the positive and negative terms cancel out. This makes intuitive sense because we don't want the energy function to change once we have perfectly fit the data. Mathematically, this procedure is an approximation to the gradient of the log likelihood function.

Defining $p_{\theta} = \frac{e^{-E_{\theta}}}{Z(\theta)}$, start by decomposing the gradient of the log likelihood into two terms, which will play the role of positive and negative terms:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \nabla_{\theta} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})] &= \nabla_{\theta} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\log \frac{e^{-E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})}}{Z(\theta)}]\\
    &= -\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\nabla_{\theta} E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})] - \nabla_{\theta} \log Z(\theta)
\end{aligned}$$

The first term is the positive term gradient, which tries to modify parameters to decrease the energy placed on data samples. The second term is the negative term gradient; it appears as an intractable integral, so we rewrite it as an expectation, which can be approximated via sampling:

$$\begin{aligned}
\nabla_{\theta} \log Z(\theta) &= \frac{1}{Z(\theta)}\nabla_{\theta}Z(\theta) \\
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
\nabla_{\theta} \log Z(\theta) &= \frac{1}{Z(\theta)} \nabla_{\theta} \int_x e^{-E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})}d\mathbf{x} &&\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \text{definition of $Z$}\\
    &= \frac{1}{Z(\theta)} \int_x \nabla_{\theta} e^{-E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})}d\mathbf{x} &&\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \text{exchange sum and grad}\\
    &= \frac{1}{Z(\theta)} -\int_x e^{-E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})} \nabla_{\theta} E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x}\\
    &= -\int_x \frac{e^{-E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})}}{Z(\theta)} \nabla_{\theta} E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x}\\
    &= -\int_x p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) \nabla_{\theta} E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x} &&\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \text{definition of $p_{\theta}$}\\
    &= -\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\theta}}[\nabla_{\theta} E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})] &&\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \text{definition of expectation}
\end{aligned}$$

In @eq-generative_models-grad_log_identity we use a useful identity from the chain rule of calculus: $\nabla_{x} \log f(x) = \frac{1}{f(x)} \nabla_{x} f(x)$.

Plugging @eq-generative_models-cd_neg back into @eq-generative_models-cd, we get:

$$\begin{aligned}  \nabla_{\theta} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})] &= -\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\nabla_{\theta}E_{\theta(\mathbf{x})}] + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\theta}}[\nabla_{\theta} E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})]
\end{aligned}$$

Both expectations can be approximated via sampling: defining $\mathbf{x}^{(i)} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)} \sim p_{\theta}$, and taking $N$ such samples, we have

$$\begin{aligned}
    -\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\nabla_{\theta}E_{\theta(\mathbf{x})}] + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\theta}}[\nabla_{\theta} E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})] &\approx -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \nabla_{\theta}E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}) + \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \nabla_{\theta}E_{\theta}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)})\\
    &= \frac{1}{N} \nabla_{\theta} \sum_{i=1}^N (-E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}) + E_{\theta}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)}))
\end{aligned}$$

This shows the intuition: we contrast data samples and current model samples, then update the model to decrease this contrast, bringing the model closer to the data. Once $\mathbf{x}^{(i)}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)}$ are identically distributed, this gradient will be zero in expectation; we have perfectly fit the data and no further updates should be taken.

Under our formalization of a learning problem as an objective, hypothesis space, and optimizer, contrastive divergence is an optimizer specifically built for max likelihood objectives over energy functions. It tells us how to approximate the gradient of the likelihood function, which can then be plugged into any gradient descent method.
concepts.motivation_md: Contrastive divergence exists to efficiently approximate the gradient of the log likelihood in energy-based models, enabling learning when exact computation is intractable.
concepts.recap_md:
- Contrastive divergence modifies energy to decrease energy on data samples and increase it on model samples.
- It approximates the gradient of the log likelihood function.
- The gradient is estimated by contrasting data samples with model samples.

concepts.title: Comparing Different Kinds of Generative Models
concepts.one_liner: Some generative models give density or energy functions, others give generator functions, and still others give both.
concepts.motivation_md: Generative models differ in whether they provide density, energy, or generator functions, each with distinct advantages for modeling and sampling.
concepts.recap_md:
- Generative models may provide density, energy, or generator functions.
- Generators have latent variables controlling generated samples; density/energy models do not.
- Density/energy functions provide likelihood scores useful for anomaly detection and data synthesis.

key_passage.text: Some generative models give density or energy functions, others give generator functions, and still others give both.

motivation.text: Each of these families of model has its own advantages and disadvantages.

example.text: Generators have latent variables \mathbf{z} that control the properties of the generated image. Changing these variables can change the generated image in meaningful ways; we will explore this idea in greater detail in the next chapter.

concepts.title: Gaussian Density Models
concepts.one_liner: One of the simplest and most useful density models is the Gaussian distribution, which in one dimension (1D) is: $p_{\theta}(x) = \frac{1}{Z}e^{-(x-\theta_1)^2/(2\theta_2)}$.
concepts.content:
One of the simplest and most useful density models is the Gaussian distribution, which in one dimension (1D) is:

$$\begin{aligned}
    p_{\theta}(x) = \frac{1}{Z}e^{-(x-\theta_1)^2/(2\theta_2)}
\end{aligned}$$

This density has two parameters $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$, which are the mean and variance of the distribution. The normalization constant $Z$ ensures that the function is normalized. This is the typical strategy in defining density models: create a parameterized family of functions such that any function in the family is normalized. Given such a family, we search over the parameters to optimize a generative modeling objective.

For density models, the most common objective is max likelihood:

$$\begin{aligned}
     \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\log p_{\theta}(x)] \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \log p_{\theta}(x^{(i)})
\end{aligned}$$

For a 1D Gaussian, this has a simple form:

$$\begin{aligned}
     \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \log \frac{1}{Z}e^{-(x^{(i)}-\theta_1)^2/(2\theta_2)} = -\log(Z) + \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (x^{(i)}-\theta_1)^2/(2\theta_2)
\end{aligned}$$

Optimizing with respect to $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ could be done via gradient descent or random search, but in this case there is also an analytical solution we can find by setting the gradient to zero. For $\theta_1^*$ we have:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \frac{\partial \big(-\log Z + \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (x^{(i)}-\theta_1^*)^2/(2\theta_2^*)\big)}{\partial \theta_1^*} = 0\\
    \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N 2(x^{(i)}-\theta_1^*)/(2\theta_2^*) = 0\\
    \sum_{i=1}^N x^{(i)} - \sum_{i=1}^N \theta_1^* = 0\\
    \theta_1^* = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N x^{(i)}
\end{aligned}$$

For $\theta_2^*$ we note that $Z$ depends on $\theta_2^*$ and in particular that $\frac{\partial (-\log Z)}{\partial \theta_2^*} = \frac{1}{2\theta_2^*}$:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \frac{\partial \big(-\log Z + \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (x^{(i)}-\theta_1^*)^2/(2\theta_2^*)\big)}{\partial \theta_2^*} = 0\\
    \frac{1}{2\theta_2^*} - \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N 2(x^{(i)}-\theta_1^*)^2/(2\theta_2^*)^2 = 0\\
    2\theta_2^* - \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N 2(x^{(i)}-\theta_1^*)^2 = 0\\
    \theta_2^* = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (x^{(i)}-\theta_1^*)^2
\end{aligned}$$

You might recognize the solutions for $\theta_1^*$ and $\theta_2^*$ as the empirical mean and variance of the data, respectively. This makes sense: to maximize the probability of the data under a Gaussian, we should set the mean and variance of the Gaussian to be the empirical mean and variance of the data.

This fully describes the learning problem and solution for a 1D Gaussian density model. We can put it all together in the learning diagram below:

[FIGURE:36e43cf75cec6f8d | A block diagram representing a 1D Gaussian density model. On the left, input data $\{x^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$ enters a central box labeled '1D Gaussian density model'. Inside the box, three components are...]
concepts.motivation_md: Gaussian density models provide a simple, analytically tractable way to model data distributions, serving as a foundation for more complex models.
concepts.recap_md:
- A 1D Gaussian density model has parameters mean $\theta_1$ and variance $\theta_2$.
- Maximum likelihood estimation sets these parameters to the empirical mean and variance.
- The normalization constant $Z$ ensures the density integrates to 1.

concepts.title: Autoregressive Density Models
concepts.one_liner: Autoregressive models synthesize images pixel by pixel, predicting each pixel based on previously generated pixels.
concepts.content:
A single Gaussian is a very limited model, and the real utility of Gaussians only shows up when they are part of a larger modeling framework. Next we consider a recipe for building highly expressive models out of simple ones called an autoregressive model.

The idea of an autoregressive model is to synthesize an image pixel by pixel. Each new pixel is decided based on the sequence already generated. This is a sequence prediction problem: given a sequence of observed pixels, predict the color of the next one. We use the same learned function $f_{\theta}$ to make each subsequent prediction.

@fig-generative_models-autoregressive_prediction_schematic shows this setup. We predict each next pixel from the partial image already completed. The red bordered region is the context the prediction is based on. This context could be the entire image synthesized so far or a smaller region, like shown here. The green bordered pixel is the one we are predicting given this context. In this example, we always predict the bottom-center pixel in the context window. After making our prediction, we decide what color pixel to add to the image based on that prediction; we may add the color predicted as most likely, or sample from the predicted distribution to get randomness. Then, to predict the next missing pixel we slide the context over by one and repeat.

(see figure: An autoregressive model, $f_{\theta}$, that generates an image pixel by pixel. The black pixels are the remaining pixels to synthesize. Compare with the Efros-Leung model in @fig-sampling_efros_leung.)

This setup resembles the Efros-Leung texture synthesis algorithm, which was also an autoregressive model. The Efros-Leung algorithm was a nonparametric method that worked by stealing pixels from matching regions of an exemplar texture. Now we see how to do autoregressive modeling with a learned, parametric prediction function $f_{\theta}$, such as a deep net.

These models can be understood by first considering synthesizing one pixel, then two, and so on. It's easy to synthesize a single grayscale pixel, which can take on 256 possible values (for 8-bit grayscale). A categorical distribution can represent the probability that the pixel takes each possible value. Fitting this categorical distribution to training data amounts to counting how often each value occurs and normalizing.

To model the distribution over a second grayscale pixel given the first, we model $p(\mathbf{x_2} \mid \mathbf{x_1})$ where $\mathbf{x_1}$ is the first pixel and $\mathbf{x_2}$ is the second. Treating $\mathbf{x}_2$ as a categorical variable, we use softmax regression, as seen in @sec-intro_to_learning-image_classification.

For the third pixel conditioned on the first two, we again model a 256-way softmax regression conditioned on observations. Inductively, modeling each next pixel in the sequence is a softmax regression problem modeling
$p(\mathbf{x}_n \mid \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{n-1})$. The cross-entropy loss is computed as in @fig-generative_models-autoregressive_softmax_regression.

(see figure: Autoregressive prediction as next-pixel-classification.)

For color images, we predict three values per pixel (red, green, blue) sequentially: first predict red as a 256-way classification, sample it, then predict green, and so on. To turn an image into a pixel sequence, a common method is vectorizing the 2D grid row by row.

We can model the probability of each subsequent pixel given preceding pixels. To generate an image, sample the first pixel, then the second given the first, then the third given the first two, etc. This is a valid model of the joint distribution $p(\mathbf{X})$ according to the chain rule of probability, which factorizes any joint distribution into a product of conditionals:

$$\begin{aligned}
    p(\mathbf{X}) &= p(\mathbf{x_n} \mid \mathbf{x_1}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{n-1})p(\mathbf{x}_{n-1} \mid \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{n-2}) \quad \ldots \quad p(\mathbf{x}_2 \mid \mathbf{x}_1)p(\mathbf{x}_1)\\
    p(\mathbf{X}) &= \prod_{i=1}^n p(\mathbf{x}_i \mid \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{i-1})
\end{aligned}$$

As a convenience, define $p(\mathbf{x}_i \mid \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{i-1}) = p(\mathbf{x}_1)$ when $i=1$. This factorization shows that sequential sampling draws a valid sample from $p(\mathbf{X})$ because all conditional distributions are independent of each other.
concepts.motivation_md: Autoregressive models allow building expressive generative models by sequentially predicting each pixel based on previously generated pixels, enabling tractable density estimation and sampling.
concepts.recap_md:
- Autoregressive models generate images pixel by pixel, conditioning each pixel on previous ones.
- Each pixel prediction is modeled as a categorical distribution over possible pixel values.
- The joint distribution factorizes as a product of conditional distributions by the chain rule of probability.

concepts.title: chain rule of probability
concepts.one_liner: The chain rule of probability factorizes any joint distribution into a product of conditional distributions.
concepts.content:
Sampling a valid sample from $p(\mathbf{X})$ can be done according to the chain rule of probability. This rule allows us to factorize any joint distribution into a product of conditionals as follows:

$$\begin{aligned}
    p(\mathbf{X}) &= p(\mathbf{x_n} \mid \mathbf{x_1}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{n-1})p(\mathbf{x}_{n-1} \mid \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{n-2}) \quad \ldots \quad p(\mathbf{x}_2 \mid \mathbf{x}_1)p(\mathbf{x}_1)\\
    p(\mathbf{X}) &= \prod_{i=1}^n p(\mathbf{x}_i \mid \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{i-1})
\end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: The chain rule of probability enables modeling complex joint distributions as products of simpler conditional distributions, facilitating sequential sampling and density estimation.
concepts.recap_md:
- The chain rule factorizes joint distributions into products of conditionals.
- It allows sequential sampling from complex distributions.
- Formally, $p(\mathbf{X}) = \prod_{i=1}^n p(\mathbf{x}_i \mid \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{i-1})$.

key_passage.text:
This rule allows us to factorize *any* joint distribution into a product of conditionals as follows: $$\begin{aligned} p(\mathbf{X}) &= p(\mathbf{x_n} \bigm | \mathbf{x_1}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{n-1})p(\mathbf{x}_{n-1} \bigm | \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{n-2}) \quad \ldots \quad p(\mathbf{x}_2 \bigm | \mathbf{x}_1)p(\mathbf{x}_1)\\ p(\mathbf{X}) &= \prod_{i=1}^n p(\mathbf{x}_i \bigm | \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{i-1})
\end{aligned}$

concepts.title: Training an Autoregressive Model
concepts.one_liner: Training an autoregressive model involves extracting supervised input-output pairs from sequences of pixels.
concepts.content:
To train an autoregressive model, you extract supervised pairs of desired input-output behavior. For an autoregressive model of pixels, this means extracting sequences of pixels $\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{n-1}$ and the corresponding observed next pixel $\mathbf{x}_n$. These pairs can be extracted by traversing training images in raster order. The full training and testing setup looks like this (@fig-generative_models-autoregressive_train_predict):

(see figure: Training an autoregressive model, then sampling images from it.)
concepts.motivation_md: Training autoregressive models as supervised learning problems on sequences of pixels allows effective learning of conditional distributions for image generation.
concepts.recap_md:
- Training data consists of input sequences $\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{n-1}$ and next pixel $\mathbf{x}_n$.
- Pairs are extracted by traversing images in raster order.
- The model learns to predict the next pixel given previous pixels.

key_passage.text: To train an autogressive a model, you just need to extract supervised pairs of desired input-output behavior, as usual. For an autoregressive model of pixels, that means extracting sequences of pixels $\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{n-1}$ and corresponding observed next pixel $\mathbf{x}_n$.

example.text: These can be extracted by traversing training images in raster order.

concepts.title: Sampling from Autoregressive Models
concepts.one_liner: Sampling from autoregressive models is done sequentially by sampling each pixel conditioned on previously sampled pixels.
concepts.content:
Autoregressive models give us an explicit density function, @eq-generative_models-autoregressive_likelihood. To sample from this density, we use the process described previously: sample the first pixel from $p(\mathbf{x}_1)$, then conditioned on this pixel, sample the second from $p(\mathbf{x}_2 \mid \mathbf{x}_1)$, and so forth. Since each of these densities is a categorical distribution, sampling is easy: one option is to partition a unit line segment into regions of length equal to the categorical probabilities and see where a uniform random draw along this line falls.

Autoregressive models do not have latent variables $\mathbf{z}$, which makes them incompatible with applications that involve extracting or manipulating latent variables.
concepts.motivation_md: Sequential sampling from autoregressive models enables explicit and tractable generation of data without latent variables.
concepts.recap_md:
- Sampling proceeds sequentially from $p(\mathbf{x}_1)$, then $p(\mathbf{x}_2 \mid \mathbf{x}_1)$, etc.
- Each conditional distribution is categorical, allowing straightforward sampling.
- Autoregressive models lack latent variables, limiting some applications.

concepts.title: Geometric Transformations as Convolutions
concepts.one_liner: Once geometry is added to the representation, all of the transformations we discussed before can be implemented as one-dimensional (1D) convolutions over the locations.
concepts.content:
### Geometric Transformations as Convolutions

In @sec-linear_image_filtering we showed how certain geometric transformations can be written as convolutions (such as the translation) while others cannot (such as rotations, scalings, shears, etc.). However, things change when adding geometry explicitly to the image representation!

Once geometry is added to the representation, all of the transformations we discussed before can be implemented as one-dimensional (1D) convolutions over the locations as shown in the diagram in @fig-rotation_as_convolution.

(see figure: Geometric transformation as a convolution. The input and output signals are represented as pixel sets with explicit geometry. The convolution kernels are $w_x$ and $w_y$, corresponding to one...)

In the diagram (@fig-rotation_as_convolution), each input element is a vector $(x_i,y_i,\ell_i)$ where $x_i$, $y_i$ are the pixel location, and $\ell_i$ is the pixel intensity at that location. The convolution kernels are: $w_x=[\cos ( \theta), \sin ( \theta)]$ and $w_y=[-\sin ( \theta), \cos ( \theta)]$. The weights are the same for all inputs. The output is also represented using position explicitly: $(x'_i,y'_i,\ell'_i)$.
concepts.motivation_md: Representing images with explicit geometry allows all geometric transformations, including rotations and scalings, to be implemented as convolutions, unifying and simplifying their computation.

- Some geometric transformations can be expressed as convolutions, e.g., translation.
- Adding explicit geometry to image representation enables all transformations to be implemented as 1D convolutions.
- Convolution kernels correspond to rotation parameters $w_x$ and $w_y$.

concepts.title: Lines and Planes in Homogeneous Coordinates

position.section_title: Lines and Planes in Homogeneous Coordinates

concepts.one_liner: In homogeneous coordinates, the equation of a line is the dot product: $\boldsymbol{l} ^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{p} = 0$ where $\boldsymbol{l}^\mathsf{T}= \left [a, b, c\right ]$.
concepts.content:
One interesting application of homogeneous coordinates is to use it to describe lines and planes and perform operations with them. In 2D, the equation of a line is $ax+by+c=0$, which can be written in homogeneous coordinates as $$ax+by+c=0 \rightarrow 
    \begin{bmatrix}
    a & b & c 
    \end{bmatrix}
    \begin{bmatrix}
    x \\
    y \\
    1
    \end{bmatrix}
    = 0$$

In homogeneous coordinates, the equation of a line is the dot product:
$$\boldsymbol{l} ^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{p} = 0$$ where $\boldsymbol{l}^\mathsf{T}= \left [a, b, c\right ]$. Therefore, a point $\mathbf{p}$, belongs to the line when $\boldsymbol{l}$ and $\mathbf{p}$ are perpendicular.

This representation of the line is in homogeneous coordinates because it is scale invariant. This is, $\left [a, b, c\right ]$ is the same line as $\left [a/c, b/c, 1\right ]$. Therefore, it is also useful to describe the equation of the line with $\boldsymbol{l}^\mathsf{T}= \left [n_x, n_y, -d\right ]$ where $(n_x,n_y)$ is the normal to the line and $d$ is the distance to the origin.

Using homogeneous coordinates makes obtaining geometric properties of points and lines very easy. Given two points $\mathbf{p}_1$ and $\mathbf{p}_2$ in homogeneous coordinates, the line that passes by both points is the cross product (@fig-points_and_lines_homogeneous_imggeo):
$$\boldsymbol{l} = \mathbf{p}_1 \times \mathbf{p}_2$$ This is because if the line passes by both points, it has to verify that $\boldsymbol{l}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{p}_1=0$ and $\boldsymbol{l}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{p}_2=0$. That is, the vector $\mathbf{l}$ has to be perpendicular to both $\mathbf{p}_1$ and $\mathbf{p}_2$. The cross product between $\mathbf{p}_1$ and $\mathbf{p}_2$ gives a vector that is perpendicular to both.

Following a similar argument, you can show that given two lines $\boldsymbol{l}_1$ and $\boldsymbol{l}_2$ the intersection point between them is the cross product (@fig-points_and_lines_homogeneous_imggeo):
$$\mathbf{p} = \boldsymbol{l}_1 \times  \boldsymbol{l}_2$$ The coordinates of $\mathbf{p}$ computed that way will be given in homogeneous coordinates. So you need to divide by the third component in order to get the actual point coordinates in heterogeneous coordinates.

(see figure: Using homogeneous coordinates to get the line that passes by two points, and to obtain the intersection of two lines. Both operations are analogous.)

If three 2D points are colinear, then the determinant of the matrix formed by concatenating the three vectors, in homogeneous coordinates, as columns is equal to zero: $\det( [\mathbf{p}_1~\mathbf{p}_2~\mathbf{p}_3 ])=0$. If three lines intersect in the same point we have a similar relationship: $\det( [\boldsymbol{l}_1~\boldsymbol{l}_2~\boldsymbol{l}_3 ])=0$.

It is also interesting to point out that a 3D vector can be interpreted as a 2D line or as a 2D point in homogeneous coordinates.

We can also do something analogous to represent planes in 3D. The equation of a 3D plane is $aX+bY+cZ+d=0$, which can be written in homogeneous coordinates as:

$$\mathbf{\pi}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{P} = 0$$ where $\mathbf{\pi} = [a,b,c,d]^\mathsf{T}$ are the plane parameters and $\mathbf{P}=[X,Y,Z,1]^\mathsf{T}$ are the 3D point homogeneous coordinates.

Representing 3D lines with homogeneous coordinates is not that easy and
concepts.motivation_md: Homogeneous coordinates simplify the representation and computation of lines and planes, enabling easy calculation of intersections and colinearity using vector operations.
concepts.recap_md:
- A 2D line in homogeneous coordinates is $\boldsymbol{l}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{p} = 0$ with $\boldsymbol{l} = [a,b,c]$.
- The line through two points is $\mathbf{p}_1 \times \mathbf{p}_2$; intersection of two lines is $\boldsymbol{l}_1 \times \boldsymbol{l}_2$.
- Planes in 3D are represented as $\mathbf{\pi}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{P} = 0$ with $\mathbf{\pi} = [a,b,c,d]^\mathsf{T}$.

concepts.title: Image Warping
concepts.one_liner: The best approach is to use what is called backward mapping which consists of looping over all the pixels of the target image and applying the inverse geometric transform, then using interpolation to get the correct color value.
concepts.content:
Now that we have seen how to describe simple geometric transformations to pixel coordinates, we need to go back to the representation of the image as samples on a regular grid. This will require applying image interpolation.

The first algorithm that usually comes to mind when transforming an image is to take every pixel in the original image represented as $[\ell_i,x_i,y_i]$, apply the transformation, $\mathbf{M}$, to the coordinates, and record the pixel color into the resulting coordinates in the target image (@fig-warping_sketch). As coordinates might result in non-integer values, we can simply round the result to the closest pixel coordinate (i.e., nearest neighbor interpolation as we discussed in @sec-interpolation). This algorithm is called **forward mapping**. It is an intuitive way of warping an image but it is really not a good idea. We will have all sorts of artifacts such as missing values and aliasing as shown in @fig-warping_sketch and @fig-warping_forward_backward.

(see figure: Comparison between forward and backward mapping using nearest neighbor interpolation. Forward mapping will produce missing values.)
 
The best approach is to use what is called **backward mapping** which consists of looping over all the pixels of the target image and applying the inverse geometric transform, $\mathbf{M}^{-1}$; we then use interpolation (as described in @sec-interpolation in chapter @sec-downsampling_and_upsampling) to get the correct color value (@fig-warping_sketch). This process guarantees that there will be no missing values (unless the coordinates go outside the frame of the input image) and there will be no aliasing if the interpolation is done correctly. To avoid aliasing, blurring of the input image might be necessary if the density of pixels in the target image is lower than in the input image. Figures @fig-warping_sketch and @fig-warping_forward_backward compare forward and backward mapping.

(see figure: Comparison between forward and backward mapping. Forward mapping produces many artifacts. In both cases we use nearest neighbor interpolation.)

To achieve high image quality warping it is important to choose a high quality interpolation filter such as bilinear, bicubic, or Lanczos. MIP-mapping @Lance1983 is another popular technique for high quality and efficient interpolation. MIP-mapping relies on a multiscale image pyramid to efficiently compute the best neighborhood structure needed to perform the interpolation at each location, which can be very useful when warping an image onto a curved surface.

Image warping can be applied to arbitrary geometric transformations and
concepts.motivation_md: Image warping applies geometric transformations to images; backward mapping with interpolation avoids artifacts like missing pixels and aliasing, ensuring better image quality.
concepts.recap_md:
- Forward mapping applies transformation to original pixels but causes missing values and aliasing.
- Backward mapping applies inverse transform to target pixels and interpolates colors, avoiding artifacts.
- High-quality interpolation filters like bilinear or Lanczos improve warping results.

key_passage.text: The best approach is to use what is called backward mapping which consists of looping over all the pixels of the target image and applying the inverse geometric transform, \mathbf{M}^{-1}; we then use interpolation (as described in \sec-interpolation in chapter \sec-downsampling_and_upsampling) to get the correct color value. This process guarantees that there will be no missing values (unless the coordinates go outside the frame of the input image) and there will be no aliasing if the interpolation is done correctly.

concepts.title: Implicit Image Representations
concepts.one_liner: An implicit image representation via a function $f_\theta$ trained to reproduce the image pixels is a function such that, $\ell(x,y) = f_{\theta}(x,y)$ where now $x,y$ can take on any real value.
concepts.content:
An image is an array of values, $\boldsymbol\ell\in \mathbb{R}^{N \times M \times 3}$, where each value is indexed as $\ell[n,m]$ when $n,m$ take only on discrete values. We can say that interpolation is a way of transforming the discrete image into a continuous signal: $\ell(x,y)$.

An implicit image representation via a function $f_\theta$ trained to reproduce the image pixels is a function such that,
$$\ell(x,y) = f_{\theta}(x,y)$$ where now $x,y$ can take on any real value.

### Interpolation

In the case of nearest neighbors or bilinear interpolation, the parameters of the interpolation function $\theta$ is the input image itself. For example, using a functional form, nearest neighbors interpolation can be written as:
$$\ell(x,y) = \ell\left[ \text{round}(x), \text{round}(y) \right]$$

What is really interesting about thinking about interpolation in this way is that we can now extend the space of possible functions $f_{\theta}(x,y)$ to include other functional forms. For instance, this function could be implemented by a neural network that will take as input the two image coordinate values $x$ and $y$ and will output the intensity value at that location. The training set for the neural network is the image itself, and it will consist of the input-output pairs $[(x_i, y_i); \ell(x_i,y_i)]$ (i.e., location as input and intensities/colors as output). During training the neural network will memorize the image. The training will contain only values at discrete positions but in test time we can use any continuous input values. For this formulation to work, the neural network should be able to generalize to non-integer coordinate values, that is, it should be able to interpolate between samples.
concepts.motivation_md: Implicit image representations model images as continuous functions, enabling interpolation and transformations beyond discrete pixel grids, often using neural networks.
concepts.recap_md:
- Images are discrete arrays $\ell[n,m]$ but interpolation creates continuous signals $\ell(x,y)$.
- Implicit representation models $\ell(x,y) = f_\theta(x,y)$, with $f_\theta$ trained to reproduce pixels.
- Neural networks can implement $f_\theta$ to generalize interpolation beyond discrete samples.

concepts.title: Image Warping with Implicit Representations
concepts.one_liner: Image warping is implemented by applying the inverse geometric transformation to output coordinates and using the implicit function representation to get interpolated values.
concepts.content:
Once the neural network, $f_{\theta}(x,y)$, has learned to reproduce the image, we can reconstruct the original image or apply transformations to it. Image warping is then implemented by simply applying the inverse geometric transformation to the discrete coordinates of the output grid and use the functional representation of the image to get the interpolated values:
$$\hat{\ell} (x,y) = f_{\theta} \left( \mathbf{M}^{-1}(x,y,1)^\mathsf{T}\right)$$
In this equation the input location is written in homogeneous coordinates, so the function $f$ will first have to divide by the third component to translate the input back to heterogeneous coordinates.
concepts.motivation_md: Using implicit image representations for warping allows smooth interpolation and transformation by applying inverse geometry to output coordinates and querying the learned function.
concepts.recap_md:
- Neural network $f_\theta$ models the image implicitly.
- Warping applies inverse transform $\mathbf{M}^{-1}$ to output coordinates.
- The warped image intensity is obtained by evaluating $f_\theta$ at transformed coordinates.

concepts.one_liner: The goal is to identify the transformation $\mathbf{M}$ between two images where one is a transformed version of the other; this problem is called image alignment.

- It is the reverse problem of applying a known transformation.
- Essential for tasks involving multiple images and geometric consistency.

concepts.title: Camera Modeling and Calibration
concepts.one_liner: We will use homogeneous coordinates to describe a camera projection model that is more general than what we have done until now, enabling coordinate system changes and camera calibration.
concepts.content:
# Camera Modeling and Calibration {#sec-camera_parameters}

## Introduction

In @sec-imaging we described the image formation process assuming that the camera was the central element and we placed the origin of the world coordinates system in the pinhole. But, as we will be interested in interpreting the scene in front of the camera, other systems of reference might be more appropriate. For instance, in the simple world model of @sec-simplesystem we placed the origin of the world coordinates system on the ground, away from the camera. What formulation of the image formation process will allow us changing coordinate systems easily? This is what we will study in this chapter.

In the sketch shown below, a standing person is holding a camera and taking a picture with it of someone sitting at a table (sorry for our drawing skills but hopefully this description compensates for our poor artistry). We will be answering questions about the scene based on the picture taken by the camera: for instance, how high and large is the table? We will also answer questions about the camera, like how high is the camera above the floor?

(see figure: Camera-centric and world-centric camera coordinate systems.)

In settings where we have multiple cameras we will have to be able to transform the coordinates frames between cameras. And finally, to translate the two-dimensional (2D) images into the underlying three-dimensional (3D) scene, we need to know how 2D points relate to 3D world coordinates, which is called calibrating the cameras.

In this chapter we will show how to use homogeneous coordinates to describe a camera projection model that is more general than what we have done until now. This formulation will be key to building most of the approaches we will study from now until the end of this book; therefore it is important to be familiar with it. It is also often used both in classic computer vision approaches and in deep learning architectures.

But before we move into the material, we are sure you would like to see the picture that the standing character from the previous sketch took. Here it is:
concepts.motivation_md: Camera modeling and calibration enable interpreting 2D images in terms of 3D world coordinates and allow coordinate transformations between cameras, essential for scene understanding and multi-camera setups.
concepts.recap_md:
- Camera modeling relates 3D world coordinates to 2D image points.
- Calibration determines how 2D points correspond to 3D scene geometry.
- Homogeneous coordinates provide a flexible framework for these transformations.

concepts.title: Trick 2: Efficient approximation via importance sampling
concepts.one_liner: When approximating the likelihood integral for $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$, try to only sample $\mathbf{z}$ values that place high probability on $\mathbf{x}$, called importance sampling.
concepts.content:
The previous trick works decently for modeling low-dimensional distributions. Unfortunately, this approach does not scale well to high dimensions. The reason is that in order for our Monte Carlo estimate of the integral to be accurate, we may need many samples from $p_{\mathbf{z}}$, and the higher the dimensionality of $\mathbf{z}$, the more samples we will typically need.

Consider the sum approximation of the likelihood integral:

$$\begin{aligned}    p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) &\approx \frac{1}{M} (p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z}^{(1)}) + p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z}^{(2)}) + p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z}^{(3)}) + \ldots)
\end{aligned}$$

In general, some of the terms $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z}^{(j)})$ will be larger than others. In fact, in our example in @fig-generative_modeling_and_representation_learning-IGMM_training_iters, most of these terms are near zero. This is because, to maximize likelihood, the model spreads out the Gaussians so that each places high density on a different part of the data distribution. A datapoint $\mathbf{x}$ will only have substantial probability under the Gaussians whose means are near $\mathbf{x}$.

Consider the example in @fig-generative_modeling_and_representation_learning-vae_importance_sampling1, where we try to estimate the probability of the point $\mathbf{x}$ (blue circle).

(see figure: To estimate $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$ we only need to consider the Gaussian components (gray circles) that place significant probability on $\mathbf{x}$.)

The mixture components are shaded according to the probability they assign to $\mathbf{x}$. Almost all are so far from $\mathbf{x}$ that we have:

$$\begin{aligned}
    p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) &\approx \frac{1}{M} (0 + p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z}^{(2)}) + 0 + \ldots)
\end{aligned}$$

If we had only sampled $\mathbf{z}^{(2)}$, we would have had almost as good an estimate!

This brings us to the second trick of VAEs: when approximating the likelihood integral for $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$, try to only sample $\mathbf{z}$ values that place high probability on $\mathbf{x}$, that is, those $\mathbf{z}$ values for which $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z})$ is large. Then, a few samples will suffice to well approximate the entire expectation. This trick is called importance sampling. It is a general trick for approximating expectations. Rather than sampling $\mathbf{z}^{(i)} \sim p_{\mathbf{z}}$, we sample from some other density $\mathbf{z}^{(i)} \sim q_{\mathbf{z}}$, and multiply by a correction factor $\frac{p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})}{q_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})}$ to account for the fact that we are sampling from a biased distribution:

$$\begin{aligned}
p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) &= \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim p_{\mathbf{z}}}\Big[p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z})\Big]
= \int_{\mathbf{z}} p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z}) p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z}) d\mathbf{z}
= \int_{\mathbf{z}} q_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})\frac{p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})}{q_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z}) d\mathbf{z}\\
&= \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim q_{\mathbf{z}}}\Big[\frac{p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})}{q_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z})\Big]
\end{aligned}$$

Using the intuition developed previously, the distribution $q$ we would really like to sample from is the one whose samples maximize $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z})$. It turns out that the optimal distribution is $q^* = p_{\theta}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})$.

See chapter 9, section 1 of @mcbook for a proof that

- $q^*(\mathbf{z}) \propto \lvert p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z}) \rvert p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})$,
- from which it then follows that
- $q^*(\mathbf{z}) \propto p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z})p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z}) = p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z}) \propto p_{\theta}(\mathbf{z} \bigm | \mathbf{x})$,

yielding our result.

This distribution minimizes the expected error between a Monte Carlo estimate of the expectation and its true value (i.e., minimizes the variance of our Monte Carlo estimator). The intuition is that $p_{\theta}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})$ is precisely a prediction of which $\mathbf{z}$ values are most likely to have generated the observed $\mathbf{x}$. The optimal importance sampling way to estimate the likelihood of a datapoint will therefore look like this:

$$\begin{aligned}    &p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) \approx \frac{1}{M} \sum_{j=1}^M\frac{p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z}^{(j)})}{p_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}^{(j)} \bigm | \mathbf{x})} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z}^{(j)}) \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad\text{Optimal importance sampling}\\
    &\quad\quad \mathbf{z}^{(j)} \sim p_{\theta}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x}) \nonumber
\end{aligned}$$

Visually, rather than sampling from all over $p_{\mathbf{z}}$ and wasting samples on regions that place nearly zero likelihood on the data, we focus our sampling on just the region that places high likelihood on the data, and we can get away with far fewer samples to well approximate the data likelihood, as indicated @fig-generative_modeling_and_representation_learning-vae_importance_sampling2.

(see figure: Optimal importance sampling estimates $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$ by drawing samples from $p_{\theta}(Z \\| \mathbf{x})$.)
concepts.motivation_md: Sampling from the prior $p_{\mathbf{z}}$ in high dimensions requires many samples for accurate Monte Carlo estimates, so importance sampling focuses on sampling $\mathbf{z}$ values that place high probability on the data point $\mathbf{x}$ to efficiently approximate the likelihood integral.
concepts.recap_md:
- Monte Carlo estimates of $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$ require many samples in high dimensions.
- Importance sampling samples $\mathbf{z}$ from a distribution $q$ biased towards high likelihood on $\mathbf{x}$.
- The optimal importance sampling distribution is $q^* = p_{\theta}(Z \mid \mathbf{x})$, minimizing estimator variance.

concepts.title: Trick 3: Variational inference to approximate the sampling distribution
concepts.one_liner: VAEs use a strategy called variational inference to approximate the complicated sampling distribution $p_{\theta}(Z \mid \mathbf{x})$.
concepts.content:
Now we know what distribution we should be sampling $\mathbf{z}$ from: $p_{\theta}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})$. The only remaining problem is that this distribution may be complicated and hard to sample from.

Remember, we have defined simple forms for only $p_{\theta}(X \\| \mathbf{z})$ and $p_{\mathbf{z}}$ (both are Gaussians), but this does not mean $p_{\theta}(Z \\| \mathbf{x})$ has a simple form.

Sampling from arbitrary distributions is a standard topic in statistics, and many algorithms have been proposed, including the Markov chain Monte Carlo methods we encountered in previous chapters. VAEs use a strategy called variational inference.
concepts.motivation_md: Sampling from the ideal distribution $p_{\theta}(Z \mid \mathbf{x})$ is difficult because it may be complex and hard to sample from directly, so variational inference provides a tractable approximation.
concepts.recap_md:
- The ideal sampling distribution is $p_{\theta}(Z \mid \mathbf{x})$.
- This distribution may be complicated and hard to sample from.
- Variational inference is used to approximate this sampling distribution.

key_passage.text: Now we know what distribution we *should* be sampling $\mathbf{z}$ from: $p_{\theta}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})$. The only remaining problem is that this distribution may be complicated and hard to sample from.

motivation.text: Sampling from arbitrary distributions is a standard topic in statistics, and many algorithms have been proposed, including the Markov chain Monte Carlo methods we encountered in previous chapters.

example.text: VAEs use a strategy called **variational inference**.

concepts.title: variational inference
concepts.one_liner: Variational inference approximates an intractable density $p$ by finding the nearest density in a tractable family $q_{\psi}$ parameterized by $\psi$.
concepts.content:
The name variational inference comes from the "calculus of variations," which studies functionals (functions of functions). Integrals of probability densities are functionals. Variational inference is commonly (but not always) used to approximate densities expressed as the integral of some other densities, hence functionals, hence the name variational.

The idea of variational inference is to approximate an intractable density $p$ by finding the nearest density in a tractable family $q_{\psi}$, parameterized by $\psi$. In VAEs, we approximate our ideal importance density $p_{\theta}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})$ with a $q_{\psi}$ in a family we can efficiently sample from; the most common choice is to again use a Gaussian, conditioned on $\mathbf{x}$:

$$q_{\psi} = \mathcal{N}(f_{\psi}^{\mu}(\mathbf{x}), f_{\psi}^{\Sigma}(\mathbf{x})).$$

The $f_{\psi}$ is a function that maps from $\mathbf{x}$ to parameters of a distribution over $\mathbf{z}$; in other words, $f_{\psi}$ is a probabilistic encoder! This function is shown next in

(see figure: A VAE's encoder, $f_{\psi}$, models $p(Z \\| \mathbf{x})$ as a Gaussian parameterized by $f_{\psi}(\mathbf{x})$.)
concepts.motivation_md: Variational inference provides a tractable way to approximate complex or intractable probability densities by optimizing over a simpler family of distributions, enabling efficient sampling and learning.
concepts.recap_md:
- Variational inference approximates intractable densities by a tractable family $q_{\psi}$.
- In VAEs, $q_{\psi}$ is often a Gaussian conditioned on $\mathbf{x}$.
- The encoder $f_{\psi}$ maps $\mathbf{x}$ to parameters of $q_{\psi}$.

key_passage.text: The idea of variational inference is to approximate an intractable density $p$ by finding the nearest density in a tractable family $q_{\psi}$, parameterized by $\psi$.

motivation.text: Variational inference is commonly (but not always) used to approximate densities expressed as the integral of some other densities, hence functionals, hence the name variational.

example.text: In VAEs, we approximate our ideal importance density $p_{\theta}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})$ with a $q_{\psi}$ in a family we can efficiently sample from; the most common choice is to again use a Gaussian, conditioned on $\mathbf{x}$: $q_{\psi} = \mathcal{N}(f_{\psi}^{\mu}(\mathbf{x}), f_{\psi}^{\Sigma}(\mathbf{x}))$. The $f_{\psi}$ is a function that maps from $\mathbf{x}$ to parameters of a distribution over $\mathbf{z}$; in other words, $f_{\psi}$ is a probabilistic encoder!

concepts.title: KL divergence objective for $q_{\psi}$
concepts.one_liner: We choose $q_{\psi}$ to minimize the KL divergence to $p_{\theta}(Z \mid \mathbf{x})$, maximizing the objective $J_q$ defined as the negative KL divergence.
concepts.content:
We want $q_{\psi}$ to be the best approximation of $p_{\theta}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})$, so our goal is to choose the $q_{\psi}$ that minimizes the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between these two distributions. We could have chosen other divergences or notions of approximation, but using the KL divergence yields some nice properties. We call the objective for $q_{\psi}$ as $J_{q}$, defined as the negative KL-divergence, so our goal is to maximize this quantity. Using the definition of KL-divergence, we expand this objective as follows:

$$\begin{aligned}    J_q(\mathbf{x},\psi) &= -\mathrm{KL}\left(q_\psi(Z \mid \mathbf{x}) \| p_\theta(Z \mid \mathbf{x})\right)\\
    &= -\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z} \sim q_{\psi}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})}[ \log q_{\psi}(\mathbf{z} \bigm | \mathbf{x}) - \log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{z} \bigm | \mathbf{x})]\\
    &= -\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z} \sim q_{\psi}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})}[ \log q_{\psi}(\mathbf{z} \bigm | \mathbf{x}) - \log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z}) - \log p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z}) + \log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})]\\
    &= \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z} \sim q_{\psi}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})}[ -\log q_{\psi}(\mathbf{z} \bigm | \mathbf{x}) + \log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z}) + \log p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})] - \log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})
\end{aligned}$$

The last line follows from the fact that $\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$ is a constant with respect to the distribution we are taking expectation over.

The learning problem for $q_{\psi}$ is to maximize $J_q$ over all images in our dataset $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$ with respect to parameters $\psi$. Notice that the term $\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$ is constant with respect to these parameters, so we can drop that term, yielding:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \psi^* &= \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{\psi} \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N J_q(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \psi)\\
    &= \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{\psi} \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z} \sim q_{\psi}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x}^{(i)})}[ -\log q_{\psi}(\mathbf{z} \bigm | \mathbf{x}^{(i)}) + \log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)} \bigm | \mathbf{z}) + \log p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})]}_{J}
\end{aligned}$$

Here we have defined a new cost function, $J$.
concepts.motivation_md: Minimizing the KL divergence between $q_{\psi}$ and $p_{\theta}(Z \mid \mathbf{x})$ ensures $q_{\psi}$ closely approximates the true posterior, enabling efficient inference.
concepts.recap_md:
- The objective $J_q$ is the negative KL divergence between $q_{\psi}(Z \mid \mathbf{x})$ and $p_{\theta}(Z \mid \mathbf{x})$.
- Maximizing $J_q$ finds the best approximation $q_{\psi}$.
- The term $\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$ is constant and can be dropped during optimization.
