concepts.title: Shortcomings
concepts.one_liner: Image classification has important limitations, including ambiguous class definitions and reliance on dataset biases.
concepts.content:
The task of image classification is plagued with issues. Although it is a useful task to measure progress in computer vision and machine learning, one has to be aware of its limitations when trying to use it to produce a meaningful description of a scene, or when developing a classifier for consumption in the real world.

One very important shortcoming of this task is that it assumes that we can actually answer unambiguously the question *does the image contains object c?* But what happens if class definitions are ambiguous or class boundaries are soft? Even in cases were we believe that the boundaries might be well defined, it is east to find images that will challenge our assumption, as shown in @fig-whatisacar.

[FIGURE:360abab54729bcf5 | A photograph of an older, white Renault 4 hatchback with a blue hood parked on a gravel surface. The car is shown from a front-three-quarter angle, with buildings and other modern cars in the...]

[FIGURE:a64dd9969f9fe987 | A photograph of two cars, a blue sedan in the foreground and a green SUV behind it, both heavily covered in a thick layer of snow. The snow forms a large, rounded mound on top of each vehicle...]

[FIGURE:2e461a626376ea7e | A photograph taken from the driver's seat of a car looking through the windshield into a dark rock tunnel. The car's dashboard and rearview mirror are visible in the foreground, framing the view of...]


[FIGURE:2f43ff582bf7c58e | A photograph of a car body shell in an assembly plant, held by a red robotic arm and a red 'SMART Cart' base. The car is incomplete, lacking windows, wheels, and interior components, illustrating the...]

[FIGURE:479c0a519751a2ba | A small yellow toy car with a strawberry decal on its roof and hood is parked in front of a cardboard castle. The image illustrates the ambiguity of object classification, questioning whether a toy...]

[FIGURE:aee6e4196eafb081 | A photograph of a white plate containing a slice of watermelon. A piece of the red fruit has been carved out into the silhouette of a car and placed separately on the plate, illustrating the...]

Which of these images contains a car? This is a simple question that does not have a simple answer.

Which of this images of @fig-whatisacar contains a car? A simple question that does not have a simple answer. The top three images contain cars, although with increasing difficulty. However, for the three images on the second row, it is not clear what the desired answer it is. We can clearly recognize the content of those images, but it feels as if using a single word for describing those images leaves too much ambiguity. Is a car under construction already a car? Is the toy car a car? And if we play with food and make a car out of watermelon, would that be a car? Probably not. But if a vision system classifies that shape as a car, would that be a mistake like any other?

Although it is not clearly stated in the problem definition, language plays a big role in object classification. The objects in @fig-object_recognition_pepper are easily recognizable to us, but if we ask the question "Is there a fruit in this picture?," the answer is a bit more complex than it might appear at first glance.

(see figure: A pepper is a fruit according to botanics, and it is a vegetable according to the culinary classification.)

What if the object is present in the scene but invisible in the image? What if there are infinite classes? In our formulation, $\hat {\bf y}$ is a vector of a fixed length. Therefore, we can only answer the question "is object class $c$ present in the image?" for a finite set of classes. What if we want to be able to answer an infinite set of questions? The next sections introduce more sophisticated formulations of object recognition that address some of these questions.

Is it possible to classify an image without localizing the object? How can we answer the question "Is object class $c$ present in the image?" without localizing the object? One possibility is that the function $f$ has learned to localize the object internally, but the information about the location is not being recorded in the output. Another possibility is that the function has learned to use other cues present in the image (biases in the dataset). As it is not trying to localize an object, the function $f$ will not get penalized if it uses shortcuts such as only recognizing one part of the object (e.g., such as the head of a dog, or car wheels), or if it makes use of contextual biases in the dataset (e.g., all images with grass and blue skies have horses, or all streets have cars) or detects unintended correlations between low-level image properties and the image content (e.g., all images of insects have a blurry background). As a consequence, image classification performance could mislead us into believing that the classifier works well and that it has learned a good representation of the object class it classifies.
concepts.motivation_md: Image classification is limited by ambiguous class definitions, soft boundaries, and dataset biases, which complicate meaningful scene description and real-world classifier deployment.
concepts.recap_md:
- Image classification assumes unambiguous class definitions, which is often unrealistic.
- Ambiguities arise from unclear boundaries and diverse object representations.
- Classifiers may rely on dataset biases or partial cues, misleading performance evaluation.

concepts.title: Concluding Remarks
concepts.one_liner: The four different approaches we have described use a common set of building blocks: image classifiers, region proposals, pixelwise classifiers, and bounding box regression.
concepts.content:
@fig-pictorialsummary shows a pictorial summary of the different methods we have seen in this chapter to represent objects in images. The four different approaches we have described use a common set of building blocks: image classifiers, region proposals, pixelwise classifiers, and bounding box regression.

(see figure: A family of object recognition definitions.)

However, the representations we have described in this chapter feel very incomplete. If you are building a robot or an autonomous vehicle, such object representations are very hard to act on. A robot planning to grasp an object will need an accurate three-dimensional (3D) modeling of the object as well as an understanding of some of its physical properties in order to plan for the best grasping points. An autonomous vehicle will also need an accurate 3D description of the locations of objects in the world, together with a characterization of their dynamics. Therefore, object segmentation and classification only provide one part of the information needed.

The techniques we have described in this chapter rely on language to define what an object is (e.g., image tagging, captioning, etc.). What else can we do besides associating an object with a word? Here there are other questions that an object recognition system could try to answer:

- Is this piece of matter an object? could I find other instances that might belong to the same class or is it just a random arrangement of things with little chances of being found somewhere else?

- What is its 3D shape?

- Is it resting on the ground? How is it supported?

- What are its mechanical properties? Is it soft? Does it has parts? Is it rigid or deformable?

- How will it react to external actions? Can I grasp the object? How?

- What might this object be useful for? If I have to solve a task, can I use this object?

- Is it alive? Can I eat it?

- What is the physical process that created it? Is it artificial or natural?

- How did the object arrived to its current location?

- Is it stable? What will it do next?

Those are the questions that scientist would ask themselves when observing a new natural phenomena, and a computer vision system should behave as a scientist when confronted with a new visual stimuli. A system should formulate hypothesis about its visual input, devise experiments and perform interventions to answer them. One can rely on language to answer some or all of those questions, but language does not need to be the only internal representation used.
concepts.motivation_md: Object recognition methods use common building blocks but lack the full 3D and physical understanding needed for robotics or autonomous vehicles. This motivates deeper representations beyond language-based object tagging.
concepts.recap_md:
- Object recognition methods use image classifiers, region proposals, pixelwise classifiers, and bounding box regression.
- Current methods provide incomplete representations for tasks like robotic grasping or autonomous driving.
- A vision system should answer deeper questions about 3D shape, physical properties, and dynamics beyond labeling.

concepts.title: Vision and Language
concepts.one_liner: The last few decades have seen enormous improvements in both computer vision and natural language processing.
concepts.content:
The last few decades have seen enormous improvements in both computer vision and natural language processing. Naturally, there has been great interest in putting these two branches of artificial intelligence (AI) together.

At first it might seem like vision has little to do with language. This is what you might conclude if you see the role of language as just being about communication. However, another view on language is that it is a representation of the world around us, and this representation is one the brain uses extensively for higher-level cognition @fodor1975language. Visual perception is also about representing the world around us and forming mental models that act as a substrate for reasoning and decision making. From this perspective, both language and vision are trying to solve more or less the same problem.

It turns out this view is quite powerful, and indeed language and vision can help each other in innumerable ways. This chapter is about some of the ways language can improve vision systems, and also how vision systems can support language systems.

## Background: Representing Text as Tokens

In order to understand **vision-language models** (**VLMs**) we first need to understand a bit about **language models**. There are many ways to model language and indeed there is a whole field that studies this, called **natural language processing** (**NLP**). We will present just one way, which follows almost exactly the same format as modern computer vision systems: tokenize the text, then process it with a transformer. In chapter @sec-transformers we saw how to apply transformers to images and now we will see how to apply them to text. 

The amazing thing about transformers is that they work well for a wide variety of data types: in fact, the same architectures that we saw in chapter @sec-transformers also works for text processing. To apply transformers to a new data modality may require nothing more than figuring out how to represent that data as numbers.

So our first question is, how can we represent text as numbers? One option, which we have already seen, is to use a word-level encoding scheme, mapping each word in our vocabulary to a unique one-hot code. This requires $K$-dimensional one-hot codes for a vocabulary of $K$ different words.

A disadvantage of this approach is that $K$ has to be very large to cover a language like English, which has a large vocabulary of over 100,000 possible words. This becomes even worse for computer languages, like Python. Programmers routinely name variables using made up words, which might never have been used before. We can't define a vocabulary large enough to cover all the strange strings programmers might come up
concepts.motivation_md: Vision and language have both advanced greatly and combining them helps solve shared problems of world representation and reasoning.
concepts.recap_md:
- Vision and language both represent the world and support higher-level cognition.
- Transformers can process both images and text by representing data as numbers.
- Word-level one-hot encoding requires very large vocabularies, which is a limitation.

key_passage.text: From this perspective, both language and vision are trying to solve more or less the same problem.

concepts.one_liner: A happy middle ground can be achieved using byte-pair encodings.
concepts.content: A happy middle ground can be achieved using **byte-pair** encodings @gage1994new. In this approach, we assign a one-hot code to each small chunk of text. concepts.title: Direct Linear Transform
concepts.one_liner: If we have six correspondences, then, under certain conditions, we can recover the projection matrix $\mathbf{M}$ by solving a linear system of equations.
concepts.motivation_md: The Direct Linear Transform (DLT) algorithm exists to recover the camera's projection matrix from known 3D points and their 2D image correspondences, enabling camera calibration from real-world measurements.
concepts.recap_md:
- The projection matrix $\mathbf{M}$ relates 3D points $\mathbf{P}_i$ to image points $\mathbf{p}_i$ via $\mathbf{p}_i = \mathbf{M}\mathbf{P}_i$.
- Stacking equations from $N$ correspondences yields a homogeneous linear system $\mathbf{A} \mathbf{m} = \mathbf{0}$.
- The solution minimizing $\|\mathbf{A} \mathbf{m}\|^2$ gives $\mathbf{m}$, from which $\mathbf{M}$ is formed (DLT algorithm).

key_passage.text: This method to obtain the projection matrix is called the **direct linear transform** (DLT) algorithm.

motivation.text: Let's assume that we know the exact locations of several 3D points in our scene in world coordinates and we also know the locations in which those 3D points project into the image. Can we use them to recover the intrinsic and extrinsic camera parameters?

concepts.title: Recovering Intrinsic and Extrinsic Camera Parameters
concepts.one_liner: Once $\mathbf{M}$ is estimated, we can decompose it to recover intrinsic camera parameters, translation, and rotation.
concepts.motivation_md: Recovering intrinsic and extrinsic camera parameters from the projection matrix $\mathbf{M}$ allows us to understand the camera's internal settings and its position and orientation in the world.
concepts.recap_md:
- The projection matrix $\mathbf{M}$ can be decomposed as $[\mathbf{K}\mathbf{R} ~|~ -\mathbf{K}\mathbf{R}\mathbf{T}]$.
- Camera translation $\mathbf{T}$ is recovered as $-\mathbf{B}^{-1}\mathbf{b}$ where $\mathbf{M} = [\mathbf{B} ~ \mathbf{b}]$.
- $\mathbf{K}$ and $\mathbf{R}$ are obtained from the QR decomposition of $\mathbf{B}^{-1}$, with sign adjustments to ensure positive diagonal entries in $\mathbf{K}$.

key_passage.text: Let's say that you start with a $3 \times 4$ matrix $\mathbf{M}$ obtained by calibrating the camera using DLT (or any other calibration method), and you want to extract the matrices $\mathbf{K}$, $\mathbf{R}$, and $\mathbf{T}$. It is possible to decompose the matrix $\mathbf{M}$ such that it can be written as: $$\mathbf{M} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{K}\mathbf{R} ~ \mid ~ -\mathbf{K}\mathbf{R}\mathbf{T} \end{bmatrix}$$

motivation.text: Once $\mathbf{M}$ is estimated, we would like to recover the intrinsic camera parameters, and also camera translation and rotation. Can it be done? It turns out that the answer is yes!

concepts.title: Nonlinear Optimization by Minimizing Reprojection Error
concepts.one_liner: The reprojection error is the difference between the estimated image coordinates of a 3D point and its ground-truth image coordinates.
concepts.motivation_md: Minimizing reprojection error refines camera parameters by reducing the difference between projected 3D points and their observed 2D image locations, improving calibration accuracy.

- It is computed as $\sum_{i=1}^N \|\mathbf{p}_i - \mathbf{p}'_i \|^2$.
- Minimizing this error via gradient descent refines $\mathbf{K}$, $\mathbf{R}$, and $\mathbf{T}$, often initialized by DLT.

concepts.title: A Toy Example
concepts.one_liner: We applied the DLT algorithm to real office measurements and recovered camera parameters close to expected values.
concepts.content:
The last few pages were full of math, and although everything seems sound, it is good to remain suspicious about what subtleties might be hidden behind the math that might make everything break. Can we run a simple test to see if the theory meets the practice?

We wanted to try it out so here is what we did. We started by taking a picture of one office and measure some distances as shown in @fig-office_measurements. The goal is to get real 3D coordinates measured in the world and use them to calibrate the camera.

(see figure: Office picture and real distances between a sparse set of points measured in centimeters.)

We took a picture, @fig-office_measurements, with the same iPhone we used in @sec-simple_unreliable_calibration_method, holding the camera at eye height (which is around 67 in, or 170 cm above the ground). The camera was looking downward at an angle of around 15 degrees with respect to the vertical. Would we be able to recover these extrinsic camera parameters, together with the intrinsic camera parameters, using the theory described in this chapter?

First we need to decide where we will place the origin of the world coordinates and the axis direction. As shown in the following picture, we place the origin on the ground floor, in the corner between the column and the glass wall in the back. Now we can get a list of 3D points from the office measurements and their corresponding 2D coordinates. The following figure shows a list of easily identifiable 3D points and their corresponding image coordinates. The image coordinates are approximated also and are collected manually. We use Adobe Photoshop to read the pixel coordinates.

(see figure: Office picture and a table with the 3D world coordinates of 12 points, extracted using the measurements from @fig-office_measurements)

Photoshop has the image coordinates origin on the top left. Our convention has been to put the origin on the bottom and the $x$-axis point from right to left. Therefore, we need to change the coordinates first (or just deal with it later). It is just simple to replace the image coordinates by $y_i \leftarrow 3{,}024-y_i$ and $x_i \leftarrow 4{,}032-x_i$.

In order to estimate the projection matrix we need a minimum of eight correspondences. Here we have 12, which will help to reduce the noise (and we assure you there is a lot of noise on those manual measurements). Applying the DLT algorithm we recover the following projection matrix: $$\mathbf{M} = 
    \begin{bmatrix}
    -8.1    &       -1.8      &     -0.2    &     1{,}845.5\\
      -3    &        5.4      &     -4.8    &     1{,}262.5\\
       0    &          0      &        0    &          1
    \end{bmatrix}$$ The matrix has been scaled so that the bottom-right element is a 1. Using this matrix, the mean reprojection error is 12.3 pixels, which is reasonably small for an image of size $4{,}032 \times 3{,}024$ pixels. That is, the reprojection error is $<0.5$ percent of the image height.

We now need to recover the intrinsic and extrinsic camera parameters. Using equation (@eq-recover_translation) we recover first the translation vector which gives us $\mathbf{T} = (182.3; 171.8; 347.6)$. From our definition of the world-coordinates frames, the middle element of $\mathbf{T}$ is the camera height with respect to the ground plane. The value of 171.8 cm is very close to our initial guess! Given a scene with known measurements and a picture, one can find out details about the camera and also about the observer. 

A picture reveals information about the camera and the photographer, even when there is no one on the picture. It is important to keep this in mind when thinking about privacy.


Let's now see if we can recover the camera angle and the intrinsics. Using the QR decomposition as described in @sec-recovering_intrinsic_and_extrinsic, we get
$$\mathbf{K} = 
    \begin{bmatrix}
    2{,}960    &      -24.9    &     1{,}979.7\\
       0    &       3{,}019    &     1{,}433.6\\
       0    &          0    &          1
    \end{bmatrix}$$ The values are very close to the ones from equation (@eq-intrinsic) which were obtained using a calibration pattern and also from the camera technical specifications. The off-diagonal elements, which would account for a skew pixel shape in the camera, are small relative to the focal length and probably just due to the annotation noise. Also, both scaling factors are very similar, and their difference might just be due to noise. The camera is likely to have square pixels. The last column is the location of the optical image center, as we defined the image coordinates with the origin in the bottom right instead of that in the image center, and is quite close to what one would expect: $[W/2, H/2,1]$.

Now let's look at the camera orientation. The rotation matrix obtained with the QR decomposition is $$\mathbf{R} = 
    \begin{bmatrix}
   -0.8576  & -0.0162  &  0.5141 \\
    0.1928  & -0.9368  &  0.2921\\
   -0.4769  & -0.3496  & -0.8064
   \end{bmatrix}$$ The viewing direction of the camera can be obtained as $\mathbf{R}^\mathsf{T}[0, 0, 1]^\mathsf{T}$ (this is the direction of the $Z$-axis in the camera-coordinates system).  


Another potential bug when extracting the camera orientation is to use the rotation matrix instead of its inverse. We defined $\mathbf{R}^\mathsf{T}$ as the rotation needed to move the world coordinate axes to be aligned with the camera-coordinate axes.

The angle of the camera with respect to the vertically can be computed in multiple ways. Here is one: $$\begin{aligned}
\arccos \left( [0,1,0] \mathbf{R}^\mathsf{T}[0,1,0]^\mathsf{T}\right) &= \arccos (R[2,2]) \nonumber \\
&= \arccos (-0.9368) \nonumber \\
&= 20.5 \text{~degrees}
\end{aligned}$$ Here we just computed the camera $Y$-axis and then computed the dot product with a unit vector along the $Y$-axis of the world-coordinates. This angle is also quite close to the approximate value that we gave at the beginning of the section.
concepts.motivation_md: Testing the camera calibration theory with real-world measurements helps verify the accuracy and robustness of the methods.
concepts.recap_md:
- Real 3D points and their 2D image coordinates were manually measured and used.
- The DLT algorithm estimated the projection matrix with a low reprojection error.
- Intrinsic and extrinsic parameters recovered closely matched expected physical values.

concepts.title: camera projection matrix
concepts.one_liner: In the rest, we will usually refer to the camera projection matrix, which includes both intrinsic as extrinsic parameters as: $$\mathbf{M} = \mathbf{K} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R} & -\mathbf{R}\mathbf{T} \\ \mathbf{0}^T & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$
concepts.motivation_md: The camera projection matrix compactly represents both intrinsic and extrinsic parameters, simplifying the transformation from 3D world coordinates to 2D image coordinates.
concepts.recap_md:
- The camera projection matrix $\mathbf{M}$ combines intrinsic matrix $\mathbf{K}$ and extrinsic parameters $\mathbf{R}$ and $\mathbf{T}$.
- It is expressed as $\mathbf{M} = \mathbf{K} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R} & -\mathbf{R}\mathbf{T} \\ \mathbf{0}^T & 1 \end{bmatrix}$.
- This matrix is fundamental for projecting 3D points into 2D images.

concepts.title: camera projection equations for parallel projection
concepts.one_liner: In heterogeneous coordinates, the parallel projection camera equations are $x = -a X$ and $y = a \cos (\theta) Y - a\sin(\theta) Z$.
concepts.content:
The second constraint from the simple world chapter is that the origin of the world coordinates is where the camera optical axis intersects the ground plane, imposing the restriction $\tan (\theta) = h/d$. Therefore, $d \sin(\theta) - h \cos (\theta) = 0$. In heterogeneous coordinates, this results in:

$$\begin{aligned}x &= -a X\\
y &= a \cos (\theta) Y - a\sin(\theta) Z
\end{aligned}$$

These equations are similar to equation (@eq-projection) from @sec-simplesystem (with $a=1$). The difference is that $x$ has the opposite sign due to a different convention for the sign of the $x$-axis in image coordinates. This is acceptable as various books and publications use different conventions, and one should adapt formulations accordingly.
concepts.motivation_md: These equations model the parallel projection camera under specific geometric constraints, linking camera parameters to world coordinates for simplified projection.

- Parallel projection equations are $x = -a X$ and $y = a \cos (\theta) Y - a\sin(\theta) Z$.
- Sign conventions may vary across sources and should be adapted.

concepts.title: Camera Calibration
concepts.one_liner: A camera is said to be calibrated if we know the transformations relating 3D world coordinates to pixel coordinates within the camera.
concepts.content: A camera is said to be **calibrated** if we know the transformations relating 3D world coordinates to pixel coordinates within the camera. Those transformations involve two types of parameters: (1) parameters that depend on where the camera is physically located in the world, and (2) parameters that are a function of the camera itself. These two types of parameters are called extrinsic and intrinsic parameters, respectively.
concepts.motivation_md: Camera calibration is essential to determine the parameters needed to accurately map 3D world points to 2D image pixels, enabling precise computer vision and imaging tasks.
concepts.recap_md:
- Camera calibration determines transformations from 3D world to 2D pixel coordinates.
- Extrinsic parameters depend on camera location in the world.
- Intrinsic parameters depend on the camera's internal characteristics.

concepts.title: "Slow down to speed up."
concepts.one_liner: The first piece of advice can go on a bumper sticker: "Slow down to speed up."
concepts.content:
The first piece of advice can go on a bumper sticker: **"Slow down to speed up."** In classes, the world is rigged. There's a simple correct answer and the problem is structured to let you come to that answer. You get feedback with the correct answer within a day after you submit anything.

Research is different. No one tells you the right answer, and we may not know if there is a right answer. We don't know if something doesn't work because there's a silly mistake in the program or because a broad set of assumptions is flawed.

How do you deal with that? Take things slowly. Verify your assumptions. Understand the thing, whatever it is—the program, the algorithm, or the proof. As you do experiments, only change one thing at a time, so you know what the outcome of the experiment means.

It may feel like you're going slowly, but you'll be making much more progress than if you flail around, trying different things, but not understanding what's going on.

(see figure: Research advice for a bumper sticker.)
concepts.motivation_md: Research problems lack clear answers and immediate feedback, so slowing down to verify assumptions and understand each step helps avoid wasted effort and leads to more meaningful progress.
concepts.recap_md:
- "Slow down to speed up" means taking time to understand and verify assumptions in research.
- Change only one thing at a time in experiments to interpret results correctly.
- Progress feels slow but is more effective than flailing without understanding.

concepts.title: Please don't tell me "it doesn't work."
concepts.one_liner: Please don't tell me "it doesn't work."
concepts.content: **Please don't tell me "it doesn't work."** Of course, it doesn't work. If there's a single mistake in the chain, the whole thing won't work, and how could you possibly go through all those steps without making a mistake somewhere? What I want to hear instead is something like, "I've narrowed down the problem to step B. Until step A, you can see that it works because you put in X and you get Y out, as we expect. You can see how it fails here at B. I've ruled out W and Z as the cause."
concepts.motivation_md: Instead of vague failure reports, detailed diagnostics help isolate where and why a problem occurs, facilitating effective debugging and progress.
concepts.recap_md:
- Saying "it doesn't work" is unhelpful without specifics.
- Narrow down the problem to a particular step.
- Explain what works before the failure and what has been ruled out as causes.

concepts.title: "This sounds like hard work."
concepts.one_liner: "This sounds like hard work."
concepts.content:
**"This sounds like hard work."** Yes. It's no longer about being smart. By now, everyone around you is smart. In graduate school, it's the **hard workers** who pull ahead. This happens in sports, too. You always read stories about how hard the great players work, being the first ones out to practice, the last ones to leave, and so on.

A co-author, who generally works harder than I do, tells me I should add comments here about the importance of taking time off from work and maintaining a good life/work balance. That is true: you should work at a pace you can sustain, and you should refresh yourself by making time for the things that matter more than work, such as relationships, service, and relaxation. Perhaps the point is to protect your time so you will have enough time to do the research well.
concepts.motivation_md: Success depends more on sustained hard work than innate intelligence, balanced with rest and life priorities to maintain long-term productivity.
concepts.recap_md:
- Hard work, not just intelligence, drives success in graduate school.
- Great achievers often work harder and longer than others.
- Maintaining work-life balance is important for sustainable research.

concepts.title: "How do I get myself to work hard enough to do research well?"
concepts.one_liner: "How do I get myself to work hard enough to do research well?"
concepts.content: **"How do I get myself to work hard enough to do research well?"** It all plays out if you love what you're doing. You become good at it because you spend time at it and you do that because you enjoy it. So pick something to work on that you can love. If you're not the type who falls in love with a problem, then just know that working hard is what you have to do to succeed at research.
concepts.motivation_md: Loving your research motivates sustained effort and skill development; without passion, hard work remains essential for success.

- Loving your work helps you work hard and improve.
- Choose research problems you can be passionate about.
- If not passionate, recognize that hard work is still necessary.

concepts.title: The above isn't completely true.
concepts.one_liner: Beyond working hard, there's also steering.
concepts.content: **The above isn't completely true.** Beyond working hard, there's also **steering**. We're like boats. We need motors—that's the part about working hard. But we also need a rudder for steering—that means stepping back periodically to make sure we're working on the right thing. On the topic of steering, I find time management books to be very helpful. They teach you how to spend your time solving the right problems.

- Steering means stepping back to check if you're on the right path.
- Time management helps focus on solving the right problems.

concepts.title: Strategies for success.
concepts.one_liner: Strategies for success.
concepts.content:
**Strategies for success.** Here is a parable, as told by my friend Yair Weiss. There is a weak and a strong graduate student. They are both asked by their advisor to try a particular approach to solving a research problem. The weak student does exactly what the advisor has asked. But the advisor's solution fails, and the student reports that failure. The strong student starts doing what the advisor has asked, sees that it doesn't work, looks around within some epsilon ball of the original proposal to find what does work, and reports that solution.

concepts.title: only the good papers count
concepts.one_liner: Only the really good papers matter for your career.
concepts.content: Many graduate students we know feel it is important to coauthor many papers. While the number of papers a student has can be a rough measure of research productivity, it is our experience as mentors, faculty search committee members, and industrial research managers that *only the good papers count*. (We acknowledge that this is not true everywhere, and some institutions simply count papers. But you should still strive to make all your papers good!) This emphasis is shown in @fig-impact, a plot of made-up data that summarizes our impression, formed over many years, of the relationship between paper quality and its impact on one's career. Only the really good papers matter for your career. So it makes sense to learn how to write the best possible paper.
concepts.motivation_md: Focusing on producing high-quality papers rather than many mediocre ones is crucial because only good papers significantly impact your career.

concepts.title: Organization
concepts.one_liner: Start by stating the problem, then discuss other solutions, explain your own solution, and end with related work.
concepts.content:
The Ph.D. thesis advisor of two of us, Prof. Edward Adelson, wrote some good advice in response to a student's question of how to write a good paper @Adelson92:

- Start by stating which problem you are addressing, keeping the audience in mind. They must care about it, which means that sometimes you must tell them why they should care about the problem.

- Then state briefly what the other solutions are to the problem, and why they aren't satisfactory. If they were satisfactory, you wouldn't need to do the work.

- Then explain your own solution, compare it with other solutions, and say why it's better.

- At the end, talk about related work where similar techniques and experiments have been used, but applied to a different problem.

That structure fits well with a progression of section headings typical
concepts.motivation_md: Organizing a paper clearly helps readers understand the problem, existing solutions, your contribution, and related work, making your research more accessible and persuasive.
concepts.recap_md:
- Begin by stating the problem and why it matters.
- Summarize other solutions and their shortcomings.
- Explain your solution and compare it to others.
- End with related work applying similar techniques elsewhere.

concepts.title: The Paper's Introduction
concepts.one_liner: You must write a dynamite introduction that makes your paper easy to read and understand up front.
concepts.content: Regarding paper introductions, Kajiya @Kajiya1993 writes, "You must make your paper easy to read. You've got to make it easy for anyone to tell what your paper is about, what problem it solves, why the problem is interesting, what is really new in your paper (and what isn't), why it's so neat. And you must do it up front. In other words, you must write a dynamite introduction."
concepts.motivation_md: A strong introduction helps readers quickly grasp the paper's purpose, novelty, and significance, making the research accessible and engaging from the start.

- Clearly state what the paper is about and the problem it solves.
- Highlight what is new and interesting upfront.

concepts.title: Main Idea
concepts.one_liner: It can be very helpful to show a simple example that captures the main idea of the paper.
concepts.content:
When appropriate to the paper, it can be very helpful to show a simple example that captures the main idea of the paper. Here is a figure from a different paper @Simoncelli92 that conveys the main idea very simply. The paper's main idea was that wavelets lacked important desirable features for an image representation. @fig-wavelet shows the failure of a wavelet representation to form a translation invariant representation. The top row shows two versions of the same signal, differing only in a one-sample translation. The bottom three rows show the coefficients of the high-, mid-, and low-frequency bands of a wavelet representation of that signal. The figure points out in a simple way the drawback of a wavelet representation with aliased subbands that was the focus of the paper: as the signal translates, the signal representation energy moves to different frequency bands and changes form within the mid-frequency band.

(see figure: Effect of translation on the wavelet representation of a signal (caption and figure after @Simoncelli92. (a) An input signal. (b-d) The high-, mid-, and low-frequency coefficients within a wavelet...)

concepts.title: Experimental Results
concepts.one_liner: Modern standards require that assertions in a paper be backed up with experimental evidence.
concepts.content:
In earlier days of computer vision research, good ideas could be presented with only plausibility arguments to support them. However, modern standards require that assertions in a paper be backed up with experimental evidence. Readers will be expecting a table quantitatively comparing the performance of your algorithm with that of the previous state-of-the-art. If you are proposing a new task for which there aren't previous benchmarks, you should still compare with an algorithm that solves a related task, noting that the algorithm was designed for a different task.

(see figure: prototypical table of results, from \cite{Owens2016} Rows are different algorithms, or ablations of a favored algorithm. Columns are datasets or tasks, and the numbers indicate performance, with the...)
concepts.motivation_md: Experimental evidence is essential to validate claims and demonstrate the effectiveness of your algorithm compared to prior work, meeting modern research standards.
concepts.recap_md:
- Assertions must be supported by experimental evidence.
- Include quantitative comparisons with prior state-of-the-art.
- Compare with related tasks if no direct benchmarks exist.

concepts.title: How to End the Paper
concepts.one_liner: Resist the temptation to end the paper by listing unfinished work; instead, emphasize contributions and new research directions.
concepts.content:
A cautionary note on how *not* to end the paper. Conference papers are often written under deadline pressure, and there is inevitably a list of results that the authors wanted to obtain that have been left uncompleted. You should resist the temptation to describe the items that were left unfinished in a section on "Future Work." It is hard to imagine a weaker way to end the paper than to enumerate all the things the paper doesn't accomplish, providing a summary of where it falls short.

Instead, the paper can finish with a review what has been presented, emphasizing the contributions. How has the world changed, now that the reader has read this paper? What new research directions have been opened up; what can we do now that we couldn't do before?
concepts.motivation_md: Ending the paper by listing unfinished work weakens its impact; focusing on contributions and future possibilities leaves a stronger impression.
concepts.recap_md:
- Avoid ending by listing unfinished work.
- Emphasize the paper's contributions in the conclusion.
- Highlight new research directions opened by the work.

concepts.title: General Writing Tips
concepts.one_liner: Keep the reader uppermost in mind: what they know, expect next, and why.
concepts.content:
Donald Knuth, the author of the classic book series, *The Art of Computer Programming*, wrote @Knuth1989,"Perhaps the most important principle of good writing is to keep the reader uppermost in mind: What does the reader know so far? What does the reader expect next and why?"

Our mental image is that of a great host, who anticipates every need of their house guest: after you arrive, they say, "Can I take your coat? Would you like something to drink?" At every moment, they know what you might be wanting and how to help you find it.
concepts.motivation_md: Good writing anticipates the reader's knowledge and expectations, guiding them smoothly through the material like a thoughtful host.
concepts.recap_md:
- Keep the reader's knowledge and expectations in mind.
- Anticipate what the reader might want next.
- Guide the reader smoothly through the material.

concepts.title: dense optical flow
concepts.one_liner: We can model motion over time as a sequence of dense optical flow images: $$\left[ u(x,y,t), v(x,y,t) \right]$$ where $u(x,y,t)$ and $v(x,y,t)$ indicate pixel velocity at $(x,y)$ and time $t$.
concepts.content: We can model motion over time as a sequence of dense optical flow images: $$\left[ u(x,y,t), v(x,y,t) \right]$$. The quantities $u(x,y,t)$ and $v(x,y,t)$ indicate that a pixel at image coordinates $(x,y)$ at time $t$ moves with velocity $(u,v)$. The problem with this formulation is that we do not have an explicit representation of the trajectory followed by points in the scene over time. As time $t$ changes, the location $(x,y)$ might correspond to different scene elements.
concepts.motivation_md: Dense optical flow models pixel-wise motion over time, providing a detailed velocity field for each image location, which is crucial for understanding dynamic scenes.
concepts.recap_md:
- Dense optical flow represents motion as velocity vectors $(u,v)$ at each pixel $(x,y)$ over time $t$.
- It models motion as a sequence of images showing pixel velocities.
- The formulation lacks explicit trajectories for scene points over time.

key_passage.text: We can model motion over time as a sequence of **dense optical flow** images: $$\left[ u(x,y,t), v(x,y,t) \right]$$ The quantities $u(x,y,t)$and $v(x,y,t)$ indicate that a pixel at image coordinates $(x,y)$ at time $t$ moves with velocity $(u,v)$.

concepts.title: sparse set of moving points
concepts.one_liner: An alternative representation is to model motion as a sparse set of moving points (tracks): $$\left\{ \mathbf{P}^{(i)}_t \right\}_{i=1}^N$$.
concepts.content: An alternative representation is to model motion as a sparse set of moving points (tracks): $$\left\{ \mathbf{P}^{(i)}_t \right\}_{i=1}^N$$. This has the challenge that we have to establish the correspondence of the same scene point over time (tracking). The appearance of a 3D scene point will change over time due to perspective projection and other variations such as illumination changes over time. It might be difficult to do this on a dense array. Therefore, most representations of motion as sets of moving points use a sparse set of points.
concepts.motivation_md: Sparse sets of moving points simplify motion representation by tracking distinct points over time, avoiding the complexity of dense pixel-wise motion and handling appearance changes.
concepts.recap_md:
- Motion can be represented as a sparse set of moving points (tracks).
- Tracking requires establishing correspondences of scene points over time.
- Appearance changes and perspective effects complicate dense tracking, favoring sparse representations.

concepts.title: brightness constancy assumption
concepts.one_liner: The brightness constancy assumption says that as a scene element moves, the brightness captured by the camera from that element does not change over time.
concepts.content:
The brightness constancy assumption says that as a scene element moves in the world, the brightness captured by the camera from that element does not change over time. Mathematically, this assumption translates into the following relationship, given a sequence $\ell(x,y,t)$: 

$$\ell(x +u, y+v, t + 1)  = \ell(x,y,t)$$

where $u$ and $v$ are the element displacement over one unit of time and are also a function of pixel location, $u(x,y)$ and $v(x,y)$, but we will drop that dependency to simplify the notation. The previous relationship is equivalent to saying that $\ell(x, y, t + 1) = \ell(x-u,y-v,t)$. To make sure that the reader remains onboard without getting confused by the indices and how the translation works, here is a simple toy example of a translation with $(u=1, v=0)$:

(see figure: Translation to the right of a simple $6 \times 6$ size image.)

The constant brightness assumption only approximately holds in reality. For it to be exact, we should have a scene with Lambertian objects illuminated from a light source at infinity, with no occlusions, no shadows, and no interreflections. Few real scenes check any of those boxes. This equation assumes that all the pixels in $\ell(x, y, t)$ are visible in $\ell(x, y, t+1)$, but in reality, some pixels might be occluded in the first frame and new pixels might appear around the image boundaries and behind occlusions.
concepts.motivation_md: This assumption allows relating pixel intensities across frames to estimate motion, simplifying the problem by assuming brightness remains constant despite movement.
concepts.recap_md:
- Brightness constancy assumes pixel brightness does not change as scene elements move.
- Mathematically, $\ell(x +u, y+v, t + 1) = \ell(x,y,t)$ relates pixel intensities across frames.
- The assumption is approximate; real scenes have occlusions, shadows, and illumination changes.

concepts.title: Gradient-Based Optical Flow Estimation
concepts.one_liner: Gradient-based optical flow estimation uses a Taylor approximation and the brightness constancy assumption to derive a linear constraint for optical flow at each pixel.
concepts.content:
The most popular version of a gradient-based method for optical flow estimation was introduced by Lucas and Kanade in 1981 @Lucas1981.

Let's start describing the method in words, and we will see next how it translates into math. We will start by approximating the change between two consecutive frames by a linear equation using a Taylor approximation. This linear approximation combined with the constant brightness assumption will result in a linear constraint for the optical flow at each pixel. We will then derive a big system of linear equations for the entire image that, when solved, will result in an estimated optical flow for each image pixel. Let's now see, step by step, how this algorithm works.

If the motion $(u,v)$ is small in comparison to how fast the image $\ell$ changes spatially, we can use a first-order Taylor expansion of the image $\ell(x +u, y+v, t + 1)$ around $(x,y,t)$:
$$\ell(x +u, y+v, t + 1)  \simeq \ell(x,y,t) + u \ell_x  + v \ell_y + \ell_t + \mbox{h. o. t.}$$

Combining equations (@eq-constancy_brightness_assumption) and (@eq-motion_taylor), and ignoring higher order terms, we arrive at the **gradient constraint equation**: $$u \ell_x  + v \ell_y + \ell_t  = 0$$

This equation constrains the motion $(u,v)$ in location $(x,y)$ to be along a line perpendicular to the image gradient $\nabla \ell= \left( \ell_x, \ell_y \right)$ at that location. This is the same relationship that we discussed before when describing the aperture problem. This is not enough to estimate motion and we will need to add additional constraints. The second assumption that we will add is that the motion field is constant (or smoothly varying) over an extended image region. By solving for the gradient constraints over an image patch, we hope there will be only a unique velocity that will satisfy all the equations. We can implement this constraint in a different way. One simple way of implementing this constraint is by summing over a neighborhood using a weighting function $g(x,y)$. If $g(x,y)$ is a Gaussian window centered in the origin, the optical flow, $(u,v)$, at the location $(x,y)$ can be estimated by minimizing:
$$\mathcal{L}(u, v) = \sum_{x',y'} g(x'-x,y'-y) \left| u(x,y) \ell_x (x',y',t) + v(x,y) \ell_y(x',y',t) + \ell_t(x',y',t) \right| ^2$$

The previous equation is a bit cumbersome because we wanted to make explicit the spatial variables, $(x',y')$, over which the sum is being made and the factors that are function of the location $(x,y)$ at which the flow is computed. From now, to simplify the derivation, we will drop all the arguments and write the loss in a single location as:

$$
\mathcal{L}(u, v) = \sum g \left| u \ell_x  + v \ell_y + \ell_t \right| ^2
$$
where only $u$ and $v$ are constant.

The solution that minimizes this loss can be obtained by computing where the derivatives of the loss with respect to $u$ and $v$ are equal to zero: 

$$\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}(u, v)}{\partial u } =
\sum g \left( u \ell_x ^ 2 + v \ell_x \ell_y + \ell_x \ell_t  \right) = 0 \\
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}(u, v)}{\partial v } = 
\sum g \left( u \ell_x \ell_y + v \ell_y^2 + \ell_y \ell_t  \right) = 0
\end{aligned}$$

We can write the previous two equations in matrix form at each location $(x',y')$ as: 

$$\begin{bmatrix}
\sum g \ell_x ^ 2  & \sum g \ell_x \ell_y \\
\sum g \ell_x \ell_y & \sum g \ell_y ^ 2 
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
 u \\
 v
\end{bmatrix}
=
- 
\begin{bmatrix}
\sum g \ell_x \ell_t \\
\sum g \ell_y \ell_t
\end{bmatrix}
$$

We will have an equivalent set of equations for each image location. The solution at each location can be computed analytically as $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{A}^{-1} \textbf{b}$ where $\mathbf{A}$ is the $2 \times 2$ matrix of equation (@eq-lk). The motion at location $x,y$ will only be uniquely defined if we can compute the inverse of $\mathbf{A}$. Note that the matrix $\mathbf{A}$ is a function of the image structure around location $(x,y)$. If the rank of the matrix is 1, we can not compute the inverse and the optical flow will be constrained along a 1D line, this is the aperture problem. This will happen if the image structure is 1D inside the region of analysis that will be defined by the size of the Gaussian window $g(x,y)$.

In order to implement this approach we can make use of convolutions in order to compute all the quantities efficiently in a compact algorithm @alg-gradient_algorithm:

- Assumes motion is constant over a local region to solve for $(u,v)$.
- Solves a weighted least squares problem using image gradients and Gaussian window $g(x,y)$.

concepts.title: Iterative Refinement for Optical Flow
concepts.one_liner: Iterative refinement improves optical flow estimates by minimizing photometric reconstruction error over multiple scales.
concepts.content:
The gradient-based approach is efficient but it only provides an approximation to the motion field because it ignores higher order terms in the Taylor expansion in equation (@eq-motion_taylor). A different approach consists of directly minimizing the photometric reconstruction error:
$$L(\boldsymbol\ell_1,\boldsymbol\ell_2,\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v})= 
\sum_{x,y} \left| \ell_1 (x+u,y+v,t+1) - \ell_2 (x,y,t)) \right| ^2$$

We can now run gradient descent on this loss. Running only one iteration would be similar to the gradient-based optical flow algorithm described in the previous section. However, adding iterations will provide a more accurate estimate of optical flow. At each iteration $n$, the estimated optical flow will be used to compute the warped frame $\ell_1 (x+u_n,y+v_n,t+1)$ and we will compute an update, $\Delta u_n$ and $\Delta v_n$, of the optical flow: $u_{n+1} = u_n+\Delta u_n$ and $v_{n+1}= v_n + \Delta v_n$. To improve the results, the optical flow estimation is done on a Gaussian pyramid. First, we run a few iterations on the lowest resolution scale of the pyramid (where the motion will be the smallest). The estimated motion is then upsampled and used as initialization at the next level. We iterate this process until arriving at the highest possible resolution. This process is shown in @fig-multiscale_iterative_optical_flow.

(see figure: Multiscale iterative refinement for optical flow. Optical flow estimation is done on a Gaussian pyramid. (left) First, we run a few iterations on the lowest resolution scale of the pyramid (where the...)

@fig-comparison_gradient_vs_iterative compares the optical flow computed using the gradient-based algorithm (i.e., one iteration) and the multiscale iterative refinement approach. Note how the gradient-based approach underestimates the motion of the left car. The displacement between consecutive frames is close to four pixels and that makes the first-order Taylor approximation very poor. The multiscale method is capable of estimating large displacements.

(see figure: Comparison between the optical flow estimated using the gradient-based algorithm and the multiscale iterative refinement approach.)

- Updates optical flow iteratively: $u_{n+1} = u_n + \Delta u_n$, $v_{n+1} = v_n + \Delta v_n$.
- Uses a Gaussian pyramid to handle large displacements progressively.

A different approach consists of directly minimizing the **photometric reconstruction** error:
$$L(\boldsymbol\ell_1,\boldsymbol\ell_2,\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v})= \sum_{x,y} \left| \ell_1 (x+u,y+v,t+1) - \ell_2 (x,y,t)) \right| ^2$$ We can now run gradient descent on this loss. Running only one iteration would be similar to the gradient-based optical flow algorithm described in the previous section. However, adding iterations will provide a more accurate estimate of optical flow. At each iteration $n$, the estimated optical flow will be used to compute the warped frame $\ell_1 (x+u_n,y+v_n,t+1)$ and we will compute an update, $\Delta u_n$ and $\Delta v_n$, of the optical flow: $u_{n+1} = u_n+\Delta u_n$ and $v_{n+1}= v_n + \Delta v_n$.

concepts.title: slow prior
concepts.one_liner: A slow prior penalizes large velocities by regularizing the sum of squared velocity components.
concepts.content:
There are several popular regularization terms. One penalizes large velocities (slow prior): 

$$
R(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = 
\sum_{x,y} \left( u(x,y) \right)^2 +
\left( v(x,y)  \right)^2
$$

- Encourages smooth, realistic motion estimates.

concepts.title: Parameter setting heuristics for recovering world coordinates
concepts.one_liner: To apply the world coordinate recovery equation, we set parameters $d_0=0$, $n_0=N/2$, $m_0=M/2$, $a=N$, and $	heta=\pi/4$ as heuristics.
concepts.content:
In order to apply the equation for recovering world coordinates, we need to define certain parameters: $d_0$, $n_0$, $m_0$, $a$, and $\theta$. Although these parameters could be determined using a calibration image, we opt for a simpler heuristic approach:

- $d_0$: Set to 0.

- $n_0$, $m_0$: Define the camera center point, where $n_0 = N/2$ and $m_0 = M/2$, with $N \times M$ as the input image size.

- $a$: Accounts for image size and camera focal length; a standard setting is $a = N$, where $N$ is the image width.

- $\theta$: Represents the angle between the optical camera axis and the ground plane. Although it could be estimated accurately by measuring the surface normal direction in pixels corresponding to the ground, we simply set $\theta = \pi / 4$, approximately the angle at which the pictures were taken.

Now we are ready to use the world coordinate recovery equation and the output.
concepts.motivation_md: Setting these parameters heuristically allows applying the world coordinate recovery without complex calibration, simplifying the 3D reconstruction process.

- Parameters $d_0$, $n_0$, $m_0$, $a$, and $\theta$ must be set to recover world coordinates.
- $d_0=0$, $n_0=N/2$, $m_0=M/2$, $a=N$, $\theta=\pi/4$ are heuristic choices.
- These simplify applying the recovery equation without calibration.

concepts.title: From 2D Images to 3D
concepts.one_liner: Apply a neural network to an input image to obtain disparity and transform it into world coordinates for 3D reconstruction without detecting edges or features.
concepts.content:
Let's start running the model on the same input image used as a running example in the simple system section. We apply the neural network to the input image, obtain the output disparity, and transform the disparity into world coordinates. We do not need to detect edges or other features computed previously; instead, the neural network has learned to compute whatever features it deems necessary to solve the task. We will not retrain the network using images from our simple visual world.

Just as before, to show that the algorithm for 3D interpretation gives reasonable results, we can re-render the inferred 3D structure from different viewpoints.

(see figure: 3D reconstruction using a pretrained model. The images show multiple view points of the reconstructed 3D scene from @fig-simplesystem_revisited_img1)

It is remarkable that it works somewhat well even though this system was trained with natural images, which differ from our simple world. However, errors remain: the ground is not recovered as a flat surface but appears concave; cubes' edges are not straight and faces are twisted instead of flat.

We can compare this result with the 3D images recovered using the algorithm defined in the simple system section:

(see figure: 3D reconstruction using the simple visual system from @sec-simplesystem)

While the learned-based model may lose accuracy in this example fitting our simple world assumptions, it gains robustness and generalization. The following figure compares results from MiDaS (learning-based) and the simple world model (hand-crafted).
concepts.motivation_md: This approach demonstrates how neural networks can infer 3D structure from 2D images without manual feature detection, enabling more robust and generalizable 3D reconstruction.

- Neural networks can infer disparity from 2D images without explicit feature detection.
- Disparity is transformed into world coordinates for 3D reconstruction.
- Learned models trade some accuracy for robustness and generalization.

concepts.title: A Simple Vision System---Revisited
concepts.one_liner: Hand-crafted vision systems produce beautiful results under ideal conditions but are fragile, while learning-based approaches yield good quality results more robustly.
concepts.content: When images fit the assumptions of the world model, the hand-crafted approach can produce beautiful results. However, it is very fragile; poor illumination can break edge detectors, causing a cascade of errors that propagate to the output. Conversely, the learning-based approach produces results of good (although never perfect) quality regardless of conditions. The hand-crafted approach completely fails even with small scene changes, such as changing the ground plane from white to black.
concepts.motivation_md: Comparing these approaches highlights the trade-off between accuracy under ideal conditions and robustness to real-world variability.
concepts.recap_md:
- Hand-crafted vision systems work well when assumptions hold.
- They are fragile and sensitive to illumination changes.
- Learning-based approaches are more robust but not perfect.

Another option is to use GPT4-v to interpret the scene. GPT4-v can take images as inputs and allows asking questions about them. The figure shows the result of asking GPT4-v to describe a simple world image.

concepts.title: unsolved solved computer vision problems
concepts.one_liner: Some computer vision problems seem solved but often are illusions; for every solved problem, many unsolved ones remain.
concepts.content: Computer vision is making amazing progress, but beware of the unsolved solved computer vision problems. For some vision tasks, it might appear as if one method perfectly resolves the task or that foundational problems are solved. It might seem impossible to make progress on certain questions. But more often than not, this is an illusion, and the solved problem was not really solved at all. Even when a problem was genuinely solved (and probably is not), remember that for every solved problem, many unsolved problems lurk in the background.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept reminds us to remain cautious about claims of solved problems and to recognize ongoing challenges in computer vision.
concepts.recap_md:
- Some vision problems appear solved but often are not.
- Progress can seem stalled but usually is not.
- Many unsolved problems remain behind solved ones.

concepts.title: Vanishing Point
concepts.one_liner: As time goes to infinity, the projected point converges to a vanishing point given by $\lim_{t \to \infty} x(t) = f \frac{V_X}{V_Z}$ and $\lim_{t \to \infty} y(t) = f \frac{V_Y}{V_Z}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the vanishing point helps explain how points moving in 3D project onto 2D images and how their projections behave over time, especially for points moving towards or away from the camera.
concepts.recap_md:
- A 3D point moving with velocity $\dot{\mathbf{P}} = (V_X, V_Y, V_Z)^\mathsf{T}$ projects to 2D coordinates $x(t), y(t)$.
- If $V_Z \neq 0$, the 2D projection converges to a vanishing point as $t \to \infty$.
- The vanishing point coordinates are $x_\infty = f \frac{V_X}{V_Z}$ and $y_\infty = f \frac{V_Y}{V_Z}$.

concepts.title: Camera Translation Motion Field
concepts.one_liner: For a camera moving with velocity $\mathbf{V} = (V_X,V_Y,V_Z)^\mathsf{T}$, the 2D motion field is given by $\begin{bmatrix}\dot{x} \\ \dot{y}\end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{Z} \begin{bmatrix}-f & 0 & x \\ 0 & -f & y  \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}V_X\\ V_Y \\ V_Z \end{bmatrix}$.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept models how the camera's translation causes apparent motion in the image, crucial for understanding motion fields in computer vision.
concepts.recap_md:
- Camera translation velocity is $\mathbf{V} = (V_X,V_Y,V_Z)^\mathsf{T}$.
- Scene points move relative to camera with velocity $-\mathbf{V}$.
- The 2D motion field is $\frac{1}{Z} \begin{bmatrix}-f & 0 & x \\ 0 & -f & y \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{V}$.

key_passage.text: Let's now assume that the scene is static and that only the camera is moving. In this case, all the observed motion in the image will be due to the motion of the camera.

motivation.text: Let's now assume that the scene is static and that only the camera is moving. In this case, all the observed motion in the image will be due to the motion of the camera.

example.text:
Let's assume the camera is moving in a straight line with a velocity
$\dot{\mathbf{T}} = \mathbf{V} = (V_X,V_Y,V_Z)^\mathsf{T}$. The
translation of the camera after time $t$ will be
$\mathbf{T} = \mathbf{V} t$. A point in space
$\mathbf{P} = (X,Y,Z)^\mathsf{T}$, will move with velocity, relative to
the camera, equal to $\dot{\mathbf{P}} = -\mathbf{V}$. The moving camera
is equivalent to the case where all the scene points move relative to
the camera with the same velocity.

concepts.title: Camera Translation Motion Field Explicit Form
concepts.one_liner: The 2D motion field can be expressed explicitly as $\begin{bmatrix}\dot{x} \\ \dot{y}\end{bmatrix} = -\frac{f}{Z} \begin{bmatrix}V_X\\ V_Y \end{bmatrix} + \frac{V_Z}{Z} \begin{bmatrix}x\\ y \end{bmatrix}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Expressing the motion field explicitly clarifies how lateral and forward components of camera velocity contribute separately to image motion.
concepts.recap_md:
- The 2D motion field splits into lateral and forward components.
- Lateral motion term: $-\frac{f}{Z} \begin{bmatrix}V_X \\ V_Y \end{bmatrix}$.
- Forward motion term: $\frac{V_Z}{Z} \begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \end{bmatrix}$.

concepts.title: Lateral Camera Motion
concepts.one_liner: Under lateral camera motion with zero forward velocity ($V_Z=0$), the apparent velocity of a 3D point's projection is $\begin{bmatrix}\dot{x} \\ \dot{y}\end{bmatrix} = -\frac{f}{Z} \begin{bmatrix} V_X \\ V_Y  \end{bmatrix}$.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains how lateral camera movement affects the apparent motion of scene points in the image, important for understanding motion parallax.
concepts.recap_md:
- Lateral camera motion means $V_Z=0$.
- The apparent image velocity is $-\frac{f}{Z} \begin{bmatrix} V_X \\ V_Y \end{bmatrix}$.
- This models motion seen through a side window of a moving car.

concepts.title: Parallax Effect in Lateral Camera Motion
concepts.one_liner: Objects close to the camera appear to move faster than distant objects under lateral camera motion, illustrating the parallax effect used to recover depth.

The motion field depends on the depth at each location $Z$ as illustrated in the lateral camera translation flow figure. Objects close to the camera appear to move faster than objects farther away. Objects that are very far will appear as not moving. This parallax effect is the same one used in stereo vision to recover depth. The 2D motion in the image plane is in the opposite direction to the camera motion.

concepts.recap_md:

- Closer objects appear to move faster than distant ones.
- Far objects appear stationary, illustrating parallax used for depth recovery.

concepts.title: Camera Forward Motion and Focus of Expansion
concepts.one_liner: For forward camera motion with $V_X=V_Y=0$, the motion field is $\begin{bmatrix}\dot{x} \\ \dot{y}\end{bmatrix} = \frac{V_Z}{Z} \begin{bmatrix}x \\ y  \end{bmatrix}$, defining the focus of expansion.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept describes how forward camera motion causes image points to appear to expand from a focus of expansion, important for motion analysis.
concepts.recap_md:
- Forward camera motion means $V_X=V_Y=0$, $V_Z \neq 0$.
- The motion field is proportional to $\frac{V_Z}{Z} \begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \end{bmatrix}$.
- This defines the focus of expansion in the image.

concepts.title: Time to Contact
concepts.one_liner: The observed motion depends on the ratio $V_Z/Z$, the inverse of the time to contact, which is the time for the camera to reach an object at distance $Z$ moving at velocity $V_Z$.
concepts.content: Equation (@eq-motion_projection_focus_expansion) provides insights: the rate of expansion does not depend on the focal length $f$, and the observed motion depends only on the ratio $V_Z/Z$, which is the inverse of the time to contact. The time to contact, $Z/V_Z$, is the time it will take the camera to reach the object located at distance $Z$ when moving at velocity $V_Z$.
concepts.motivation_md: Time to contact quantifies how soon the camera will reach an object, linking image motion to real-world distances and speeds, crucial for navigation and collision avoidance.
concepts.recap_md:
- Rate of expansion is independent of focal length $f$.
- Observed motion depends on $V_Z/Z$, the inverse time to contact.
- Time to contact is the time for the camera to reach an object at distance $Z$.

concepts.title: Motion Field for Arbitrary Camera Translation
concepts.one_liner: For arbitrary camera translation, the motion field is $\begin{bmatrix}\dot{x} \\ \dot{y}\end{bmatrix} = \frac{V_Z}{Z} \begin{bmatrix}x - x_{\infty} \\ y - y_{\infty} \end{bmatrix}$.
concepts.motivation_md: This general formula describes the image motion field for any camera translation direction, relating motion to the vanishing point and depth.
concepts.recap_md:
- Camera translation velocity components $V_X, V_Y, V_Z$ are arbitrary.
- Motion field depends on $\frac{V_Z}{Z}$ and displacement from vanishing point.
- Motion field is $\frac{V_Z}{Z} \begin{bmatrix}x - x_{\infty} \\ y - y_{\infty} \end{bmatrix}$.

concepts.title: Focus of Expansion
concepts.one_liner: The observed motion is zero at the focus of expansion, $(x_{\infty}, y_{\infty})$.
concepts.content: The observed motion is zero at the **focus of expansion**, $(x_{\infty}, y_{\infty})$.
concepts.motivation_md: The focus of expansion identifies the point in the image where motion appears stationary, helping to understand motion patterns in visual scenes.
concepts.recap_md:
- The focus of expansion is the point where observed motion is zero.
- Denoted as $(x_{\infty}, y_{\infty})$.
- It is a key concept in analyzing motion fields.

key_passage.text: The observed motion is zero at the **focus of expansion**, $(x_{\infty}, y_{\infty})$.

concepts.title: Camera Rotation Motion Model
concepts.one_liner: The camera motion field for small motions is given by $\mathbf{P}_{t+\Delta t} = - \mathbf{T}_{\Delta t} + \mathbf{R}_{\Delta t} \mathbf{P}_t$.
concepts.content:
Let's consider a general camera motion undergoing both translation and rotation. To compute the motion field with a compact expression, we will do a number of simplifications assuming a small motion between consecutive frames. After a small time interval, $\Delta t$, the camera will move, generating a displacement in the points with respect to the camera coordinate system equal to:

$$\mathbf{P}_{t+\Delta t} = - \mathbf{T}_{\Delta t}  + \mathbf{R}_{\Delta t} \mathbf{P}_t
$$
where $\mathbf{T}_{\Delta t}$ is the camera translation and $\mathbf{R}_{\Delta t}$ is the camera rotation that took place over that time interval, $\Delta t$. The velocity of a 3D point with respect to the camera will be:
$$
\dot{\mathbf{P}} = \frac{\mathbf{P}_{t+\Delta t} - \mathbf{P}_{t}}{\Delta t} = - \mathbf{V} + \frac{\mathbf{R}_{\Delta t} -\mathbf{I}}{\Delta t} \mathbf{P}_t
$$
concepts.motivation_md: This model describes how points move relative to the camera when it undergoes both translation and rotation, essential for understanding motion fields in video sequences.
concepts.recap_md:
- Camera motion combines translation $\mathbf{T}_{\Delta t}$ and rotation $\mathbf{R}_{\Delta t}$.
- Point displacement: $\mathbf{P}_{t+\Delta t} = - \mathbf{T}_{\Delta t} + \mathbf{R}_{\Delta t} \mathbf{P}_t$.
- Velocity is the difference quotient of point positions over $\Delta t$.

concepts.title: Euler Angles for Camera Rotation
concepts.one_liner: The rotation matrix can be decomposed using Euler angles (yaw, pitch, roll) as rotations along the three axes.
concepts.motivation_md: Euler angles provide a systematic way to represent 3D rotations by decomposing them into rotations about the principal axes, simplifying rotation matrix construction.
concepts.recap_md:
- Euler angles represent rotation as yaw, pitch, and roll.
- Rotation matrix is a product of three axis rotations.
- Each angle corresponds to rotation about a camera-coordinate axis.

key_passage.text: To derive the rotation, we consider the **Euler angles** and decompose the rotation using rotations along the three axes (yaw, pitch, roll): Each angle measures the rotation along the camera-coordinate axes. Using this representation of the rotation, the rotation matrix can be written as: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{R}_{\Delta t} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos \theta_Z & \sin \theta_Z & 0\\ -\sin \theta_Z & \cos \theta_Z & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \cos \theta_Y & 0 & -\sin \theta_Y\\ 0 & 1 & 0\\ \sin \theta_Y & 0 & \cos \theta_Y \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & \cos \theta_X & \sin \theta_X \\ 0 & -\sin \theta_X & \cos \theta_X \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned} $$

concepts.title: Small Angle Approximation for Rotation Matrix
concepts.one_liner: For small angles, $\cos \alpha \approx 1$ and $\sin \alpha \approx \alpha$, simplifying the rotation matrix.
concepts.motivation_md: Approximating trigonometric functions for small angles simplifies rotation matrices, making calculations more tractable for small camera motions.
concepts.recap_md:
- For small angles, $\cos \alpha \approx 1$ and $\sin \alpha \approx \alpha$.
- Second-order terms like $\sin \alpha \sin \beta$ are approximated as zero.
- Rotation matrix simplifies to a linear form in $\theta_X, \theta_Y, \theta_Z$.

key_passage.text: For a small $\Delta t$, the angles will be small, and we can approximate the trigonometric functions, $\cos$ and $\sin$, by $\cos \alpha \approx 1$ and $\sin \alpha \approx \alpha$. We can also approximate the product $\sin \alpha \sin \beta \approx 0$ as it will result in a second-order term.

motivation.text: For a small $\Delta t$, the angles will be small, and we can approximate the trigonometric functions, $\cos$ and $\sin$, by $\cos \alpha \approx 1$ and $\sin \alpha \approx \alpha$.

concepts.title: Cross Product Matrix Form for Rotation
concepts.one_liner: The rotation-induced displacement can be expressed as a cross product matrix form: $\mathbf{P}_{t+\Delta t} - \mathbf{P}_t = - \mathbf{T}_{\Delta t} - \boldsymbol{\theta} \times \mathbf{P}_t$.
concepts.content:
$$\mathbf{P}_{t+\Delta t} - \mathbf{P}_{t} = - \mathbf{T}_{\Delta t} + (\mathbf{R}_{\Delta t} - \mathbf{I}) \mathbf{P}_t = 
- \mathbf{T}_{\Delta t} - 
\begin{bmatrix}
0 &  -\theta_Z & \theta_Y\\
\theta_Z & 0 &  -\theta_X \\
-\theta_Y &  \theta_X &  0 
\end{bmatrix}
\mathbf{P}_t$$ 

The last term corresponds to the cross product in matrix form (note that we changed the sign of the matrix to make the cross product form more obvious). Therefore, we can rewrite the previous expression as: 

$$\mathbf{P}_{t+\Delta t} - \mathbf{P}_{t} = 
- \mathbf{T}_{\Delta t} - \boldsymbol{\theta} \times \mathbf{P}_t
$$

where
concepts.motivation_md: Expressing rotation displacement as a cross product matrix form simplifies the representation and computation of 3D point motions due to rotation.
concepts.recap_md:
- Rotation displacement can be written as $- \mathbf{T}_{\Delta t} - \boldsymbol{\theta} \times \mathbf{P}_t$.
- The cross product matrix is antisymmetric.
- This form clarifies the effect of rotation on point displacement.

key_passage.text:
The last term corresponds to the cross product in matrix form (note that we changed the sign of the matrix to make the cross product form more obvious). Therefore, we can rewrite the previous expression as: $$\mathbf{P}_{t+\Delta t} - \mathbf{P}_{t} = \mathbf{T}_{\Delta t} - \boldsymbol{\theta} \times \mathbf{P}_t
$$

concepts.title: Angular Velocity and 3D Point Motion
concepts.one_liner: The velocity of a 3D point is $\dot{\mathbf{P}} = - \mathbf{V} - \mathbf{W} \times \mathbf{P}_t$.
concepts.content:
$$\dot{\mathbf{P}} = - \mathbf{V} - \mathbf{W} \times \mathbf{P}_t =
-\begin{bmatrix}
V_X\\
V_Y \\
V_Z 
\end{bmatrix}
-
\begin{bmatrix}
-W_Z Y + W_Y Z\\
W_Z X - W_X Z \\
-W_Y X + W_X Y 
\end{bmatrix}$$
concepts.motivation_md: This formula relates the 3D point velocity to the camera's translational velocity and angular velocity, essential for modeling motion in 3D space.
concepts.recap_md:
- 3D point velocity: $\dot{\mathbf{P}} = - \mathbf{V} - \mathbf{W} \times \mathbf{P}_t$.
- $\mathbf{V}$ is translational velocity vector.
- $\mathbf{W}$ is angular velocity vector.

concepts.title: 2D Motion Field from Camera Translation and Rotation
concepts.one_liner: The 2D motion field from camera translation and rotation is given by a formula involving $\mathbf{V}$ and $\mathbf{W}$ and image coordinates.
concepts.motivation_md: This formula models how 3D camera motion translates into 2D image motion, combining translation and rotation effects on image points.
concepts.recap_md:
- 2D motion field depends on camera translation $\mathbf{V}$ and rotation $\mathbf{W}$.
- Uses image coordinates $x,y$ and depth $Z$.
- Expressed as a matrix equation combining translation and rotation terms.

concepts.title: 2D Motion Field for Camera Rotation Only
concepts.one_liner: The 2D motion field for camera rotation only is given by a matrix expression involving $\mathbf{W}$ and image coordinates.
concepts.motivation_md: Focusing on rotation-only motion isolates the rotational component's effect on the 2D image motion field, simplifying analysis.
concepts.recap_md:
- When $\mathbf{V}=0$, motion field depends only on rotation $\mathbf{W}$.
- 2D motion field is given by a matrix times $\mathbf{W}$.
- Uses image coordinates $x,y$ and focal length $f$.

motivation.text: In the previous section we saw what happens when there is no rotation; now we can focus on the case when there is only camera rotation, that is $V_X=V_Y=V_Z=0$,

concepts.title: Very Short Talks (2 -- 10 minutes)
concepts.one_liner: Short talks are often advertisements, designed to persuade the listener to read your paper, or to listen to a longer version of the talk.
concepts.content:
Short talks are often advertisements, designed to persuade the listener to read your paper, or to listen to a longer version of the talk. Rather than trying to convey many details about your work, you should aim to have the audience remember the main idea behind your work, and to share your excitement about the work.

For five minute talks describing students' final project class presentations, we suggest that the students cover these points:

1.  What problem did you address?

2.  Why is it interesting?

3.  Why is it hard?

4.  What was the key to your approach?

5.  How well did it work?

That structure can be used for other short talks, too. For very short
concepts.motivation_md: Short talks exist to quickly convey the main idea and excitement about your work, persuading listeners to engage further without overwhelming them with details.
concepts.recap_md:
- Short talks aim to persuade listeners to explore your work further.
- Focus on the main idea and your enthusiasm.
- Cover problem, interest, difficulty, approach, and results in about five minutes.

concepts.title: Preparation
concepts.one_liner: We believe the keys to both a good talk and to overcoming nerves are the same: prepare and practice.
concepts.content:
(see figure: The key to a good talk: preparation and practice.)

We believe the keys to both a good talk and to overcoming nerves are the same: prepare and practice. Think through your talk. It's almost always better to give a talk from notes than to read it from a script--the audience feels you're speaking to them so it's easier for them to pay attention. But for people giving a talk in a language that they are not comfortable with, writing out a script ahead of time may be a better solution. There may be parts of the talk that you feel are difficult to get through. For those parts, even for a native speaker, it may help to write out what you plan to say. When you give the talk, you may ignore the script, but having written it out once will make it easier to say.

Think through the talk and find the story--how one part relates to the next. If you can't find that story, you may want to reorder the presentation to create a good story.

When you can, you should visit the room you'll be speaking in to identify any issues that may come up. Will you be blocking anyone as you stand at the lectern to give the talk? Will there be someone there to help you set up? You should decide how to position yourself so that you can see your presentation, and also engage well with the audience.
concepts.motivation_md: Preparation and practice help deliver a clear, engaging talk and reduce nervousness by familiarizing you with your material and environment.
concepts.recap_md:
- Prepare and practice to improve your talk and reduce nerves.
- Use notes rather than a script unless language comfort is an issue.
- Visit the speaking room beforehand to plan your setup and engagement.
