concepts.title: Nervousness
concepts.one_liner: A great cure for nervousness is to practice the talk aloud.
concepts.content:
One of us writes, "I used to be a nervous public speaker. I still find the hours before giving a presentation to be stressful. I'm always reviewing my talk to try to improve it or to track down the answers to questions I think someone might ask me. The more I prepare, and the better I know the lecture material, the less stressed I am."

A great cure for nervousness is to practice the talk aloud. Practice by yourself. Practice in front of your friends.

One approach @Hoogterp to calming nervousness is to remind yourself, "Get over it. They're not there to see you, they're there to hear the information. Just convey the information to them."

Some find this quote, attributed to Dr. Rob Gilbert @Gilbert, to be helpful: "It's all right to have butterflies in your stomach. Your job is to get them to fly in formation."
concepts.motivation_md: Nervousness can hinder public speaking, but practicing aloud and adopting calming mental strategies help speakers gain confidence and focus on conveying information.
concepts.recap_md:
- Nervousness is common but decreases with preparation.
- Practice aloud alone and with friends to build confidence.
- Use mental reminders to focus on sharing information, not on yourself.

concepts.title: Your Distracted Audience
concepts.one_liner: Before giving a talk, your mental image of the audience may be of many people, listening to your every word.
concepts.content: Before giving a talk, your mental image of the audience may be of many people, listening to your every word. In reality, on most every speaking situation, your audience is a collection of people who are checking their social media or email, looking on their laptops for other talks to attend, or are hungry or fidgety. How does one speak to such an audience? We have to practise and prepare in order to engage the audience.
concepts.motivation_md: Speakers must recognize that audiences are often distracted and prepare strategies to engage them effectively during talks.
concepts.recap_md:
- Audiences are often distracted by devices or other concerns.
- Expect less than full attention during talks.
- Practice and preparation help engage distracted listeners.

concepts.title: Ways to Engage the Audience
concepts.one_liner: The answer, of course, is to ask them questions.
concepts.content:
In the middle of Patrick Winston's talk about public speaking @WinstonSpeaks, he asks the audience the question, "Can you think of a technique to get the audience more engaged in the talk?" The answer, of course, is to ask them questions.

Bill Hoogterp @Hoogterp expands on that: "The audience is like a sheep dog, always wanting to be working. Give the audience something to work on while they're listening to you. 'Four' pushes people back, while 'two plus two' draws them in." You might pose a sub-problem to them that you had to address in your work, to get them thinking about how to solve that problem. Then they'll be more receptive to hear your solution.
concepts.motivation_md: Engaging the audience by asking questions keeps them mentally active and attentive during a talk.
concepts.recap_md:
- Asking questions is an effective way to engage the audience.
- Give the audience something to think about while listening.
- Pose sub-problems to draw listeners into your presentation.

concepts.title: Layer Your Talk
concepts.one_liner: It's often easier for the audience to listen to your talk if you layer it—provide verbal cues for new concepts and transitions between sections of the talk.
concepts.content:
### Layer Your Talk

It's often easier for the audience to listen to your talk if you layer it---provide verbal cues for new concepts and transitions between sections of the talk. This helps even the attentive listener to follow the structure of your talk. It keeps the distracted listener from being completely lost. The distracted listener, only listening for the verbal headings of your talk, may hear, "The probability of an observation has three terms to it. $ blah blah blah blah $ So that gives us the objective function we want to optimize. Now, how do we find the optimal value? There are two approaches you can take. $ blah blah blah blah So now, with these tools in hand, we can apply this methods to real images. $ blah blah blah blah $" Your verbal cues can help even a distracted listener follow your main points.

You can also make your talk easier to follow if you add verbal dynamics---variations in speed or intensity. Find a part of the talk that is particularly special to you and let that show through. One of us writes, "When I gave talks about image deblurring, I would emphasize one aspect that I particularly enjoy: 'I love this problem; it's beautifully underdetermined. There are many ways we can explain a blurry image. It could be that that's what was there in the world--- we took a sharp picture of a world that happened to look blurry. Or we took a blurred image of a sharp world.' " The audience loves to watch you be excited about something!
concepts.motivation_md: Layering your talk with verbal cues and dynamics helps all listeners follow your main points, especially those who are distracted.
concepts.recap_md:
- Use verbal cues to signal new concepts and transitions.
- Layering helps both attentive and distracted listeners.
- Add verbal dynamics to convey your enthusiasm.

concepts.title: People Like to See a Good Fight
concepts.one_liner: The audience loves to watch a good fight.
concepts.content:
As described by @Adelson95, the audience loves to watch a good fight. You can set up a fight between two competing conjectures. For example, you might say, "The flat earth theory predicts that ships will appear on the horizon as small versions of the complete ship. Under that theory, you’d expect approaching ships to appear as in @fig-boats-a. Conversely, the round earth theory predicts that the top of the sails will appear first, then gradually the rest of the ship below it, resulting in approaching ships looking as in @fig-boats-b. The audience waits with anticipation as you show them the result from your experiment, @fig-boats-c, thus revealing the winning theory."


(see figure: The appearance of ships approaching a port, from the flat-earth theory.)

(see figure: Their appearance as predicted by the round-earth theory.)

(see figure: The experimental evidence: a photograph of ships approaching a port.)

Fig (a) The appearance of ships approaching a port, from the flat-earth theory. (b) Their appearance as predicted by the round-earth theory. (c) The experimental evidence: a photograph of ships approaching a port @mnsomero
concepts.motivation_md: Setting up a conflict between competing theories engages the audience by creating anticipation for the resolution.
concepts.recap_md:
- Audiences enjoy seeing a 'good fight' between competing ideas.
- Present contrasting predictions to build suspense.
- Reveal experimental evidence to show which theory wins.

concepts.title: Show Yourself to the Audience
concepts.one_liner: An audience wants a technical talk to make sense, teach a few things, and connect with the speaker's excitement for the topic.
concepts.content:
In a lovely video, the actor Alan Alda describes the importance of connecting with the audience in scientific presentations @AlanAlda. Alda noted the improvement in scientific speaking of volunteers after they engaged in improvisational theater exercises. After the exercises, the volunteers were primed to engage and connect with others, and their scientific talks sparkled.

Here's what we think an audience wants from a technical talk: (a) To have one part follow from another and make sense. (b) To learn a few things. (c) To connect with the speaker, to share their excitement for the topic. They want to watch you love something!
concepts.motivation_md: Connecting with the audience makes technical talks more engaging and effective, helping listeners follow the talk, learn, and share the speaker's enthusiasm. This improves communication and impact.
concepts.recap_md:
- Audiences want talks that logically flow and make sense.
- They want to learn a few things during the talk.
- They want to connect with the speaker's excitement for the topic.

concepts.title: How to End the Talk
concepts.one_liner: Better to close a talk with "Thank you." so the audience knows when to applaud, then ask for questions.
concepts.content:
How should you end your talk? A common, but awkward, way is to end by asking, "Are there any questions?" The audience wants to clap at the end of a talk, but with that ending, they don't know whether to applaud or to ask a question, and they're likely to give only scattered applause @Adelson95. Better is to close with "Thank you." The audience then knows it's their time to applaud, and they will. Then you can ask for questions.

We note that Patrick Winston disagrees with ending a talk with "thank you" @WinstonSpeaks. He didn't like the implication that the audience was doing you some favor for attending your talk, and preferred to remind the audience of how he has kept his earlier promise to them regarding what they would learn after they listened to his talk.
concepts.motivation_md: Ending a talk clearly signals to the audience when to applaud and when to ask questions, avoiding awkward pauses and scattered applause.
concepts.recap_md:
- Ending with "Are there any questions?" can confuse the audience.
- Closing with "Thank you." signals the audience to applaud.
- Some prefer reminding the audience of the talk's promise instead of "thank you."

Follow-up with the references in this chapter to find the collection of talk tips that works best for you. Preparation and rehearsal are the best cures we know of for nervousness about giving a talk.

- Show your enjoyment of the topic to the audience.

concepts.title: A Simple Neural Network
concepts.one_liner: From a user's perspective, a neural network trained end-to-end for 3D perception is just a function call.
concepts.content:
When we introduced the simple world in chapter @sec-simplesystem, our goal was to recover the three-dimensional (3D) structure of the scene from a single image (@fig-simplesystem_revisited_img1).

(see figure: Image from the simple world.)

We derived an algorithm to recover the 3D scene structure from first principles: we started studying the image formation process, then reasoned where the information might be preserved, how to build a representation that makes the information explicit, and finally how to integrate all the evidence left in the image in order to recover the 3D information that was lost during the image formation process.

In this chapter, we will instead download a pretrained model that has been trained to solve the 3D perception problem from single images. The current state of the art is MiDaS @Ranftl2021, @Ranftl2022. The system is a neural network trained end-to-end using a diverse set of real images that had ground truth depth information and also using stereo images.

Maybe the neural net is not so simple, but at the end, from a user's perspective, it is just a function call. Before running the system out of the box, it is worth understanding how it was trained, what the output means, and how it can be adapted to our task.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding a pretrained neural network for 3D perception helps us apply it effectively and adapt its outputs to our needs.
concepts.recap_md:
- The goal is to recover 3D structure from a single image.
- Earlier, an algorithm was derived from first principles.
- Now, a pretrained neural network (MiDaS) solves this as a function call.

concepts.title: How Was It Trained?
concepts.one_liner: MiDaS was trained on a mix of four real-image datasets with ground-truth depth, using an invariant loss to handle scale and camera ambiguities.
concepts.content:
This model has been trained using a mix of four datasets with real images. The images below (@fig-examples_training_midas) show one sample from each dataset alongside their ground-truth depth.

(see figure: Images and depth maps from the training set. *Source*: Image from @Ranftl2022)

As the model is trained with a diverse collections of data sources, there is an ambiguity on the overall scale, camera parameters, and stereo baselines. Therefore, the loss is defined in a way that it can be invariant to all those ambiguities. The invariant loss makes the training more robust, but it also makes the output less convenient to use.
concepts.motivation_md: Training on diverse datasets with an invariant loss makes the model robust to scale and camera differences, improving generalization.
concepts.recap_md:
- MiDaS trained on four diverse real-image datasets.
- Ground-truth depth was used for training.
- Loss is invariant to scale and camera parameter ambiguities.

concepts.title: Adapting the Output
concepts.one_liner: To convert MiDaS disparity output to world coordinates, invert disparity plus an unknown constant and apply camera intrinsic and extrinsic parameters.
concepts.motivation_md: Converting disparity to world coordinates allows practical use of MiDaS outputs for 3D reconstruction by applying camera parameters and adjusting for unknown constants.
concepts.recap_md:
- MiDaS outputs disparity values up to an unknown constant $d_0$.
- Depth is computed as $z = 1/(d + d_0)$.
- World coordinates are recovered using camera intrinsic and extrinsic parameters.

key_passage.text: MiDaS returns disparity values, up to an unknown constant ($d_0$), but what we need are world coordinates ($X,Y,Z$) for each pixel. To perform this transformation, we will use what we learned in chapter We will need to know the intrinsic and extrinsic camera parameters and also decide the value of $d_0$.

motivation.text: To translate the returned disparity for a given pixel $d\left[n,m \right]$ into depth values $z\left[n,m \right]$, we need to invert the disparity after adding the constant:

concepts.title: Recover world coordinates from disparity
concepts.one_liner: World coordinates for a pixel are obtained by multiplying depth with the inverse camera matrix applied to pixel coordinates.
concepts.motivation_md: This equation provides a direct method to compute 3D world coordinates from disparity and camera parameters, essential for 3D scene reconstruction.

- Depth $z$ is computed as the inverse of disparity plus $d_0$.

concepts.title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: One approach of learning visual representations is to set up a pretext task that requires arriving at a good representation of the scene, using language association as supervision.
concepts.content:
In chapter @sec-representation_learning, we saw that one approach of learning visual representations is to set up a pretext task that requires arriving at a good representation of the scene. In this section, we revisit this idea, using language association as a pretext task for representation learning.

Historically, one of the most popular pretext tasks has been image classification, where an image is associated with one of $K$ nouns. In a sense, this is already a way of supervising visual representations from language. However, human languages are much more than just a set of $K$ nouns, raising the question of whether richer linguistic structure could be used to supervise vision.

The answer is yes, and it works really well. Researchers have tried using all kinds of language structures to supervise vision systems, including adjectives and verbs @StatesAndTransformations, words indicating relationships between objects @visualgenome, and question-answer pairs @antol2015vqa. What seems to work best, once you reach a certain scale of data and compute, is to use *all* the structure in language, and the simplest way to do this is to train a vision system that associates images with free-form natural language.

This is the idea of the highly popular CLIP.
concepts.motivation_md: Using language as supervision enables richer, more flexible visual representations beyond simple noun classification, leveraging the full structure of natural language to improve vision systems.
concepts.recap_md:
- Visual representation learning can use language association as a pretext task.
- Image classification with nouns is a historical example of language supervision.
- Using all natural language structure to associate images with text works best at scale.

concepts.title: CLIP training process

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: The CLIP training process uses a symmetric InfoNCE loss with image and text encoders outputting unit vectors to align image-text pairs.
concepts.content:
[FIGURE:7d5ab02809b91736 | A diagram illustrating the CLIP training process. It shows input data as a set of pairs $\{\mathbf{t}^{(i)}, \boldsymbol{\ell}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$ entering a box labeled 'CLIP'. Inside the box, the...]

Here, $\boldsymbol\ell$ represents an image, $\mathbf{t}$ represents text, $\mathbb{S}^{d_z}$ represents the space of unit vectors of dimensionality $d_z$ (i.e., the surface of the $[d_z-1]$-dimensional hypersphere), $f_{\ell}$ is the image encoder, and $f_t$ is the text encoder. Image inputs are represented as $[3 \times N \times M]$ pixel arrays, text inputs as $d_t$ dimensional tokens, and $d_z$ is the embedding dimensionality.

The objective is a symmetric version of the InfoNCE loss defined in @eq-representation_learning-infonce. Both $f_\ell$ and $f_t$ output unit vectors, achieved using $L_2$-normalization before computing the objective; this ensures the denominator cannot dominate by pushing negative pairs infinitely far apart.
concepts.motivation_md: CLIP's training aligns images and text in a shared embedding space using a symmetric contrastive loss, ensuring meaningful similarity measures between modalities.
concepts.recap_md:
- CLIP uses image encoder $f_\ell$ and text encoder $f_t$ to embed inputs.
- Both encoders output unit vectors on a hypersphere via $L_2$-normalization.
- Training uses a symmetric InfoNCE loss to align matching image-text pairs.

concepts.title: CLIP training

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: CLIP training embeds batches of image-text pairs, maximizing dot products for positive pairs and minimizing for negative pairs.
concepts.motivation_md: This training method teaches CLIP to associate matching image-text pairs closely in embedding space while pushing apart mismatched pairs, enabling effective cross-modal understanding.
concepts.recap_md:
- CLIP trains on batches of image-text pairs embedding both modalities.
- Dot products between embeddings measure similarity.
- Positive pairs' dot products are maximized; negative pairs' minimized.

key_passage.text: First we sample a batch of $N$ language-image pairs, $\{\mathbf{t}^{(i)}, \boldsymbol\ell^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$ ($N=6$ in the figure). Next we embed measure the dot product between all these text strings and images using a language encoder $f_t$ and an image encoder $f_\ell$, respectively. This produces a set of text embeddings $\{\mathbf{z}^{(i)}_t\}_{i=1}^N$ and a set of image embeddings $\{\mathbf{z}^{(i)}_\ell\}_{i=1}^N$. To compute the loss, we take the dot product $\mathbf{z}^{(i)}_\ell\cdot \mathbf{z}^{(j)}_t$ for all $i, j \in \{1,\ldots,6\}$. Terms for which $i \neq j$ are the negative pairs and we seek to minimize these dot products (denominator of the loss); terms for which $i == j$ are the positive pairs and we seek to maximize these dot product (they appear in both the numerator and denominator of the loss).

concepts.title: Making a novel image classifier on the fly using CLIP

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: CLIP enables creating novel image classifiers on the fly by embedding descriptive text and comparing to image embeddings.
concepts.content:
Using language as one of the views may seem like a minor variation on the contrastive methods we saw previously, but it's a change that opens up a lot of new possibilities. CLIP connects the domain of images to the domain of language. This means that many of the powerful abilities of language become applicable to imagery as well.

One ability that the CLIP paper showcased is making a novel image classifier on the fly. With language, you can describe a new conceptual category with ease. Suppose I want a classifier to distinguish striped red circles from polka dotted green squares. These classes can be described in English just like that: "striped red circles" versus "polka dotted green square." CLIP can then leverage this amazing ability of English to compose concepts and construct an *image* classifier for these two concepts.

Here's how it works. Given a set of sentences $\{\mathbf{t}^{a}, \mathbf{t}^{b}, \ldots\}$ that describe images of classes $a$, $b$, and so on,

1.  Embed each sentence into a $\mathbf{z}$-vector, $\mathbf{z}_t^{a} = f_t(\mathbf{t}^{a}), \mathbf{z}_t^{b} = f_t(\mathbf{t}^{a}),$ and so on.

2.  Embed your query image into a $\mathbf{z}$-vector, $\mathbf{z}_{\ell}^{q} = f_{\ell}(\boldsymbol\ell^{q})$.

3.  See which sentence embedding is closest to your image embedding; that's the predicted class.

These steps are visualized in @fig-vision_and_language-clip_inference.
concepts.motivation_md: CLIP's language-image alignment allows flexible, on-the-fly image classification by describing new classes in natural language without retraining.
concepts.recap_md:
- CLIP links images and language enabling novel classifiers.
- Describe new classes with natural language sentences.
- Classify images by embedding and comparing to text embeddings.

concepts.one_liner: Custom binary classifiers can be created by comparing image embeddings to text embeddings representing two classes using angular distance.
concepts.content:
@fig-vision_and_language-clip_clocks gives more examples of creating custom binary classifiers in this way. The two classes are described by two text strings ("triangle" versus "cricle"; "purple" versus "teal"; and "arrowhead" versus "ball"). The embeddings of the text descriptions are the red and green vectors. The classifier simply checks where an image embedding is closer, in angular distance, to the red vector or the green vector. This approach isn't limited to binary classification: you can add more text vectors to partition the space in more ways.

concepts.title: Translating between Images and Text
concepts.one_liner: Translating between different data modalities like images and text is possible by composing encoders and decoders with alignment strategies.
concepts.content:
In chapter @sec-conditional_generative_models, we saw how to translate between different image domains. Could we be even more ambitious and translate between entirely different data *modalities*? It turns out that this is indeed possible and is an area of growing interest. For any type of data X, and any other type Y, there is, increasingly, a method X2Y (and Y2X) that translates between these two data types. Go ahead and pick your favorite data types---X,Y could be images and sounds, music and lyrics, amino acid sequences and protein geometry---then Google "X to Y with a deep net" and you will probably find some interesting work that addresses this problem. X2Y systems are powerful because they forge links between disparate domains of knowledge, allowing tools and discoveries from one domain to become applicable to other linked domains.

One approach to solving X-to-Y translation problems is to do it in a modular fashion by hooking up an *encoder* for domain X to a decoder for domain Y. This approach is popular because powerful encoder and decoder architectures, and pretrained models, exist for many domains. If we have an encoder $f: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Z}$ and a decoder $g: \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}$, then we can create a translator simply by function composition, $g \circ f$.

Of course, the output of our encoder might not be interpretable as a proper input to the decoder we selected. For example, suppose $f$ is a text encoder and $g$ is an image decoder and we have $\boldsymbol\ell= g(f(\mathbf{t}))$, where $\boldsymbol\ell$ is a generated image from the text input $\mathbf{t}$. Then nothing guarantees that $\boldsymbol\ell$ semantically matches $\mathbf{t}$.

To *align* the encoder and decoder we can follow several strategies. One is to simply finetune $g \circ f$ on paired examples of the target translation problem, $\{\mathbf{t}^{(i)}, \boldsymbol\ell^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$. Another option is to freeze $f$ and $g$ and instead train a translation function in latent space, $h: \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathcal{Z}$, so that $g \circ h \circ f$ correctly maps each training point $\mathbf{t}^{(i)}$ to the target output $\boldsymbol\ell^{(i)}$. See @rombach2022high for an example of this latter option.

In the next sections, we will look at a few specific architectures for solving this problem of text-to-image translation as well as the reverse, image-to-text.
concepts.motivation_md: Translating between different data modalities enables cross-domain knowledge transfer and new applications by linking disparate data types through learned mappings.
concepts.recap_md:
- Translation between data modalities like images and text is increasingly possible.
- Modular translation uses encoders and decoders composed as $g \circ f$.
- Alignment strategies include finetuning or latent space translation functions.

concepts.title: text-to-image
concepts.one_liner: Text-to-image is the problem of generating an image just from a text description using conditional generative models.
concepts.content:
Text-to-image is the problem of generating an image just from a text description. This can be achieved using any of the conditional generative models we saw in chapter @sec-conditional_generative_models. We simply have to find an effective way to use text as the conditioning information to these models. @fig-vision_and_language-text2im_schematic_mapping shows how this problem looks as a mapping from the space of text to the space of images:

(see figure: Text-to-image.)

On the right is an example of such a system translating input text $\mathbf{t}$ to an output image $\hat{\boldsymbol\ell}$ that matches what the text describes. Recall the similar diagrams in the chapters on representation learning and generative modeling and think about how they relate (see and @fig-generative_modeling_and_representation_learning-genrep_schematic). This new problem is not so different from what we have seen before!

Now let's build some concrete architectures to solve this mapping. We will start with a conditional variational autoencoder (cVAE; @sec-conditional_generative_models-cVAE). This was the architecture used by the DALL-E 1 model @dalle1, which was one of the first text-to-image models that caught the public's imagination.

A cVAE for text-to-image can be trained just like a regular cVAE; the special thing is just that the encoder is a text encoder, that is, a neural net that maps from text to a vector embedding. @fig-vision_and_language-text2im_VAE_training shows what the training looks like; it's conceptually the same as @fig-conditional_generative_models-cVAE_ball_bouncing_example_nets, which we saw previously.

(see figure: Training a cVAE to perform text-to-image. The dotted lines indicate that the image encoder is only used during training; at test time, usage follows the solid path. In this cartoon we draw the output...)

After training this model, we can sample from it by simply discarding the image encoder and instead inputting a random Gaussian vector to the decoder, in addition to providing the decoder with the text embedding. @fig-vision_and_language-text2im_VAE_sampling shows how to sample an image in this way.

This is how text-to-image generation can be done with a cVAE. We could perform the same exercise for any conditional generative model. Let's do

- A cVAE can be adapted for text-to-image by using a text encoder as the encoder.
- After training, sampling discards the image encoder and uses text embeddings plus Gaussian noise to generate images.

concepts.title: conditional diffusion model for text-to-image
concepts.one_liner: A conditional diffusion model inserts text embeddings into multiple layers of a denoising U-Net to generate images from text.
concepts.content:
One more approach is a conditional diffusion model. This is the approach followed by the second version of the DALL-E system, DALL-E 2 @ramesh2022hierarchical, as well as other popular systems like the one described in @rombach2022high. The difficulty we will focus on here is as follows: how do you most effectively insert the text embeddings into the decoder, so that it can make best use of this information? @fig-vision_and_language-text2im_diffusion_model shows one way to do this, which is roughly how it is done in @rombach2022high: we insert text embedding vectors into each denoising U-Net, and even into multiple layers of each U-Net. This makes it very easy for the diffusion model to condition all of its decisions on the text information.

(see figure: Sampling from a trained cVAE.)

(see figure: A text-to-image diffusion model.)

Notice that @fig-vision_and_language-text2im_diffusion_model is actually very similar to @fig-vision_and_language-text2im_VAE_sampling. A conditional diffusion model is in fact very similar to a cVAE. At sampling time, both take as input text and Gaussian noise. The VAE uses a network that directly maps these inputs to an image, in a single forward pass. The diffusion model, in contrast, maps to an image via a chain of denoising steps, each of which is a forward pass through a neural network. See @NEURIPS2021_b578f2a5 for a discussion of the connection between diffusion models and VAEs.
concepts.motivation_md: Conditional diffusion models improve text-to-image generation by integrating text embeddings into multiple layers of the denoising U-Net, enabling fine-grained conditioning.
concepts.recap_md:
- Conditional diffusion models insert text embeddings into multiple layers of a denoising U-Net.
- Sampling involves iterative denoising steps conditioned on text and Gaussian noise.
- Diffusion models are similar to cVAEs but generate images via multiple denoising passes.

concepts.title: image-to-text
concepts.one_liner: Image-to-text or image captioning translates images into text using an image encoder and a text decoder.
concepts.content:
Naturally, we can also translate in the opposite direction. We just need to use an *image encoder* (rather than a text encoder) and a *text decoder* (rather than a text encoder). In this direction, the problem can be called **image-to-text** or **image captioning**. This kind of translation is very useful because text is a ubiquitous and general-purpose interface between almost all domains of human knowledge (we use language to describe pretty everything we do and everything we know). So, if we can translate images to text then we link imagery to many other domains of knowledge.

As an example of an image-to-text system, we will use a transformer to map the input image to a set of tokens, and we will then feed these tokens as input to an autoregressive text decoder, which is also implemented with a transformer. See @li2023blip2 for an example of a

- Image-to-text uses an image encoder and a text decoder.
- Also called image captioning, it translates images into descriptive text.
- Text serves as a universal interface linking images to knowledge.

concepts.title: cross-attention layer
concepts.one_liner: A cross-attention layer lets text tokens attend to image tokens by mixing their value vectors based on attention weights.
concepts.motivation_md: Cross-attention layers enable text models to incorporate information from image tokens by letting text tokens attend to image tokens, facilitating multimodal fusion.
concepts.recap_md:
- Cross-attention lets text tokens attend to image tokens by mixing their value vectors.
- Queries come from text tokens; keys and values come from image tokens.
- Outputs combine cross-attention and self-attention with learnable weights.

key_passage.text: There is one special layer to point out, the **cross-attention** layer (`cross-attn`). This layer addresses the question of how to insert image tokens into a text model. The answer is quite simple: just let the text tokens attend to the image tokens. The image tokens will emit their value vectors which will be mixed with the text token value vectors according to the attention weights to produce the next layer of tokens in the text decoder.

motivation.text: This layer addresses the question of how to insert image tokens into a text model.

concepts.title: text decoder autoregressive model
concepts.one_liner: The text decoder is an autoregressive model that uses causal attention to predict the next word given previous words.
concepts.content: The text decoder is an autoregressive model (@sec-generative_models-autoregressive) that uses causal attention (@sec-transformers-masked_attention) to predict the next word in the sentence given the previous words generated so far. In this strategy, the input to the text decoder is the tokens representing the previous words in the training data caption that describes the image. At sampling time, the model is run sequentially, where for each next word generated it autoregressively repeats, with that word being added to the input sequence of tokens. The text tokens themselves are produced by tokenizing the input words, for example, via byte-pair encodings or word-level encodings (the latter is shown in the figure).
concepts.motivation_md: Autoregressive text decoders predict the next word based on previous words, enabling coherent text generation conditioned on prior context.
concepts.recap_md:
- Text decoder predicts the next word autoregressively using causal attention.
- Input tokens represent previous words in the caption.
- Tokens are produced by tokenizing input words (e.g., byte-pair encoding).

key_passage.text: The text decoder is an autoregressive model that uses causal attention to predict the next word in the sentence given the previous words generated so far.

motivation.text: In this strategy, the input to the text decoder is the tokens representing the previous words in the training data caption that describes the image.

example.text: At sampling time, the model is run sequentially, where for each next word generated it autoregressively repeats, with that word being added to the input sequence of tokens.

concepts.title: Text as a Visual Representation
concepts.one_liner: Text can serve as a visual representation of an image, linking it to language models for reasoning.
concepts.content:
One way of thinking about image-to-text is as yet another visual encoder, where text is the visual representation. Just like we can represent an image in terms of its frequencies (Fourier transform), its semantics and geometry (scene understanding), or its feature embeddings (DINO @caron2021emerging, CLIP @radford2021learning, and others), we can also represent it in terms of a textual description of its content.

In @fig-vision_and_language-different_visual_representations we show an image represented in several ways (the depth map is produced by MiDaS @Ranftl2022 and the text is produced by BLIP2 @li2023blip2):

(see figure: Four representations computed from the input on the left. The input image itself (its pixel values) is in fact a fifth representation of the scene.)

Think about the relative merits of each of these representations, and what advantages or disadvantages text might have over these other kinds of visual representation.

Text is a powerful visual representation because it interfaces with language models. This means that after translating an image into text we can use language models to reason about the image contents.
concepts.motivation_md: Representing images as text links visual data to language models, enabling reasoning and understanding through natural language.
concepts.recap_md:
- Image-to-text can be viewed as a visual encoder producing text representations.
- Images have multiple representations: frequency, semantics, embeddings, and text.
- Text representation enables reasoning via language models.

key_passage.text: One way of thinking about image-to-text is as yet another visual encoder, where text is the visual representation.

motivation.text: Text is a powerful visual representation because it interfaces with language models. This means that after translating an image into text we can use language models to reason about the image contents.

concepts.title: Visual question answering
concepts.one_liner: Visual question answering (VQA) maps an image and a textual question to a textual answer.
concepts.content:
As AI systems become more general purpose, one goal is to make a vision algorithm that is fully general, so that you can ask it any question about an image. This is akin to a Turing test @turing2009computing for visual intelligence. **Visual question answering** (**VQA**) is one formulation of this goal @antol2015vqa. The problem statement in VQA is to make a system that maps an image and a textual question to a textual answer, as shown in @fig-vision_and_language-VQA_examples.

(see figure: An example VQA system.)
concepts.motivation_md: VQA aims to create vision systems that can answer any question about an image, testing visual intelligence like a Turing test.
concepts.recap_md:
- VQA maps an image and a textual question to a textual answer.
- It aims for fully general vision algorithms answering any image question.
- VQA is a form of visual intelligence evaluation.

key_passage.text: Visual question answering (VQA) is one formulation of this goal. The problem statement in VQA is to make a system that maps an image and a textual question to a textual answer, as shown in fig-vision_and_language-VQA_examples.

motivation.text: As AI systems become more general purpose, one goal is to make a vision algorithm that is fully general, so that you can ask it any question about an image. This is akin to a Turing test for visual intelligence.

concepts.title: Cascade of classifiers
concepts.one_liner: Cascade of classifiers divides the search into a sequence of classifiers of increasing computational complexity and accuracy to efficiently localize objects in images.
concepts.content:
Trying to localize an object in an image is like finding a needle in a haystack: the object is usually small and might be surrounded by a complex background. Selective search reduced the complexity of the search by dividing it into two steps: a first, fast, and cheap classification function that detects good candidate locations; and a second, slow, and expensive classification function capable of accurately classifying the object, applied only to a subset of all possible locations and scales. Cascade of classifiers pushes this idea further by dividing the search into a sequence of classifiers with increasing computational complexity and accuracy.

The algorithm for the cascade of classifiers is:

(see figure: Cascade of classifiers algorithm.)

Cascades of classifiers became popular in computer vision when Paul Viola and Michael Jones introduced it in 2001 with a ground-breaking real-time face detector based on a cascade of boosted classifiers. In parallel, Fleuret and Geman also proposed a system that performs a sequence of binary tests at each location, where each test checks for the presence of a particular image feature. Early versions of this strategy were inspired by the game "Twenty Questions".

In a cascade, computational power is allocated to image regions more likely to contain the target object, while flat or feature-poor regions are quickly rejected with minimal computation. The following figure from Fleuret and Geman illustrates how a cascaded classifier allocates computing power when trained to detect faces. The heat map intensity is proportional to the number of cascade levels applied at each location.

(see figure: (left) Input image with the output of a face detector from 1999. (right) The heat map reports the computational cost at each location. Most of the computation was allocated into the wrong detections...)

It is interesting to note that the scanning window approach (Levels = 1) and the selective search procedure (Levels = 2) are special cases of this algorithm. The cascade of classifiers usually does not include a bounding box refinement stage since it starts with a full list of bounding boxes, but such a stage could be added to incorporate new transformations not available initially (e.g., rotations).
concepts.motivation_md: Localizing objects in images is challenging due to their small size and complex backgrounds. Cascade of classifiers efficiently allocates computation by quickly discarding unlikely regions and focusing resources on promising candidates, improving detection speed and accuracy.
concepts.recap_md:
- Cascade of classifiers uses a sequence of classifiers with increasing complexity to localize objects efficiently.
- Early classifiers quickly reject unlikely regions, saving computation.
- The approach generalizes scanning windows and selective search methods.

key_passage.text: Cascade of classifiers pushes this idea to the limit by dividing the search in a sequence of classifiers of increasing computational complexity and accuracy.

motivation.text: Trying to localize an object in an image is like finding a needle in a haystack: the object is usually small and might be surrounded by a complex background.

example.text: Cascades of classifiers became popular in computer vision when Paul Viola and Michael Jones introduced it in 2001 with a ground-breaking real-time face detector based on a cascade of boosted classifiers.

concepts.title: Object Localization Loss
concepts.one_liner: The object localization loss combines classification and localization losses to train object detectors end-to-end by comparing predicted bounding boxes and labels with ground truth.
concepts.content:
The object localization loss accounts for two complementary tasks: classification and localization.

- Classification loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}$): For each detected bounding box, does the predicted label match the ground truth at that location?

- Localization loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}}$): How close is the detected location to the ground truth object location?

For each image, the object detector outputs a set of bounding boxes $\{\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \hat{\mathbf{y}}_i\}_{i=1}^B$, where $B$ is likely larger than the number of ground truth bounding boxes in the training set. The first step is to associate each detection with a ground truth label, yielding $\{\mathbf{b}_i, \mathbf{y}_i\}_{i=1}^B$. Predicted bounding boxes overlapping ground truth instances are optimized to improve predicted locations and labels. Remaining boxes that do not overlap ground truth are assigned to the background class ($\mathbf{y}_i=0$), and the model is optimized to reduce their predicted class scores.

This process is illustrated in the figure showing detector outputs compared with ground truth bounding boxes, where each detected box is assigned a ground truth label or background.

For classification loss, since each bounding box has one class, cross-entropy loss is used:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i, \mathbf{y}_i) = -  \sum_{c=1}^{K} y_{c,i} \log(\hat{y}_{c,i})$$

where $K$ is the number of classes.

To measure localization loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \mathbf{b}_i)$, a common similarity measure is the Intersection over Union (IoU):

[FIGURE:10874378d0fc5d26 | Sketch of the computation of intersection over union for two bounding boxes.]

IoU ranges from 0 (no overlap) to 1 (identical boxes). The localization loss is defined as:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b})= 1 - IoU (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b}).$$

IoU is translation and scale invariant and frequently used to evaluate object detectors. A simpler alternative is the L2 regression loss:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b}) = (\hat{x}_1 - x_1)^2 + (\hat{x}_2 - x_2)^2 + (\hat{y}_1 - y_1)^2 + (\hat{y}_2 - y_2)^2$$

The L2 loss is translation invariant but not scale invariant and is larger for bigger bounding boxes. The next graph compares IoU loss and L2 regression loss for two square bounding boxes as a function of relative $x$-displacement.

(see figure: (left) Input image with the output of a face detector from 1999. (right) The heat map reports the computational cost at each location. Most of the computation was allocated into the wrong detections...)

IoU loss becomes 1 when boxes do not overlap, resulting in no gradient information during backpropagation.

The overall loss combines classification and localization losses:

$$
\mathcal{L}( \{\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \hat{\mathbf{y}}_i\}, \{\mathbf{b}_i, \mathbf{y}_i\})
     =  \mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i, \mathbf{y}_i) +
     \lambda \mathbb{1} (\mathbf{y}_i \neq 0)
     \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} 
     (\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \mathbf{b}_i)
$$

where the indicator function $\mathbb{1} (\mathbf{y}_i \neq 0)$ zeroes the localization loss for bounding boxes not overlapping ground truth. The parameter $\lambda$ balances the relative strength of both losses. This loss enables end-to-end training of the detection algorithm, though localization and classification stages can also be trained independently.
concepts.motivation_md: Object detection requires both classifying what is in a bounding box and precisely localizing it. The object localization loss combines classification and localization terms to train detectors end-to-end, improving accuracy in both tasks.
concepts.recap_md:
- Object localization loss combines classification loss and localization loss.
- Classification loss uses cross-entropy to compare predicted and true labels.
- Localization loss often uses IoU or L2 regression to measure bounding box accuracy.

key_passage.text: The object localization loss has to take into account two complementary tasks: classification and localization.

motivation.text: For each of the predicted bounding boxes that overlaps with the ground truth instances, we want to optimize the system parameters to improve the predicted locations and labels.

example.text: The detector produces a set of bounding boxes for candidate car locations. Those are compared with the ground truth data. Each detected bounding box is assigned one ground truth label (indicated by the color) or assigned to the background class (indicated in white). Note that several detections can be assigned to the same ground truth bounding box.

concepts.title: Intersection over Union
concepts.one_liner: Intersection over Union (IoU) measures similarity between two bounding boxes as the ratio of their intersection area to their union area.
concepts.content:
**Intersection over Union** (IoU) is a measure of similarity between two bounding boxes, computed as the area of their intersection divided by the area of their union.

[FIGURE:10874378d0fc5d26 | Sketch of the computation of intersection over union for two bounding boxes.]
concepts.motivation_md: IoU provides a scale- and translation-invariant measure to evaluate how well predicted bounding boxes overlap with ground truth, essential for object detection accuracy.
concepts.recap_md:
- IoU measures overlap between two bounding boxes.
- IoU = (area of intersection) / (area of union).
- Values range from 0 (no overlap) to 1 (perfect overlap).

concepts.title: Precision-recall curve
concepts.one_liner: Precision-recall curve measures detection performance as a function of the decision threshold based on confidence scores.
concepts.content:
The **Precision-recall curve** measures the performance of a detection system as a function of the decision threshold. Each bounding box has a confidence score $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i$, and a threshold $\beta$ is used to decide if an object is present at location $\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i$.

Given threshold $\beta$, the number of detections is $\sum_i  \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta)$, and the number of correct detections is $\sum_i  \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta) \times \mathbf{y}_i$.

Precision is the percentage of correct detections:

$$
Precision(\beta) = \frac{\sum_i  \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta) \times \mathbf{y}_i} {\sum_i  \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta)}
$$

Precision alone does not account for missed detections. Recall measures the proportion of ground truth instances detected:

$$Recall (\beta) = \frac{\sum_i  \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta) \times \mathbf{y}_i} {\sum_i \mathbf{y}_i}$$

Both precision and recall range from 0 to 1, with high values indicating better performance. The following graph shows a precision-recall curve as a function of $\beta$.

(see figure: Example of a precision-recall curve. This is a standard plot to evaluate detection algorithms. It is usually summarized by the area under the curve. In this example, note that recall stops around...)
concepts.motivation_md: Precision-recall curves help evaluate detection algorithms by showing the trade-off between correctly detected objects and missed detections as the decision threshold varies.
concepts.recap_md:
- Precision-recall curve evaluates detection performance over thresholds.
- Precision = correct detections / total detections.
- Recall = correct detections / total ground truth instances.

motivation.text: The precision only gives a partial view on the detector performance as it does not account for the number of ground truth instances that are not detected (misdetections).

example.text: The next graph ( shows the precision-recall curve as a function of $\beta$ (decision threshold).

concepts.title: stuff and objects
concepts.one_liner: Stuff refers to regions without well-defined boundaries, like grass or sky, contrasting with distinct object instances in images.
concepts.content:
It is useful to differentiate between **stuff** and **objects**. Stuff refers to things that do not have well-defined boundaries such as grass, water, and sky (discussed previously in textures). The distinction between stuff and objects is not very sharp. In some images, object instances might be easy to separate, like two trees in the left image below, or become a texture where instances cannot be detected individually, as shown in the right image. In cases with many instances, bounding boxes might not be appropriate; it is better to represent the region as "trees" than to try to detect each instance.

(see figure: Bounding boxes are not an appropriate representation of the location of trees. This is true for many object classes with extended shapes that are hard to approximate with a box.)
concepts.motivation_md: Differentiating stuff and objects helps choose appropriate representations: stuff regions lack clear boundaries and are better represented as textures or regions, while objects are distinct instances.
concepts.recap_md:
- Stuff refers to amorphous regions without clear boundaries (e.g., grass, sky).
- Objects are distinct instances that can be separated.
- Bounding boxes may not suit stuff with extended shapes or many instances.

key_passage.text: It is useful to differentiate between **stuff** and **objects**. Stuff refers to things that do not have well-defined boundaries such as grass, water, and sky (we already discussed this in chapter

concepts.title: semantic segmentation
concepts.one_liner: Semantic segmentation classifies each pixel in an image with an object class.
concepts.content:
Semantic segmentation involves classifying each pixel in an image with an object class. This per-pixel classification of object labels is illustrated in the figure below.

(see figure: Semantic segmentation. Every pixel is annotated with a semantic tag (red = car, blue = building, green = road, yellow = sidewalk, and cyan = sign).)
concepts.motivation_md: Semantic segmentation provides detailed understanding of images by labeling every pixel, enabling precise scene interpretation beyond bounding boxes.
concepts.recap_md:
- Semantic segmentation assigns a class label to every pixel.
- It provides detailed scene understanding.
- Illustrated by color-coded pixel annotations for different classes.

key_passage.text: Per-pixel classification of object labels, illustrated in fig-semantic_class_segmentation, is referred to as **semantic segmentation**.

example.text: Every pixel is annotated with a semantic tag (red = car, blue = building, green = road, yellow = sidewalk, and cyan = sign).

concepts.title: semantic segmentation loss
concepts.one_liner: Semantic segmentation loss is the cross-entropy loss applied to each pixel over all classes and training examples.
concepts.content:
The multiclass semantic segmentation loss is the cross-entropy loss applied to each pixel:

$$\mathcal{L}_{seg}(\hat{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y})
     = -\sum_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{c=1}^{K} \sum_{n,m}  y^{(t)}_c \left[n,m \right] \log(\hat{y}^{(t)}_c \left[n,m \right])$$

where the sum is over all training examples, all classes, and all pixel locations.
concepts.motivation_md: Applying cross-entropy loss per pixel enables training semantic segmentation models to accurately classify each pixel into the correct class.
concepts.recap_md:
- Semantic segmentation loss uses cross-entropy per pixel.
- Summed over all classes, pixels, and training examples.
- Enables pixel-wise classification training.

key_passage.text:
multiclass semantic segmentation loss is the cross-entropy loss applied to each pixel: $$\mathcal{L}_{seg}(\hat{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y}) = -\sum_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{c=1}^{K} \sum_{n,m} y^{(t)}_c \left[n,m \right] \log(\hat{y}^{(t)}_c \left[n,m \right])$$
where the sum is over all the training examples, all classes, and all pixel locations.

concepts.title: Instance Segmentation
concepts.one_liner: Instance segmentation outputs pixel-level masks for each object instance, combining object detection and semantic segmentation.
concepts.content:
Instance segmentation combines object detection and semantic segmentation by outputting a set of localized objects represented as pixel-level masks rather than bounding boxes, as shown in the figure below.

(see figure: Instance segmentation. Each instance of the class car is assigned to a different color.)

Unlike semantic segmentation, which aggregates pixels of the same class without distinguishing instances, instance segmentation outputs $K$ masks for $K$ objects of the same type, delineating overlapping objects.

One approach follows the object localization pipeline: after proposing and labeling bounding boxes, the cropped image within each box is fed to a binary semantic segmentation function that predicts, for each pixel in box $\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i$, whether it belongs to the object or not, producing an instance mask for each box. This approach was introduced by He et al. The architecture is illustrated below.

(see figure: Architecture for instance segmentation. This architecture combines several of the components we have seen previously. The image is first broken into overlapping regions, and then class segmentation...)

Here, $f_0$ is a low-cost detector proposing regions likely to contain target object instances. The function $f_1$ performs classification and segmentation of the instance:

$$\left[\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i,   \hat{\mathbf{s}}_i \right]= f_j(\mathbf{x}, \hat{\mathbf{b}}_i)$$

where $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i$ is the binary label confidence, and $\hat{s}_i \left[ n,m \right]$ is the instance segmentation mask.

The loss combines classification, localization, and segmentation losses:

$$
\mathcal{L}( \{\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \hat{\mathbf{y}}_i\}, \{\mathbf{b}_i, \mathbf{y}_i\})
     =  \mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i, \mathbf{y}_i) +
     \mathbb{1} (\mathbf{y}_i \neq 0)
     \left( 
     \lambda_1 \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \mathbf{b}_i)
     +
     \lambda_2 \mathcal{L}_{\text{seg}} (\hat{\mathbf{s}}_i, \mathbf{s}_i)
     \right)
$$

The first classification loss corresponds to classifying the crop as containing the object or not; if present, the second term measures bounding box accuracy, and the third term measures whether the segmentation mask matches the ground truth instance segmentation. Parameters $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ weight each loss.

This formulation can be extended to richer representations, such as regressing $u-v$ coordinates per pixel in an instance-centered frame, shape maps, or part segmentations.
concepts.motivation_md: Instance segmentation provides detailed object localization by combining detection and pixel-wise segmentation, enabling distinction between overlapping instances of the same class.
concepts.recap_md:
- Instance segmentation outputs pixel masks for each object instance.
- Combines object detection and semantic segmentation.
- Loss combines classification, localization, and segmentation terms.

key_passage.text: We can combine the ideas of object detection and semantic segmentation into the problem of instance segmentation. Here the idea is to output a set of localized objects, but rather than representing them as bounding boxes we represent them as pixel-level masks as shown in fig-instance_segmentation.

motivation.text: The difference from semantic segmentation is that if there are $K$ objects of the same type, we will output $K$ masks; conversely, semantic segmentation has no way to telling us how many objects of the same type there are, nor can it delineate between two objects of the same type that overlap; it just gives us an aggregate region of pixels that are all the pixels of the same object type.

example.text: One approach to instance segmentation is to follow the object localization pipeline but, after the bounding boxes have been proposed and labeled, feed the cropped image within each bounding box to a binary semantic segmentation function that simply predicts, for each pixel in box $\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i$ whether it belongs to the object or not. This way we get an instance mask for each box. Such an approach was introduced in he2017. The architecture is illustrated in fig-instance_segmentation_architecture.

concepts.title: Use Fewer Words
concepts.one_liner: "Vigorous writing is concise. A sentence should contain no unnecessary words, a paragraph no unnecessary sentences."
concepts.content: In *The Elements of Style* @Strunk, Strunk and White write, "Vigorous writing is concise. A sentence should contain no unnecessary words, a paragraph no unnecessary sentences, for the same reason that a drawing should have no unnecessary lines and a machine no unnecessary parts." To illustrate this in scientific writing, an original paragraph of 149 words is shown, which conveys the technical information but in a roundabout way. It describes a locality assumption for nodes depending only on nodes within a patch, justifies it for skin images, explains cropping the image into smaller windows and computing the inverse J matrix for these windows to reduce computational cost, and notes that only part of xMAP is used to avoid blocky artifacts. The paragraph is then rewritten to 88 words without changing its meaning, making it more concise and direct while preserving the technical content.
concepts.motivation_md: Concise writing avoids unnecessary words and sentences, making scientific communication clearer and more efficient, which helps readers understand complex ideas more easily.
concepts.recap_md:
- Vigorous writing is concise, avoiding unnecessary words and sentences.
- Scientific writing benefits from clear, direct phrasing without roundabout explanations.
- Rewriting can reduce word count significantly without losing meaning.

key_passage.text: Vigorous writing is concise. A sentence should contain no unnecessary words, a paragraph no unnecessary sentences, for the same reason that a drawing should have no unnecessary lines and a machine no unnecessary parts.

motivation.text: While the text above conveys the desired technical information, it describes things in a roundabout way.

example.text: We assume local influence---that nodes only depend on other nodes within a patch. This condition often holds for skin images, which have few long edges or structures. We crop the image into small windows, as shown in Fig. 5, and compute the inverse J matrix of each small window. This is much faster than computing the inverse J matrix for the input image. To avoid artifacts from the block processing, only the center region of xMAP is used in the final image, as shown in Fig. 5.

concepts.title: Tone
concepts.one_liner: The tone of your writing is important; papers written from a generous, clear, and reliable point of view are more pleasant and build lasting friendships.
concepts.content: The tone of your writing is important. You may feel pressure to oversell, hide drawbacks, and disparage others' work. It is in both your short-term and your long-term interest not to succumb to that pressure! If your work has a shortcoming, it is much better that you point it out than to have someone else do so later. Papers written from the point of view that "we're all good researchers, doing our best" are much more pleasant to read than papers written from the standpoint that everyone else is an idiot. Note the delightful sentences written by Efros @Efros01 when he was a graduate student, "*A number of papers to be published this year, all developed independently, are closely related to our work. The idea of texture transfer based on variations of \[6\] has been proposed by several authors (in particular, see the elegant paper by Hertzmann et al. in these proceedings). Liang et al. propose a real-time patch-based texture synthesis method very similar to ours. The reader is urged to review these works for a more complete picture of the field.*" This generous tone wins over the reader and promotes long-lasting friendships with people who study the same problems you do. You should develop a reputation for being clear and reliable. Always convey an accurate impression of the performance of an algorithm. If something doesn't work in important cases, let the readers know. In @Fergus2006, we noted that our deblurring algorithm didn't work for a case where we had been sure it should work for a maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation of the deblurred image. Some years later we learned, and described in @Levin2011, that we had been wrong to believe that MAP estimation of the deblurred image was feasible. We were glad we had described our counterintuitive result years before.
concepts.motivation_md: Maintaining a generous and honest tone in writing fosters trust, clarity, and positive relationships, while accurately reporting limitations helps readers understand the true performance of your work.
concepts.recap_md:
- Avoid overselling and disparaging others; be honest about your work's limitations.
- A generous tone promotes pleasant reading and lasting professional relationships.
- Clearly convey algorithm performance, including failures or counterintuitive results.

key_passage.text: The tone of your writing is important. You may feel pressure to oversell, hide drawbacks, and disparage others' work. It is in both your short-term and your long-term interest not to succumb to that pressure!

The idea of texture transfer based on variations of [6] has been proposed by several authors (in particular, see the elegant paper by Hertzmann et al. in these proceedings). Liang et al. propose a real-time patch-based texture synthesis method very similar to ours. The reader is urged to review these works for a more complete picture of the field." This generous tone wins over the reader and promotes long-lasting friendships with people who study the same problems you do.

concepts.title: Author List
concepts.one_liner: The quality of the papers you write matters so much more than your positions within the author lists of the papers.
concepts.content: The quality of the papers you write matters so much more than your positions within the author lists of the papers. If adding more authors will make a paper better, then you should add more authors. If a collaborator feels they should be an author, but you yourself are not sure, we find it is generally a good idea to trust the collaborator and to add them as a coauthor. It's much better to be one of many authors on a great paper than to be one of just a few authors on a mediocre paper.
concepts.motivation_md: Prioritizing paper quality and collaboration over author order encourages better research and more inclusive credit.
concepts.recap_md:
- Paper quality is more important than author order.
- Add authors if it improves the paper.
- Trust collaborators who feel they deserve authorship.

key_passage.text: The quality of the papers you write matters so much more than your positions within the author lists of the papers.

motivation.text: If adding more authors will make a paper better, then you should add more authors.

example.text: If a collaborator feels they should be an author, but you yourself are not sure, we find it is generally a good idea to trust the collaborator and to add them as a coauthor.

concepts.title: Avoiding Rejection
concepts.one_liner: Avoid giving easy reasons for rejection such as missing references, incremental results, poor writing, or mistakes.
concepts.content:
With the task of rejecting at least three-quarters of the submissions, conference area chairs, who make the acceptance decisions, are grasping for reasons to reject a paper. Here's a summary of reasons that are commonly used, and it is best not to provide the area chair with any of these easy reasons to reject your paper:

- Do the authors not deliver what they promise?

- Are important references missing (and therefore one suspects the authors not up on the state of the art for this problem)?

- Are the results too incremental (too similar to previous work)?

- Are the results believable, with sufficient tests to support the claims?

- Is the paper poorly written?

- Are there mistakes or incorrect statements?

As an area chair, the very good and the very bad papers are easy to deal with, and most of the decision-making effort goes to the borderline papers. One of us writes, "I find that much of my time is spent dealing with two kinds of borderline papers: cockroaches and puppies with six toes."

"Cockroaches" have no exciting contributions, but the reviews are ok and the results show incremental improvement to the state of the art. They're hard to kill (hence the nickname), and maybe two-thirds are accepted as posters, and one-third are rejected. As an author, it's best to work harder for the fresh results, to bring papers like this out of the cockroach category.

At the other end of the spectrum of borderline papers are "puppies with six toes." These are delightful papers, but with an easy-to-see flaw. The flaw may not matter (like six toes on a puppy) but makes the paper easy to reject, even though the paper may be fresh and wonderful. Maybe two-thirds of those papers get rejected, and one-third maybe accepted as posters. As an author, it may be better to wait for another submission cycle with a paper like this, to remove the easy to spot flaw. Then the paper might receive an oral presentation at a subsequent conference submission cycle.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding common rejection reasons helps authors avoid easy grounds for rejection and improve their papers' chances of acceptance.

- Avoid missing references, incremental results, poor writing, and mistakes.
- Borderline papers often fall into "cockroach" (incremental) or "puppy with six toes" (flawed but delightful) categories.
- Fix easy-to-spot flaws before resubmitting to improve acceptance chances.

concepts.title: Concluding Remarks
concepts.one_liner: Good writing involves lots of rewriting, and improving clarity before submission is often more valuable than last-minute result improvements.

concepts.title: Introduction
concepts.one_liner: Giving good talks is important and can greatly help your work's impact, much like a big serve helps in tennis.
concepts.content: Giving good talks is important for people who use the material of this book--for students, researchers, and engineers. One might think, "It is the work itself that really counts. Giving a talk about it is secondary." But the ability to give a good talk is like having a big serve in tennis---by itself, it doesn't win the game for you, but it sure helps. And the very best tennis players all have great serves. So we include in this chapter material that we have found helpful in giving talks.
concepts.motivation_md: Effective talks enhance the impact and communication of your work, complementing the quality of the research itself.

- Like a big serve in tennis, it helps but doesn't replace the work itself.

concepts.title: A Taxonomy of Talks
concepts.one_liner: Talks vary widely in length and audience familiarity, requiring inclusion of material accessible to both novices and experts.
concepts.content: There are different kinds of talks. Conference and workshop talks may range in length between 3 minutes for a "fast-forward" talk to 45 or 60 minutes for a keynote address. You may be one of many speakers, sometimes speaking in different rooms at the same time. Sometimes you will visit a university or company and speak in a special seminar. (Here @MITFacultyJobTalks2022 is a list of tips regarding faculty job talks from the MIT faculty.) It is very often the case that the audience will have a wide range of familiarity with the work and topic that you will present about. In a small seminar to a competing research group, there may be many people who are very familiar with your work. But even in such a small seminar, and especially to a larger group, there may be many people who don't know your area, nor perhaps not even your broad area. So you will to include material to let the uninitiated not be lost. Even people who are very familiar with the topic will appreciate hearing material they already understand presented clearly and well.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the types of talks and audience diversity helps tailor presentations to be clear and engaging for all listeners.
concepts.recap_md:
- Talks vary from 3-minute fast-forward to hour-long keynotes.
- Audiences often have mixed familiarity with your topic.
- Include material accessible to novices and clear to experts.

concepts.title: Robust Model Fitting: Random Sampling with Consensus
concepts.one_liner: RANSAC (random sampling with consensus) robustly fits models to data by iteratively sampling minimal sets, computing model parameters, and selecting the model with the largest consensus set of inliers.
concepts.content:
To perform image stitching, we need to find the homography parameters that best describe the transformation from one image to another. Because feature point detection can be noisy, homography fitting must be robust against inevitable feature mismatches. A good algorithm for robust model fitting is RANSAC (random sampling with consensus) @Fischler1981.

The RANSAC procedure is simple and its name describes its steps. First, randomly select a minimal set of datapoints sufficient to fit the model parameters (e.g., line parameters, homography). Then compute the model from these points. Next, determine the inliers in the dataset—points fitting the model within some tolerance. Repeat this process $N$ times. Finally, compute the model from the largest consensus set of inliers.

@fig-ransac illustrates RANSAC for fitting a line to datapoints. Two points (minimal set) are randomly selected (green points in @fig-ransac (b)), defining a line. The number of inliers (points within $\epsilon$ of this line) is counted. This repeats for $S$ samplings. The final model is fitted from the inliers of the model with the most inliers.

(see figure: RANSAC applied to robust estimation of line parameters. (a) Datapoints for which robust line estimation is sought. (b) Two points (in blue) are selected at random, sufficient to estimate line model...)

@Fischler1981 derives a heuristic for the number of samples $S$ needed to ensure a good fit. Let $n$ be the number of points needed to specify the model, and $w$ the probability a selected point is an inlier. Then $w^n$ is the probability all selected points are inliers, and $1 - w^n$ the probability at least one is an outlier. The probability that $k$ trials select only bad models is $(1 - w^n)^k$. If $p$ is the desired probability of selecting a good model, then:
$$1-p = (1 - w^n)^k$$
Taking logarithms and solving for $k$:
$$k = \frac{\log(1-p)}{\log(1-w^n)}$$

For example, in @fig-ransac, with $w=0.18$ and $n=2$, to achieve 95% confidence, $k=91$ iterations are needed.

In homography estimation, eight equations are needed (four points, each contributing two equations) to use the DLT algorithm. Multiple random sets of four points can be sampled and RANSAC used to estimate the homography robustly.
concepts.motivation_md: Robust model fitting is needed because feature detection is noisy and contains mismatches. RANSAC provides a way to fit models by iteratively sampling minimal sets and selecting the model with the largest consensus, ensuring robustness against outliers.
concepts.recap_md:
- RANSAC fits models by randomly sampling minimal point sets and selecting the model with the largest inlier consensus.
- The number of iterations needed depends on the inlier ratio and model complexity via $k = \frac{\log(1-p)}{\log(1-w^n)}$.
- For homography estimation, sample sets of four points and use RANSAC to robustly estimate parameters.

key_passage.text: A good algorithm to fit models to data robustly is RANSAC, which stands for random sampling with consensus. The procedure for RANSAC is simple, and the name contains most of the steps of the algorithm. First, randomly select a sufficient set of datapoints to fit the parameters of some model. Then, compute the model parameters from the randomly sampled set of points. Compute the inliers in the dataset, that is, the datapoints that fit the model (or achieve consensus) to within some tolerance. Repeat that procedure some number of times, $N$. Compute a final model from the set of inlier points corresponding to the largest number of inlier datapoints.

motivation.text: Because the detection of the feature points can be noisy, the homography fitting needs to be robust against inevitable feature mismatches between images.

example.text: RANSAC applied to robust estimation of line parameters. First, a number of datapoints, sufficient to uniquely specify the model parameters, are drawn from the dataset. For this problem, that is two points. Two randomly selected points are marked in green. After finding the line that passes through those two points, the number of inliers (datapoints within $\epsilon$ of the model) are determined. For the line, the number of inliers is three. This process is repeated until some desired number of samplings, $S$, have been drawn. The output model is fitted from all the inlier datapoints corresponding to the model that led to the most inlier datapoints.

concepts.title: Concluding Remarks
concepts.one_liner: Homographies are important geometric transforms with many applications, including measuring planes, camera calibration, and neural network regression.
concepts.content: Homographies are an important class of geometric transforms between images with many applications. They can be used to take measurements on a plane given a reference measure. While we have focused on computing homographies using correspondences between images, homographies can also be computed in other ways. For example, to produce a bird's-eye view of a plane, one can compute the homography using the horizon line to determine camera rotation. For an uncalibrated camera, vanishing points can be used to estimate intrinsic camera parameters. Additionally, homographies can be extracted using neural networks trained to regress the homography given two input images @abbas2019geometric.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding homographies enables applications like plane measurements, camera calibration, and novel view synthesis; multiple methods exist to compute them beyond correspondences.
concepts.recap_md:
- Homographies relate images via geometric transforms with many applications.
- They can be computed from correspondences, horizon lines, or vanishing points.
- Neural networks can also regress homographies from image pairs.

key_passage.text: Homographies are an important class of geometric transforms between images and they have lots of applications.

motivation.text: Homographies can be used to take measures on a plane given a reference measure.

example.text: For instance, to produce a bird's-eye view of a plane one can compute the needed homography using the horizon line to get the camera rotation and, for an uncalibrated camera, we can use vanishing points to get the intrinsic camera parameters. The homography can also be extracted using a neural networks trained to regress the homography given two input images.

concepts.title: Single View Metrology
concepts.one_liner: Single view metrology recovers 3D scene information from a single 2D image using geometry, perspective, and visual cues.
concepts.content:
The goal of this chapter is to introduce techniques that recover three-dimensional (3D) information about a scene from a single image, such as the office picture used before (@fig-finding_depth_office).

(see figure: Is it possible to recover three-dimensional (3D) scene information from a single two-dimensional (2D) image? How tall is the desk? How wide is the bookshelf? What do we need to know about the scene...)

Single view metrology relies on understanding the geometry of image formation, the rules of perspective, and other visual cues present in the image to answer questions about the 3D structure of the scene. This contrasts with methods like stereo vision, structure from motion, or multiview geometry, which use multiple images to reconstruct 3D information. For deeper analysis, consult specialized monographs such as Hartley and Zisserman's book on multiview geometry @Hartley2004.
concepts.motivation_md: Single view metrology allows extracting 3D scene structure from just one image by leveraging geometric and perspective cues, unlike multi-image methods.
concepts.recap_md:
- Single view metrology recovers 3D information from a single 2D image.
- It uses image formation geometry, perspective rules, and visual cues.
- Multi-image methods like stereo vision differ by using multiple views.

key_passage.text: Single view metrology relies on understanding the geometry of the image formation process, the rules of perspective, and other visual cues present in the image to answer questions about the 3D structure of the scene.

motivation.text: The goal of this chapter is to introduce a set of techniques that allows recovering three-dimensional (3D) information about the scene from a single image like the picture of the office we used before.
